Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster …

papers.title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
papers.abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. …

papers.title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
papers.abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions. Further analyses reveal that winners with previous competition medals are more likely to favor contributing content over competing again, whereas winners with more prior contribution medals are less inclined to further increase contributions. Moreover, team winners exhibit a lower tendency than solo winners to shift their efforts from competition to contribution. We add to the symbolic awards literature by uncovering a novel goal-shifting effect induced by contest medals, where award receipt redirects user effort from the focal rewarded domain to other forms of platform engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. …

papers.title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
papers.abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. We show that this asymmetry in the diversity of transaction methods in issuances and repurchases and the size-method relation in issuances are natural consequences of the single informational friction of a firm having superior information to investors. Moreover, although this friction always leads firms to issue inefficiently little, it leads firms to repurchase too little if they maximize long-term shareholder value but too much if the primary goal is to boost short-term share prices. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: Y. Yuan acknowledges support from the Paul Woolley Centre, the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Projects 72342020 and 72495152], and University College London. H. Zhong acknowledges support from the Economic and Social Research Council [New Investigator Grant ES/T003758/1]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03301 .

papers.title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
papers.abstract: While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

papers.title: Cross-Cluster Referrals and Subsidy Schemes in Multi-Cluster Healthcare Systems
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Excessive and highly variable waiting times for specialty services are a long-standing problem for public healthcare systems. Healthcare authorities in some jurisdictions have begun to experiment with schemes to improve system performance, including cross-cluster referrals which allow patients to switch from their home cluster to other clusters with shorter waiting times, and opt-out subsidies which help patients seeking services from private providers outside the public system. However, few studies in the literature have examined the structure of the problem or offered analytical insights to the design of such schemes. Methodology/results: We construct a multi-cluster service network model to study optimal routing policies under both individual and system optimization. We define externalities in a network setting and establish their properties, and further identify conditions under which referrals are effective or counterproductive in reducing system costs. We also show that lowering the switching cost could inadvertently degrade overall system performance. In contrast to the classic result for single-cluster systems (e.g. Naor 1969), our analysis of opt-out and switching incentives reveals that fixed subsidies generally cannot fully coordinate a multi-cluster system due to the cross-cluster effect of externalities. However, they can effectively reduce system costs in wide ranges of system parameter values. We further show that dynamic (state-dependent) …

papers.title: A Decision-Support Framework for Food Bank Operations: Overcoming Waste and Uncertainty in Food Distribution
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Food banks face the complex operational challenge of allocating uncertain and per- ishable food donations to maximize community benefit. This requires navigating difficult trade-offs between effectiveness (delivering nutritious and fresh food relative to need), efficiency (maximizing food distributed and minimizing waste), and equity (ensuring fair distribution), a task for which traditional myopic poli- cies are often ill-equipped. Our research addresses how food banks can design practical, forward-looking allocation strategies in this dynamic and challenging environment. Methodology/results: We develop a comprehensive dynamic programming framework to model the food bank allocation problem. From this, we derive two practical and implementable policies: a simple, static Scaled Fluid (SF) policy and an adaptive Re-Optimized (ReOPT) policy. We provide rigorous theoretical proofs that both policies are asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, extensive simulations using both synthetic and real data show that our proposed strategies yield significant utility gains. Managerial implications: This research provides food bank man- agers and decision-makers with theoretically sound and empirically validated tools to improve their opera- tions. Our framework offers a clear path to enhance the impact and sustainability of food distribution efforts, enabling organizations to better serve their communities by making more efficient, effective, and equitable decisions with …

papers.title: Humanitarian Aid Management under Corruptible Distribution and Oversight Agents
papers.abstract: Problem Definition: In many crisis contexts, such as armed conflicts, natural disasters, or refugee emergencies, one of the most pressing challenges is to regulate the delivery of humanitarian aid to the final beneficiaries in the presence of both corruptible agents (those responsible for delivering aid) and corruptible inspectors (who may be bribed not to report uncovered misappropriations). Strengthening anti-corruption efforts by hiring more inspectors and/or rewarding inspectors’ truthful reporting can reduce corruption but draws on the finite humanitarian aid financing, reducing the aid delivered to the beneficiaries. Methodology/Results: We develop a three-stage game-theoretic model in which a government agency chooses inspection intensity and the reward rate for inspectors’ truthful reporting, managers decide how much aid to misappropriate, and inspectors decide whether to report detected misconduct or accept a bribe to conceal misappropriation. The government agency aims to maximize the amount of humanitarian aid reaching the beneficiaries. We find that the role of inspectors depends on the financing available. When the financing is low, inspectors serve to detect misconduct; when the financing is sufficiently high, inspectors also affect managers' behavior and deter misappropriation. The reward can also serve two purposes. It can either induce truthful reporting and eliminate bribery, or increase the bribe that managers must pay, thereby reducing their incentive to …

papers.title: Technology-Mediated Services in Health Care: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
papers.abstract: This study examines how telehealth delivery models are associated with access to care and protocol adherence in underserved populations. While prior research reports mixed evidence on telehealth’s effectiveness, we argue that these inconsistencies arise because telehealth is not a single intervention but is implemented through distinct service configurations that address different barriers. Drawing on the theoretical framework of digital economics, we conceptualize telehealth as a technology-mediated service that can alter key economic frictions, including search and verification, transportation, tracking, and setup costs. We focus on two widely adopted models—specialist-facilitated telehealth and remote telehealth—and theorize that each addresses different subsets of these frictions, leading to distinct effects on care access and protocol adherence across settings. Using panel data from U.S. Community Health Centers on mental health services, we document three findings. First, adoption of the specialist-facilitated model is associated with increased access to mental health care, particularly in areas with greater clinical need. Second, remote telehealth is not associated with increased access on average but is associated with higher adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. These effects are consistent with improvements in screening and documentation processes rather than increases in utilization. Third, the estimated effects of both models …

papers.title: Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
papers.abstract: What is the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on healthcare value? Does PE ownership reduce healthcare value, and if so, can its effect be mitigated using health information technologies (IT)? Given the significant investments by PE firms in the healthcare sector in recent years, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policy makers, care providers, and patients, to understand their likely impact and whether PE ownership is aligned with their interests. Because PE firms seek to improve efficiency and generate short-term financial returns, the cost-cutting strategies used to achieve these goals may come at the expense of care quality, leading to competing hypotheses on the impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. We argue that IT-enabled health information sharing capabilities can help PE-owned hospitals to better manage this cost-quality tension and achieve higher healthcare value. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach and data from US hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we estimate changes in healthcare value following PE acquisition and ownership. Overall, we find that PE ownership of hospitals reduces healthcare value. This decline is partially driven by reduction in clinical staffing following PE ownership. We further find that pre-existing, hospital health information sharing capabilities mitigate the negative impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. Specifically, such capabilities can strengthen the effect of PE ownership on cost …

papers.title: Collective Attention Configurations in Open-Source Software Development: Interlacing for High Performance1
papers.abstract: Coordinating open-source software (OSS) development requires both the division and integration of developers’ attention. How to combine these contradictory logics effectively, however, remains unclear. Adopting a configurational lens, we distinguish between developers’ primary attention, or their top-priority focus, and secondary attention, or their spare capacity. Along these two lines, division and integration take on different forms. Recombining these forms yields two new coordination logics: interlacing, which combines primary division with secondary integration, and interlocking, which combines primary integration with secondary division. Applying the same or different logics across OSS’s two key work types—discursive and technical—produces a broader set of coordination configurations. Analyzing 4,291 release cycles from 1,004 GitHub machine-learning projects, we find that isomorphic interlacing—applying interlacing in both work types—delivers the strongest performance of development speed, novelty, and quality. Configurations pairing interlacing with division or integration also perform well under particular contingencies of task interdependence, project ownership, and release-cycle length. By contrast, configurations involving interlocking consistently underperform. Our study advances OSS coordination theory by identifying a high-performing configuration that systematically combines division and integration and clarifying when alternative configurations can substitute …

papers.title: Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
papers.abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. The optimal policy may include partial conditional approval for drugs with low expected efficacy, and leniency in granting final approval below conventional standards. Our calibration suggests these tools can generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual social value. This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Funding: The authors received no external funding for this research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03836 .

papers.title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
papers.abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. Our empirical evidence supports the model’s prediction that payoff structures and investor disagreement account for the distinct price dynamics across asset classes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge research support from the Center for Investing at HKUST. Y. Xiong thanks the support by National Natural Science Foundation of China [NSFC 72422007] and the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Project 16501523]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07966 .

papers.title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
papers.abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

papers.title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
papers.abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

papers.title: Operational Implications of Diagnostic Discrepancies: The Weigh-In of Focal and Related Physician Experience
papers.abstract: Problem Definition: Diagnostic discrepancies, defined as mismatches between patients’ admitting and principal diagnoses, are common but heterogeneous claims-based markers. These discrepancies represent a misalignment in the diagnostic process, reflecting diagnostic updating, reprioritization, residual clinical complexity, documentation practices, or error, without establishing clinical preventability, and may signal latent operational burden in subsequent physician decision-making. We examine whether this retrospective operational flag identifies inpatient stays with larger adjusted resource-use differentials and whether those differentials vary with physician experience. Methodology/Results: Leveraging a patient-level dataset of 5.7 million emergency-department-origin inpatient stays from Florida hospitals, we examine the operational burden associated with diagnostic discrepancies, measured by total costs per hospitalization. Our results show that discrepancy-flagged inpatient stays have a 6.62% higher adjusted total cost after rich patient risk adjustment and high-dimensional fixed effects. The adjusted differential is smaller at higher focal experience (treating similar diagnoses) and larger at higher related experience (treating diverse diagnoses). The pattern remains qualitatively similar across alternative discrepancy definitions, richer diagnosis and service-line controls, risk-adjusted benchmarking, physician matching, alternative experience measures, and alternative …

papers.title: Gendered Effects of a Crisis-induced Work-from-Home Shock: A Time-Motion Study Using Digital Footprints
papers.abstract: Problem definition: While organizations are adopting hybrid and even remote-first work schedules, the potentially gendered impact of work-from-home (WFH) on operational outcomes remains poorly understood. Methodology/results: To examine this question, we combine a crisis-induced shock (i.e., the Covid-19 lockdown) that forced a shift to WFH due to stay-at-home orders, with a novel methodology to gather contextualized digital trace data. We examine the online time allocation — akin to a time-motion study for white collars — of 1,094 individuals across various activities and industries, when in-person work related and leisure activities were abruptly curtailed by the pandemic, inducing a shift to home-based work and online activities. Analysis of over 30 million website visits reveals that overall, this crisis-induced WFH increased the time devoted to both work-related and leisure pursuits online. However, these gains are significantly larger for men, giving rise to new gender gaps. We observe notable disparities in online work and leisure activities, including on smartphones, suggesting that crisis-induced WFH reshapes workers’ daily activities differently across genders. These gender differences are amplified among parents — a pattern consistent with increased household obligations placing greater constraints on women’s ability to fully benefit from the flexibility offered by WFH. Furthermore, we observe a substantial relative decline in women’s job search activities after …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Assortment Optimization Given Basket Shopping Behavior Using the Ising Model
papers.abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Improving Operational Performance through Boarding Time Slack: Evidence from the U.S. Airline Industry
papers.abstract: Flight delays have a significant impact on airlines, passengers, and the U.S. economy. Airlines also use flight on-time performance (OTP) – a metric based on the proportion of delayed flights – to attract travelers by demonstrating service reliability. It is well established that adding buffers to flight time and ground time improves on-time arrivals. However, such buffers can impose significant costs. The flight and ground times comprise multiple activities, and prior research has primarily focused on studying the impact of aggregate buffers. In this paper, we study the impact of increasing the buffer of a critical ground time activity, namely boarding time, potentially without increasing the aggregate ground time buffer, on flight delays. To do so, we use the context of Delta Air Lines' recent policy changes wherein the airline increased the boarding time for domestic narrow-body flights by 5 minutes and started compensating flight attendants for pre-flight boarding. Using a Difference-in-Difference-in-Differences framework, we analyze and quantify the impact of these policies on Delta’s flight delays. Our findings indicate a significant reduction in departure delays following the policy changes, with increased boarding time playing a critical role in improving on-time departures. Our analysis finds no evidence that boarding compensation contributed to the improvement in on-time departures. We show that the increase in boarding time can improve the likelihood of on-time …

papers.title: Action-oriented Narratives. How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
papers.abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities …

papers.title: Designing AI-Enabled Pronunciation Training for Digital Learning
papers.abstract: AI-enabled learning environments are reshaping how communication skills can be taught at scale in higher education and talent development. This study conceptualizes pronunciation training as a digital pedagogy problem and examines how two configurable features of AI-enabled learning environments, instruction illustration and AI-generated verbal narration, jointly affect pronunciation accuracy. Drawing on cognitive fit theory, we argue that learning outcomes depend on whether instructional representations match the cognitive demands of pronunciation practice tasks. We propose a 2-by-2 experiment comparing description-only illustrations versus descriptions with visualized illustrations and local versus foreign-accented narration. This study further theorizes that cognitive effort and emotional confusion mediate this relationship. This study contributes to digital learning research by explaining when AI-enabled pronunciation training can support scalable, ethical, and effective skill development.

papers.title: Designing Prompt-Level Scaffolds for Student Agency in GenAI-Supported Learning
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet its educational value depends on whether students remain active agents in AI-supported learning rather than passive recipients of generated content. This study investigates how prompt-level scaffolding can support student agency through more deliberate and reflective prompting. Following a design science research approach, we derived design principles from a literature review and 15 student interviews, instantiated them in Prompt Coach, a browser-based prompt-feedback artifact, and evaluated the artifact with 25 university students. The artifact provides feedback on four prompt-quality dimensions, clarity, context, depth, and scope, and embeds brief reflective prompts into the interaction process. Findings show that students revised prompts more deliberately, developed a clearer vocabulary for prompt quality, and became more aware of how prompt wording shapes AI responses. The paper contributes design knowledge for educational GenAI tools that strengthen prompt literacy, metacognitive reflection, and student agency.

papers.title: CS1 in the Age of GenAI: Affordance Dissolution and Assessment Governance
papers.abstract: Forty-five percent of students who earned top grades on weekly programming exercises scored zero on a monitored final exam. We see this as a sign of a deeper change: generative AI (GenAI) breaks the old assumption that finished coursework shows learning. Using affordance theory and validity theory, we name this change affordance dissolution and test it with three kinds of evidence from three Finnish introductory programming (CS1) courses: grades from over 1,000 students, 883 paired student-and-AI code submissions, and surveys of 602 students. When one course added exam monitoring, top grades fell from 73% to 24%. Two student groups at the same university also described their AI use in clearly different ways. Rules alone cannot undo this change, so we outline how institutions can redesign assessment and what future research is needed.

papers.title: A Nascent Design Theory for Meaningful Soft Skills Acquisition in Immersive Learning Environments: An Action Design Research Study
papers.abstract: Immersive Learning Environments (ILEs) offer new opportunities for experiential learning, yet design knowledge for supporting meaningful soft skills acquisition remains underdeveloped. This study develops a nascent design theory for meaningful soft skills acquisition in ILEs through a three-year Action Design Research project on conflict management training with a Swedish train operating company. Across two iterative design cycles, empirical insights from stakeholder workshops, prototype evaluations, and focus groups were integrated with justificatory knowledge on soft skills acquisition and meaningful learning. The resulting design theory comprises five meta-requirements and six design principles organized around integration, interactivity, realism, and multimodality, together with propositions for future empirical testing. An expository instantiation demonstrates how the principles materialize in an ILE for conflict management training. The study contributes actionable design knowledge that integrates pedagogical, socio-technical, and experiential dimensions of ILE design while identifying opportunities for further evaluation across soft skills contexts.

papers.title: From Post-Hoc to Pre-Assessment Evaluation: LLMs as Collaborative Partners for Simulating Student Performance
papers.abstract: Ensuring the quality of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) remains a complex challenge in higher education, as traditional post-hoc psychometric analyses often identify flaws only after students have been negatively impacted. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential for simulating student performance to validate items before delivery, they are frequently hindered by a “high-accuracy bias” that prevents larger models from realistically mimicking student errors. This paper proposes the Triadic Pedagogical Fit (TPF) framework, which triangulates Model Scale, Task Complexity via Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Instructional Persona to optimize pre-assessment evaluation. Through two studies, we demonstrate that while Mid-scale (12B) models effectively mirror undergraduate performance via high task sensitivity, Large-scale (27B) models require a “Teacher Persona” to bypass their high-accuracy bias. This pedagogical positioning transforms advanced models into superior “Item Auditors” for identifying ambiguous questions. We conclude with a decision matrix to guide instructors in selecting the optimal LLM configuration for assessment evaluation.

papers.title: Designing for Professional Competence: A Competence Architecture for IS Curriculum Design
Distorted Deliberation:  A Field Study of Metacognitive Miscalibration in AI-Assisted Legal Education
papers.abstract: The human-in-the-loop paradigm relies on accurate oversight to safely integrate generative AI into professional workflows. This study investigates a critical vulnerability in this assumption: metacognitive miscalibration, the divergence between users' perceived and actual alignment with AI-generated reasoning. In a field experiment, students and an LLM reasoned from identical legal cases. We anchored students' deliberation using the IRAC framework, then benchmarked their evaluations of the AI's output against an objective semantic measure. Panel data analysis reveals miscalibration is dynamically induced by task complexity, producing "distorted deliberation" where evaluative accuracy collapses despite structured engagement. Students competently detect errors in simple tasks, but this competence breaks down under analytical depth. Furthermore, recognizing novel AI insights remains a persistent blind spot amplified by case complexity. These findings reframe miscalibration as a predictable breakdown, demonstrating that procedural oversight is an insufficient safeguard in high-stakes domains.

papers.title: A Classroom Trial of Vibe Coding in Information Systems Education
papers.abstract: This paper reports a classroom trial of vibe coding in information systems analysis and design education for undergraduate social informatics students. We implemented "MindCode," a web-based environment that supports AI-assisted web-system development and process logging for learning analytics. We also designed a curriculum that encouraged learners to avoid uncritical acceptance of AI-generated results and to refine prompts and design intentions while developing a system from a given specification. We analyzed work logs from 34 learners and their questionnaire responses. The results suggest that learners recognized the importance of expressing specifications clearly, proceeding incrementally, and understanding the relationship among views, data, and object-oriented models. Two representative cases also illustrated clear differences in prompt-design skills.

papers.title: What Do Students Ask ChatGPT? An Analysis of Prompting Practices in a Course Assignment
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in higher education, yet little is known about how students' prompting practices relate to their experiences during complex, practice-oriented tasks. This study investigates students' reported benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT in a master's-level Information Systems course, where students developed an information security policy. Self-evaluation reports from ten student groups were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis followed by an interaction analysis. As part of an ongoing study, this short paper illustrates two recurring interaction patterns—GenAI-driven and challenge-driven—that demonstrate how students' interactions with ChatGPT evolve throughout the assignment. The study contributes to research on human–AI interaction and Information Systems education by providing a process-oriented perspective on students' engagement with GenAI during authentic, complex knowledge work.

papers.title: The Combination of GenAI and Immersive Technologies in Higher Education – The Perspective from Educators
papers.abstract: Higher education (HE) is increasingly challenged to integrate emerging technologies such as generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and immersive technologies into teach-ing and learning practices. While prior research has mainly focused on text-based AI applications, the combined use of GenAI and immersive technologies remains underex-plored, particularly from the perspective of educators. This study investigates educa-tors’ acceptance of these technologies using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM3). To address the research questions, 19 semi-structured expert interviews were conducted and analyzed using qualitative content analysis based on an adapted TAM3 frame-work. The findings show that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are key drivers of acceptance. While GenAI is already widely used and perceived as easy to use, immersive technologies remain less established but offer significant potential. The study contributes by extending TAM3 to a combined GenAI-immersive context and provides insights for research and practice.

papers.title: When AI Credibility Fractures: Human vs. AI Feedback Sources in Global Virtual Student Team Projects
papers.abstract: Students increasingly receive feedback from professors, coaches, and generative AI tools within the same learning cycle. This paper examines whether Source Credibility Theory, originally developed for human communicators, transfers intact to AI feedback in digital learning environments. Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm, we compare credibility perceptions of professors, program coaches, and generative AI tools in an 11-week global virtual student team project. Using data from 3,776 students across 31 countries, we model credibility perceptions measured at week 9 and self- and peer-evaluated performance measured at week 11. Results show that human-source credibility behaves as a global evaluation, whereas AI-source credibility remains differentiated into competence, trustworthiness, and goodwill. AI competence is positively associated with peer-evaluated performance, while AI trustworthiness is negatively associated with it. The findings suggest that effective GenAI pedagogy requires calibrated reliance rather than generic trust in generative AI feedback.

papers.title: Pathways to AI-Ready Entry-Level Talent for Industry Domains: Modular, Adaptive Design Principles for Business-School Curriculum
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reconfiguring the entry pathway into business work faster than university curricula can adapt. This disruption erodes the apprenticeship layer through which graduates historically developed expertise. This study employs a Design Science Research approach to develop and instantiate the AIX Hub, an industry-partnered AI curriculum co-designed by two R1 hub institutions. The design follows a no-code to low-code to full-code progression grounded in cognitive apprenticeship theory, aligns learning objectives to a 35-skill labor market taxonomy, and embeds work-based learning through a stage-based industry partnership model. Spring 2026 deployment reached 1,060 students across 12 sections of four courses at a minority-serving institution, with eight work-based learning opportunities spanning eight industry partners. From this instantiation, we formalize three preliminary design principles (derived progression, adaptive industry co-design, and equity-relevant deployment) for curricula that prepare AI-ready entry-level talent.

papers.title: When Introduction Falls Short: Stereotype Exposure and the Mitigating Effect of Intrinsic Interest in IS Introductory Events
papers.abstract: Since women are still underrepresented in information systems (IS), IS education seeks to attract more young women to the field. Although introductory events have been argued to be an important intervention against underrepresentation, little is known about the potential risks and barriers associated with them. Our study contributes to this body of knowledge by demonstrating that IS introductory events should be examined in light of risks from contextual social factors, particularly negative stereotypes. Linear regression analysis of an experiment with 96 young women from Germany in upper secondary education shows that exposure to stereotype-relevant cues before engaging in introductory, practical IS tasks increases stereotype endorsement. Importantly, we identify that intrinsic interest in the practical IS tasks mitigates this effect. Consequently, we emphasize that, although stereotypes pose a risk to IS introductory events, interesting IS tasks can help IS introductory events to fully realize their intended benefits.

papers.title: When AI Shapes Learning: Decision Authority and Accountability in AI-Augmented Consulting
papers.abstract: This case examines how an AI-based knowledge system, initially introduced as a learning support tool, gradually evolves into a decision-influencing actor in organizational settings. Drawing on a consulting firm implementing a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, the case highlights how system design features, such as traceability and structured outputs, shape perceived authority and influence user judgment. As AI becomes embedded in onboarding and project preparation, it transforms not only knowledge access but also learning processes, cognitive engagement, and accountability structures. The case presents a strategic dilemma between restricting use, implementing governance, or scaling adoption, providing a basis for examining the role of AI in digital learning environments and its implications for decision authority and professional development.

papers.title: From Producing Lectures to Governing Transformations: Teacher Orchestration in Agentic Lecture-Production Workflows
papers.abstract: Generative AI can support lecture production through text generation, summarization, slide drafting, narration, and media transformation. However, when these capabilities are embedded in stateful workflows, the issue is how teaching work is redistributed between teachers, AI services, and institutional systems. Drawing on prototype-development records, a course-based production case, formative walkthroughs with six university teachers, field notes, and transcript-derived material, this paper examines an agentic lecture-production prototype in higher education. The paper develops a model of accountable delegation-boundary orchestration, distinguishing delegated transformations, teacher-supervised co-production, and non-delegable pedagogical responsibilities. The findings show that responsible AI-supported lecture production depends on recurring orchestration: setting direction, reviewing outputs, adapting transformations, preserving traceability, and maintaining pedagogical and institutional accountability. Teacher control should therefore be designed as a workflow property, not treated as a final approval step. This shifts attention from automation efficiency to governing professional work in AI-supported educational production.

papers.title: Building community in an audio-first platform economy
When the Forecast Cannot Forecast: Designing Decision Support for a Retail Buyer at a Multi-Channel University Merchandise Store
papers.abstract: A two-student analytics team builds a forecasting and decision-support platform for a multi-channel university merchandise retailer. After a successful final presentation, the client reveals that an unexplained August revenue spike, which the team had treated as a one-time anomaly through statistical winsorization, is the first observation of a recurring structural change: the athletics department has begun routing student-athlete gear orders through the retail channel. A single observation cannot anchor a forecast, yet the change is genuine and recurring. The case ends with the faculty advisor and student team facing an open decision: leave the platform as delivered, tighten the winsorization without further change, or redesign the architecture to combine model-generated forecasts with human-supplied inputs for the non-forecastable component. For master's-level analytics courses, the case develops decision-support architecture for non-technical users, distinguishes outliers from structural change, and highlights the professional dimensions of post-delivery revision.

papers.title: What Makes One Mechanism More Plausible Than Another? A Critical Realist Framework for Causal Adjudications
papers.abstract: Critical realist research provides powerful tools for generating causal explanations through abductive and retroductive reasoning, yet researchers often face a subsequent problem: multiple candidate mechanisms may plausibly explain the same phenomenon. Existing methodological guidance offers limited direction on how such competing explanations should be scrutinized and comparatively adjudicated. This paper develops a Critical Realist Framework for Causal Adjudication that distinguishes mechanism generation from the subsequent evaluation of causal explanations. The framework comprises six interconnected analytical movements. We demonstrate its application using qualitative evidence from a public-sector organization, focusing on budget allocation for cybersecurity initiative and five candidate mechanisms inferred from interviews, observations, and documents. The demonstration shows how candidate mechanisms can be challenged, comparatively assessed, and positioned as competing or complementary causal processes. The paper contributes a systematic methodological logic for making critical realist causal reasoning more explicit, contestable, and theoretically defensible.

papers.title: Attending to Systems: Matters of Care in Information Systems Research
papers.abstract: Every solution brings new problems in tow. Digital technologies designed to make life easier, faster, and more efficient also create new dependencies, vulnerabilities, and uncertainties. Research on digitalization often treats these “dark sides” independent from the benefits from digital innovations. We argue that this division obscures the interdependence through which beneficial and harmful outcomes are produced simultaneously. Drawing on theories of care, we develop a more-than-human care lens for studying sociotechnical systems. Rather than viewing care as a moral virtue or ethical add-on, we conceptualize it as a jointly generative and destructive force that both maintains and repairs heterogenous relations that make sociotechnical worlds possible while enabling others to unravel as a necessary feature of how care is directed across sociotechnical relations. We develop four conceptual principles of care and propose a research agenda for examining how digital systems are sustained, transformed and displaced.

papers.title: Mechanismic items in survey research: conceptualization and concerns about their use
papers.abstract: In survey research, items are typically assumed to measure the values of properties (e.g., the "ease of use" of a system). Yet some items instead ask respondents to validate mechanisms linking two or more properties—for instance, that "using ICTs blurs boundaries between my job and my home life." We label such items mechanismic and reflect on the epistemological implications of their use. A preliminary review of 1,517 items published in MIS Quarterly and JAIS (2015–2025) suggests that roughly 15% of survey items are mechanismic, and that about one in three of these appears problematic. We identify three validity threats that they pose: multidimensionality, multifinality, and scope-validity violations. We argue that mechanismic items, while in need of scrutiny from a scale-validity standpoint, can be used to problematize and inspire research that decomposes and respecifies the mechanisms they encode, turning measurement weaknesses into opportunities for theory development.

papers.title: Designing Multimodal Conversational Agents for Laddering Interviews
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based conversational agents are increasingly used to collect qualitative data, but their suitability for cognitively demanding interview techniques remains underexplored. We examine how to design such agents to support laddering interviews in which participants are guided from concrete attributes to consequences and ultimately to personal values. Drawing on echeloned design science research (eDSR), we developed and evaluated design knowledge across linked design echelons. The study produced three design principles concerning agent reasoning, probing strategy, and multimodal interaction. We instantiated these principles and evaluated the artifact through a between-subjects experiment with 90 participants and a workshop demonstration with 18 doctoral researchers. A hybrid voice-and-text design achieved the highest observed response volume and proportion of complete means-end chains among the three conditions. We contribute prescriptive design knowledge for automated laddering interviews and show how multimodal interaction can jointly support response elaboration and the structural completeness required for laddering analysis.

papers.title: Beyond Fit: An Organizational Flux Theory of AI Governance
papers.abstract: Contingency theory explains organizational effectiveness through fit between organization and environment and presumes that observations remain valid long enough to inform governance. This premise is challenged when governance-relevant technological mutation outpaces organizational review and intervention. Formalizing technological mutation cycle time and governance cycle time, we distinguish three governance regimes. When the mismatch becomes extreme, the temporal commensurability assumption breaks down and fit becomes structurally non-identifiable at the governance cadence. To account for such circumstances, we propose Organizational Flux Theory (OFT) as a process-based lens. OFT explains temporal lag, agency inversion, and boundary volatility and shifts effectiveness from point-in-time fit to adaptability within authorized bounds. It also yields one design implication, an Algorithmic Constitution, that separates human normative amendment from runtime monitoring, constraint enforcement, containment, and telemetry. OFT is a boundary-conditioned conceptual theory; its regime thresholds and design prescriptions require empirical evaluation.

papers.title: Advancing Literature Review Automation through API-Based Searches: Design of an Independent Emulator
papers.abstract: The automation of literature search execution is becoming increasingly important as publication volumes grow and AI-based, agentic systems augment academic search activities. However, some Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) lack support for academic search queries consisting of nested subqueries and Boolean operators. This constraint complicates systematic and reproducible searches, increases manual effort, and decreases search efficiency. To resolve this issue, we present the Query Emulation for Academic Literature Searches (QuEALS) technique, which allows researchers to conduct automated API-based searches with academic search queries even when APIs do not support them natively. This approach works by recursively processing the query, retrieving literature from the API, and filtering the results for subqueries. We followed a Design Science Research approach to design, implement, and evaluate QuEALS. The prototype was implemented and evaluated for Crossref, which offers one of the most comprehensive and open research APIs, but lacks support for academic search queries.

papers.title: Fit for What Purpose?
papers.abstract: Fit was introduced to Information Systems (IS) through Task Technology Fit (TTF), drawing on socio-technical systems, contingency theory, and satisfactoriness. Across these research traditions, fit is generally understood as how the relationship between two or more elements influences an outcome. However, seminal papers often lack clear conceptualisations of fit, stemming from loosely defined elements, inconsistent terminology describing the relationship between elements, and, most critically, a tendency to take outcomes for granted, leaving fit for what purpose unspecified. Consequently, this leads to ambiguous, inconsistent conceptualisations hindering the cumulative research tradition, and impeding the progress of IS research. Through a literature survey and interpretive meaning-in-use analysis informed by a Wittgensteinian worldview, we demonstrate that these issues, not identified before, persist in contemporary research. Therefore, we propose three key ingredients for conceptualising fit, hoping to bring much-needed clarity to fit research in IS.

papers.title: Revisiting Digital Government and Digital Democracy: Theorizing Digitalization Beyond Government Efficiency
papers.abstract: Rapid technological progress, recurrent political crises, and a global erosion of democratic forms of government make the relationship between digital technologies and democracy a pressing issue. Critical information systems researchers have drawn on approaches from the social sciences to scrutinize the entanglement of digital technologies and politics and to inform design science research (DSR). Yet the prominent fields of digital government and digital democracy exhibit shortcomings. Where digital government research may at times be disengaged from the normative exploration of government, digital democracy is dominated by Habermasian approaches limiting its scope largely to the digital public sphere. We argue for a conception of digital democracy that reaches into the field of digital government, understood as democratic self-rule by and through digital technologies. We propose two design principles to guide the development of artifacts in the field and argue that normative-democratic criteria belong in the relevance and evaluation stages of DSR.

papers.title: From Design Insights to Design Knowledge:  A Taxonomy for Structuring the Development of Design Principles
papers.abstract: Design principles (DPs) in design science research (DSR) often lack transparency regarding their structure, scope, and underlying assumptions, making them difficult to interpret, compare, and reuse across contexts. This ambiguity limits their generalizability and can lead to inconsistent application and redundant effort. To address this issue, this paper develops a taxonomy that systematically captures the components and characteristics of DPs. The taxonomy is derived through a multi-iteration approach combining expert workshops, literature analysis, and empirical validation, resulting in 16 dimensions across the areas of derivation and synthesis, formulation, and evaluation. Building on this, a cluster analysis identifies four archetypes, consisting of conceptual, procedural, situated, and transferable DPs, representing different maturity levels of design knowledge. Thereby, the taxonomy enhances transparency and provides a structured foundation for the systematic development, communication, and evaluation of DPs in DSR.

papers.title: LLM Uncertainty in Strategic Decisions
papers.abstract: This paper examines the growing use of large language models to support strategic decisions in organizations, where questions such as whether to explore or exploit have no objectively correct answer. It highlights an emerging challenge: existing methods for eliciting model confidence were developed and validated against tasks with known ground truth, leaving open how they behave under genuine ambiguity. To address this gap, the study benchmarks six elicitation methods across seven organizational tensions, nine settings, and seven open-weight models, and proposes deviation from neutrality as a measure of bias, since balanced evidence should yield a probability near 50%. Initial experiments reveal that method choice alone explains over half the variance in measured bias, that logit-level methods substantially outperform generation-based ones, and that verbalized confidence, the practitioner default, degrades as models scale. The findings underscore the need for access to internal uncertainty measures in decision-support interfaces.

papers.title: A New Conceptual Paradigm for Narrowing the IS Research-Practice Gap
papers.abstract: The research-practice gap ranks among the most persistent problems in information systems (IS) research, made more urgent by the explosive deployment of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across organizations worldwide. This paper argues that the gap has resisted resolution because it has been misdiagnosed as either a problem of knowledge transfer, topic selection, or communication. We contend it is based on a false ontological separation between theory and practice, inherited from the division between pure and applied science and reproduced in IS scholarship's institutional structures. Drawing on Foucault's account of the mutual constitution of discursive and non-discursive practices, the paper proposes a paradigm shift grounded in the inseparability of theory and practice, and derive implications for IS research practice, IS professionalism, and the transformation of the IS field itself.

papers.title: Toward Knowledge-Traceable AI-Assisted Design Science: A Prompt-Code-Reflection Traceability Method Artifact
papers.abstract: Generative AI increasingly participates in design work, posing a methodological challenge for design science research (DSR): design knowledge may be generated in AI responses, externalized in prompts, materialized in code, rejected during debugging, or retrospectively interpreted by designers. Human-AI interaction traces alone provide useful but incomplete evidence. This paper addresses this knowledge traceability gap by developing a Prompt-Code-Reflection Method, a method artifact for identifying, qualifying, and characterizing Design Knowledge Externalization Events (DKEEs) in AI-assisted DSR. The method integrates framework-based qualitative coding of human-AI interaction traces, artifact-uptake qualification, and reflection-based cross-checking. We instantiate and preliminarily evaluate the method through an educational software design task using seven core cases. The evaluation identifies 22 qualified DKEEs and shows how cross-layer evidence distinguishes prompt-visible knowledge from artifact uptake and participant-side interpretation. The study contributes a traceability method for qualifying what prompt, code, and reflection evidence can and cannot support in AI-assisted DSR knowledge claims.

papers.title: Configurational Meta-Analysis: A Set-Theoretic Approach to Cross-Study Evidence Synthesis in Information Systems
papers.abstract: Configurational Meta-Analysis (CMA) extends set-theoretic reasoning from primary empirical cases to published studies as cases for cross-study evidence synthesis. We formalize an IS-oriented protocol integrating corpus construction, construct harmonization, calibration from textual evidence, truth-table analysis, robustness assessment, and reporting. We demonstrate the protocol with 35 studies of agentic AI systems, calibrated for autonomy, coordination architecture, institutional embeddedness, governance clarity, and operational viability. The analysis identifies a concentrated configuration associated with outcome presence and multiple equifinal configurations associated with outcome absence. These patterns are interpreted as provisional insights from a recent, heterogeneous evidence base rather than direct causal estimates. CMA complements systematic reviews, bibliometric analysis, statistical meta-analysis, and primary-data fsQCA by enabling explicit assessment of conjunction, equifinality, and configurational asymmetry across calibrated study-level evidence.

papers.title: Agentic AI and the Reconfiguration of Methodological Risk in Qualitative Research
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used in qualitative research, but methodological debate has largely centred on conversational chatbots. We review this literature and organise recurring concerns into ten methodological challenges, alongside five epistemic risks identified in prior work. We then use an illustrative multi-agent workflow for reflexive thematic analysis, with ChatGPT as a point of comparison to examine how these methodological challenges and epistemic risks are reconfigured under a different configuration. The analysis shows that agentic design can constrain challenges associated with data handling, model control, and transparency, while non-replicability, hallucination, and evaluation uncertainty are shifted into more inspectable parts of the workflow. Bias and environmental burden remain largely unresolved. The workflow does not remove the underlying epistemic limits of LLM-based analysis or the need for reflexive researcher judgement. The study’s primary contribution is a risk-reconfiguration account showing how GenAI configuration redistributes methodological dependence while interpretive responsibility remains with the researcher.

papers.title: The Methodological Black Box of LLM-Assisted Topic Modeling
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly delegated analytical tasks in research workflows, yet what large language models actually do when asked to “run topic modeling” remains opaque. We compare five consumer LLM systems (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok) performing topic modeling on the same corpus of 77 articles through one-shot, deliberately underspecified delegation, in November 2025 and again — three same-instruction runs and two paraphrases per system — in August 2026. Systems diverged at the level of the algorithm family, not merely its parameters; divergence recurred across runs, versions, and phrasings, and included form-preserving methodological substitution, undisclosed alternatives, and simulated results acknowledged only under disclosure probing. We propose the Six-Gate Framework for Accountable LLM-Assisted Topic Modeling. The framework decomposes the task into six methodological decision gates and replaces monolithic delegation with adaptive human–AI dialogue and explicit researcher authorization. Its ongoing validation compares the autonomous baseline with a framework-guided condition.

papers.title: What Management Scholarship Brings to the IS Debate on AI-Augmented Literature Reviews: An Epistemic Contribution
papers.abstract: Information Systems scholarship has produced a robust diagnosis of the epistemic and methodological tensions raised by AI-augmented literature reviews, together with operational guidance on how generative AI may support the review process and on what it should be allowed to do. Less formalized is the normative question that precedes both: why should particular review activities remain under human responsibility?  Drawing on a comparative reading of 81 full-text articles we identify four epistemic resources that management scholarship contributes to four tensions already formalized in the IS discourse, and translate them into four principles for deciding what to delegate: strategic inefficiency, reflective agency, instrumental triangulation, and criteria-centric evaluation. The contribution is epistemic rather than procedural.

papers.title: What Kind of AI? Introducing Three Material Properties of AI Systems
papers.abstract: IS research often groups materially different systems under the label “AI,” making it difficult to compare findings or know when they generalize. We introduce three material properties—task latitude, output latitude, and action latitude—for specifying what kind of AI system a study examines. The properties describe where the task is fixed, what the system can express, and how model output becomes organizational action. The framework distinguishes systems that are collapsed by broad labels such as predictive, generative, and agentic AI. This vocabulary helps researchers compare empirical findings, assess the scope of claims about AI, and trace how organizations domesticate broad AI capabilities into specific applications and workflows. By making the material configuration explicit, the framework provides a baseline for more cumulative research on AI in organizations.

papers.title: Conducting Rigorous AI-Led Interviews in Qualitative IS Research – Practical Advice
papers.abstract: Qualitative interviewing is a cornerstone of information systems (IS) research, yet it remains resource-intensive, difficult to scale, and constrained by interviewer-related variability. Recent advances in conversational artificial intelligence (AI) make it possible, for the first time, for the interviewer to be non-human, opening methodological opportunities while challenging the relational, interpretive, and reflexive facets of qualitative inquiry. Despite the growing availability of AI-led interviewing tools, methodological guidance for their rigorous integration into IS research is largely absent. Drawing on a systematic literature review, sixteen AI-led interviews on conspiracy beliefs, and sixteen subsequent human-led reflection interviews, we develop a framework that includes key insights and practical advice for conducting rigorous AI-led interviews. We find that methodological rigor shifts from interpersonal performance toward design rigor, and that the researcher’s positionality is relocated upstream into prompts, interface, and system architecture, calling for an expanded standard of methodological transparency in qualitative IS research.

papers.title: Skeptical Yet Engaged: Unpacking Engagement Mechanisms of Generative AI Influencers in Mixed-Reality Contexts
papers.abstract: Despite the rise of GenAI influencers on social media, many still struggle to attract users, raising questions about why some GenAI influencers consistently engage users while others don’t. Accordingly, this study explores whether and how GenAI influencers foster positive attitudes and engagement. Using exploratory topic modeling and sentiment analysis of user comments on Instagram, we identified that GenAI influencers engage users through two attitudinal patterns: skepticism about authenticity and immersion in virtual beauty. Informed by these mechanisms, we subsequently conducted a controlled experiment examining the anthropomorphism of GenAI influencers’  appearances and the mixed-reality environments they inhabit, revealing how these factors differentially influence attitudinal patterns and user engagement. This study offers practical guidance for GenAI influencer designers and organizations seeking to attract users and advance Information Systems research by emphasizing the factors and mechanisms that influence user engagement with GenAI influencers.

papers.title: Same Structure, Different Trajectories: Community Dissolution on an AI Agent Social Platform
papers.abstract: Multi-agent platforms where participants are AI agents are beginning to emerge. While theories of human online communities are well developed, there is a need to examine whether these theories can be applied to agent-based platforms and, if not, how they differ and why. We study Moltbook, a Reddit-like platform populated entirely by large language model (LLM) agents, and compare it with its reference platform, Reddit. We find that collective behaviors observed in human communities weaken on Moltbook. Topic differentiation across communities decreases, valued contribution signals such as voting and disagreement are weak, and interaction patterns, such as who responds to whom, become less distinctive. We refer to this joint weakening across topics, valued contribution, and interaction as Community Dissolution. We propose two agent-level limitations as candidate explanations: a norm enforcement deficit and the homogenization of LLM outputs. This study offers a foundation for future research on LLM agent communities.

papers.title: InfoPsych-MoE: An Information-Theoretic Case-Based Reasoning Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Mental Health Detection
papers.abstract: Mental health assessment in social media is challenging because psychological expressions are implicit, heterogeneous, and difficult to interpret using purely data-driven models. While integrating domain knowledge has emerged as a primary strategy, existing approaches largely rely on static knowledge bases that fragment holistic clinical reasoning into rigid fact entries, limiting their ability to foster domain-specific reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose InfoPsych-MoE, an information-theoretic case-based reasoning mixture-of-experts framework that enables LLMs to acquire and coordinate domain-specific reasoning expertise. Specifically, we develop a Case-Based Reasoning Internalized Prompting (CBRIP) pipeline to construct transferable reasoning patterns through the Retrieve–Reuse–Revise–Retain cycle. We further introduce a PMI-based dual-level utility assessment mechanism that evaluates the contribution of reasoning patterns, guiding reasoning refinement and expert routing. Experiments on three mental health assessment tasks demonstrate that InfoPsych-MoE achieves superior performance and provides an effective framework for adaptive mental health assessment.

papers.title: Across Exposure Stages: Framing Incongruence and User Engagement on Social Media
papers.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly present content in stages, exposing users first to limited external cues and only later to fuller internal content. This study examines how cross-layer framing incongruence—the discrepancy between pre-entry presentation and post-entry content—shapes different forms of user engagement on social media. Drawing primarily on Expectancy Violation Theory, we argue that users form expectations from initial exposure cues such as preview titles and cover text and respond when post-entry content deviates from those expectations. We propose a sequential research design combining large-scale post-level platform data with online experiments. The study will examine how cross-layer framing incongruence influences comments, likes, and favorites, and whether these relationships are strengthened when the pre-entry presentation is more emotionally intense than the post-entry content. By differentiating these engagement behaviors, the study aims to clarify how expectancy violations translate into distinct behavioral responses in layered social media environments.

papers.title: Beyond Emotional Contagion: How Sensemaking Shapes Reactions to Digital Outrage on Social Media
papers.abstract: Social media has become a common digital platform for venting moral outrage, an intense feeling of anger and indignation triggered by perceived injustice or immorality. Understanding how observers respond to such outrage has important implications for users, targets, and platforms. Prior research suggests that emotionally charged content spreads via emotional contagion at the collective level, but these effects may not hold at the individual level. Integrating Tripartite Reactions to Emotions (TRE) theory with sensemaking theory, we propose that observers engage in sensemaking by evaluating the rationality of outrage expressers. A negative appraisal of this rationality may prevent individual observers from developing their own feelings of outrage and thereby counteract the contagion of outrage and associated information sharing. Across two experiments, we find support for this cognitive-emotional mechanism. Our findings advance understanding of how individuals respond to digital outrage, and provide theoretical and practical implications.

papers.title: When Reframing Becomes Misinformation: An Agent-Based Model of Vaccine Discourse on Social Media
papers.abstract: People may encounter misinformation even when the original news report is accurate, because user comments beneath news posts can misinterpret and reframe the report. Yet misinformation research pays limited attention to how misleading content is generated before it spreads. This study develops an agent-based model grounded in framing theory to examine how user reframing of news posts leads to the emergence of misinformation. The model represents reframing as evolving semantic divergence from news post and models a socially amplified pathway in which substantial frame drift combines with emotional activation. Using Weibo Covid-19 vaccine data, the simulated discourse remains semantically close to observed commentary, and the calibrated model reproduces the broad temporal pattern of misinformation prevalence. The study extends framing research by conceptualising reframing as recursive and cumulative process, and contributes to misinformation research by explaining how misinformation can emerge from initially accurate information through user interactions.

papers.title: A Tri-Dimensional Network Perspective on Social Media Framing and Polarization in Climate Disasters
papers.abstract: Social media induced polarization (SMIP) divides public discourse and limits shared understanding. This challenge intensifies during climate disasters, when news publishers shape how audiences interpret events. While prior research has examined framing and polarization, we lack a clear understanding of how frame packages are constructed and diverge across publisher groups. We examine how climate-consensus and climate-skeptical publishers construct divergent frame packages. We develop a GenAI-augmented computational approach to extract tri-dimensional frame packages—manifest connectivity, narrative logic, and expressive evocation—from coverage of Hurricane Ian and the 2022 Western U.S. wildfires. Our analysis identifies eight frame packages and shows that divergence is uneven: total at the manifest dimension, substantial at the narrative dimension, and minimal at the expressive dimension. This study conceptualizes digital frames as dynamic semantic networks, specifies the internal structure of the communicative process within SMIP, and introduces a scalable approach for analyzing multimodal social media discourse.

papers.title: Making Sense of the Feed: A Recursive Process Model of Finfluencer Influence
papers.abstract: Financial influencers (finfluencers) increasingly shape how young retail investors form judgments within algorithmically curated social media environments, where decisions carry irreversible consequences. Yet prior research treats influence mostly as a linear pathway from exposure to behavior, leaving unexplained how investors interpret, revise, and enact financial meaning through sustained interaction. Following the Gioia methodology, we conducted a qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews with young German investors. The findings yield a recursive process model of five interdependent dimensions, whose self-modifying dynamic continuously reshapes investors’ interpretive frames, challenging static vulnerability assumptions. The model extends Information Systems (IS) research on algorithmic mediation from content distribution to context formation, with implications for platform governance and financial education.

papers.title: Am I Actually Satisfied With What I See? How Information-Limiting Environments Shape Social Media Switching Intentions
papers.abstract: Recommender systems on social media increasingly personalize information, creating information-limiting environments that may shape how users evaluate social media platforms and whether they intend to switch. This research-in-progress paper examines how two characteristics of such environments, information slant and information diversity, influence user satisfaction and switching intentions on social media. Drawing on switching literature, we argue that both opinion-congruent information and diverse information can – whilst being opposingly associated with information-limiting environments – increase satisfaction, which in turn reduces switching intentions. We further propose that truth bias, critical consuming media literacy, and issue involvement moderate these relationships. We will analyze data from Twitter (now X) users using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Exploratory results from a pre-test indicate that perceived information slant and perceived information diversity positively influence satisfaction, while satisfaction negatively affects switching intentions. We will contribute to literature by linking information-limiting environments and their characteristics to social media switching.

papers.title: AI Sanitization Paradox in Online Discourse: Declining Participation and Rising Toxicity
papers.abstract: Discourse about social issues on social media platforms has expanded rapidly in both scale and toxicity, challenging platforms’ ability to sustain constructive debate. Over the last few years, platforms have adopted opinion summarizers powered by generative AI to help users quickly understand existing viewpoints.
