However, these summaries often sanitize toxic content, potentially distorting users’ perceptions of the opinion landscape. The behavioral consequences of such algorithmic curation remain unclear. This study examines how AI summaries affect the volume and toxicity of subsequent user comments. Drawing on the collective effort model and psychological reactance theory, we develop and test a set of hypotheses using a natural experiment to identify the causal effects of displaying AI-generated summaries. Our findings show that AI-generated comment summaries significantly reduce subsequent comment volume while increasing comment toxicity. Mechanism analyses reveal that the reduced participation is driven by the summary’s opinion coverage ratio, whereas increased toxicity stems from AI sanitization bias—the underrepresentation of toxic opinions in the summaries. Robustness checks and supplementary experiments support these results. The findings provide potentially important implications for the design of AI summarization systems and content moderation strategies.

papers.title: How Does Early Random Exploration Shape Content Allocation on Platforms? Evidence from a Large-scale Field Experiment
papers.abstract: Digital content platforms must recommend new content before knowing its quality or audience fit, while early feedback is selectively shaped by prior allocation rules. Although exploration may support learning, direct evidence is limited regarding whether early random exploration improves the subsequent organic recommendation performance of new content by generating more informative feedback. Using a randomized traffic allocation experiment with over 65,000 new videos on a major Chinese short-video platform, we show that early random traffic increases subsequent views and like ratios and reduces skip ratios. To identify the mechanism, we construct a video-level measure of feedback informativeness from the dispersion and depth of engagement states and instrument it using pre-treatment heterogeneity in assigned viewers’ historical engagement propensities. Videos that generate more informative feedback achieve larger gains later, especially in views and skips. Effective cold-start recommendation, therefore, requires diagnostic early exposure, not simply more traffic.

papers.title: Is Decentralizing Democratizing? Self-Organization and Unintended Centralization in Decentralized Social Media
papers.abstract: Decentralized social media platforms promise to redistribute control over content curation from centralized algorithms to ordinary users, but whether this redistribution is genuinely democratizing user influence and broadening user participation remains largely untested. We examine Bluesky's starter packs, user-curated bundles of recommended accounts, using two complementary empirical methods. A relational hyperevent model of pack creation reveals that pack generators systematically feature already-prominent, non-reciprocating accounts, concentrating rather than distributing visibility. A generalized synthetic control analysis of adopters shows a 53.7% increase in weekly likes sent during the first three weeks post-adoption, but a 45.2% decrease in weekly likes to non-followed, outside-pack users over the following ten weeks. These results suggest that user self-organizing through curation produces hierarchy that crowds out organic discovery. We contribute evidence that decentralized infrastructure's aim to grant user autonomy does not imply a decentralization of influence, and instead show a patterned emergence of centralized attention.

papers.title: Examining Naturalness of Synthetic Conversations: A Framework and Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM-based simulations of social media conversations are increasingly used to examine phenomena such as opinion dynamics and polarization. However, the naturalness of such synthetic conversations lacks comprehensive evaluation, limiting our ability to assess whether they mimic real conversations and support valid inferences. This paper proposes a multi-dimensional, multi-level framework for evaluating such naturalness across three complementary dimensions i.e., lexical, dialog, and semantic, at the word/ sentence, interaction, and thread levels, with five pre-registered metrics. We apply the framework to Reddit-style synthetic conversations across several topics that we generate with a base model and a fine-tuned Llama3.3 model. We validate the metrics’ rankings against human evaluations for a popular topic. The results show that fine-tuning improves performance across all three dimensions, with the automated metric rankings broadly aligned with human judgments. This study contributes towards a holistic evaluation framework for assessing the naturalness of synthetic social media conversations that can be extended to other synthetic dialog data.

papers.title: Making Sense of Deepfakes – How Online Communities Exchange Technological Frames on Reddit
papers.abstract: The commodification of deepfake technology led to a proliferation of interpretations of its uses. In online communities, where collective sense-making occurs, these interpretations (frames) may diffuse and converge across communities through shared membership. Understanding whether and how frames converge across communities, and toward which types of interpretations, is critical for assessing how collective sense-making shapes perceptions of and possibly future developments in deepfake technology.  This study examines Reddit discussions following the release of a deepfake of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in March 2022. We construct an inter-community network based on users’ posting activity and identify frames using a semi-supervised approach. We find that membership overlap fosters convergence, penalizing particularly harmful frames such as the generation of non-consensual sexual imagery. Furthermore, convergence toward specific frames largely depends on community specialization in discussing deepfake technology; while entertainment frames characterize these communities, they also spread both non-harmful frames, such as entertainment, and more problematic ones, such as disinformation.

papers.title: Content Credibility Signaling and Trust in Professional Social Networks: Evidence from LinkedIn
papers.abstract: AI technologies are changing digital professional environments  facilitating the large-scale production of realistic but potentially misleading content. This study explores signaling dynamics on LinkedIn, examining how professional identity, credibility, and trust are constructed and evaluated in the context of AI-driven content. Based on 25 semi-structured expert interviews analyzed through the Gioia methodology, we identify key elements shaping these dynamics: (1) platform use and signaling, (2) trust and credibility construction, (3) AI and information integrity challenges, (4) verification and adaptive user responses, (5) user typologies. Findings reveal a tension between costly and low-cost signals due to AI-generated content, resulting in increased ambiguity and reduced transparency in professional evaluations. Users and platforms develop strategies such as verification practices and transparency-enhancing features to navigate these challenges. This study developed a framework for signaling dynamics on professional social media, offering insights for creating more trustworthy digital platforms and improving online identity signaling in the age of AI.

papers.title: How do Social Media Managers Manage Algorithms? Uncovering Folk Theories of Algorithm Management
papers.abstract: This study examines how social media managers manage opaque algorithms to achieve professional goals such as visibility, reach, and commercial success. Drawing on five qualitative interviews with social media managers and thematic analysis, preliminary findings identify three approaches to algorithm management: continuous experimentation, reliance on a settled formula, and a solely content-focused approach with limited attention to algorithms. Five folk theories are identified, including authenticity, consistency, quality, branding, and boosting, that reflect social media managers’ beliefs about how algorithms can be influenced. These findings extend research on algorithm sensemaking and folk theories by shifting attention from private users to professional actors who actively seek to manage algorithms as part of their work.

papers.title: A Deer in the Digital Forest: Social Media Use in Times of Adversity
papers.abstract: What does social media become when life is disrupted by illness, loss or trauma? For some, it becomes far more than a platform for sharing. Drawing on Uses and Gratifications theory and identity and narrative perspectives, this study examines how individuals experiencing significant life disruption use social media and how the gratifications associated with such engagement evolve over time. Using longitudinal social media data and interviews, the findings show that social, hedonic and cognitive gratifications are not static motivations but can be reconfigured as circumstances, relationships and identities change. Narrative and identity work operate as cross-cutting processes through which these gratifications acquire new meanings and functions. The study contributes a processual perspective on social media use during adversity, showing how changing circumstances can reconfigure established gratifications and how sustained social media engagement may become embedded in ongoing practices of adaptation and identity reconstruction, potentially developing into a socio-technical coping infrastructure.

papers.title: When the Story Survives the Scandal: Understanding Social Media Audiences’ Post-Scandal Support for Deceptive Entrepreneurs
papers.abstract: Entrepreneurial scandals create public evidence that undermines the validity of prior claims, yet online audiences often continue to accept or defend the entrepreneur and their narrative. We examine why legitimacy persists, fragments, or recovers following such a breakdown of validity. Using more than 2.6 million Reddit posts concerning 36 scandalized digital entrepreneurship gurus, we combine event-time analysis of expressed propriety, community validity, and community consensus with structural topic modeling and qualitative process analysis. Our preliminary findings identify four post-scandal trajectories and suggest distinct audience-side mechanisms underlying each. We contribute to social evaluations research by showing how legitimacy dimensions can decouple after public disconfirmation, to cultural entrepreneurship by theorizing audience (dis)enchantment and narrative regeneration as processes through which online communities sustain or reconstruct entrepreneurial legitimacy after scandal, and to information systems research by explaining how networked audiences collectively reinterpret disconfirming evidence and sustain divergent social judgments after validity breakdowns.

papers.title: When Trust Does Not Translate into Engagement: A Decoupling Perspective on AI Disclosure in Short-Form Video Platforms
AI Moderation as an Accommodating Force: Evidence from Retail Investor Discourse
papers.abstract: LLM-assisted moderation outperforms keyword filtering technically, but its effect on collective investor discourse is unclear. Using the launch of an AI moderator on r/WallStreetBets in October 2024, with 152,626 posts and 8.8 million comments matched to 3,258 CRSP-listed stocks, we examine how GenAI-based platform governance reshapes community discussion. Grounded in the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm and communication accommodation theory, we argue the moderator earns legitimacy by linguistically aligning with the posts it moderates, driving topical convergence. Community attention concentrates on larger firms and retreats from earnings events and institutionally held stocks. Return predictability improves for large caps only. AI moderation narrows the discourse diversity that crowd wisdom depends on.

papers.title: Eroding Policy Legitimacy: A Policy Triangle Analysis of Australia’s Social Media Minimum Age Restriction Policy
papers.abstract: Governments are increasingly adopting restrictive measures to address risks associated with young people’s social media use, yet such interventions may face legitimacy erosion when concerns about policymakers, policy processes, regulatory design, and socio-technical conditions reinforce one another. This study examines how the legitimacy of Australia’s Social Media Minimum Age policy is eroded through interactions among actors, process, content, and context. Guided by Walt and Gilson’s Policy Triangle, we analyze parliamentary submissions and Reddit discourse using deductive and inductive analysis. Findings show that institutional distrust, procedural deficits, content ambiguity, and concerns about surveillance, rights, and enforceability interact to produce cascading legitimacy deficits. We conclude that legitimacy erosion is relational and multidimensional, arising from misalignment across actor credibility, procedural integrity, content viability, and contextual resonance. The study extends the Policy Triangle by theorizing these dimensions as interdependent legitimacy mechanisms and proposes an anticipated compliance paradox associated with discursive resistance and anticipated circumvention.

papers.title: Not All Data Are Alike: Rethinking Data Domains in Information Systems Research
papers.abstract: Data are central to Information Systems research, yet the field increasingly studies different kinds of data under a single, undifferentiated label. From government data, through biometric data, personal data, synthetic data, natural world data, to trace data, researchers work across distinct data domains, defined as socio-technical contexts in which data are produced, governed, interpreted, and used, with implications for organizational and societal outcomes. This panel opens a debate among scholars working across distinct data domains to examine what in data constitutes a unified phenomenon and what requires domain-specific theorizing, whether core data studies constructs travel across domains, and whether methods from one data domain can be productively applied to others. By making both convergence and divergence visible, the panel invites a rethinking of core assumptions about data in Information Systems research, with implications for research questions, theory building, and methods.

papers.title: Reconstituting Organizations in the Age of Agentic AI: Agency, Governance, and Organizational Boundaries Beyond Human-Centered Organizations
papers.abstract: The rise of agentic AI challenges organizational assumptions by shifting the role of technology from tool to actor. As AI systems increasingly perform cognitive tasks, participate in decision-making, and reshape governance. Organizations must renegotiate agency, accountability, and trust. Subsequently, this panel explores how AI transforms organizational structures, decision processes, and control mechanisms and addresses three key questions: How does AI reshape organizational agency? How are decision rights governed to handle agentic systems? And what are the implications for theory and research designs? The brings together varied perspectives on the topic, inviting and stimulating discourse on the future of organizing in the age of agentic AI.

papers.title: Information Systems in Outer Space: Imaginaries and Realities of the New Space Economy
papers.abstract: Outer Space has received hardly any attention from the IS field to this day. This lack of engagement is surprising. After all, SpaceTech, an offspring of the cybernetic revolution, is a truly digital-born domain of human endeavor. Likewise, the success of the Artemis II mission not only reignited imaginaries about humanity’s future but also escalated the race to dominate Outer Space. Finally, with the invention of reusable rockets, SpaceTech is transforming from a centralized, government-led industry to a New Space Economy marked by loosely coupled innovation ecosystems. In this purview, SpaceTech is becoming a new all-purpose platform comparable to the Internet in terms of its impact on innovation, governance, organization, and other areas of IS research. Against this backdrop, the panel discusses how Outer Space, a radically hostile environment, pushes IS research and practice to their epistemological, conceptual, methodological, and ethical limits. By way of discussion, the panel explores how IS can contribute to a more equitable, responsible, and sustainable New Space Economy.

papers.title: AI in Healthcare: Effective, Compassionate, Efficient – or None of the Above?
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) diffuses across the healthcare industry, its impact on the core pillars of effective, compassionate, and efficient care remains uncertain. Grounded in Glouberman and Mintzberg’s "four worlds" model, this panel examines how AI reshapes the distinct logics of cure (clinical), care (nursing), control (administrative), and community (governance). Panelists will debate critical tensions, including clinician deskilling versus expertise augmentation, the potential for "algorithmic control" in resource allocation, and the challenge of maintaining authentic human compassion in AI-mediated interactions. By identifying trade-offs and complementarities across these domains, the panel seeks to outline a future research agenda for the Information Systems community to foster the responsible design and governance of AI in healthcare.

papers.title: Human-in-the-Loop AI Research: A Hands-on Workshop on Integrating AI into the Research Workflow
Autonomous Scholarship: An AI-led Research Experience
papers.abstract: This Professional Development Workshop (PDW) examines autonomous scholarship through a transparent, end-to-end AI-led research experience. Generative AI tools are used to create the call for papers, conduct research, produce submissions, and review manuscripts, while human participants serve as orchestrators, auditors, presenters, and accountable editors. At ICIS 2026, selected teams will present both their AI-generated papers and the processes behind them, including prompts, interventions, failures, and lessons learned. Audience assessment and panel discussion will explore implications for authorship, novelty, quality, legitimacy, peer review, and governance. The workshop will generate reusable protocols, artifacts, reflections, and policy recommendations for responsible AI-enabled scholarship in Information Systems research.

papers.title: Generative AI and Computational Theory Construction: Challenges and Opportunities
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI—specifically, large language models (LLMs)—are expanding the possibilities of computational theory construction (CTC) by enabling new approaches to data generation and analysis. At the same time, these developments raise important questions about transparency, reproducibility, and validation. This PDW provides a space to critically reflect on and discuss both the opportunities and the challenges of using generative AI in CTC. The workshop will include a panel discussion with scholars who have been leveraging generative AI for theory development, followed by roundtable sessions in which participants receive developmental feedback from mentors on their ongoing projects.

papers.title: Computational Design in the Age of Generative AI: Opportunities and Demonstrations
Digital Enforcement and Dignity Disequilibrium: A CARE-Capability Perspective on Digital Public Services
papers.venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: Digital technologies are essential to modern governance, as governments rely on them to deliver vital public services. Although these initiatives aim to enhance efficiency, scalability, and transparency, they also raise concerns about digitally mediated access for citizens with varying levels of capability. When access to entitlements depends on technology, barriers can arise that constrain citizens’ freedom to realise their entitlements and affect their sense of dignity. Despite increasing focus on digital inequality, the dignity implications of digitally enforced public services remain unexplored in Information Systems (IS) research. Drawing on CARE Theory and Sen’s Capability Approach, this study examines how digitally mediated governance reshapes citizens’ freedoms and generates dignity tensions. Through an interpretive multiple-case study of two large-scale public digital governance systems in India: the CoWIN vaccination platform and the Jeevan Pramaan digital life certificates, we develop the concept of digital enforcement to explain how institutional reliance on digital infrastructure reconfigures access to benefits. The findings uncover a mechanism in which narratives of reform translate into technology-conditioned access that limits capability conversion and creates a dignity disequilibrium. The study advances IS research by extending CARE Theory to digital governance and conceptualising digital enforcement as a governance mechanism shaping citizens’ lived …

papers.title: Local Level Resistance, Wickedness and State-Mandated ICTD Programmes: A Case of Agriculture E-Market Platform in Karnataka, India
papers.venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: Situated in critical interpretivist traditions, this paper examines a state-mandated programme to transform agricultural markets into E-markets in Karnataka, India. We problematise the top-down, deterministic framing of this ICTD initiative, in which the state’s dominant success narratives marginalise local voices and explore how situated actors within the societal system perceive and respond to this transformation. We undertake a layered analysis, first applying Scott’s counter-discourse theory to establish a dissonance between state narratives and local realities. This analysis serves as the foundation for a two-pronged inquiry. The first prong, informed by Scott’s resistance theory, demonstrates that dissonance with programme objectives leads local actors to adopt everyday resistance tactics such as foot-dragging, false reporting, and false compliance, producing a condition of ‘cosmetic compliance’ amid low adoption. The second prong, based on Rittel and Webber’s wicked problem lens, shows that the templated ICT intervention has deepened existing traits of wickedness and generated new ones rooted in resistance. We argue that these new traits are not merely disruptive but reflect adaptive local agency and the evolving character of wicked problems. The study challenges the top-down orientation and epistemic preferences of state-led development, advocating greater attention to indigenous practices, situated knowledge, and the evolving nature of wickedness in societal systems …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Evaluating the Impacts of Bundling on a Firm’s Product Demand and Operational Decisions
papers.abstract: Firms use bundles to influence customer demand, but supplying those bundles often requires operational capacity that is shared across the portfolio. Changing the price, composition, or availability of one bundle can therefore trigger two reallocations: customers reallocate expenditure across bundles, and the firm reallocates operational capacity across the demand those bundles generate. We develop a data-driven framework that links these two decisions. Heterogeneous consumers choose discrete bundle quantities subject to a common budget, while the firm jointly chooses bundle prices and quantities subject to bundle-specific and shared-resource requirements. We estimate the demand and supply models from observed discrete decisions using Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo, retaining the integer structure in estimation and counterfactual analysis. We apply the framework to three empirical settings: public bike sharing, online retail, and theme-park services. The empirical analyses reveal several consequences of evaluating bundles as part of a portfolio. Customer value and profit contribution need not be aligned: a bundle that creates substantial customer value can make little or no incremental contribution to optimized profit, and removing some bundles can increase profit after the remaining portfolio is re-optimized. Price responses differ across bundles because discrete purchases adjust at different thresholds. A bundle's response to tighter shared-resource requirements depends …

papers.title: Green IS Affordances for Sustainable Mega-Events: A Conceptual Model for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics
papers.abstract: Mega-events generate substantial environmental footprints while relying increasingly on complex information systems (IS) capabilities to coordinate venues, transport, energy, supply chains, and legacy outcomes. This paper develops a Green IS affordance model for sustainable mega-events and applies it to the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Drawing on Green IS and IS affordance theory, we conceptualize how digital infrastructures enable sustainability across heterogeneous actor groups and temporal phases. The model identifies four categories of sustainability affordances: operational affordances for Games-time resource management, structural affordances for sustainable design and construction, governance affordances for transparency and accountability, and legacy affordances for post-Games sustainability outcomes. We also introduce the concept of temporally deferred sustainability affordances, which captures IS capabilities designed today for future actualization by post-Games actors. The paper extends Green IS theory to mega-events and outlines a research agenda for empirically studying the Brisbane 2032 Games.

papers.title: Unlocking Local Energy Transitions through Monetary Innovation
papers.abstract: Photovoltaic Community Currencies (PVCCs) have emerged as a promising approach to simultaneously address energy poverty, financial exclusion, and the transition to renewable energy by linking decentralized solar energy generation to community-based digital currencies. However, research integrating these domains remains fragmented. This study addresses this gap through a systematic literature review following Okoli’s methodology. From 543 records identified in Web of Science, AIS eLibrary, and Scielo, 24 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using inductive thematic synthesis. The review proposes a socio-technical framework comprising four analytical elements—initial conditions, enabling ICTs, local community, and broader implications—and identifies six affordances for PVCC implementation: inclusive financial participation, behavioral engagement and energy literacy, sustainable community currency engagement, infrastructure accessibility, regulatory and policy stability, and energy justice. The framework advances digital sustainability research and provides a theoretical foundation for designing and evaluating PVCC initiatives in underserved communities.

papers.title: Inter-Organisational Systems for Circular Value Chains: A Simulation of Digital Product Passport Adoption
papers.abstract: Circular value chains rely on effective information sharing to recover materials from waste, reducing dependence on virgin resources and improving industrial sustainability. To support circular value chains, the EU has introduced the Digital Product Passport, an inter-organisational information system for disclosing product information. The effect of the DPP on the sustainability of circular value chains has not been explored, and extant literature focuses only on its technical design. Drawing on organisational information processing theory, we model the DPP characteristics as capabilities that address different information needs in each phase of a circular value chain for the recovery of photovoltaic waste, and simulate 500 random adoption scenarios. The findings indicate that the DPP increases the amount of material processed and improves environmental and social sustainability, while costs grow faster than revenues and the additional material is not matched by proportional downstream processing. These dynamics reveal tensions and trade-offs in both implementation and policy decisions regarding DPP adoption.

papers.title: Push for Transparency: Mitigating Information Asymmetries with the Digital Product Passport
papers.abstract: The Digital Product Passport (DPP) is becoming mandatory in the European Union across product groups, requiring extended data sharing for physical products along the supply chain. Our paper focuses on the implications for suppliers and manufacturers through the lens of information asymmetry. By conducting 57 interviews, we revealed how the DPP is reducing information asymmetries and the risks and opportunities arising for suppliers and manufacturers. The DPP overrules previous barriers of data sharing through regulatory enforcement. We follow three information asymmetry constructs, private information, hidden information and the information impactedness, to reveal the underlying processes. Reduced information asymmetries pose risks, for example, by unveiling competitive advantages. But for suppliers and manufacturers, the DPP also creates opportunities through extended, digitalized and standardized product data, laying the groundwork for improved processes and decision support.

papers.title: Advancing Sustainability in AI Strategy: A Design Principles Perspective
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes central to business transformation, sustainability gains importance for future ready AI strategy design. Our study examines how sustainability is integrated in the organisational design of AI strategies. Following a design science research approach, we develop a prescriptive strategy design framework based on the people–process–technology framework and the strategic alignment model. Our study builds on a structured literature review of 87 publications and 27 expert interviews. We derive 19 meta requirements and 15 design principles across economic, environmental, and social sustainability dimensions. The results identify leadership and culture, AI process governance, and green AI technology as central for integrating sustainability into organisational AI strategies. The proposed framework provides reusable design knowledge, supporting organisations in aligning AI strategies with sustainability goals. Our study contributes to research and practice by offering actionable guidance for sustainability-oriented AI strategy design and development.

papers.title: Disclosing Information System Affordances for Digital Resilience: A Large Sustainability Reporting Analysis
papers.abstract: Digital resilience is increasingly important for firms in a geopolitically tense environment and accelerating climate change. Prior research has primarily examined either specific information systems or individual major shocks, offering limited insight into how firms use information systems to build digital resilience across disruptive contexts. We address this gap by analyzing how firms disclose information systems use in response to major shocks in sustainability reports. Methodologically, we combine LLM-assisted retrieval and qualitative document analysis across 613 reports and 7,501 verbatim quotes, complemented by an in-depth Gioia analysis of 74 full reports. Drawing on affordance theory, we shift attention away from the difficult measurement of resilience toward IS-enabled interaction possibilities that firms report. We identify six affordances and show that firms place emphasis on affordances that support operational business activities, with a focus on mitigation and reactive measures. Our results clarify how information systems support mitigation and adaptation to major shocks.

papers.title: Help Yourself: Chatbot-Based First Aid Support for Citizens in Flood Situations
papers.abstract: Flood disasters increasingly expose citizens to situations in which professional help may be delayed and immediate first-aid action is required. Existing crisis apps primarily provide one-way warnings and general information, offering limited interactive support for laypersons. Following a Design Science Research approach, this study investigates how AI-based chatbots should be designed to assist citizens in performing first-aid measures during flood disasters. Based on a literature review and expert interviews, we identify twelve issues, formulate ten meta-requirements, and derive five initial design principles. These principles are instantiated in a retrieval-augmented generation chatbot prototype and evaluated in scenario-based tests with twelve participants. The findings provide exploratory support for the relevance of multimodal interaction, stepwise guidance, transparent source grounding, adaptive dialogue, and escalation mechanisms. Four additional principles extend the design knowledge toward continuous support, audiovisual scaffolding, accessibility, and coordinated escalation. The study contributes design knowledge for trustworthy AI-based self-aid systems in crisis contexts.

papers.title: How Congestion Pricing Reshapes Platform-Mediated Urban Mobility: Evidence from New York City
papers.abstract: Digitally enabled mobility platforms have become central to urban transportation systems and, as a result, are subject to increasing regulatory scrutiny. However, little is known about how regulatory interventions reshape demand across these interconnected modes. We study the introduction of congestion pricing in New York City, which imposes a surcharge on trips in Manhattan’s central business district. Leveraging machine-learning-based counterfactual prediction, we estimate system-wide treatment effects in the absence of a natural control group. Our preliminary results suggest substantial demand reallocation: subway, bike-sharing, and yellow cab usage increase, while aggregate ride-hailing declines. We uncover platform-level heterogeneity, with Uber losing ridership and Lyft gaining. A plausible explanation is differences in cost pass-through strategies the providers adopted in response to the policy intervention. Our findings highlight how regulation may induce asymmetric competitive responses and redistribute demand across mobility ecosystems, with implications for platform strategy and urban policy design.

papers.title: From Digital Sustainability to Sustainability Transitions: A Multi-Level Framework for Information Systems Research
papers.abstract: Information systems (IS) research increasingly addresses sustainability, yet digital sustainability initiatives are often studied as organizational or technology-centered interventions. This focus risks obscuring how digital technologies are entangled with broader sustainability transitions involving everyday practices, organizational capabilities, incumbent regimes, societal pressures, planetary constraints, and cultural narratives. To address this gap, this paper develops an Extended Multi-Level Perspective (E-MLP) for IS research on sustainability transitions. Drawing on sustainability transitions research, the Multi-Level Perspective, and the X-curve framework, the E-MLP offers a heuristic for analyzing digital technologies, organizations, and infrastructures across six interdependent levels: mini, micro, meso, macro, mundo, and meta. We illustrate the framework through ÖrebroBostäder’s AI-supported heating management system in Sweden. The paper shifts IS research from asking whether digital technologies improve sustainability outcomes in isolated settings toward examining how they support, stabilize, or redirect transition pathways, providing a vocabulary for studying digitalization’s role in systemic sustainability transformations.

papers.title: Navigating Renewable Energy Tensions Through Agentic Human–AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Household decisions about renewable energy technologies involve persistent competing demands, including short-term versus long-term outcomes and individual versus collective interests. These tensions can be reinforced by psychological distance, which makes future and collective consequences less salient than immediate and individual considerations. This research-in-progress paper examines how agentic AI can support households in navigating such tensions rather than resolving them through simple optimization. Drawing on paradox theory, psychological distance, agentic AI, sensemaking, and human–AI collaboration, we derive five initial meta-requirements: surfacing competing demands, counteracting asymmetric salience, providing context-sensitive agentic support over time, supporting ongoing sensemaking, and calibrating human and AI agency. We outline a mixed-method, interpretive design science approach to empirically examine and refine these meta-requirements through qualitative inquiry, artifact development, and scenario-based evaluation. The study conceptualizes agentic AI as support for ongoing paradox navigation in complex sustainability decisions.

papers.title: Sensemaking under Twin Transition Hype
papers.abstract: The twin transition — the convergence of digital transformation and sustainability — is widely promoted as a coherent strategic pathway, yet small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) exposed to the same institutional pressures respond in markedly different ways. Drawing on sensemaking theory, this study argues that these differences stem not from resource constraints alone but from how firms interpret an ambiguous, hype-driven transformation agenda. Using a Gioia-based qualitative methodology applied to interviews and observations from a large-scale regional initiative supporting 184 SMEs, we identify four recurring sensemaking patterns — breakdown, reduction, exploration, and integration — through which firms construct meaning around digital and sustainability pressures. We further show that hype's influence is filtered through each firm's interpretive capacity, and we advance five propositions linking hype, capability, and learning to these patterns. The study contributes a processual, firm-centric account of SME engagement with the twin transition.

papers.title: Putting Digital Sustainability into Practice through Business Processes
papers.abstract: Organizations are required to produce verifiable sustainability reports under European Union legislation like the CSRD and ESPR. They respond with digital sustainability initiatives, which use digital technologies to pursue sustainability objectives, yet these initiatives consistently fail to deliver efficiency gains combined with positive ecological outcomes. Viewing business processes as the boundary object where digital and sustainability transformation converge, we ask how organizations operationalize digital sustainability and what explains success or failure. Drawing from a literature review with 25 articles and eleven expert interviews, we propose a three-layer framework encompassing a diagnostic, an instrumental and an impact layer. We find that operationalization follows a sequencing logic in which sustainability objectives, process-level data foundation, and accountability precede technology deployment, and that practitioners apply evaluation criteria diverging from prior research. We thus complement value-creation perspectives on digital sustainability with prescriptive knowledge on operationalization, offering practitioners a sequential approach for managing such initiatives.

papers.title: Defining Green ITSM: A Taxonomy for Sustainable IT Service Management
papers.abstract: Despite IT Service Management’s (ITSM) role in digital transformation, its systematic integration of sustainability remains underexplored with no classification of this construct. To address the identified construct-specification and classification gap at the intersection of Green Information Systems and ITSM, this paper develops a taxonomy-based definition of Green ITSM. An iterative process combines two systematic literature reviews, additional literature, practitioner interviews, practice-oriented guidance, and academic expert evaluation. The resulting morphological taxonomy comprises 16 dimensions and associated characteristics. Green ITSM is defined as the configuration of ITSM beliefs, practices and learning mechanisms – embedded in a management context – that aligns the design, delivery, evaluation, and improvement of IT services and their ecosystems for economic, ecological, and social sustainability outcomes. Evaluation indicates high relevance, novelty, and clarity, while highlighting operationalization and practical validation needs. Overall, the taxonomy provides a conceptualization of Green ITSM and a reproducible classification scheme to assess, compare, and improve sustainability-oriented IT services.

papers.title: Signals That Don't Add Up: How Markets Reconcile CEO Digital Orientation and Firm Innovation in the Twin Transformation
papers.abstract: How do markets value firms pursuing the twin transformation? Building on signaling theory and recent work on signal-set incongruence, we theorize that equity-market receivers assemble twin transformation signals across organizationally distinct internal senders within the same firm, reading their configurational coherence as evidence of strategic integration or misalignment. Examining CEO digital orientation rhetoric (a low-cost signal) and firm patent output (a costly signal) within CEO tenures across 6,530 CEO-firm-tenure-year observations from 913 S&P 1500 firms (2001–2024), we find that co-intensification of digital orientation and green patenting is associated with a valuation penalty as the two point toward different technological domains. The penalty attenuates as the firm's portfolio combines green and integrated innovation. We contribute a cross-scale signal-set perspective, an asymmetric-cost coherence mechanism through which a costly third signal may restore contested credibility, and the first within-firm market-based evidence that twin transformation integration is materially priced.

papers.title: How Digital Information Systems Enable Sustainable Procurement: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Digital technologies, including artificial intelligence, machine learning, blockchain, and e-procurement systems, are transforming procurement practices. Firms increasingly prioritize economic efficiency while also adhering to environmental requirements and social responsibility to ensure long-term value creation. Despite this, the literature remains fragmented across the domains of purchasing, sustainability, and information systems. This systematic literature review, conducted using the PRISMA method, synthesizes evidence that digital technologies facilitate sustainable procurement across the Triple Bottom Line. Four primary enabling mechanisms are identified: process integration and efficiency, visibility and traceability, supplier assessment and governance, and lifecycle intelligence. Economic and environmental outcomes are more thoroughly addressed than social outcomes, revealing a structural gap in the literature. The review adopts a mechanism-based approach and develops a conceptual research model grounded in socio-technical systems theory and information technology (IT) business value logic, providing guidance for practitioners to align digital investments with procurement sustainability objectives.

papers.title: Tracknography: Developing a Method Artifact for Studying Environmental Sustainability in Supply Chains
papers.abstract: Environmental sustainability research often depends on empirical access that is mediated by the very organizations whose practices are being studied. Interviews, surveys, disclosures, audits, and trace data provide valuable evidence, but they can also be selective, retrospective, aggregated, or strategically curated. This paper addresses this problem by developing tracknography, a method artifact for using digital tracking technologies to generate external empirical access to materially enacted, environmental sustainability-related supply chain processes. Drawing on design science research, the problem is established, design objectives and principles are derived, and tracknography is presented as an eight-step process for generating, contextualizing, and interpreting object-centered digital traces. The artifact is evaluated through three empirical instantiations. This study contributes to the IS literature by providing methodological guidance for studying opaque material flows, extending digital trace data research toward researcher-configured trace generation, and strengthening Green IS scholarship on environmental accountability in interorganizational supply chain contexts.

papers.title: One Ring to Rule Them All: An Allegory of Artificial Intelligence, Corruptive Drift, and the Limits of Organizational Governance
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence’s most consequential organizational effects may be its slowest: the cumulative transformation of professional judgment, evaluative criteria, and governance capacity that sustained engagement can produce. This paper reads the One Ring of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, which amplifies capability while reconfiguring its bearer, as an analytical lens on these dynamics. My core contribution is corruptive drift, the gradual reshaping of professional judgment through sustained AI engagement, from which I derive strategic restraint as an organizational capability. I develop five propositions and a temporal process model (power amplification, uneven usability, illusion of control, corruptive drift, and dependency and lock-in). The implication for governance is that frameworks designed to catch discrete violations cannot detect a transformation that moves the standard itself, so audits return clean results while auditor and audited drift together. The paper contributes to responsible AI scholarship a middle-range theory of moral consequence and temporal unfolding.

papers.title: Ethical Uncertainty in Human-AI Collaborative Decision-Making: A Study of AI-Assisted Radiology
papers.abstract: Decision-making in professional work is often ethically charged, and underlying ethical principles are rarely unambiguous. This ambiguity extends to human-AI collaboration, yet the literature says little about how professionals navigate different ethical principles (e.g., tacit and formal) when working with AI. We address this gap through an empirical study of AI-assisted clinical decision-making, examining how healthcare professionals perceive and exercise professional discretion under ethical uncertainty. We find that professionals are reluctant to override an AI recommendation under ethical uncertainty, and situational pressures increase the contextual appeal of adherence to the AI recommendations. Our analysis further identifies two distinct forms of AI adherence: precautionary adherence, by which professionals suppress their uncertainty in fully accepting an AI recommendation, and signalling adherence, by which professionals adhere to AI recommendations while signalling their reservations in communicating the decisions. These two types of adherence produce varied effects on downstream decision-making tasks.

papers.title: When Clicking Accept Is Not Enough: Adolescents' Experience of Consent Opacity on Social Media
papers.abstract: Adolescents (aged 13–17) are vulnerable to risks on social media. The problem begins at sign-up, where users agree to terms of conditions that are legally valid but ethically weak. We aim to develop a theory of the problem and a theory of the solution using a sequential mixed-methods design. We conduct semi-structured interviews with adolescent–parent dyads to examine how consent is interpreted. Our preliminary findings identify consent opacity as a mechanism through which ethical consent fails, driven by adolescents’ bounded rationality and resulting in mechanical acceptance of complex terms. We then identify authentic consent design as a solution through cognitive load reduction and assessment mechanisms that support comprehension before agreement. In the next phase, we will continue data collection and design an experiment to test our ethical consent design. This study contributes to IS research by explaining why consent fails and offering a design-based path toward ethical consent.

papers.title: When AI Enables Misconduct and Detection: Research Integrity in Scholarly Publishing
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is transforming research integrity in scholarly publishing by making misconduct easier to produce, harder to detect, and increasingly difficult to govern. We conducted a scoping thematic review of 68 peer-reviewed studies published from 2016 to 2026, analysed through inductive thematic analysis. Our review shows that, while prior studies document specific phenomena such as AI-generated text, hallucinated citations, paper mills, statistical anomalies, and post-publication scrutiny, the literature remains fragmented and largely descriptive. We identify five themes and fifteen sub-themes capturing the social, technical, and institutional dimensions of AI-mediated research integrity. The paper makes three contributions: it conceptualises AI-mediated research integrity as a sociotechnical governance problem; develops a constitutive mechanism-based model showing how interacting components produce and reproduce system-level integrity vulnerability; and identifies three persistent tensions: escalation between AI-enabled misconduct and AI-enabled detection, threshold ambiguity around acceptable AI use, and governance lag between technological change and institutional response.

papers.title: Decolonizing Digital Dialogues: A Critical Theory Analysis of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models have rapidly diffused into work and decision-making, yet their default operation reproduces dominant epistemologies and reshapes how users articulate problems, evaluate evidence, and reach conclusions. Existing critiques concentrate on model bias and training data, leaving the broader sociotechnical conditions of use underexamined. This paper offers a critical theory analysis of large language models conceptualized as a sociotechnical ecosystem of training data, learning algorithms, provider governance, prompts, and outputs. Four oppressive features emerge: collapsing epistemological differences, economizing deliberation, foreclosing communication moderation, and discounting substance. Together, they constrain user freedoms across the ecosystem regardless of provider intent or user awareness. Because four of the five ecosystem elements remain closed to ordinary users, the prompt is the principal site at which user agency can be exercised and the natural locus for future emancipatory design research.

papers.title: Responsible Innovation Behavior in the Generative AI Era
papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in organizational innovation has raised ethical concerns, particularly regarding employees’ innovation-related behaviors. However, limited research has examined how GAI’s intrinsic characteristics affect employees’ responsible innovation behavior (RIB). To address this gap, this study investigates the influence of key GAI characteristics on RIB. Using a mixed-method design, we first conduct a qualitative study to identify five ethically concerning characteristics of GAI, including hallucination, homogeneity, deficiency, unexplainability, and bias. Building on Social Cognitive Theory, we develop a theoretical model and test it using structural equation modeling. Results show that these characteristics indirectly undermine RIB by reducing GAI-driven moral efficacy and increasing GAI-driven moral disengagement. In addition, formal and informal punishment moderate the relationships between moral cognition and RIB. This study advances understanding of the ethical implications of GAI-enabled innovation and offers practical implications for responsible use of generative technologies.

papers.title: A Multi-faceted Evaluation of LLM Explanations for AI Credit Scoring Models
papers.abstract: This paper examines the growing use of AI-driven decision systems in high-stakes domains such as credit scoring, where concerns about transparency, fairness, and accountability are critical. It highlights the emerging challenge of evaluating explanations generated through multi-step pipelines involving both machine learning models and large language models (LLMs), which add an additional layer of opacity. To address the lack of consensus in explanation evaluation, the study proposes a comprehensive framework comprising five dimensions and 20 metrics derived from prior literature. These are implemented as an open-source benchmarking pipeline that integrates model prediction, XAI methods, and LLM-based explanation generation. Initial experiments on four LLMs reveal variations in explanation quality and trade-offs across key dimensions such as fidelity and clarity. The findings underscore the need for systematic, multi-dimensional evaluation approaches to support responsible deployment of AI explainability systems in regulated contexts.

papers.title: Unwilful Regulatory Work: Defining Appropriate Generative AI Use in Higher Education
papers.abstract: The rapid uptake of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in organizations raises questions on how to regulate emerging technologies whose risks and uses remain in flux. In the absence of comprehensive external regulation, organizations are compelled to engage in regulatory work despite limited control, expertise, and regulatory templates to rely on. Prior research on regulation and information technology focuses largely on compliance with exogenous rules or deliberate self-regulation, leaving undertheorized how regulation unfolds while both a technology and its appropriate uses are still in the making. Drawing on a field study at a leading European business school, we examine what we conceptualize as unwilful regulatory work: a necessity-driven process of defining appropriate technology use without clear mandates or stable reference points. Initially reactive, this work becomes increasingly distributed and purposive as organizational members confront and learn from recurrent tensions between agnostic rules and the situated realities in which they are enacted.

papers.title: Does Transparency Always Benefit? The Effect of Explicit Disclosure of Incentivized Reviews on Review Usefulness
papers.abstract: Policymakers such as the U.S. Federal Trade Commission mandate explicit disclosure of incentivized reviews. This paper examines the consequences of such mandatory disclosure. Given that the ultimate purpose of incentivized reviews is to assist consumer decision making, this study focuses on how disclosure affects perceived review usefulness. The results show that explicit disclosure indirectly enhances perceived usefulness by improving review quality. However, disclosure labels also directly reduce perceived usefulness by triggering fairness concerns and discouraging consumers from reading these reviews. Importantly, the negative direct effect outweighs the positive indirect effect, resulting in an overall decline in perceived usefulness. To mitigate this adverse effect, this paper further proposes and empirically tests the role of platform-based quality certification in alleviating the negative impact of disclosure on perceived usefulness.

papers.title: Cultural Bias in Generative AI Negotiation Advice: Evidence from a Large-Scale Audit
papers.abstract: The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for financial advice has become increasingly prevalent. While GenAI can provide accessible guidance for high-stakes decisions, including salary negotiations, such advice may also reproduce unequal recommendations through seemingly irrelevant prompt details, such as names, phrasing, or community references, that implicitly signal cultural orientation. Using a large-scale factorial audit, we generate 14,400 responses via OpenAI API calls to controlled salary-negotiation prompts that vary cultural orientation, cultural cue type, location anchoring, model version, and negotiation stakes. We find that collectivistic cues lead to lower recommended salary opening offers than individualistic cues. This disparity is strongest for name-based cues, attenuated but not eliminated by location anchoring, and persistent in newer GenAI models. A low-stakes bicycle-purchase replication shows weaker effects. Our findings reveal a responsibility and contestability gap: equivalent users can receive unequal economic advice through subtle cues that remain difficult to observe or challenge.

papers.title: From Surprise to Astonishment: An Alternative Perspective for Futures-Oriented IS Research
papers.abstract: The field of Information Systems (IS) has become increasingly concerned with the responsibility it shares in digital futures. With technologies poised to drastically change society, whether the resulting world will be a better one remains uncertain. Futures-oriented IS addresses this challenge by directly researching digital futures to generate theories which inform responsible behavior in the present. However, such research risks framing responsibility as an uncertainty problem. Drawing on Tim Ingold and Alexis Shotwell, this paper problematizes this assumption as one based on a surprised attention from which the purpose of research is the reduction of uncertainty. As an alternative, I propose an astonished attention: An attention continuously open to the world-in-becoming. Perceiving the future as the immanent possibility of the present, uncertainty is instead framed as a condition of existence. Acknowledging our implication in it, we can become complicit with others to realize possible, more responsible, worlds.

papers.title: The Decontextualisation of Data in AI Policy
papers.abstract: Shared AI infrastructures, such as AI factories, are emerging around a policy vision of data as portable across public authorities and available for future computational use. This paper examines how data are constructed and framed in AI policy documents, and how these constructions shape the visibility of data practices and the assignment of responsibility. Building on classification and infrastructure studies, we show how policy constructs data as reusable and infrastructural, foregrounding their capacity to travel while backgrounding the situated practices through which classifications acquire meaning. We argue that this separation has consequences for responsibility: as classifications are prepared to travel across infrastructures and into only partly specified futures, responsibility becomes both distributed across infrastructures and deferred across time. In public authorities, this is politically consequential because classifications made today may later shape the exercise of public power.

papers.title: Analyzing the Relationship Between News Sentiment and AI-Based Risk: Evidence from the Russia–Ukraine War
papers.abstract: This study examines whether sentiment framing in conflict-related news is associated with text-based risk assessment. Using 878,117 Russia–Ukraine war news articles from the GDELT 2.0 Global Knowledge Graph, we construct a rule-based event-severity proxy (AI_Risk) and examine its relationship with news sentiment (TONE) through correlation, regression, propensity score matching, event fixed effects, within-event analysis, and mixed-effects models. The results consistently show that more negative sentiment is associated with higher assessed risk, including within comparable events. To examine whether this relationship extends beyond the rule-based measure, we conduct a multi-LLM validation using Qwen, Mistral, and Llama on a stratified sample of 8,000 observations. The negative TONE–risk association is consistently observed across all three models. These findings show that linguistic framing is systematically associated with text-based risk assessment and highlight the importance of considering sentiment-related variation when AI-supported systems use news data for risk evaluation.

papers.title: Three Properties, Three Signals: Testing Consumer-Facing Governance in Real-Time Generative AI Video Advertising
papers.abstract: Generative AI can now produce a video advertisement in the moment it is viewed, for a single viewer, with no human having reviewed the output. This configuration removes the institutional signals (pre-exposure review, shared exposure, documented provenance) that consumer-response theories implicitly assume. We identify three properties that co-occur in real-time generative advertising (audit opacity, psychological proximity of data use, and provenance ambiguity), show how each pulls one theory (the Persuasion Knowledge Model, IUIPC, and the trust literature) into a regime where its standard predictions require adjustment, and map each onto one consumer-facing governance signal: transparency disclosure, consent signaling, and human oversight indication. We pre-register a 2×2×2 between-subjects factorial design to test individual signal effects, a signal-coherence prediction for the full bundle against an explicit cognitive-load alternative, and two moderation hypotheses. Because consumers cannot observe a generative backend, the design manipulates governance signals against a held-constant perception of real-time generation; we state that scope explicitly and argue for it.

papers.title: From Digital Accountability to Accountable Digitality Through Needs-Aware Information Systems: The Case of Auditable Child-Welfare Judgments
papers.abstract: Digital accountability research asks how digital systems can, among other aims, be made transparent, explainable, auditable, contestable, and supportive of learning and improvement. This paper reverses the question: how can digital transformation make established institutions more accountable? It theorizes this reversal as accountable digitality and specifies needs-aware information systems as a mediating mechanism linking rights to institutional reasoning and review. The hard and paradigmatic case is child-welfare judgment, where best-interest procedures must give effect to children’s rights, preserve confidentiality, and respect judicial independence while enabling aggregate learning about needs, reasons, exceptions, and disparities. The case is used diagnostically and illustratively to derive and examine the design logic. Conceptual design-oriented analysis decomposes and recombines digital and legal accountability under child-rights constraints, deriving a theory-to-design chain, contingent mechanisms, implications, and safeguards. It advances IS responsibility and ethics research, showing how privacy-preserving, co-created, needs-aware information systems can support institutional self-knowledge and auditable justice.

papers.title: Suspect Futures: Surveillant Assemblages and Approximate Policing
papers.abstract: Contemporary policing is being reordered through digital and AI technologies that expand capacities to collect, connect, analyse, and act upon data. This paper examines how these capabilities form a surveillant assemblage, reordering suspicion, intervention, and democratic accountability through probabilistic approximation. Drawing on 20 interviews, the study examines three Swedish policing mandates: Secret Data Reading, Forensic DNA Genealogy, and Real-Time Facial Recognition. The findings show how suspicion emerges through partial information, relational proximity, resemblance, and connections across data environments. Their cumulative operation widens the conditions under which individuals become visible, suspicious, and subject to intervention. The paper contributes a critical perspective to IS scholarship by showing how approximation emerges across digital and AI capabilities, data flows, legal mandates, and institutional practices, making state power increasingly difficult to locate, reconstruct, and contest. Keywords: policing; surveillance; approximation; surveillant assemblage; democratic accountability

papers.title: Developing a Theory of the Problem of Acoustic Surveillance
papers.abstract: When public institutions deploy algorithmic surveillance against the communities they govern, stakeholders fundamentally disagree about what problem the technology constitutes. This short paper develops a theory of the problem of state-deployed algorithmic surveillance, drawing on Majchrzak et al.’s (2016) theory of the problem and Beck’s (2009) digital risk society, and treating acoustic surveillance—ShotSpotter, deployed in over 150 U.S. cities—and Reddit as revelatory empirical contexts. Gioia-methodology analysis of 8,417 Reddit comments across 71 communities and 152 threads identifies four constitutive and internally contested dimensions: the Efficacy Paradox, Racialised Spatial Logic, Epistemic Control, and Democratic Consent Deficit. The paper advances a preliminary triadic vendor–institution–community model of epistemic asymmetry that extends the dyadic accounts dominant in the IS algorithmic governance literature. The work establishes the problem space as the foundation for subsequent causal loop modelling and for interview-based fieldwork in Cape Town that addresses the limits of platform-mediated discourse.

papers.title: Clean Slates and Lasting Scars: Assessing Reintegration and Policy Design under Colorado's Clean Slate Act
papers.abstract: Automatic record-sealing laws — exemplified by Colorado's Clean Slate Act (SB 22-099), which began phased rollout in July 2024 — represent a new generation of state-mandated information removal aimed at reducing the labor-market ``scarring'' effects of past convictions. Yet whether such policies achieve their intended reintegration outcomes is theoretically ambiguous in a digital ecosystem where conviction information persists in private background-check databases, data broker repositories, and third-party screening systems that operate independently of state record infrastructures. We propose to evaluate Colorado's Clean Slate Act by leveraging cross-system administrative data linked through the Linked Information Network of Colorado (LINC), which integrates judicial, unemployment insurance, postsecondary education, and homelessness management records under a privacy-preserving identifier. Using a matched difference-in-differences design with an event study on staggered treatment timing, together with a group-time estimator as an extension, we estimate the average and heterogeneous effects of automatic versus petition-based sealing on quarterly wages, postsecondary engagement, housing stability, and recidivism. We pay particular attention to heterogeneity along three dimensions: sealing pathway (automatic vs. petition), industry exposure to formal background screening, and demographic subgroups. By situating record sealing within the broader literatures on digital …

papers.title: Data Extractivism and the Role of Licensing – A Critical Realist Case Study in East African Data Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Data extractivism refers to the appropriation of data from underrepresented communities typically by large technology firms from the Global North without fair acknowledgment, compensation, or collaboration. Thereby it exploits open data ecosystems at the expense of local communities and reinforces existing asymmetries in ownership, control, and value capture. To understand how data extractivism emerges in the African data ecosystem and how tiered licenses affect it, we conduct a qualitative case study drawing on 20 interviews and document analysis. We apply critical realism as a theoretical lens to identify events, stakeholders, structures, and retrodict the underlying mechanisms at play. Our findings present an analysis of the mechanisms promoting data extractivism and the effects of tiered licenses on them. Our paper contributes to academic research by enriching the discussion on open data ecosystems, explaining the emergence of data extractivism, and applying critical realism in the analysis of ecosystem interventions.

papers.title: The Morphogenetic Process of Post-Intervention Survival and Long-Term Sustainability in Digital Development
papers.abstract: The survival and sustainability of digital development initiatives largely depend on the post-funding and technology handover phase—a period marked by intricate, non-deterministic, and uncertain realities. This study ventures into this underexplored area by investigating how the socio-technical structures of multiple rural villages undergo transformation following digital development projects. We conducted a two-stage longitudinal multiple-case study of Indonesian digital village initiatives, tracking these projects over three years to capture divergent outcomes ranging from total collapse to persistent survival and independent expansion. Using Margaret Archer’s morphogenetic analysis, we delineate the temporally sequenced interplay between inherited structural conditions, reflexive actors, and the activation of generative mechanisms. We propose a process theory mapping four distinct paths of transformation— total morphogenesis, strategic adaptation, operational adaptation, and total morphostasis—demonstrating that long-term digital sustainability relies on the continuous, reflexive reconfiguration of structural, cultural, and material components.

papers.title: Psychic Algorithms: Digitalization of the Rituals of Coffee Divination
papers.abstract: This study explores the digitalization of coffee divination, also known as tasseography, an intangible cultural heritage recognized by UNESCO. As cultural practices become digitally mediated, questions arise regarding their authenticity, symbolism, and social value. Therefore, drawing on the experiential computing perspective, this study examines users’ experiences with AI-based mobile coffee divination apps compared with in-person coffee divination, focusing on perceived differences, effects, benefits, and concerns. To this end, we analyzed two data sources: trace data from public discussion forums and interviews with 30 participants. Preliminary findings indicate that digital coffee divination transforms the practice along four dimensions—space, time, actors, and artifacts—while providing many of the same benefits as in-person coffee divination. However, users emphasize the importance of physical privacy and physical materiality for continued engagement with these apps. These initial findings extend experiential computing by introducing boundary conditions for digital transformation at the service layer.

papers.title: Digital Platforms and Housing Market Transparency for Young Tenants
papers.abstract: Young tenants face housing burdens as they enter rental markets with limited experience, little savings and weak bargaining power. This vulnerability stems from information frictions, where landlords and agents often possess better knowledge of local prices, unit quality, and contract terms. This study examines whether digital intermediary platforms can improve market transparency by reducing such information frictions. We exploit the nationwide expansion of Zigbang, South Korea’s first mobile rental intermediary platform, as an information shock and analyze administrative actual rental transaction data from 2011 to 2014. Using a difference-in-differences design, we compare non-apartment small units, the segment most exposed to Zigbang’s aggregation function, with small apartment units. Preliminary results show that platform entry reduced rental price level by 4.3%. The findings extend IS research on platform-driven information effects to rental housing and highlight digital platforms’ societal implications for transparency and housing access.

papers.title: Actors or Actions? Rethinking Platform Governance in Pre-Platform Crisis Settings
papers.abstract: Crises expose the limits of governance characterized by predefined roles and stable structures. This study examines how governance emerges in the pre-platform stage under conditions of urgency, unpredictability, and fragmented authority. Using four dimensions of platform governance, i.e. roles, decision rights, control, and ownership, we analyze three crisis actions during the Ukrainian refugee crisis in Switzerland: communication via online refugee communities, identification of refugees, and civic-led host-refugee matching. Findings show that governance emerges through action rather than formal authority: roles become overlapping, decision rights shift to those who can act, control relies on local norms, and ownership becomes collective and negotiated. We conceptualize this as governance-by-action, that explains how coordination arises before a coherent platform is established, extending platform governance theory to pre-platform contexts.

papers.title: Mobile Information Technology for Survival: The Case of Irregular Migration in the Mediterranean Sea
papers.abstract: International migration is increasingly shaped by geopolitical instability and environmental pressures, leading to growing flows of irregular migrants. While Information Systems (IS) research has largely focused on the role of digital technologies in supporting refugees’ social inclusion after arrival, limited attention has been paid to their use during earlier stages of migration. This short paper addresses this gap by examining how irregular migrants mobilize ICTs for survival and social inclusion. Drawing on qualitative data, the paper explores migrants’ experiences along Mediterranean routes, with a particular focus on departures from the Tunisian coast. The findings highlight that ICTs enable access to information, facilitate coordination, and sustain transnational ties, yet are used under conditions of uncertainty, infrastructural fragility, and legal precarity. By shifting attention beyond post-arrival integration, this study contributes to IS research by conceptualizing irregular migration as a sociotechnical process shaped by uneven access to digital resources and capabilities.

papers.title: Unmasking E-Government Trajectories: Heterogeneity in Corruption Control
papers.abstract: Electronic government or E-government (EGOV) has become embedded in the institutional infrastructure through which public services are delivered, yet its consequences are neither uniform nor inevitable. EGOV, as a key manifestation of the redesign of government processes, can reshape how public administration is organized and delivered. This study examines how EGOV becomes instrumental for Corruption Control (CC) through its interaction with administrative institutions, and how these effects differ across EGOV developmental trajectories and forms of corruption. Drawing on Technology Enactment and Path Dependency perspectives, we demonstrate that Government Effectiveness (GE) is a critical channel through which EGOV impacts are transmitted. Across 122 countries over 2012–2024, this pathway varies substantially: EGOV is most effectively translated into CC where technological and administrative capacities are aligned, while other settings exhibit limited, direct, or adverse effects. We further show that EGOV has greater short-run reach over routine public-sector corruption than deeper systemic corruption.

papers.title: Am I My True Self? Identity Formation in Online Spaces: Investigating Transgender Identity
papers.abstract: Identity has long remained an important area of study within the field of information systems. Information systems research has shown how platforms can both enable and constrain the formation of one’s sense of self. Yet while these contributions exist, research relating to transgender identity has been overlooked. Transgender people exist in a tangential category to cisgendered people regarding how they experience disenfranchisement from the gender they are assigned at birth. This leads many transgender people to re-visit their identity after adolescence and begin to perform, rehearse, and re-build who they are. In this paper, through a systematic literature review we explore identity, identity formation, and transgender identity both within information systems literature and in other disciplines. We present emergent themes and apply these to transgender identity formation in socio-technical environments. We discuss the applicability of transgender identity to existing information systems theories and provide direction for future research.

papers.title: Managing Tensions Between Speed and Safety: Digital Responsibility in Hybrid AGI Organizations
papers.abstract: The safe and responsible development of artificial general intelligence (AGI) is among the most consequential challenges facing organizations and society today. Yet how AGI-pursuing organizations construct and articulate digital responsibility remains not well understood. Drawing on hybrid organization theory, we examine, through a case study of OpenAI and Anthropic, how these organizations manage field-level tensions between development speed and model safety. Organizations respond by deploying a portfolio of five practice types, of which four constitute an organizational responsibility architecture, while the subthemes of ‘market positioning’ appear to serve as legitimacy signal or acceleration-supporting mechanism. The responsibility architecture has a seemingly strong impact on AI safety, weak impact on broader sustainability implications, and is largely internally controlled. These findings reveal structural limits of voluntary self-governance, highlight the need for governance frameworks that extend beyond organizational discretion, and illustrate how engineering overlaps between the commercial and welfare logic can steer responsible behavior.

papers.title: Theorising Constitutional Corruption: A Typology and Research Agenda for IS Scholarship on Anti-Corruption Technology
papers.abstract: Information systems scholarship has produced sophisticated theory for how corruption persists within deployed digital systems — workarounds, co-optation, opportunity displacement, design-reality gaps — but has thin apparatus for the corruption that shapes systems before deployment: procurement scope, configuration choices, evaluation criteria, and replacement timing. We distinguish operational corruption, enacted by users at the point of system use, from constitutional corruption, enacted by procurement officers, vendors, officials, and donors across a system's lifecycle. Drawing on Ghana customs' three-decade digitalisation record (ASYCUDA, TradeNet, ICUMS), we show constitutional corruption reproducing as a stable rent-generation cycle masked as sequential anti-corruption reform. We argue this blind spot is structural, not incidental — produced by access asymmetries, methodological repertoires, and theoretical inheritances that bias IS research toward what is observable at the operational layer. The paper offers a consolidating typology, arranged across multiple dimensions, and a research agenda for studying constitutional corruption, with implications for research design, evaluation methodology, and theory development.

papers.title: From Description to Intention: How Goal-Oriented Labels Drive Engagement in Online Peer Support Platforms
