papers.abstract: Online communities for mental health have become valuable in raising awareness, providing accessible support, and enabling long-term self-care. However, many users seeking assistance receive inadequate engagement, leaving vulnerable individuals without support. This study investigates how labels shape user behavior in online peer support communities, challenging conventional assumptions about effective labeling. We distinguish between goal-oriented labels, which signal posters’ intentions, and content-oriented labels, which summarize post topics. While conventional wisdom suggests that labels should accurately describe post content, we find the opposite using data from a large online peer support platform: label-content congruence reduces user engagement. Instead, goal-oriented labels outperform content-oriented labels, with emotional support labels increasing upvotes by 15.03% and informational support labels increasing comments by 15.03%. Using generative AI to classify content independently of user labels, we show that labels function as behavioral coordination mechanisms rather than content descriptors, offering actionable insights for designing effective digital mental health interventions.

papers.title: Anti-Immigrant Hate Crimes and Cross-Border Marriage Markets: Evidence from a Marriage Platform
papers.abstract: Cross-border matrimonial platforms connect prospective spouses across countries, where families must evaluate both individual attributes and conditions in the destination. Drawing on availability cascade theory, we examine how a high-profile hate crime against Indian immigrants in the US affected matrimonial search on a leading Indian platform. Using difference-in-differences and event studies around the February 2017 Kansas shooting, we compare US-based Indian profiles with Canada-based profiles. We find declines in profile views and expressions of interest received by US-based men, with larger point estimates among non-citizens and highly educated men and no clear corresponding declines for women. These patterns are consistent with heightened concerns about life in the US shaping the appeal of prospective spouses, although safety concerns and immigration-policy uncertainty may both contribute. Our findings highlight how salient offline events may influence attention and initial contact on platforms mediating cross-border matrimonial search.

papers.title: Translating Platform Voices into Policy: An Analytical Framework for X/Twitter Discourse on Ultra-Low Fertility in Korea
papers.abstract: South Korea’s ultra-low fertility is a severe policy challenge, yet contested meanings of responsibility, care, and social conditions expressed in platform discourse are not fully captured by demographic indicators or policy documents. This paper develops, through design science research, an analytical framework for translating Korean X/Twitter discourse into policy-relevant insight. The framework preserves jeo-chulsan and jeo-chulsaeng as separate lexical categories, structures discourse across lexical, thematic, and affective levels, and applies feminist and policy-translation lenses to reconstruct discourse problem definitions. These definitions are compared with policy through explicit decision rules for alignment, partial recognition, divergence, and omission, with policy blind spots assessed separately. A bounded worked example illustrates procedural application. The paper contributes a traceable, method-oriented artefact and reusable design principles for policy-facing analysis of contested platform discourse.

papers.title: Neurodiversity in Information Systems Research: A Review of the Literature and Research Agenda
papers.abstract: Neurodivergence research in IS has grown rapidly in the past few years, and the neurodiversity paradigm has been gaining traction in the most recent research. Adopting this paradigm comes with important implications, but no analysis of the literature has been conducted to examine its consequences for the IS discipline. We review neurodivergence research in IS and evaluate its alignment with recommendations for research under the neurodiversity paradigm. We observe that research has been increasingly focusing on adults at work. We also find that alignment with the neurodiversity paradigm is selective and limited, mainly concerning terminology change and research practices already well-established in IS. We formulate eight ways forward to further advance the adoption of the neurodiversity paradigm in IS. Together, they form a research agenda to not only make our discipline more inclusive, but enriched by incorporating and advancing a range of diverse perspectives into scholarly work.

papers.title: Designing for Relational Similarity: Facial Similarity and Racial Disadvantage in Digital Labor Platforms
papers.abstract: Digital labor platforms make worker faces visible, allowing a profile photograph to convey categorical information about perceived racial presentation and evaluator-specific relational information through buyer-seller facial similarity. We examine how these cues jointly shape hiring on Fiverr. Study 1 analyzes observed-hiring and comparison dyads using two-way clustered linear probability models, residualized similarity, and seller-stratified conditional logit. Facial similarity is positively associated with hiring, but it does not uniformly narrow racial disparities. Black-presenting sellers face the clearest baseline disadvantage and show no compensatory similarity effect, whereas race-specific associations emerge for Middle Eastern- and White-presenting sellers. Building on the continuum model of impression formation, we theorize that evaluator-specific relational information receives less evaluative weight when judgments remain strongly anchored in categorical information. Study 2 uses GenAI as a planned causal probe of this weighting mechanism under race-preserving facial manipulation. The findings identify a boundary on relational updating under persistent categorical visibility.

papers.title: How GenAI Adoption Affects Job Demand: Evidence from India
papers.abstract: How does Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) affect labor markets in emerging economies? We address this important question leveraging data from a leading job postings platform in India and exploiting ChatGPT’s launch in November 2022 as a quasi-natural experiment. The findings indicate that GenAI adoption reshapes labor demand through differential effects across GenAI-exposed versus non-exposed occupations. We document the effect of GenAI on jobs across IT outsourcing (ITO)/business process outsourcing (BPO) jobs versus other industries, and partial mediation through GenAI exposure. The study contributes to debates on technological displacement versus skill transformation, offering implications for policy design, and workforce reskilling strategies.

papers.title: Indigenous Resurgence through Artificial Intelligence: Reconnecting Wendat Myths and Legends with Storied Places
papers.abstract: Through practices of cultural Resurgence, Indigenous Peoples seek to create decolonized spaces and futures by strengthening their sacred relationships with the land, reaffirming their cultural traditions, and reclaiming self-determination. Artificial intelligence (AI) can support Resurgence practices but can also reinforce settler-colonial narratives if not designed with due care. An action design research project is underway in collaboration with Wendat First Nation storytellers to explore how AI solutions can be designed for Resurgence practices. This research aims co-create an AI solution to connect places central to Wendat myths and legends to natural physical landmarks. Drawing on theoretical perspectives of Indigenous Resurgence and digital sovereignty as well as co-creation conversations with Wendat storytellers, this paper presents three initial meta-requirements of AI solutions for Resurgence practices: sovereignty, relationality, and intergenerationality. These meta-requirements inform subsequent research including the design and implementation of AI artifacts and formalization of new design knowledge.

papers.title: Do Better Conditions Always Lead to More Use? Evidence from Digital Payments in Brazil
papers.abstract: Digital financial technology use is commonly expected to be greater in more favorable socioeconomic and infrastructural contexts. This study questions whether this expectation holds when digital payment systems become widely adopted. Using municipal-level data from Brazil, it examines the relationship between Pix usage and four structural conditions: income, education, digital connectivity, and physical banking presence. The results reveal contrasting patterns. Higher connectivity and education are associated with greater Pix usage, as expected, whereas municipalities with lower income and lower physical banking presence exhibit higher levels of usage. These findings challenge the assumption that favorable structural conditions systematically correspond to greater technology use and caution against interpreting intensive usage as straightforward evidence of financial inclusion. As a short paper, this study provides a basis for further examining how digital financial technology use should be interpreted and studied across different structural contexts.

papers.title: Worker Dignity in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: AI increasingly shapes not just how work is performed, but who is assigned work, how it is evaluated, and how workers are valued. This raises pressing questions about dignity at work, particularly on digital labor platforms. In this paper, we examine how AI both erodes and enables workers' dignity through an interpretive multi-case study of three platforms: Outlier AI, Upwork, and Fiverr. Our preliminary analysis identifies three dignity tensions arising from AI's reconfiguration of platform work: fragmentation of knowledge, mediation of visibility, and constrained autonomy. These tensions are especially consequential for vulnerable workers. The study contributes to research on human dignity, digital labor platforms, and responsible AI by developing a preliminary theoretical understanding that can form the basis of worker-centered design principles for dignity-preserving AI systems.

papers.title: May the Source Be with You—Paradoxes in Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: Synthetic data (SD) is increasingly adopted in domains such as finance, to overcome privacy, scale, and access constraints. Although SD enables experimentation and data sharing, it also raises fundamental questions about the relationship between data and reality. Ironically, this is particularly salient in the same domains, as decisions have far-reaching monetary and socioeconomic consequences. Drawing on 17 interviews with practitioners in banking and finance, this paper examines the drivers, affordances, and challenges of SD. We identify three paradoxes that characterize SD use: scarcity versus validity, fluidity versus anchoring, and fidelity versus drift. From these, we develop a higher-order generativity–grounding paradox, showing how the capacity to generate SD simultaneously weakens the connection to empirical referents. We contribute to the information systems literature by theorizing SD as a paradoxical instantiation of data, shifting the focus from managing the tensions in data use to understanding the tensions embedded in the data itself.

papers.title: Too Much to Process?  Visual Information Competition and Sales Conversion in Short-Video Commerce
papers.abstract: Short-video commerce rewards attention, but attention does not necessarily translate into purchase conversion. We examine how multiple visual cues compete and coordinate under limited processing capacity. Building on biased competition, cognitive load theory, and perceptual fluency, we develop the Visual Information Competition Framework (VICF) and test it using 5,197 TikTok e-commerce videos, deep-learning-based visual feature extraction, XGBoost, and SHAP. Visual features increase cross-validated R² by 16.4% and reduce MAE by 4.2%, with predictive gains largely persisting across four alternative models. SHAP-LOWESS analyses reveal direction-shift, inverted-U, and U- shaped patterns; sensitivity and holdout analyses further show that stability and predictive transfer vary across features, product types, and time. The findings reposition visual layout as a problem of information competition rather than visual richness, of ering a theory-guided and computationally interpretable basis for studying high- velocity digital interfaces.

papers.title: Collaborative Synthetic Data for Privacy-Preserving Financial Fraud Detection Across Organizational Silos
papers.abstract: Organizations seek analytical value from AI, yet relevant data are often fragmented across organizations and constrained by privacy. This is acute in financial fraud detection, where rare fraud cases and imbalanced local datasets limit decision-relevant analytics. Federated learning enables collaboration without direct data sharing but does not resolve minority-class scarcity. Synthetic data generation can help, yet lightweight methods are interpolation-bound, while generative models require substantial data and computation. Existing collaborative generative approaches often rely on federated learning, imposing considerable organization-side training burdens. In this paper, we examine CollaFuse as a collaborative diffusion-based alternative for fraud detection and evaluate it across five fraud datasets. Compared with classical oversampling, local generative baselines, and centralized diffusion benchmarks, CollaFuse does not achieve the highest local fidelity but improves downstream fraud detection more consistently across most datasets. These findings suggest that synthetic data create analytical value less through local realism than through transferable cross-organizational structure.

papers.title: Theory-Informed Dynamic Coupon Distribution via Graph-Augmented Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Dynamic coupon distribution is a data-intensive sequential decision problem in which the vast majority of coupons are either unredeemed or subsidize purchases that would have occurred without the incentive. Existing analytics pipelines under-utilize the behavioral signals available in consumer-generated text and ignore the psychological mechanisms that determine coupon response. Grounded in Promotion Reactance Theory (PRT), this study develops GRACE, an end-to-end offline reinforcement-learning framework that integrates transactional, relational, and textual data through five theory-informed modules: a reactance-modulated graph attention network, an LLM-based psychological profiler, a contrastive alignment layer, a dual-objective Q-network, and a theory-routed mixture-of-experts policy. Evaluated on 2.68 million coupon records from a major tea-beverage chain, GRACE achieves the highest point estimate on every reported metric, with statistically significant improvements in redemption and match rate against all nine baselines. The results demonstrate that behavioral theory can serve as computable design structure—shaping representation, value decomposition, and policy learning—inside AI-driven decision systems.

papers.title: From Transcripts to Insights: Data-Warehousing-Inspired Text Transformation
papers.abstract: When verbal communication data are captured for textual analysis, the harmonization  and structuring of transcript content is crucial for further processing and the accuracy  of empirical study results. This paper explores potential benefits from applying the ETL  (Extract, Transform, Load) process from Data-Warehousing, as it targets the systematic  preparation of raw data for analysis methods. The presented context of use are  automatically generated Scrum meeting transcripts that need to be prepared for  stylometric analysis. The harmonization and structuring of the transcript data are driven  by the creation of speaker-related corpora, the derivation of stylometric features and  their metadata-based documentation. Applying ETL in this way ensures analyzability of  the raw data, and the transparency, and traceability of the transformation process. The  results demonstrate that Data-Warehousing-inspired data preparation is not limited to  traditional business analysis contexts but also provides a viable methodological  framework for language-based research data.

papers.title: Authorization Work: The Case of Clinical Trial Data Repurposing
papers.abstract: While existing literature frames data repurposing as the technical alignment of data to new analytical tasks, this technical alignment alone is insufficient in scientific settings where data are often detached from their original context of collection. To address how data travels to justifiable claims, we conducted an interpretive qualitative case study of Vivli, the largest infrastructure for sharing clinical trial data. Drawing on 31 interviews and an epistemic stance lens, we find that data users engage in authorization work through which they make claims defensible before the communities that will judge them, in the absence of the collection context. We identify three mechanisms of authorization work: anchoring to authorized originals, importing community-specific interpretive resources, and warranting the inferential step to a new claim. This extends IS literature by demonstrating how making defensible claims operates alongside technical alignment, shaped by both infrastructural arrangements and the epistemic standards of the evaluating community.

papers.title: More-than-human Data Governance: The Case of Parmigiano Reggiano
papers.abstract: Data governance research has largely conceptualized data as abstract organizational assets or outcomes of sociomaterial data work practices. Based on a longitudinal qualitative case study of Parmigiano Reggiano production in Northern Italy, I investigate what happens when the biological variability of material referents shapes what counts as valid data and how data must be governed. Early results highlight that more-than-human data governance is oriented to: (i) potentiality, where breeding decisions preconfigure which future data and material phenomena can be generated; (ii) balance, where real-time calibration of microbial and process data sustains conditions for meaningful records; and (iii) judgment, where sensory assessments validate the data trail attached to each wheel. I propose understanding more-than-human data governance as a concerted effort involving material referent stewardship to decide about data through embodied collaboration between human and non-human actors embedded in biological, technological, and institutional processes.

papers.title: Jurisdictional Settlements in LLM Mediated Analytic Regimes
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to democratize organizational data work by enabling business managers to frame their analyses beyond preconfigured dashboards. However, the implications of this shift for both managers and data professionals’ authority and accountability remain under-theorized. Drawing on Abbott’s System of Professions, we examine how the rollout of a conversational LLM-mediated analytics interface in a health-technology unicorn reconfigured the jurisdiction of data work. We find that the interface redistributed rather than replaced legitimacy in the analytics chain: managers gained bounded autonomy to locate data, narrow questions, and generate provisional analyses, while data professionals’ jurisdiction shifted from routine analytic production toward ex-post certification, reviewing executive-facing and financially material outputs, and maintaining the conditions for reliable inference. We contribute to Information Systems research on data democratization with a theorization of three jurisdictional settlements between managers and data professionals around an LLM-mediated analytics regime: delegated inference, notarial legitimation, and infrastructure stewardship.

papers.title: A Taxonomy of the Invisible Work Involved in the Production of Personal Data
papers.abstract: Amid datafication, people are increasingly producing data about themselves, while organizations increasingly rely on these distributed efforts to source data for data-driven value creation. Such data production is essentially powered by sensor-based technologies incorporated into people’s everyday lives. In this paper, we apply invisible work as a theoretical lens to unpack the work individuals conduct to produce personal data. We analyzed 47 semi-structured interviews with participants who produced personal data via wearable devices and a mobile application over a 3-month period to improve their sleep health and general well-being. Through this analysis, we develop a taxonomy of five forms of invisible work involved in producing personal data: strategizing, resourcing, maintenance, interpretative, and care work. In doing so, we advance an understanding of personal data as situated and shaped through human data work, with implications for how organizations use personal data in data-driven value creation and orchestrate their production.

papers.title: Body–Data–Body Assemblages: How Embodiment and Relationality Shape Health Data Management
papers.abstract: Health data may be shared openly in one relation yet withheld or resisted in another, suggesting that what varies is not only willingness to disclose but what the data itself becomes. Drawing on 22 qualitative interviews with participants involved in health data ecosystems, we examine how data becomes meaningful as it moves through relations of illness, care, research and commercial use. We develop the concept of body-data-body assemblages to show that data is not a pre-given representation of the body: it becomes health data through relations that render embodied conditions intelligible and actionable, acquires meaning through the relations in which it circulates, and in turn participates in constituting how selves and others are understood and acted upon. We theorize this recursive process through embodied emergence, relational circulation and constitutive return. This shifts health data management from governing a stable informational object to governing an ongoing relational process.

papers.title: From Prediction to Prescription: Adaptive Video Content Optimization under Evolving Recommendation Regimes
papers.abstract: As user growth on creator platforms slows, creators face higher costs to attract audience attention, making content optimization increasingly important. A key challenge is that observed engagement reflects both intrinsic content quality and the platform’s shifting exposure-allocation logic, which changes endogenously with recommendation strategies. We conceptualize this distortion as an information systems design problem and develop an adaptive decision-support artifact for video attractiveness prediction and optimization in dynamic platform environments. The artifact integrates robustness-oriented offline learning with online reinforcement learning. The offline module uses farthest-domain centroid cross-domain matching and a domain-adversarial neural network to distinguish stable content signals from changing recommendation conditions. The online module employs a Base-Model-as-Critic dual Actor–Critic algorithm to recalibrate environmental interpretation and refine multimodal video features. Experiments on real-world platform data show that the artifact outperforms baseline methods in prediction accuracy and optimization stability, while simulations generate actionable content optimization strategies.

papers.title: How to Make Research Reach the Newsroom? Designing Open-Data Platforms Through Boundary Theory
papers.abstract: Research increasingly produces openly available datasets with high societal relevance, yet such data remain difficult to reuse beyond their original scientific context. At the same time, data journalism has become an established practice that relies on openly available data to inform public debate, but rarely draws directly on research data. This study examines how open research data platforms can support journalistic reuse. Building on boundary-spanning mechanisms as a sensitizing and interpretive lens, we analyse reuse as a cross-community challenge in which data must retain meaning across scientific and journalistic contexts. Following a design science research approach, we derive design requirements from interviews with data journalists (n=6), a co-creation workshop with data journalists (n=15), and a formative ex-ante expert evaluation (n=13). The study contributes early design knowledge by showing how syntactic and semantic platform support can enable interpretive reuse across knowledge boundaries.

papers.title: Why Do Organizations Hesitate to Participate in Data Spaces? An Empirical Study of Adoption Intentions
papers.abstract: Data spaces are gaining increasing attention as decentralized digital infrastructures for sovereign data sharing, yet organizational adoption remains limited. This study examines why organizations hesitate to participate in data spaces by investigating the drivers of adoption intention. Drawing on prior literature and Rogers’ diffusion of innovation theory, we develop and test a research model capturing seven key factors. Using survey data from 254 German-based B2B senior managers, our results show that external pressure is by far the strongest positive driver of adoption intention, followed by data sovereignty, while value opacity exhibits a significant barrier. In contrast, shared governance and cost reduction do not show significant effects. These findings suggest that data space adoption is currently driven primarily by institutional pressures rather than its intrinsic value proposition. The study contributes to the emerging literature on data spaces by providing empirical insights into early-stage adoption dynamics.

papers.title: When Data Work Runs Sideways: Sustaining Data as Assets Over Time
papers.abstract: This research-in-progress asks how data work sustains data as assets by synchronizing data journeys with the social fabric of everyday work. Drawing on flow ontology, we conceptualize synchronization as a recurrent confluence of flowing lines of action, in which the data journey, the work paths of the social fabric, and data work itself weave together. Our multiple case study spans contrasting institutional contexts, a manufacturing firm and a municipality. In both cases we observe that data work recurs in every data journey phase, runs ahead of the journey, doubles back along it, and reaches sideways into domains that routines, responsibilities, and systems hold apart. This transversal orientation extends the bidirectionality reported for data work practice. It also explains why sustaining data as assets looks messier than losing them as assets.

papers.title: When Referential Standing Becomes Unsettled: Epistemic Trouble in Data Studies
papers.abstract: Data objects increasingly organize social life because they are taken to stand for something beyond themselves. Information Systems research has examined what data stand for and how they come to be, but relied on a quieter assumption: that data remain accountable to what they are taken to stand for. We argue this assumption can no longer remain untroubled epistemic ground. Under conditions accelerated by synthetic data and generative AI, recognizing something as data no longer settles its relation to the world, how that relation was produced, or what claims it can sustain. To make this problem tractable, we examine two illustrative scenes: infection figures from pandemic reporting and carbon certificates from agri-food. We develop provenance, constitution, and consequence as analytical vocabulary for examining what data stand for and outline an agenda for staying with epistemic trouble when referential standing becomes unsettled.

papers.title: AI Ground Truth Uncertainty: The Role of Representational Inadequacy and Domain Knowledge
papers.abstract: Labeled data operationalize how real-world phenomena are represented in computational systems and underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models. Prior research largely adopts a consensus-oriented view of ground truth, overlooking divergent interpretations in domains that are inherently uncertain and contested. Drawing from representation theory, we examine ground truth uncertainty and develop a framework explaining how data label divergence arises from two forms of representational inadequacy: schema inadequacy and evidence inadequacy. We further theorize that the effects of representational inadequacy are contingent on annotators’ domain knowledge. Using a controlled experiment, we find that schema inadequacy increases divergence, whereas evidence inadequacy reduces divergence. More importantly, domain knowledge plays a contingent role: when schema and evidence are aligned (both adequate or both inadequate), domain knowledge reduces divergence; when misaligned, domain knowledge amplifies divergence. These findings show that divergence is a systematic outcome of representation and interpretation, advancing research on data work and data labeling.

papers.title: Sensors and Sentinels: Hybrid Sensing for Ontological Alignment amid Nature’s Turbulence in a Power Plant
papers.abstract: How do digital representations remain aligned with material reality when the forces of nature are inherently turbulent? Artificial intelligence and data-driven systems rely on sensor-generated data to construct real-time digital representations of physical events. Yet it is tenuous to assume that digital representations operate on stable or fully knowable phenomena. Ontological alignment is fragile when both the reality being represented and the sensing infrastructure are themselves vulnerable to nature's turbulence. Drawing on a three-year ethnographic study of a coal-fired power plant utilising AI technologies, this paper shows how two properties of nature, namely stochasticity and cascading propagation, undermine ontological alignment. The engineers enact practices to improve ontological alignment. Harnessing these findings, the paper develops a hybrid sensing framework composed of a primary Sensor regime and a field-based Sentinel regime. Their differential capabilities enhance ontological alignment under turbulent material conditions. This paper makes theoretical contributions around data, nature and ontological alignment.

papers.title: Responsibility in Data Governance has Many Faces: Theorizing Normative Reference Points
papers.abstract: Data governance research recognizes that formal governance acquires meaning through situated interpretation and enactment. Yet, little is known about the normative assumptions underlying actors' judgments when data governance is responsible. We address this gap by conceptualizing them as normative reference points (NRPs) that guide how responsibility is understood, assigned, and justified in governance practice. Drawing on an abductive analysis of qualitative interviews, we identify five NRPs and show how their relations constitute two modes of responsibility enactment: stabilizing and deliberating. The stabilizing mode renders responsibility actionable through concentration, routinization, and traceability, whereas the deliberating mode keeps responsibility open to reflection, stakeholder consideration, and case-sensitive judgment. We contribute threefold. First, we develop NRPs as a vocabulary for theorizing the plurality of responsibility in data governance. Second, we theorize the tension generated by the relation between the stabilizing and deliberating modes. Third, we show how data governance practices mediate this tension.

papers.title: Beyond Isolation: LLM-Guided Hypergraph Learning across Documents and Horizons for Volatility Prediction from Conference Calls
papers.abstract: Conference-call-based volatility prediction has mainly followed an isolated information modeling paradigm, treating each transcript as an isolated information source and each forecast horizon as an independent task. This limits comparison with economically comparable peers and the use of risk information shared across horizons. We propose an LLM-Guided Hypergraph Learning framework to address these limitations. We first use LLMs to construct a shared pool of standardized business-condition factors and then build factor-transcript hypergraphs that connect disclosures across firms through shared factors, enabling the model to retrieve comparable historical peer information. The model then explicitly compares focal and peer information and jointly predicts volatility over 5-, 10-, 20-, and 60-day horizons through multi-task learning with horizon-specific modulation. Experiments on 14,896 U.S. earnings conference calls show that the framework consistently outperforms strong transcript-based, graph-based, and financial baselines. Ablation studies confirm the importance of factor-guided peer retrieval, explicit comparison, and cross-horizon learning.

papers.title: Inferring Direct Mentor–Trainee Relationships from OpenAlex via LLM-Powered Pairwise Ranking
papers.abstract: Inferring direct mentor–trainee relationships at scale can complement curated academic genealogies and support conflict-of-interest screening. This study develops an LLM-powered learning-to-rank framework that identifies mentors from trainees’ OpenAlex coauthor networks. The framework decomposes ranking into exhaustive pairwise comparisons and aggregates preferences using the Bradley–Terry model. Rather than relying on a static prompt, it dynamically constructs each prompt from empirical feature evidence: Mann–Whitney U tests determine feature directions, SHAP values measure discriminative importance, and informative features are selected, ordered, and annotated at runtime. The resulting feature order, directional cues, and signal strengths therefore adapt to the active candidate pool instead of encoding fixed assumptions. The SHAP-pruned pairwise approach achieved Hit@1 of 0.631 and nDCG@5 of 0.786, substantially outperforming single-pass LLM ranking. The results indicate that data-driven context construction improves LLM-based inference of asymmetric academic relationships while providing interpretable evidence for ranking decisions.

papers.title: A Multi-Level Data Valuation Framework in Data Sharing Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Inter-organizational data sharing within Data Sharing Ecosystems enables organizations to co-create value through collaborative resource orchestration. With the diffusion of digital technologies making data a strategic resource, organizations are increasingly exploring innovative data sharing business models within these ecosystems. However, developing such business models remains challenging, as data valuation is highly contextual and dependent on specific use cases. Existing literature lacks evidence of a standard metric or attribute for evaluating data value within an ecosystem. Addressing this gap, this paper proposes a conceptual multi-level data valuation framework grounded in the Data Value Chain, Data Value Network, and Systems Thinking perspectives. The framework structures data valuation across three levels of the ecosystem: dataset(micro), actor (meso) and ecosystem (macro). By tracing how data value evolves from generation to use and reuse, the framework provides a structured basis for assessing value creation and value appropriation in DSEs, thereby supporting both research and practice.

papers.title: Designing an Adaptive, Speaker-Context-Aware Cross-Paradigm NLP Artifact for IT Narrative Disclosure Measurement
papers.abstract: Business communication in modern corporations is increasingly shaped by voluntary discourse channels such as earnings conference calls and merger and acquisition an- nouncement calls. A prominent element of these calls is the Information Technology (IT) narrative disclosure, where executives embed IT-related vocabulary as references to digital initiatives. However, measurement risk may arise when firms’ IT narratives diverge from actions, evading what single-paradigm dictionaries detect, a gap exacer- bated by post-Generative-AI (post-GenAI) vocabulary expansion. Adopting a design sci- ence research approach, we design NarrativeProbe, a paradigm-triangulated cascade ar- chitecture grounded in Campbell-Fiske multi-trait multi-method theory and impression- management theory. Our artifact instantiates (1) cross-paradigm triangulation with two-gate disagreement-gated escalation, routed to Large Language Models (LLM) and human review, and (2) the speaker-context-aware transcript segmentation, surfacing the asymmetry in speakers’ prepared remarks versus spontaneous question-and-answer segments. Evaluation shows that targeted human review lifts the cascade above LLM- scoring-everything and that dictionary measurement alone loses cross-era rank stability post-GenAI.

papers.title: Governing Sensitive Health Data Journeys: Toward Multi-Level Data Contracts for Portability of Data Governance
papers.abstract: Healthcare increasingly depends on sensitive health data moving across organizational, professional, and technical boundaries. Yet, while data travel across patient journeys, the governance conditions that specify legitimate use often remain embedded in local policies, systems, routines, or clarification work. This creates a mismatch between mobile data and comparatively immobile governance. This research-in-progress paper asks how a data contract architecture can be designed so that data governance conditions for sensitive health data remain portable, interpretable, and actionable across patient data journeys. Building on data governance, data contracts, and boundary resources, we propose a multi-level data contract architecture consisting of journey-level, data-level, and derived-data-level contracts connected through a data governance wrapper. We instantiate the architecture for a patient journey spanning multiple care settings, and we outline a Baustein-informed Design Science Research approach for expert-informed refinement and formative evaluation. The expected contribution is design knowledge for portable representations of data governance conditions in healthcare.

papers.title: Counterfactual Explanations for AI Model Predictions with Missing Inputs
papers.abstract: A key challenge in adopting machine learning (ML) and AI systems is the lack of transparency in “black-box” models, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance. Interpretable machine learning (IML) and explainable AI (XAI) seek to improve the interpretability of model predictions. However, most existing IML/XAI methods assume complete data and use simple imputation techniques, such as mean substitution, to handle missing values. This is problematic because missingness may arise from various causes, including lack of knowledge and intentional omission, which makes naïve imputation potentially misleading. To address this research gap, we propose a counterfactual explanation method for predictions involving incomplete inputs. Our method encourages the completion of missing values by quantifying their potential impact on model outcomes. We introduce a SHAP-based feature importance measure to evaluate the influence of missing features and guide the selection of counterfactuals. We validate our approach through experiments on real-world datasets.

papers.title: Sales Forecasting under Promotions: A Dynamic Product Network Perspective
papers.abstract: Accurate sales forecasting under promotions is critical for inventory optimization, yet promotions introduce two complexities: cross-product spillovers that reconfigure complementarity and substitution, and lingering temporal effects such as post-promotion dips that propagate through the product network. Forecasting methods that do not explicitly condition evolving product relationships on promotion information may therefore produce errors and costly stockouts or overstock. To address this gap, we adopt a dynamic-network perspective and propose the Dual-Stream Feature Fusion Network (DSFF), featuring (1) a promotion-driven dynamic sparse graph learner that infers real-time relationship shifts and (2) a dual-stream encoder with gated fusion that separates routine trends from promotional shocks and captures lingering effects. Evaluated on 7,769 SKUs against eleven state-of-the-art baselines across four multi-step horizons, DSFF achieves the best overall MAE and RMSE, with particularly pronounced MAE gains during promotional periods. The results demonstrate the value of modeling temporally reconfiguring product networks for promotional forecasting.

papers.title: Shadow AI and the Monitoring Paradox: A Typological Theory of Governance Visibility Erosion
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly face AI capabilities that evade effective oversight even when they are embedded in systems that are formally approved and actively monitored. Existing accounts of shadow IT and shadow AI do not fully explain this pattern because they assume that once relevant activity is discovered, governability can be restored. This paper develops a typological theory of shadow AI by reconceptualizing it as a governance condition rather than an authorization status. The theory identifies two generative mechanisms, visibility erosion and authorization decay, and shows how they degrade three governance capabilities: observation, attribution, and auditability. It yields four shadow AI types: Approved but Ungoverned, Unauthorized Tools, Undisclosed Vendor AI, and Ambient AI, and introduces the Monitoring Paradox, a boundary condition under which increased monitoring intensity yields diminishing returns because the constraint lies in signal availability rather than monitoring effort. The paper reframes governance from monitoring investment to delivery architecture design.

papers.title: Prosody Training for Lowering Vishing Susceptibility
papers.abstract: This short paper reports a pilot test of prosody-focused training for voice phishing (vishing). Vishing increasingly uses synthetic voices. However, most end-user security training remains text-centric (e.g., email phishing). We developed an audio-based prosody training intervention and evaluated user outcomes with Signal Detection Theory (SDT), separating sensitivity (d ′) from decision bias (criterion c). In a three-arm pilot (N = 27; AI-audio vs. human-audio vs. text-only), accuracy and sensitivity are stable from pre-test to post-test, but criterion shifts significantly toward a more conservative threshold (Δc = +0.328, p < .001), reducing both hit and false-alarm rates. Survey measures show increased perceived vulnerability and response efficacy. Pilot results suggest that prosody-focused training can meaningfully shift decision thresholds even when sensitivity is unchanged.

papers.title: Socio-Technical Conditions of Product Cyber Resilience in the Software Development Lifecycle: A Mixed-Methods Study
papers.abstract: Product cyber resilience, the ability of products with digital elements to anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to adverse conditions, is becoming a regulatory requirement, yet its implementation across the software development lifecycle remains poorly understood. Drawing on Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, this mixed-methods study derives four socio-technical conditions, three implementation layers from 14 practitioner interviews, and examines how these relate to the extent and composition of implementation in a survey of 134 professionals. Implementation is moderate across layers and systematically uneven, with technical measures most prevalent and structural measures least. The conditions are not uniformly associated with these layers: governance and resources are most strongly associated with the underdeveloped structural layer, while regulatory and managerial conditions are selectively associated with the procedural layer. This differential pattern points to a possible extension of STS theory at the implementation layer and advances the operationalisation of the IS digital resilience agenda.

papers.title: From Personal Data to Common Good: How AI Reciprocity Shapes Disclosure Intentions in AI-based Smart Energy Services
papers.abstract: AI-based smart energy services can support sustainable household energy use but require sensitive consumption data that may reveal private routines and activity patterns. Prior research suggests that collective benefits can facilitate sensitive data disclosure, yet AI reciprocity has so far been tested only in AI-based health services. This leaves open whether AI reciprocity is health-centric or a broader mechanism rooted in AI-based services’ ability to learn from aggregated user data and convert individual contributions into collective benefits. We test this boundary condition in an online vignette study with 250 tenants in Germany. Results show that perceived AI reciprocity benefits increase personal benefits, reduce perceived risks, and foster disclosure intentions, with the privacy calculus partially mediating this effect. Altruism and indebtedness further emerge as social-motivational antecedents of AI reciprocity. Our study extends AI reciprocity beyond health and positions it as a more general mechanism shaping privacy-related decisions in AI-based services.

papers.title: Employees’ Psychosocial Responses to Cybersecurity Attacks on Organizations
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity attacks on organizations increasingly disrupt not only technical and economic operations but also employees. Yet behavioral IS security research has largely focused on technical and economic effects and on pre‑incident threat perceptions rather than on how employees respond psychosocially to real attacks and how support shapes these responses under such conditions. Drawing on coping theory and a multiple-case study design, we examine how organizational leaders and incident response staff react to and cope with such attacks, how these processes relate to outcomes like well-being and security-relevant behaviors, and how they are shaped by perceived incident-specific organizational support. Integrating psychological and social perspectives, the study points to the often-overlooked human dimensions of cybersecurity attacks. Preliminary findings suggest that organizations may shape employees’ appraisal and coping through targeted support measures, reveal emerging ambivalent effects, and inform policymakers and regulators in assessing organizations’ compliance with occupational health and safety requirements.

papers.title: Breakthrough or Breakdown? Firm-Level Generative AI Exposure and Data Breach Risk
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) may create security vulnerabilities while supporting organizational defense. We examine whether firms more exposed to GenAI-relevant tasks experienced different breach outcomes after ChatGPT's release. Combining a pre-release task-based exposure index with a monthly panel of 5,695 U.S. Compustat firms, we estimate DID, DDD, and event-study models. Higher-exposure firms experienced fewer breaches after December 2022. Subsequent 10-K disclosures and a supplementary disclosure-timing design show that the exposure measure predicts public GenAI engagement. Mechanism evidence comes from 23,929 firm-year 10-K filings and two preregistered experiments. Higher exposure was associated with larger post-release increases in threat- and countermeasure-related disclosure. In experiment 1 (N = 267), optional GenAI access improved countermeasure knowledge and phishing detection. In experiment 2 (N = 358), task-time access produced the larger coefficients; direct comparisons between the two access conditions were statistically imprecise. The archival analysis evaluates task-based opportunity, while the experiments manipulate assistant access.

papers.title: Cyber-Safe Autonomous Drone Operations: An AI-specific Risk Assessment Framework
papers.abstract: AI-enabled autonomous drone operations are expanding across critical sectors, from healthcare logistics to infrastructure inspection, yet existing risk frameworks address only exogenous threats and overlook the endogenous risks introduced by AI infrastructures. Through Action Design Research conducted within the XADOT project on autonomous drone organ transportation, this paper proposes an AI-specific risk assessment framework that articulates three interrelated components: AI infrastructure vulnerabilities (algorithmic bias, decisional opacity, accountability gaps), endogenous and exogenous threats, and distributed operational activity domains. Each component is anchored to established IS theoretical lenses on algorithmic fairness, responsible AI, and AI risk management, and mapped onto the European regulatory landscape – Including the AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2, and GDPR – revealing coordination gaps for AI-enabled autonomous infrastructures. The framework is offered as a first analytical step toward a governance-actionable conceptual model in subsequent design cycles.

papers.title: Exchange Rate and the Supply of Hacking Goods: Evidence from an International Panel
papers.abstract: Many underground transactions are denominated in U.S. dollars, and exchange rate fluctuations may thereby alter vendors’ local currency income and shape their supply incentives. Using a unique dataset that links anonymous vendors’ geographic locations to their activity in the Hack Forums marketplace, we find that local currency appreciation is positively associated with vendor supply. Analyses of extensive and intensive margins reveal divergent responses. Local currency appreciation reduces new vendor entry, and this negative effect is weaker when the unemployment rate is higher. In contrast, appreciation increases supply among incumbent vendors, leading them to post more selling threads, introduce new products, and become more likely to offer innovative and malicious products. This positive supply response is more pronounced among vendors who sell time-sensitive products. This study contributes to IS research on cybersecurity and underground digital platforms. We draw related implications for cybersecurity governance and intervention.

papers.title: Cybersecurity Knowledge Transfer in Software Outsourcing: A Boundary‑Spanning and Sensemaking Perspective
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity failures in outsourced software projects are often rooted not in technical flaws alone, but in breakdowns in how cybersecurity knowledge is transferred, interpreted, and legitimized across organizational boundaries. This short paper examines cybersecurity knowledge transfer (CKT) in software outsourcing through an integrated boundary spanning and sensemaking perspective. Drawing on exploratory interviews with experienced software professionals, we show that CKT is a process of cross boundary sensemaking conducted under conditions of epistemic asymmetry, where team members cannot independently verify cybersecurity claims. Boundary spanners, shared artifacts, and recurring coordination routines enable cybersecurity knowledge to move across client–vendor boundaries, while interpretive and legitimation processes determine whether that knowledge is accepted and enacted. The findings demonstrate that effective cross boundary sensemaking is critical to perceived cybersecurity effectiveness in outsourced projects. The study contributes theoretically by integrating boundary spanning and sensemaking, and practically by highlighting socio-technical processes that shape cybersecurity outcomes.

papers.title: The Weakest Link Fallacy between Hembigs and Self-Fulfilling Prophecies
papers.abstract: Claiming that humans are the weakest link in cybersecurity is pervasive among both researchers and practitioners, yet the claim is rarely examined for its conceptual clarity or organizational consequences. This study investigates how cybersecurity practitioners understand and deploy this metaphor and whether it achieves its intended effects. Based on 22 interviews with cybersecurity professionals and informed by Speech Act Theory, we deconstruct the metaphor in terms of its locutionary meaning, illocutionary intent, and perlocutionary effects. We find that the metaphor operates as a rhetorical device rather than an analytical diagnosis. Although practitioners are aware of its potentially demotivating effects, its use often reinforces a tribal divide and normalizes low expectations of nontechnical employees. Conceptually, we argue that it functions as a hembig—hegemonic, ambiguous, weakly grounded; yet performatively powerful. The study calls for greater reflexivity in cybersecurity discourse, warning that uncritical language use may undermine engagement and organizational security outcomes.

papers.title: Revelation Without Cue-Based Instruction: Rethinking Phishing Simulations as Learning Interventions
papers.abstract: Phishing simulations are a standard tool for assessing and reducing phishing susceptibility. Research treats them as either measurement instruments or delivery channels for cue-based instruction. We explore a third possibility: that the simulation experience itself fosters learning, regardless of cue-based instructional content. Based on 31 interviews conducted after a CEO impersonation simulation at a European multinational, we analyze how managers process the experience across three dimensions: affective disruption, cognitive recalibration, and social sensemaking. Without cue-based instruction, revelation alone appears sufficient to trigger a learning process in which trapped employees identify missed cues, reassess their susceptibility, and discuss the experience with colleagues. We make three arguments: phishing simulations function as learning interventions; susceptibility in cue-fluent populations is an application rather than a recognition problem; and revelation and cue-based instruction are distinct functions of resolution pages, the latter appearing redundant and possibly counterproductive for these populations.

papers.title: Disentangling Reactions to Data Breaches: Evidence from Mobile Service Providers
papers.abstract: When consumers learn of a data breach, do they react based on personal risk or moral judgment? We draw on cognitive appraisal theory and construal level theory, which generate opposing predictions, to investigate whether potential victims or unaffected non-customers react more strongly to a data breach. Across three experiments on Prolific (one scenario-based experiment with 568 U.S. participants and two real-life replications following breaches at Telus in Canada and Odido in the Netherlands), we consistently find that unaffected non-customers react more negatively than the firm’s own customers, who are potential victims. This pattern holds across attitude, trust, satisfaction, and word-of-mouth, supporting a construal level explanation in which data breaches are primarily construed as corporate scandals rather than personal privacy threats. Reputational consequences extend beyond the affected customer base. We discuss implications for the archetypical problem behind a data breach, research on privacy violations, and possible avenues for future research.

papers.title: "You can't just trust having the most expensive EDR": Using case-based learning to help cybersecurity leaders engage with complex sociotechnical systems
papers.abstract: Modern cybersecurity leaders must be able switch into crisis mode without warning, at a time and under conditions selected by an adversary. Between attacks, they must also run daily operations and ensure organisational learning from cybersecurity incidents. The competencies needed to implement organisational learning and align strategy and posture are crucial but not routinely taught. In this study, we designed a case-based learning experience to help cybersecurity leadership learners reflect on the complex sociotechnical factors at play during incidents. We delivered the workshop four times with successive learners, reflecting on our method and analysing participants' responses. Findings show learners engaging with 'fractured cybersecurity terrain', both in their organisations and within themselves. This study contributes an empirically validated educational design that can be used with updated cases as technology and tactics evolve.

papers.title: Framing Cyber Resilience in Higher Education: Diagnosing Readiness and Response
papers.abstract: Cyber resilience is increasingly critical as cyber threats disrupt digitally dependent institutions. Existing frameworks provide valuable technical guidance but often underplay how resilience is enacted by heterogeneous stakeholders in decentralized socio-technical settings. This limitation is salient in higher education, where students, academic staff, and administrative staff depend on shared digital infrastructures but differ in responsibility, authority, confidence, and continuity practices. Using Design Science Research (DSR), this study operationalizes cyber resilience through three stakeholder-sensitive artefacts: a readiness-response matrix, stakeholder-specific self-assessment tools, and empirically grounded personas. Drawing on 35 semi-structured interviews and three stakeholder-specific focus groups in a European business school, the study shows that cyber resilience maturity is configurational rather than linear. Stakeholders may exhibit readiness without response, response without readiness, both, or neither. The study contributes by conceptualizing cyber resilience as a distributed socio-technical capability and by offering diagnostic artefacts for identifying stakeholder-specific resilience gaps.

papers.title: The Clash of the Head and the Heart in Empathic Artificial Intelligence: Decision Accuracy and Security Tradeoffs
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) systems designed to provide empathic and socially responsive interactions, yet the consequences of empathic alignment for other organizationally important objectives remain unclear. We examine whether strengthening empathic alignment creates tradeoffs with epistemic performance and cybersecurity robustness. Using controlled healthcare experiments with open-weight large language models, we progressively manipulate empathic alignment through domain-specific and empathy-oriented fine-tuning and evaluate decision accuracy and vulnerability to social–cognitive adversarial attacks. Results show that stronger empathic alignment is associated with lower decision accuracy and greater susceptibility to adversarial manipulation within the examined settings. These patterns remain qualitatively consistent across multiple model specifications and five target models. Constitutional AI substantially reduces attack success but does not eliminate vulnerability and introduces additional accuracy costs. We conceptualize these findings as a conditional “head–heart” tradeoff and highlight the importance of jointly managing socio-emotional quality, epistemic performance, and cybersecurity robustness when designing empathic AI systems.

papers.title: How Can Organisations Absorb Cyber Threat Intelligence: A Multiple-Case Study
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity practice operates under an attacker-defender asymmetry that incident response (IR) cannot close on its own, and cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is positioned in the literature as the capability that closes it. Existing CTI research has been dominated by the technology perspective, leaving the empirical question of how the capability to absorb intelligence is distributed across organisational stakeholder roles substantively underexamined. We address this through a multiple-case study of nine organisations across two stakeholder roles, CTI Practitioner and Cybersecurity Management, using Zahra and George’s (2002) absorptive capacity (ACAP) as the analytical lens. Our contribution is a stakeholder-activity process model of CTI practice that reveals a structural pattern in which management performs gatekeeping, combining, codification, and routine-refining work while practitioners perform volume processing, source validation, and audience tailoring; a modal asymmetry concentrated at Transformation that supports disaggregating realised absorptive capacity (RACAP); and a diagnostic instrument for CISOs and CTI leads.

papers.title: Strategic Silence, Strategic Signal:  Network Proximity to Data Breaches and Digital Strategic Initiative Disclosure
Extending the Integrative Trust Model to Smart Home Intrusion Detection Adoption
papers.abstract: Smart home intrusion detection systems are only as effective as the households willing to install them, and installing one means trusting an unfamiliar provider with monitoring authority over the home network. We examine how trust relates to adoption intention through a between-subjects vignette experiment with 983 smart home device owners, extending an integrative trust typology to household security technology and pairing it with UTAUT2 constructs and perceived security. First, the results support the trust typology: disposition is associated with institution-based trust, then with provider beliefs and app-level intentions, and provider beliefs show the strongest relationship with app-level intentions. Second, perceived security and performance expectancy demonstrated separate relationships with adoption intention. Third, hedonic motivation related to adoption intention as strongly as performance expectancy, and perceived completeness was associated with hedonic motivation but not performance expectancy. We find that trust formation and hedonic motivation shape household adoption of security technology.

papers.title: How Cyber Fraud Triggers Behavioral  Responses: A Stimulus-Organism-Response  View of Victims' Behavior
papers.abstract: Cyber fraud against individuals has surged in digitalizing economies. India alone reports  900% rise in complaints over four years, despite high awareness campaigns. IS security  research, framed around the organizational employee protected by institutional controls,  under-theorises the societal individual who faces fraud alone in real time. It treats  victims’ behavioral responses as a single event decision rather than a process well planned by fraudsters. Drawing on Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework and  thirteen interviews with victims and institutional actors in India, we identify six fraud  stimuli, three organism mechanisms, and five forms of victims’ behavioral response. Our  central contribution is to show that these cues are sequences and interact. As we saw how  authority impersonation and urgency and threat cues produce trust displacement and  cognitive overload, social proof normalises the response, and technological triggers  convert mental states into action. This reorients intervention design from awareness  raising toward mechanism disruption.

papers.title: A Breach on the Resume: Organizational Data Breaches and IT Employees’ Subsequent Career Prospects
papers.abstract: Data breaches can impose substantial consequences on organizations and their stakeholders, yet their downstream effects on affiliated employees remain underexplored. Drawing on the theory of organizational stigma and stigma by association, we theorize that organizational stigma created by data breaches may affect affiliated IT employees in the external labor market. We further propose that this effect varies with employees’ functional proximity to the functional areas implicated by the breach and breach publicity. We identify perceived competence and perceived contaminating risk as two psychological mechanisms through which organizational stigma shapes prospective employers’ evaluations. We propose a multi-study, multimethod research design combining econometric analysis with a controlled experiment. Theoretically, this study extends data breach and stigma research by examining how breach-related stigma can shape affiliated employees’ subsequent career prospects. Practically, this study informs employees, employers, and organizations about the broader career implications of data breaches.

papers.title: Technology-Related Misconduct: A Review and Explanatory Pathway Model
papers.abstract: Digital technologies are implicated in diverse forms of misconduct that can harm organizations, individuals, and society. Although information systems (IS) research has generated rich insight into specific forms of technology-related misconduct, this knowledge remains fragmented across different labels, empirical contexts, and theoretical lenses. Consequently, it remains unclear what this fragmented literature collectively explains and how its explanations relate to one another. We address this issue by systematically reviewing 42 empirical studies published in premier IS journals and reconstructing 146 explanatory routes, each capturing how prior research explains misconduct. Comparing these routes, we identify six recurring explanatory pathways, showing that seemingly different forms of technology-related misconduct often share common explanations. By integrating this fragmented literature at the level of explanation, we provide a foundation for cumulative theorizing on technology-related misconduct.

papers.title: Leveraging Generative AI for SETA: Designing an Interactive Comic-Based Security Awareness Artifact
papers.abstract: Security Education, Training, and Awareness (SETA) programs remain central to reducing human-related cybersecurity risks, yet many existing approaches struggle to provide engaging, realistic, and efficiently developed training experiences. This research-in-progress study investigates how generative artificial intelligence can support the design of an interactive comic-based SETA artifact. Applying Design Science Research, we draw on role identity theory, Protection Motivation Theory, and prior SETA studies to derive requirements for target-group-specific content and consequential branching that guide AI-assisted comic development. The artifact combines realistic security-related decision situations, narrative consequences, and evaluation alignment with established awareness constructs. Initial insights suggest that generative artificial intelligence can facilitate the efficient creation of narrative SETA content, while also raising challenges related to visual consistency, tool complexity, and artifact refinement. The study contributes an initial design-oriented account of AI-assisted SETA artifact development.

papers.title: Quantifying the Hydra Effect: Measuring the Resilience of Darknet-Market Cryptocurrency Network through Role-Invariant Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Darknet-market cryptocurrency networks in Southeast Asia generate billions annually by coordinating through messaging platforms and settling payments on public blockchains. Despite enforcement, they remain resilient: disrupted nodes are quickly replaced, a Hydra-like effect. Existing measures struggle because adversaries deliberately rotate identities, breaking node-level continuity. We address this with RIFT (Role-Invariant Functional Trajectory learning), a graph learning framework developed under the Design Science Research paradigm that shifts resilience measurement from individual node survival to functional role trajectories. Using a cross-modal dataset linking messaging records with blockchain transactions across two enforcement waves, we show that resilience depends less on disposable front-desk addresses than on the recovery of hub and layering roles. The two waves are also consistent with the hypothesis that infrastructure-focused enforcement produces more durable disruption than channel bans alone. Effective governance should therefore track role continuity, target structurally important settlement functions, and combine platform, financial, and physical interventions.

papers.title: When Decentralized Market Centralized:  The Oracle Failure in Prediction Market
papers.abstract: Decentralized prediction markets settle real-world events through oracles whose token-weighted governance is intended to ensure no single actor can determine market outcomes. Yet when this trustless settlement mechanism is publicly shown to fail, it remains theoretically unclear whether users continue to trust decentralization and through what behavioral channel they respond. We address this question by exploiting a natural experiment in Polymarket—the manipulation of the Optimistic Oracle by a single large tokenholder together with on-chain trading records. Following the oracle failure, treated users are 5.3% more likely to exit the platform and a subsequent oracle governance repair does not bring them back. Together, these findings introduce design-premise violation as a distinct class of trust violation and show that ex-post governance repair cannot substitute for ex-ante governance, carrying important implications for protocol designers and platform operators of DeFi.

papers.title: How to Unite Energy Certificates Across Carriers? Exploring Distributed Ledger Technology for Guarantee of Origin Schemes in Multi-Carrier Energy Systems
papers.abstract: Guarantees of Origin (GO) are the principal instrument for tracking renewable energy attributes in European energy markets. The revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) extends GO schemes from electricity to renewable gases and heating and cooling, making interoperability between previously siloed registries an operational necessity. Energy carrier conversion such as power-to-hydrogen requires cross-domain data sharing that current centralized architectures cannot support. Following a Design Science Research approach, we derive five design principles for interoperable multi-carrier GO systems, validated through interviews with seven domain experts, and instantiate them in CrossGO, a Hyperledger Fabric prototype with 10 chaincode namespaces and 85 functions covering the full GO lifecycle. A dual-channel benchmark sustains up to 41.9 TPS for intra-carrier writes and a three-phase cross-channel conversion protocol at 6.8 to 8.5 TPS per phase. The findings provide architectural guidance for registry operators and regulators implementing cross-carrier interoperability under RED III.

papers.title: Beyond Points: Blockchain Affordances in Loyalty Programs - A Typology of Tokenized Loyalty Programs
papers.abstract: Tokenized loyalty programs (TLPs) are emerging as a new pathway to value creation for users and to differentiate programs in a growing, yet crowded loyalty market. While prior research has treated TLPs as a monolithic category, our paper argues that materially identical blockchain substrates yield divergent action potentials depending on how a TLP is instantiated, drawing on affordance theory. Through iterative coding of 38 real-world TLPs, we identify three blockchain-specific design elements that extend established loyalty program frameworks and derive four TLP types: NFT collectibles, NFT token-gated access, FT programs with internal circulation, and FT programs with external circulation. Each type activates distinct affordance profiles and value propositions for consumers and firms. We translate the typology into 12 research propositions linking design elements to differentiated outcomes. This study extends established loyalty program frameworks and provides a foundation for empirical research on TLPs.

papers.title: To DAO or Not to DAO: Contextual Conditions, Design Choices, and Boundary Limits for DAO Viability
papers.abstract: Decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) are blockchain-based communities that coordinate activities through smart contracts and token-based governance. However, their organizational viability remains contested. This study identifies the contextual conditions, design choices, and boundary limits shaping DAO suitability compared with traditional organizational forms. Through a multi-vocal literature review integrating academic, grey, and on-chain evidence, we develop a DAO Suitability Framework and illustrate its application through contrasting cases. Findings reveal recurring constraints in technology, governance, law, and coordination. DAO failures emerge when code, governance, or legal risks remain unaddressed and critical events expose missing safeguards. Conversely, audits, legal structures, and financial buffers improve resilience. DAOs appear most suitable for digital-native, rule-intensive, and borderless contexts, while hybrid on/off-chain models are often preferable elsewhere.

papers.title: Navigating the Imagination-Implementation Divide in Blockchain Adoption
papers.abstract: We examine how the academic discourse on blockchain applications represents technological adoption and responds to changing empirical evidence. Drawing on a meta-analysis of 138 review articles published between 2009 and 2025, we combine sentiment analysis, SciBERT-based classification of adoption maturity descriptions, and systematic verification of cited real-world initiatives. Our findings reveal a persistent misalignment between academic representations and empirical developments. While the academic discourse remains neutral-to-positive in tone and heavily focused on conceptual frameworks, its representations of adoption maturity show little progression over time. Verification of cited cases from practice further shows that many referenced initiatives have been discontinued or no longer use blockchain. We conceptualize this slow adjustment to changing empirical evidence as an epistemic lag, a potential consequence of the trailing edge of fashionable information technology research. Our findings underscore the need for continuous empirical recalibration to preserve the speculative rigor of prospective research on emerging digital technologies.

papers.title: Unpacking Web3 in Information Systems Research: Complementary Framings of an Emerging Organizing Vision
papers.abstract: In this study, we interpret the conceptual heterogeneity surrounding the concept of Web3 in Information Systems research through organizing vision (OV) theory. Analyzing 30 papers from major IS outlets, we identify three complementary framings: Web3 as technical architecture, as power redistribution, and as economic paradigm. We find that each framing anchors the vision in a different constitutive domain and primarily activates one specific OV function. This domain-driven functional variation, observed within a single contributor type, challenges the community-heterogeneity explanations central to classic OV scholarship. We characterize this pattern as constitutive heterogeneity and argue that multi-domain visions such as Web3 may follow distinct closure trajectories, including domain-specific partial stabilizations, rather than achieving unified definitional closure.

papers.title: From Contribution to Participation: Tokenized Ownership under an Institutional Shock
papers.abstract: Digital platforms often use financial incentives to motivate user contributions, but sustaining them requires ongoing rewards. Tokenized ownership offers an alternative by giving users an economic stake in platform value, potentially sustaining contributions even when token value falls. We examine how this logic changes when an external institutional shock reduces the value of tokenized ownership while leaving the focal platform's fundamentals intact. Using proprietary and on-chain data from a Q&A platform, we exploit the Terra–Luna collapse and apply coarsened exact matching with a difference-in-differences design. We find that users with stronger tokenized ownership reduce value-creating core contributions and increase peripheral participation without a significant change in earned rewards. From a real options perspective, this pattern suggests that users shift toward lower-cost activities that preserve engagement and future upside. Our findings extend property rights and real options theories by showing that the value-creating effect of tokenized ownership is institutionally contingent.

papers.title: Cost, Power, and Participation in Decentralized Governance
papers.abstract: How does reducing the cost of governance participation shape activity in decentralized platforms? We examine this question in decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), whose decentralized governance intends to encourage participation but often remains concentrated among well-resourced actors. Drawing on collective action, we argue that reducing voting costs encourages governance participation and subsequent economic engagement, while generating heterogeneous effects across participants. Using a difference-in-differences design with coarsened exact matching, we study a governance redesign in Aave that substantially reduced voting costs by migrating governance to lower-cost networks. We find that lowering voting costs increases governance participation, with gains accruing disproportionately to large token holders. We further find that lowering voting costs increases transaction activities. These findings extend collective action to decentralized governance, surface a design tension between stimulated participation and unequal value capture, and show how governance design choices can shape both governance and economic activity on digital platforms.

papers.title: Beyond Sign-Up: How Prior Referee Quality Shapes Trajectory of Later Referrals in DeFi Platforms
papers.abstract: Referral research typically examines customer acquisition or the direct value of referred customers, leaving unclear whether referral sequences also shape downstream network expansion. We study 26,452 referral events from 2,433 referrers on Hyperliquid, a decentralized trading platform whose public records link referral histories to referees’ post-entry behavior. Within the same referrer, stronger realized early engagement among prior referees predicts lower subsequent trading volume and fewer active days among later referees. Behavioral alignment and profitability show shorter-lived negative associations, while later referees are consistently less likely to become referrers themselves. These patterns are consistent with sequential social-capital depletion. By connecting referral life-cycle research with referral-contagion research, we distinguish referees’ direct post-entry outcomes from first-order referral generativity and show that referral history predicts both dimensions of referral value.

papers.title: Designing for Recourse: Cost-Aware and Model Agnostic Counterfactual Explanations in Networked Decision Systems
papers.abstract: This paper presents research in progress that proposes a model-agnostic framework for generating counterfactual explanations for node classification. The proposed design science-based approach addresses the challenge of explaining black-box predictions by identifying minimal perturbations to graph structures that would flip the predicted class of a target node. Unlike most existing methods that focus exclusively on edge deletion or require full access to the model, the proposed method employs a cost-aware perturbation vector-based approach that considers both edge addition and deletion within a constrained k-hop neighborhood. The framework utilizes numerical gradient approximation to optimize a non-convex objective function incorporating context-dependent edge costs.
