Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method generates sparse, valid counterfactual explanations while remaining agnostic to the underlying model architecture. Our approach enhances the autonomy of users subjected to automated decisions by providing explanations that precisely indicate which connections need to change to achieve a desired outcome.

papers.title: MAQUETTE: A Method for Computational User Interface Instantiation
papers.abstract: Design Science Research aims to generate design knowledge, yet translating abstract design knowledge into concrete artifacts remains challenging. As design knowledge can be instantiated in many ways, current build–evaluate approaches that rely on a single artifact risk underexploring the solution space, threatening instantiation validity. Prior work on artifact sampling addresses this conceptually but remains challenging to apply given resource constraints and potential researcher biases in unstructured design activity. We propose a method for computational user interface instantiation leveraging generative artificial intelligence to support the generation and criteria-based evaluation of multiple UI artifact instantiations as an antecedent to user evaluation episodes. We develop the method, demonstrate it in a concrete case, and preliminarily evaluate it through interviews with five experts. We position our work as a methodological contribution to DSR, suggesting how automated instantiation can enable broader, more transparent solution space exploration and may help mitigate indeterminacy in design outcomes.

papers.title: Towards Collaborative Conversational Recommendation: A Multi-Agent Framework with Socratic Intent Elicitation and Experience Retrieval
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) struggle with vague user intent: existing LLM-based approaches rely on reactive questioning, underutilize experience from historical dialogues, and lack decision-theoretic sequential optimization. Adopting a design science paradigm, we develop the Socratic Collaborative Conversational Recommender System (SCCRS), a multi-agent artifact that reconceptualizes recommendation as preference co-construction under partial observability. SCCRS integrates (1) Socratic preference elicitation that actively scaffolds user sensemaking to clarify vague user intents, (2) collaborative experience retrieval that transforms historical trajectories into pseudo-gradient signals guiding dialogue planning, and (3) a POMDP formalization balancing exploration and exploitation. LLM-simulated evaluations on REDIAL and OpenDialKG show that SCCRS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in recommendation success, dialogue efficiency, and ranking accuracy. This study contributes a systematically evaluated artifact and design principles for adaptive, experience-driven conversational decision support.

papers.title: WorkScope: Towards a Design Framework and System for Uncovering Modern Slavery Through Hybrid Ontology Learning
papers.abstract: Modern slavery represents a relevant global phenomenon bearing severe consequences for individuals and societies. Prior research has largely developed theoretical knowledge, particularly due to challenges of collecting empirical data in hidden, concealed and criminal contexts. This theoretical knowledge is valuable, yet not actionable for trying to uncover and fight modern slavery in practice. Guided by a theoretical framework combining sensemaking and routine activity theory, we propose a set of meta requirements and designs for machine learning-enabled systems to uncover modern slavery as well as a particular artifact. Based upon a unique, empirically based dataset, we suggest a hybrid ontology learning approach combining theoretical knowledge with novel insights from empirical manifestations, enabling the classification of potential cases of MS and better grasping the phenomenon as a whole. We contribute to computational design research in socially relevant contexts shaped by latent and complex conditions through supporting sensemaking with fragmented and incomplete data.

papers.title: LLM-Driven Generative Fashion Outfit Algorithm Based on Consumer Intent Detection
papers.abstract: As consumers increasingly seek personalized aesthetic experiences, existing recommendation methods struggle to infer users’ underlying intentions, while large language models (LLMs) remain limited in fashion item understanding and task-specific adaptation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a generative fashion outfit recommendation algorithm based on consumer intent detection. Specifically, we encode items into hierarchical semantic IDs, enabling LLMs to perceive large-scale item catalogs, and employ chain-of-thought reasoning to extract interpretable intent descriptions from implicit user behaviors. The extracted intent is then incorporated as an explicit condition into a multi-task fine-tuning framework, achieving end-to-end coordinated outfit generation. Experiments on a public fashion outfit dataset evaluate the algorithm on hit rate, rank accuracy, diversity, and compatibility. Results show that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing baselines across all evaluated metrics, providing a comprehensive and effective solution for generative fashion outfit recommendation.

papers.title: Designing PDEL-DRK: An Ablation-Testable Architecture for Repeated Agentic Delegation
papers.abstract: Repeated delegation of operational decisions to AI-enabled systems raises architectural challenges around context, strategic intent, validation discipline, effect attribution, and reusable experience across cycles. This paper presents PDEL-DRK, an ablation-testable architecture with five typed modules: contextual perception, strategy-tactic decision, execution validation, effect attribution, and decision relation knowledge. We instantiate it in a synthetic hierarchical e-commerce seller-operation testbed and evaluate it over a 144-week paired ablation panel with an external contextual-bandit reference. Five of six pre-specified commitment ablations significantly reduce cumulative operating value after Bonferroni correction. Contextual perception is strongest; strategy-tactic separation and tactical relation retrieval form a second tier; execution validation and strategic retrieval are smaller. Effect attribution is not detectable under the pre-specified drift magnitudes, although an exploratory drift sweep suggests a boundary-sensitive role at the highest tested regime. The paper contributes nascent design theory by showing how long-horizon reliability decomposes into inspectable, typed, ablation-testable commitments.

papers.title: Governance-Responsive Social-Capital Learning for Collusive Fraud Detection
Learning Coordinated Inventory Lateral Transshipment via Graph-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Proactive lateral transshipment can rebalance inventory before shortages occur, but distributed operational information alone does not determine where reallocation is needed or how replenishment and transshipment should be coordinated. We propose TransG, a graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning decision artifact for coordinating replenishment and transshipment in multi-location inventory systems. TransG learns period-specific transshipment links from distributed retailer observations and embeds graph-theoretic constraints to suppress operationally redundant reallocation structures. It then organizes replenishment and transshipment through intention-aware sequential policy generation and feasibility-aware masking, converting these links into executable inventory adjustments while preserving entity-level decision structures. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show lower mean system costs than heuristic, optimization-based, and learning-based baselines, with analyses supporting coordination effectiveness and scalability. Overall, TransG improves proactive lateral transshipment through selective cross-location coordination and provides a design-science instantiation showing how distributed operational information can be transformed into coordinated and feasible actions in distributed operational decision environments.

papers.title: Understanding the Effects and Limitations of Reading Support Systems for Non-Native Readers in Comprehension Tasks
papers.abstract: AI-based Reading support systems increasingly assist non-native readers in working with complex texts, yet their effectiveness may depend on the reading purpose. We conducted two controlled laboratory studies with 294 non-native English readers, comparing a Conversational Interface, a Canvas Interface, and unsupported reading across an open-book reading task support setting and a closed-book reading comprehension support setting. In the open-book setting, both AI-supported groups showed descriptively higher TOEFL-based reading scores than the control group, with the Conversational Interface achieving the highest mean. In the closed-book setting, this pattern shifted: the control group achieved the highest mean, followed by the Conversational and Canvas Interfaces. This contrasting tendency suggests that support useful for immediate task performance may not translate into later unaided comprehension. Evaluation criteria for reading support systems must be aligned with reading purpose, rather than treating support effectiveness as a single, context-independent outcome across settings.

papers.title: SCORSE: A Computational Design Artifact for LLM Financial Decision Support
papers.abstract: SCORSE (Structured Contextual Orchestration and Reward Shaping Engine) is a computational design artifact for advisor-in-the-loop financial recommendation drafting. It combines parser-visible structured initialization with transparent heuristics (H), a cross-model semantic/audit judge (J), scenario performance testing (P), targeted repair, and noncompensatory gates. In a fixed-seed benchmark of 50 synthetic clients, iterative modes improve machine-measured semantic reasoning and the Reasoning Quality Index relative to scaffold-only initialization. SCORSE-HJP raises the machine pass/review-ready rate from 18% to 44%, although a simpler judge-only loop is competitive, narrowing the claim from full-stack necessity to value beyond structure plus governable evaluator separation. Sensitivity analysis shows that continuous improvements are stable under reasonable reweighting, while binary clearance depends on calibration. Boundary analysis identifies remaining failures in personalization, overclaim suppression, semantics, and feasibility. The contribution is a prototype-level design architecture for inspectable, stress-tested recommendation drafts, not evidence of practitioner-certified advice.

papers.title: When (Not) to Trust AI: An Interpretable Approach to Assessing Machine Learning Predictions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become pervasive across business, society, and research. In particular, the predictions of machine learning (ML) models are used for decision support in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance. However, ML model predictions are naturally not always correct, and false ML model predictions can have severe consequences. We propose U-EXPLORE, a novel approach for reject/trust-decisions of ML model predictions which aims to facilitate improved AI-augmented decision-making. U-EXPLORE reconstructs the decision behavior of ML models and develops a set of strongly performing ML models to exploit model multiplicity. The reject/trust-decision is based on three risk factors, thus highlighting why a prediction was rejected or trusted. An evaluation on four real-world datasets from high-stakes domains shows that U-EXPLORE provides strong decision accuracy and outperforms competing approaches. In addition, due to its interpretability, U-EXPLORE not only enhances transparency, but also can facilitate the improvement of ML models.

papers.title: LLM-Based Resume Optimization in Talent Recommendation Systems: Impact and Mitigation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled resume optimization tools to rewrite resume sections for a target job. Although such optimization can improve the clarity and organization of a resume, it may also introduce unsupported or exaggerated information. Because talent recommendation systems rely heavily on resume content to assess candidate-job fit, these changes may reduce recommendation accuracy. In this work, we examine the impact of LLM-refined resumes on the outputs of six talent recommendation models. The results show reduced recommendation accuracy for several models and upward ranking movements for optimized resumes. Human expert assessments reveal that lower authenticity scores are associated with larger matching-score gains. Motivated by this finding, we design an authenticity-aware resume processing pipeline that adds risk comments to potentially misrepresented content and removes skills or keywords that lack internal support. Our evaluation shows that the pipeline helps preserve recommendation quality by reducing accuracy losses and upward ranking movement.

papers.title: Can LLMs think like different investors? A self-reflective framework for risk-aligned stock prediction
papers.abstract: This study develops a risk-aligned financial decision support system for LLM-based stock prediction. Existing LLMs can process market information but often fail to accommodate heterogeneous investor risk preferences because preference-annotated financial data are scarce. We propose the Distillation–Attribution–Prediction (DAP) framework, which uses realized market outcomes as factual anchors and self-reflection to generate risk-preference annotations for training a lightweight LLM that produces predictions and interpretable rationales. Using Chinese industry ETF data, expert evaluation shows that the DAP-trained LLM’s generated reasoning is well aligned with different risk preferences, including both risk-averse and risk-seeking settings. The DAP-trained LLM also achieves the highest prediction accuracy (0.5913) and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (0.1725) among all evaluated models. Its preference-specific strategies outperform LLM and rule-based baselines and remain competitive with machine learning models across multiple market regimes. These findings demonstrate the value of behaviorally grounded LLM design for personalized financial decision support under uncertainty.

papers.title: From “Who” to “Why”: A Hierarchical Competition Alignment Network for Corporate Competitive Relation Discovery
papers.abstract: Accurately identifying corporate competitive relations is essential for strategic decision-making. Existing data-driven methods typically approximate competition as holistic firm-level similarity and embed firms into opaque vector spaces, limiting both granularity and interpretability. This study proposes a Large-Small Model Collaboration framework for competitive relation discovery. We first leverage a large language model to extract competition-relevant sentences from 10-K filings and map them onto a dual-level competitive dimension taxonomy grounded in Garvin's quality framework. We then develop a Hierarchical Competition Alignment Network (HCAM) that performs explicit pairwise matching at the secondary-indicator, primary-dimension, and firm levels, enabling multi-granularity identification and interpretable decomposition of competitive relations. Experiments on FactSet competitor labels demonstrate that HCAM achieves an F1 score of 0.8202, outperforming all indicator-structure and text-similarity baselines. The model further traces predictions to specific competitive dimensions with supporting textual evidence, answering not only who competes but also why.

papers.title: Identifying Organic Content Promoters: A Generative Approach to Grassroots Marketing
papers.abstract: Digital content platforms increasingly rely on algorithmic recommendation to allocate visibility, yet grassroots creators often struggle when newly uploaded content lacks sufficient interaction signals. Existing research on influencer seeding and digital promotion has not examined how platforms should select real early users whose interactions may improve the subsequent recommendation visibility of a specific item. We address this gap by developing GenPromoter, a two-stage generative artifact for organic content promoter identification. Stage 1 optimizes an ideal promoted item representation in continuous embedding space, and Stage 2 decodes it into a cardinality-constrained subset of real users. Offline evaluations on MovieLens-100K and Qilin show that GenPromoter produces stronger model-based visibility gains than comparison baselines. The findings suggest that, conditional on realized early interactions, effective grassroots promotion can depend not only on exposure volume but also on the composition of early engagement.

papers.title: From Prediction to Evidence: Detecting Harmful Short Videos with Policy-Aligned Contrastive Learning via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Short-form video platforms increasingly shape users’ mental health, yet existing detection systems remain black-box and insufficient for platform governance, which requires interpretable, policy-grounded decisions. This study reframes harmful short-video detection in toxic diet culture as a policy-aligned evidence-generation problem rather than a pure classification task. We propose the Sparse Autoencoder-based Policy-Aligned Contrastive Evidence (SPACE) framework, which transforms video segments into sparse, interpretable features, learns gated contrastive evidence for classification and segment-level localization, and aligns detected evidence with platform policy concepts. A Pareto-optimal feature selection module further balances predictive performance, interpretability, and parsimony. Preliminary results on a labeled TikTok dataset show strong predictive performance while producing segment-level, policy-aligned explanations, enabling auditable and actionable moderation decisions.

papers.title: Designing a GenAI-based Social Bot to support Crisis Communication during Natural Hazards
papers.abstract: During natural disasters, disseminating information to the public quickly can be a matter of life and death. Social media can support the rapid dissemination of information in such scenarios. However, emergency personnel typically focus on life-saving activities and lack the capacity to create online postings. This study examines the design of a generative AI (GenAI)-based social bot for crisis communication, particularly during natural hazards, to support emergency personnel. Using Peffer et al.’s design science research (DSR) approach, a prototype was designed and developed. The prototype was evaluated through expert interviews and an online survey. The results indicate that most experts would use this type of social bot for crisis communication, especially for multilingual posts. Several recommendations for a second DSR cycle were derived, providing a solid foundation for future research. A nascent design theory for GenAI-based social bots for crisis communication in natural hazards complements the theoretical contributions.

papers.title: From Detection to Decision: A Human-Centered Artifact for Regulatory Change Review
papers.abstract: Organizations in regulated industries must continuously monitor evolving legal requirements, since missed amendments translate into compliance violations and financial exposure. Manual review of large legal corpora is time-intensive and error-prone, and existing approaches address isolated subtasks without supporting the reviewer responsible for compliance decisions. We follow a design science research approach to design and evaluate an end-to-end artifact for regulatory change review. The artifact aligns regulation versions through staged structural and semantic matching, classifies changes against a six-category ontology, and presents source-grounded explanations with reviewer override controls. On a regulatory benchmark, it achieves 0.99 recall for semantic changes and outperforms all evaluated baselines. In a naturalistic study with eleven regulatory professionals, reviewers found the outputs verifiable and described the system as a structured assistant. The study shows how legal NLP and human-centered design can be combined to shift compliance work from detecting textual differences toward supporting verifiable review decisions.

papers.title: Caught between Clocks: Surfacing Temporal Boundaries and Tensions in Large-scale Agile Information Systems Development
papers.abstract: Large-scale agile information systems development (AISD) has become the prevalent mode of software development at scale. However, organizations adopting it consistently report that its promised benefits fail to materialize. We argue that an underexplored source of this shortfall lies in the incongruent temporal structures large-scale AISD endogenously generates, such as iterative versus linear rhythms, layered routines, and short-term deliverables versus long-term deadlines. Drawing on temporal structuring theory, we conducted an interview study with product owners, managers, and team leads positioned at the interfaces of agile teams and layers. Our findings uncover six temporal boundaries that generate distinct tensions for teams and individuals. We offer a framework that organizes these boundaries across three abstraction levels (understanding, organizing, and performing) and explains the mechanisms through which they produce friction. The study foregrounds time as a structurally embedded but underexamined dimension of large-scale AISD, extending coordination perspectives and opening new research directions.

papers.title: Beyond Code Generation: How AI Reshapes Agile Practices in Information Systems Development
papers.abstract: The widespread use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) could significantly impact agile development approaches, which emphasize human-centered collaboration to manage volatile requirements. Using socio-technical systems and agile coordination theory as analytical lens and responses from a survey of 111 agile workers, we explore how the use of AI affects agile practices and shapes project outcomes. We analyze the responses using a mixed-method approach that combines an inductive analysis with fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analyses (fsQCA). Our findings suggest that the introduction of AI has the potential to significantly change agile practices and coordination mechanisms across the entire work system. The fsQCA results indicate how the introduction of AI can influence project outcomes. While the combined introduction of AI into all parts of the work system seems to be required to achieve productivity benefits, a joint optimization of technical and social practices does not appear to be a prerequisite to realize quality benefits.

papers.title: Tracing the Transformation: A Digital Trace Data Perspective on AI-Augmented Information Systems Development
papers.abstract: Information systems development (ISD) is undergoing a fundamental transformation as developers increasingly augment their work with generative AI. While prior research documents productivity gains from AI-assisted coding, the longitudinal effects on ISD processes and outputs in enterprise contexts remain poorly understood. This research-in-progress aims to investigate how ISD processes and outputs change as ISD becomes AI-augmented over time. We conduct an exploratory multiple-case study of two ISD units at a large European enterprise software company, drawing on longitudinal digital trace data from GitHub spanning the periods before and after the introduction of Claude Code in March 2026. Our preliminary analysis reveals two observations: (1) a substantial volume increase in commit frequency and code churn, and (2) divergent trajectories in pull request activity. We contribute to ISD research by examining how AI-augmentation reshapes both processes and outputs longitudinally in real-world enterprise settings.

papers.title: ISD as Reconfiguring Information: A Cybernetic Perspective on How IT Interventions Shape Organizational Behavior
papers.abstract: Increasingly, information systems development (ISD) extends beyond delivering information technology (IT) tools deemed satisfactory by a client to a direct commitment to achieving organizational outcome targets. This commitment makes reasoning about the effects of IT on organizational behavior a central concern. However, we have a limited understanding of how ISD efforts can reason ex ante about how IT interventions may shape organizational behavior. We draw on a basic cybernetic understanding of organizations as self-regulating systems whose behavior is shaped by information and feedback. From this perspective, ISD is an exercise in reconfiguring information to shape organizational behavior in desirable directions. On this basis, we distinguish three forms of IT interventions: blind reinforcement of behavior, possibly amplifying undesirable behavior; regulating or enabling behavior; and influencing the reference values for self-regulation, thereby shifting the direction of system behavior. We illustrate these forms through cases from a long-term research program.

papers.title: Malleable Technologies in Digital Sourcing: A Configurational Study of Outsourcing Success
papers.abstract: Malleability, the ease with which a technology can be adapted in use, is transforming how outsourcing relationships create value. Traditional IS outsourcing assumes a service boundary separating vendor technical responsibilities from client governance. Malleable technologies such as robotic process automation challenge this boundary by enabling clients to participate directly in technical adaptation. Drawing on agency theory, the resource-based view, and relational governance theory, we develop a configurational model of outsourcing success that incorporates malleability alongside governance mechanisms and client and vendor capabilities. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) on survey data from 91 outsourced automation projects with varying degrees of malleability, we identify five configurations. In early-stage relationships, malleability substitutes for relational governance. In mature relationships, client adaptation capability substitutes for vendor capabilities and formal contracts. These findings position malleability as a central construct in IS outsourcing and show how sourcing arrangements must be configured across levels of malleability.

papers.title: Measuring Contextualized AI Alignment in Organizational Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions that depend on organizational knowledge that is partly non-codified or tacit. This creates a knowledge gap between the LLM and the organization, because textual context conveys only a subset of what past organizational decisions actually drew on. We propose the Contextualized Alignment Lens Model (CALM) to provide a quantitative estimate of the alignment to the application context. CALM captures decision policies, localizes misalignment at the cue level, supports targeted prompt-based interventions, and bounds the contribution of tacit knowledge to a given decision. We demonstrate these affordances for ten LLMs making 30,000 decisions on European Court of Human Rights Article 6 cases. CALM addresses AI alignment as an organization-specific measurement problem and gives IS researchers and developers a tool to evaluate and improve the fit between LLM decisions and their sociotechnical context.

papers.title: Domain or Software? Unpacking Knowledge Specificity and its Relational Consequences in IT Outsourcing
papers.abstract: Knowledge specificity lies at the heart of how firms govern outsourcing relationships, yet decades of research have produced conflicting findings about its effects. This study argues that this inconsistency stems from treating knowledge specificity as a unidimensional construct. It revisits the construct by distinguishing between software knowledge specificity and domain knowledge specificity, which activate relational mechanisms. Drawing on transaction cost economics (TCE) and the knowledge-based view (KBV), the study theorizes and tests how these forms of knowledge specificity influence knowledge transfer, opportunistic behavior, and coordination problems. Using matched-pair survey data from 73 outsourced software projects, the findings show that software knowledge specificity is associated with greater knowledge transfer and opportunistic behavior, whereas domain knowledge specificity is associated with greater coordination problems but shows no significant association with opportunism. These results challenge assumptions and show that TCE and KBV apply under different knowledge conditions, reframing how knowledge specificity shapes outsourcing relationships.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Role of Relational Capital for Digital Resilience
papers.abstract: This research investigates how multi-unit organizations configure their relational capital alongside their in-house digital capabilities to achieve digital resilience. While digital resilience enables organizations to overcome major disruptions, the role of relational capital as a valuable resource remains contested. While resource orchestration instates its relevance, the dynamic capabilities view offers divergent findings. Employing fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, we examine the interplay between elements of relational capital and in-house digital capabilities in multi-unit organizations. Our findings reveal that high levels of digital capabilities do not preclude, but rather condition, the strategic orchestration of relational capital elements for digital resilience. In contrast, when in-house digital capabilities are not decisive, multiple elements of relational capital are jointly present. These findings contribute to the understanding of digital resilience by demonstrating that relational capital is a valuable resource, contingent on in-house digital capabilities, and offer novel insights into managing major disruptions digitally.

papers.title: Not All Adaptations are the Same: Deciphering Asymmetric Adaptation-Fit Mechanism in IT Consumerization Behavior, Thriving at Work, and Work-to-Family Conflict
papers.abstract: This study investigates how employees’ IT consumerization behavior (ITCB) influences work-family well-being. Based on adaptive structuration theory for individuals (ASTI), we argue that ITCB directly influences four post-acceptance adaptation behaviors: exploitive (exploratory) technology (task) adaptation. Moving beyond instrumental performance output alone, we extend ASTI to involve job fit and professional fit as intermediate outcomes and propose asymmetric adaptation-fit mechanism linking ITCB to thriving at work and work-to-family conflict. We tested research model by conducting a two-wave survey to collect data from 241 employees across different industries. The results show that ITCB enables these four adaptation behaviors. Among them, only exploitive technology adaptation positively influences job fit and only exploratory task adaptation positively affects professional fit. Both fit outcomes facilitate thriving at work while only job fit attenuates work-to-family conflict. This research advances the ASTI literature by revealing mechanisms that contribute to ITCB-driven adaptation dynamics and humanistic impacts across work-family domains.

papers.title: Activating Employee’s AI Literacy for Responsible Generative AI Use: A Sensitization Framework
papers.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) diffuses rapidly into organizational practice, developing employees’ AI literacy for responsible use has become a strategic imperative. However, organizations struggle to move beyond ad-hoc training toward sustained, actionable competence. Current research has mapped what AI literacy entails but left the organizational process underexplored through which these competencies become actionable. We address this gap by theorizing GenAI sensitization as an organizationally embedded process operating at the intersection of AI literacy, governance, and organizational practice. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with human resource professionals analyzed through Gioia methodology, we identify four aggregate dimensions: organizational factors, individual factors, sensitization practices, and tensions and barriers. Four structural tensions and barriers characterize conditions that explain why responsible GenAI use fails even among AI-literate employees. The sensitization profile matrix synthesizes these findings into a diagnostic framework for organizational practice, guiding employees toward responsible GenAI use.

papers.title: Mitigating Virtualization Resistance: Design Principles for Process Virtualization in Industrial Metaverse Environments
papers.abstract: Industrial work relies on embodied, situated, and socially embedded expertise that is difficult to transfer as experienced operators retire and processes become more complex. Industrial metaverse environments may support such work, but design knowledge offers limited guidance for addressing sensory, relationship, synchronism, and identification and control requirements across workflow activities. Using Process Virtualization Theory as kernel theory, we conduct three design science cycles to derive four design requirements, twelve sub-requirements, and nine design principles. We instantiate them through five workflow mockups and a Unity-based virtual reality demonstrator for quality inspection. Three focus groups assessed the requirements, principles, and mockups; fourteen practitioners assessed the demonstrator through hands-on interaction and interviews. We contribute design knowledge for configuring a persistent shared environment, real-time multi-user interaction, bidirectional cyber-physical coupling, and instrumented process capture when multiple requirements become salient across workflow activities. The findings highlight task fit, cross-requirement tensions, and user-controlled monitoring.

papers.title: When Governance Becomes Hollow: A Motivational-Psychodynamic Framework for Understanding BPM Governance Failures
papers.abstract: Although organizations invest substantially in business process management (BPM) governance infrastructure, these initiatives remain challenging. Process owner roles, governance forums, architectures and dashboards can lose their coordination function while retaining their formal appearance. Since the mechanisms producing this divergence remain underexplained, we introduce Governance Hollowing to name this phenomenon and distinguish it from institutional decoupling and symbolic compliance. We therefore extend Motivational BPM by addressing BPM governance through self-determination theory coupled with Bion's psychoanalytic concept of attacks on linking. From an exploratory analysis of eight secondary BPM cases, we derive eight attack patterns and a three-layer framework in which need frustration and the loss of linking function reinforce each other. Dilution and fragmentation are found to be the most frequently coded patterns. The construct and framework are our main contribution, calling for primary data. Because several arrangements are information-mediated, similar research can also be relevant for IS governance.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Facilitator: Towards a Micro-Foundational Capability Framework for Effective AI Implementation in Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can significantly improve organizational performance, yet many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) struggle to implement it effectively. Existing research emphasizes organizational-level capabilities but gives limited attention to the micro-level mechanisms that enact them. To address this gap, this study introduces AI Facilitator capability as a micro-foundational mechanism that helps SMEs operationalize dynamic capabilities in AI implementation. Drawing on dynamic capability theory, this study conceptualizes AI Facilitator capability as comprising business analysis skill, AI fluency, and boundary spanning skill. These capabilities support sensing, seizing, and transforming AI opportunities, enabling SMEs to embed AI into routines, achieve socio-technical alignment, and enhance performance. The study is expected to contribute to literature by positioning the AI Facilitator and AI Facilitator capability as micro-foundational mechanisms for socio-technical alignment in AI implementation and extending dynamic capability theory.

papers.title: Digital Renewal Under Extreme Constraints: Insights From a Successful Implementation of an Election Management System
papers.abstract: Digital renewal of critical IT systems is a precarious task, particularly if incremental rollout is infeasible. This paper examines such a case by studying the renewal of Denmark’s nationwide election management system. The project’s final phase occurred under extreme constraints, including a fixed nationwide transition date with simultaneous deployment across +1,300 polling stations and 98 municipalities, heightened cybersecurity risks, and very little tolerance for errors. Drawing on High Reliability Organization theory, we identify three organizing principles that capture how the involved stakeholders coordinated development and implementation of the new system while ensuring reliable execution of the election: conservative renewal (leveraging the legacy system in design), cautious renewal (shared perception of criticality and preoccupation with failure), and collaborative renewal (aligning decentralized operation with centralized IT governance). Based on these insights, we contribute a framework for organizing digital renewal under extreme constraints.

papers.title: How Inscriptions of Automating and Augmenting AI Artifacts Reshape Organizational Routines
papers.abstract: Artifacts based on artificial intelligence are reshaping organizational routines, but their effects on routines vary markedly within the dominant framings of automation and augmentation. We argue that the inscriptions AI artifacts carry drive this variation. In a longitudinal qualitative case study at a German radiology department, we examine two AI artifacts introduced concurrently into the same prostate MRI diagnostic routine, one used to automate visual prostate segmentation, and one used to augment lesion assessment. The automating artifact carried a result inscription that enabled recognition-based verification and a compressed routine performance, while the augmenting artifact carried a proposal inscription that required reconstructive verification and produced a recursive routine performance. We extend artifact-centered routine theory by specifying the function-specific inscriptions across five action dimensions through which automating and augmenting AI artifacts reshape the ostensive and performative aspects of organizational routines.

papers.title: From TOE Dimensions to Intersections: A Spiral Model of AI Adoption Mechanisms
papers.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping processes, governance structures, and value chains, its implementation in business-to-business (B2B) contexts often lags behind expectations. Existing technology adoption models typically assume linear, stage-based processes, overlooking the dynamic and intersection-based nature of AI adoption. Based on 36 semi-structured interviews, this study examines the intersections of the technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions of the TOE framework. Focusing on TOE intersections, we identify 19 mechanisms – nine constraining and ten reinforcing – that shape AI adoption trajectories. Building on these insights, we develop an intersection-based spiral model, conceptualizing AI adoption as continuous cycles of alignment and reconfiguration, moving beyond linear stage-based frameworks. By doing so, we advance a holistic understanding of AI adoption dynamics and reposition TOE research from isolated dimensions toward their intersections.

papers.title: Provisional Stabilization of AI in a Tacit-Knowledge Work Context
papers.abstract: Drawing on actor–network theory, we analyze the integration of an AI system designed to support a manual activity grounded in tacit knowledge: agricultural harvesting. Based on a qualitative case study combining six months of participant observation, interviews, and analysis of system use and adjustments, we trace the trials of translation across the moments of problematization, interessement, enrolment, and mobilization. The findings show that stabilization remains fragile: a deficit of situated explainability, the invisibilization of human mediations, and centralized algorithmic governance constrain the network's capacity to consolidate. This article contributes to the sociotechnical literature on AI in organizations by identifying the configuration of "provisional stabilization" as a durable yet precarious organizational form in which the sociotechnical network functions without consolidating, persisting as long as minimal conditions of maintenance are met, and by specifying three interrelated mechanisms: situated explainability, human mediations, and algorithmic governance that condition its production and fragilization

papers.title: Wise Guys Into Informants: An Ethnography of Adversarial Expertise
papers.abstract: Machine learning is often understood as encoding expert judgment at scale, but this presumes an answer to a prior question: whose judgment grounds the model, and against what? Through thirty months of ethnographic fieldwork at a European betting firm, I trace how an ML sportsbook came to treat the wagers of "Wise Guys," external bettors who regularly beat it, not as a threat to curtail but as expertise to harvest, calibrating its output to the judgment of the actors it competes with. I develop the concept of adversarial expertise to name this configuration: domain expertise that is external to the firm, extracted from actors who would withhold it if they could, and rivalrous, existing only in their winning against the firm. The paper contributes a new configuration of ML-mediated expertise to IS research on algorithms, expertise, and ground truth, and specifies the conditions under which it holds beyond this case.

papers.title: AI-Driven Business Process Transformation: A Case Study on Frame Construction and Dynamics
papers.abstract: Organizations integrate artificial intelligence (AI) to transform business processes, yet many initiatives fall short of expected outcomes. We argue that a critical but underexplored reason lies in the divergent technological frames through which stakeholder groups interpret AI-driven transformation. Building on Orlikowski and Gash’s (1994) technological frames perspective, we examine how IT/AI specialists, BPM professionals, and business unit members construct divergent understandings of AI integration through a case study of two AI integration projects in a global organization. We identify four frame domains–nature of AI in process work, AI strategy and organizational embedding, AI in use and process integration, and AI ownership and responsibility– and show that frame incongruences generate expectation gaps, coordination challenges, conflicting success evaluations, and accountability uncertainty. We contribute by extending the technological frames perspective with a fourth domain specific to AI, theorizing frame incongruence as causally cascading across domains, and discussing three patterns of frame reconfiguration.

papers.title: From AI Training to Human Interaction: Examining Skill Transfer in Service Communication
papers.abstract: This study examines how AI-based training, where service employees interact with AI-simulated customers, shapes communication skills and their transfer to real customer interactions. Drawing on the theory of mind perception, we propose that AI-based training enhances information provision while reducing emotional responsiveness and persuasion efforts. Using an online experiment with human-based training as the baseline, we find that AI-based training achieves comparable performance in information provision and emotional responsiveness during training. However, AI-trained participants persistently provide more fabricated information and exhibit lower emotional responsiveness when interacting with real customers. Finally, while persuasion efforts decrease during AI-based training, they do not affect trainees’ performance in persuasion when facing human customers. These findings highlight the boundary conditions of AI-based training and offer implications for designing AI-enabled training systems.

papers.title: Power in IT Renewal: How Power Dynamics Shape the Trajectory of Large-Scale System Replacements
papers.abstract: IT renewal, replacing an organization’s core digital system while the legacy system remains operational, presents organizations with challenges distinctive from greenfield system development. This study draws on Clegg’s Circuits of Power framework to understand these challenges. Through a longitudinal case study at a government organization, we examine how power flows through episodic decisions, shared meanings, and infrastructural arrangements. We find that renewal directions change when these circuits converge around obligatory passage points; nodes through which subsequent actions must pass. External interventions such as regulatory deadlines and bureaucratic external assessments reshape the rules of meaning under which internal claims are heard, enabling such convergences to form. The paper extends IT renewal theory by showing how power operates through circuit convergence as a mechanism shaping which renewal paths persist.

papers.title: Sustaining AI Innovation Process Through Repair Practice: A Comparative Case Study
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is everywhere yet remains untamed by those seeking to harness its power for organisations. While adopting multiple perspectives in efforts to unravel AI’s knots, information-systems research has largely neglected longitudinal approaches to the evolutionary process of making and sustaining innovative AI-enabled systems. To furnish in-depth understanding of how AI innovation processes unfold, a study building on two longitudinal qualitative case studies of in-house predictive machine-learning systems examined this phenomenon via the lens of broken-world thinking. The paper tackles narration of the case organisations’ AI innovation processes in terms of innovation manifested as sites of continuous repair. Theorising on how repair and innovation weave the AI-enabled systems into their contexts and sustain performance through innovation, the authors also offer recommendations for practitioners and academia.

papers.title: Recurrent AI Assemblage Forms in Radiological Interpretation Routines
papers.abstract: AI systems are expected to improve the efficiency and reliability of radiological interpretation. Prior research has examined cognitive engagement with algorithmic outputs or treated AI reading modes as stable workflow configurations. Yet we know less about how recurrent forms of AI integration are produced within the same routine. We address this gap through a qualitative study of an AI-based pulmonary nodule detection tool used in a cancer center. Contrary to expectations of stabilized integration, we find that the same artifact is recurrently assembled in three forms: sustained as a second-look verification device, desynchronized when material or clinical misalignments prevent actionability, and aligned when available as a first-look triage filter. We document a case in which these ostensively recognized forms are navigated performatively across examinations. These findings contribute to research on AI-supported organizational routines by explaining how an artifact can be recurrently enacted in multiple forms within the same routine.

papers.title: Beyond Shared Code: The Role of InnerSource Program Offices in Organizational Knowledge Production
papers.abstract: InnerSource, the adoption of open source practices within organizations, is typically justified in terms of code reuse and efficiency. Drawing on interviews with InnerSource Program Office (ISPO) practitioners across ten organizations, group interviews with the Microsoft DevOps Dojo, a case study, survey data, and community materials, this study shows that InnerSource activity is oriented toward a dual object: shared code and shared organizational knowledge, produced through the same practices. Much of this knowledge arises in pulsating knots of cross-boundary collaboration, transient encounters that dissolve once a contribution is merged, so no single activity system sustains their recurrence. We develop a typology of four ISPO roles that address this problem, creating coherence, connecting, translating, and advising, each generated from Activity Theory dimensions and directed at a distinct contradiction. The analysis explains the resourcing constraints reported in the literature as structural, arising from how the case for InnerSource is made and measured.

papers.title: Navigating Digital Timescapes in High‑Stakes Police Intelligence Work
papers.abstract: Digital technologies shape how organisations engage with time, yet temporality remains under theorised in Information Systems (IS) research. This paper investigates how digital technologies participate in the production and reconfiguration of temporal relations in police intelligence work. Drawing on a timescapes perspective, we examine intelligence activities surrounding large-scale events such as football matches and protests, where actors must navigate uncertainty, emerging information, and future consequences. Based on an interpretive qualitative case study, our preliminary findings identify five interrelated dimensions of timescapes: synchronising layered temporalities, revisable sequences, rhythm and event-time coordination, kairotic judgement, and anticipation and persistence. These findings suggest that digital technologies continuously reconnect past experiences, present developments, and anticipated futures, keeping temporal relations open to ongoing revision and reconfiguration. We conceptualise this as temporal plasticity and outline how future research will develop it into a recursive process model explaining the ongoing reconfiguration of temporal relations in digitally mediated work.

papers.title: Interfacing IT-OT in agentic digital infrastructures: A sociomaterial practice.
papers.abstract: Digital infrastructures increasingly connect information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) yet IS research has paid limited attention to how these distinct communities of practice interface. This omission is consequential as machine-learning and agentic technologies are delegated bounded capacities to sense, infer, recommend, and act, making infrastructures generative, relational, and performative. Existing boundary-object accounts, grounded largely in socio-technical or interactional socio-material perspectives, insufficiently explain how such artefacts reconfigure communities, decision making, risks, and accountability. We address this problem through a qualitative case study of a large UK property development and management organization developing agentic capabilities across its IT-OT infrastructure. Using sociomateriality as a lens, we trace how boundary objects mediate and transform interfacing practices. We conclude that interfacing is a sociomaterial practice through which technologies, communities, operational realities, and accountabilities are jointly enacted. The study contributes by theorizing boundary objects as agentic artefacts that do, act, and perform.

papers.title: Buy a Tech, or Buy a Story? The Digital Innovation–Transformation Divide in Tech M&A
papers.abstract: While technology acquisitions by non-technology firms are prevalent, seemingly similar transactions often yield heterogeneous market reactions. The theoretical distinction between digital innovation (DI) and digital transformation (DT) provides a framework to organize this heterogeneity, yet a tractable, deal-level empirical proxy has remained elusive. We argue that the digital orientation of a technology acquisition is substantiated throughout the integration period. Accordingly, we develop an empirical proxy derived from post-deal earnings-call discourse, where executives iteratively refine strategic claims, and we apply that proxy to compare how DI- and DT-classified deals are received by the market. Our analysis reveals that the specific content of tech-aspirational vocabulary, rather than its sheer volume, is systematically associated with the acquired asset's material layer. Moreover, DI- and DT-classified deals differ in observable market behavior. By operationalizing the DI/DT distinction in firm communication, this work provides a systematic instrument for tracking how digital strategy is realized through implementation.

papers.title: The Tension of Control: How Centralized and Distributed Control Are Exercised in the Smart Grid Transition
papers.abstract: This study pursues the question of how centralized control and distributed control unfold in the transition toward smart grids. To answer this question, this study adopted a qualitative interpretive case study approach to analyze energy management system implementation. Findings depict that control is exercised across three domains, including institutional, operational, and user practices. Their interplay manifests six confrontation situations representing how each domain exercises control differently. These confrontation situations reveal how the three domains confront six objects of control. Confrontation situations were shown to be the empirical entry points for infrastructural inversion, revealing invisible background activities behind infrastructure functions. This study highlighted that smart grid transition is not about a shift from centralized to distributed control, but it concerns the coexistence of control logics that require careful consideration and balance across all domains.

papers.title: Generative AI implementation and the shift of power dynamics in established organizations
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) implementation in organizations entails substantial transformation processes that can reshape existing power relations. Despite recognition of power dynamics as critical to information systems (IS) implementation, research remains fragmented, with limited attention to AI-specific contexts. This study contributes to fill this gap by investigating how AI implementation both influences and is influenced by established power structures between organizational departments. Based on 40 interviews with Chief Officers and senior managers in Italian financial institutions, we develop a processual model of GAI implementation comprising three phases: organizing for AI development, coordination, and deployment. Our findings show that GAI-driven structural changes create power imbalances, prompting incumbents to regain control over GAI initiatives. During coordination, tensions emerge between automation resistance and augmentation narratives. These tensions are resolved through negotiated, incremental adoption. The study contributes by highlighting the interplay between AI implementation and horizontal power dynamics within established organizations.

papers.title: The Devil is in the Data: How Generative AI Reshapes Data Production Processes
papers.abstract: High-quality data depends on demanding data production processes that remain reliant on manual work and domain expertise. While prior research highlights GenAI support for data cleaning, classification or integration, it mostly focuses on model performance and evaluates GenAI in benchmark or laboratory settings. We therefore know less about how these technological capabilities translate into real-world data work. We address this gap through a multiple-case study of six GenAI use cases across four multinational firms in business partner data management. Using delegation as a sensitizing lens, we identify three configurations: task guidance, bounded review, and epistemic preparation. They show how GenAI changes the distribution of work between humans and systems, human roles, oversight, and process integration. We further find that greater analytical autonomy does not necessarily imply greater decision or execution rights: more agentic systems may remain subject to human validation, while more constrained systems may receive bounded authority to act.

papers.title: The Boundaries of AI Coding Assistance: Within and Across Modules
papers.abstract: AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software development, yet their effects on software quality may depend on where programming problems arise. Drawing on software modularity research, we distinguish between defects within modules, which involve localized implementation problems, and defects across modules, which involve dependencies across software components. Using proprietary longitudinal data from a large Chinese automobile manufacturer and a matched difference-in-differences design, we find that AI access is associated with a 32.1% reduction in defects within modules, while no statistically significant reduction is detected for defects across modules. Greater AI use intensity shows a similar pattern. Analyses for each interaction mode further show that Chat use is associated with fewer defects within modules, whereas Completion use is not significantly associated with either defect category. These findings identify software module boundaries and the distribution of information relevant to the task as important conditions shaping the quality effects of AI-assisted programming.

papers.title: The Role of Realism in NPC Avatars: A Bibliometric Review and Mixed-Method Evidence Synthesis
papers.abstract: This short paper examines how visual and behavioral realism in non-player character (NPC) avatars shape user experience in immersive virtual environments. To synthesize a fragmented research landscape, we combine a bibliometric analysis of 4,750 publications with a structured evidence synthesis of 20 empirical studies. The bibliometric results indicate a rapidly growing interdisciplinary field centered on social presence, immersion, trust, and virtual character design. Across the empirical evidence base, behavioral realism such as natural movement, expressive cues, and responsive interaction shows the most consistent positive association with social presence, emotional engagement, and acceptance. Visual realism remains relevant, but its effects appear more context-dependent and can be constrained by uncanny-valley dynamics. The findings suggest that realism should be treated as a socio-technical interface design choice, with attention to interaction quality, contextual fit, and ethical safeguards against deception and emotional manipulation. The paper derives implications for designing socially credible virtual agents across contexts.

papers.title: Thinking with Chatbots: Cognitive Offloading in Human–GenAI Interaction at Work
papers.abstract: GenAI chatbots are increasingly embedded in organizational work, yet we know little about how workers rely on them when performing cognitive tasks. Drawing on cognitive offloading theory, this study examines how workers engage with GenAI chatbots in work-related contexts. Based on 20 semi-structured interviews, we identify four recurring uses: preparing written outputs, organizing task-related information, retrieving or checking information, and comparing possible options. Building on these findings, we develop a framework of GenAI-enabled cognitive offloading based on two dimensions: perceived mental effort and perceived knowledge sufficiency. The framework distinguishes four modes of offloading: routine output offloading, knowledge-gap offloading, ambiguity-resolution offloading, and augmentation-oriented offloading. Our study contributes to research on cognitive offloading and human–technology interaction by showing how GenAI chatbots shift offloading from bounded cognitive functions toward broader task components, including writing, structuring, clarification, comparison, and elements of judgment.

papers.title: Visible Peers, Invisible Stress: The Interplay of Digital Visibility, Social Comparisons, and Technostressors in Coopetitive Work Environments
papers.abstract: In coopetitive digital work environments–where collaboration and competition coexist–technology creates digital visibility where employees are constantly exposed to their peers’ achievements. Drawing on Transactional Theory of Stress and Social Comparison Theory, this study adopts a configurational perspective to examine how social comparison in such environments interacts with technostressors to shape psychological outcomes. We conducted a time-lagged survey of 1,979 employees across different industries and organisational levels. A fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) reveals that positive and negative psychological responses can sometimes ensue from counterintuitive configurations. For instance, configurations comprising both positive social comparisons (typically associated with positive outcomes) and negative social comparisons (typically associated with negative outcomes) can, alongside challenge technostressors, lead to positive psychological responses. Our study extends technostress and social comparison research by revealing the configurational pathways underpinning psychological well-being and offers practical, actionable insights for managing technostress in a coopetitive digital work milieu.

papers.title: Algorithmic Reshaping of Human Cognition: Quantifying Latent Preference Adaptation in Human-AI Collaboration via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in high-stakes decision environments, algorithms increasingly function not only as decision aids but also as normative agents that may shape users’ latent utility preferences. This study investigates dynamic preference adaptation through a financial decision-making experiment involving 212 participants and 10,600 sequential observations. Combining digital trace data with Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning, we infer time-varying utility weights and use panel regressions to examine heterogeneity in adaptation. Results show that users’ decisions and inferred utility parameters gradually converge toward the algorithmic logic, accompanied by reduced decision latency. However, prior investment experience and financial literacy attenuate this convergence, whereas higher initial trust in AI amplifies it. This study advances human–AI collaboration research by conceptualizing algorithmic influence as dynamic preference adaptation and demonstrating inverse reinforcement learning as a computational approach for recovering latent preferences from sequential interaction data.

papers.title: HUMAID: A Theory of Human Multi-AI Agent Interaction Dynamics
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) use is shifting from one-human–one-AI dyads toward interactions with multiple differentiated agents. Yet existing research does not fully explain how users coordinate and interpret visible ensembles of knowledge-producing agents. We develop the Human Multi-Agent Interaction Dynamic (HUMAID) framework, a mid-range theory explaining how agent plurality, consensus and dissensus, relational framing, and transparency shape human judgment and action. Specifically, HUMAID identifies a span of interpretation: the bounded capacity to track agent roles, provenance, interdependence, disagreement, and aggregation. Six propositions explain when additional agents create ensemble-management demands, apparent consensus produces synthetic corroboration, structured disagreement improves scrutiny, collaborative and competitive frames alter evaluation, and locally transparent agents form a globally opaque system. The framework distinguishes visible multi-agent interaction and offers a research agenda for designing comprehensible, governable AI systems.

papers.title: The Bright Side of Social Networking Sites: A Diary Study on the Effects of Observing Prosocial Behavior on Well-Being
papers.abstract: Although social networking sites (SNSs) are often associated with a wide range of antisocial behaviors, such as cyberbullying or incivility, positive interactions are frequently overlooked. While the offline environment highlights the benefits of observing prosocial acts, there is limited evidence supporting this in the online world. Through a weekly diary study over 14 weeks, we examine the connections between observing prosocial behavior on SNSs and different dimensions of well-being. Our results reveal significant between-person associations and within-person effects of observing prosocial behavior on emotional, psychological, and social well-being. Additionally, more frequent exposure to prosocial behavior was associated with a more positive view of humanity. Amid concerns about SNSs, our findings highlight the platform's positive aspects and suggest that exposure to certain content is positively associated with well-being.

papers.title: At Home with Agentic IS: Investigating Decision-Making Latitude, Perceived Control and Trust in Smart Home Control Hubs
papers.abstract: This study investigates how the decision-making latitude of agentic information systems (IS) shapes users' home management delegation intention, and the roles of perceived control and trust in this relationship. Drawing on Baird and Maruping's (2021) IS delegation framework, we conducted a between-subjects online experiment (N = 271) in which participants were randomly assigned to one of three smart home control hub representing distinct decision-making latitude levels (supervisory, anticipatory, or prescriptive). Results reveal a pattern consistent with an authorization threshold rather than a monotonic effect: perceived control was lower under prescriptive latitude than under supervisory or anticipatory latitude. Mediation analysis demonstrates that compared to supervisory latitude, prescriptive latitude influenced delegation intention through a sequential pathway consisting of perceived control and trust. The study extends agentic IS delegation research to the domestic context and provides empirical evidence for a bounded control-trust process shaping delegation intention.

papers.title: Multisensory Experiences in VR Shopping: How Haptic and Visual Cues Shape Consumer Responses
papers.abstract: VR shopping has the potential to bridge online and physical retail by enabling embodied product interaction while introducing augmented sensory cues that extend beyond physical reality. Existing research has focused mainly on visual and auditory stimuli, while direct hand-based haptic product interaction and augmented cues uniquely enabled by VR remain underexplored. Consequently, it remains unclear how these designs shape consumer perceived value and subsequent responses, and whether VR shopping should approximate physical shopping or integrate augmented sensory interaction. We conducted a 2 × 2 between-subjects laboratory experiment with 191 participants, manipulating haptic and augmented visual feedback in VR, with a matched physical condition as a control. Preliminary descriptive results show that the physical condition generally received the most favorable evaluations. Within VR, the augmented visual-only condition showed the highest means for attractiveness, entertainment, escapism, enjoyment, and evaluation value, while non-haptic conditions tended to receive more favorable evaluations than haptic conditions.

papers.title: Configuring Decision Regret: How the Number of Options Shapes Decision Regret and Its Antecedents in Product Configuration Systems
papers.abstract: Mass customization enables firms to offer extensive product variety, yet excessive choice may overwhelm consumers and impair decision making. While choice overload has been widely studied, evidence for product configuration systems remains limited. This paper develops and tests a theoretical model explaining how the number of options in product configurators affects decision regret and its antecedents. We examine the effects of option quantity on process satisfaction, outcome satisfaction, decision confidence, and decision regret. The model is tested in a laboratory experiment (N=124) in which participants con-figured a desktop computer. Results reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between the number of options and both process and outcome satisfaction, with turning points for satisfaction at approximately six options per component. Outcome satisfaction reduces decision regret, whereas process satisfaction increases decision confidence. Additionally, higher product knowledge enhances decision confidence independently of satisfaction. The findings provide actionable insights into the design of product configuration systems.

papers.title: When Interaction Breaks Down: Technique Innovation as System-Level Realignment in Continuous Human–Technology Interaction
papers.abstract: This study examines how users sustain effective interaction with assistive technologies when artifact modification is constrained and breakdowns are consequential. Prior research offers limited insight into how users develop novel interaction patterns before routinization. We introduce technique innovation as a novel, enacted interaction pattern that becomes reliable through repeated use without altering the artifact. Drawing on a qualitative multiple-case study based on 18 interviews with para-athletes, we identify 38 technique innovations and a recurring process through which they emerge and stabilize. Most identified techniques improved interaction reliability rather than enabling new actions. Our findings contribute by (1) conceptualizing technique innovation as a distinct post-adoptive behavior and (2) advancing a system-level account of interaction breakdowns, including inter-technology misalignment.

papers.title: Context Is Everything: A Behavioral Experiment of the Effects of AI Labeling and GenAI Exposure on Attitudes toward Artists and Artwork
papers.abstract: Recent media attention has been paid to how Hollywood actors, digital artists, and photographers are threatened by AI, although the negative consumer response has received relatively little attention in the IS literature. This within- and between-subjects experiment study with 262 participants investigated how consumers react to artwork created by AI both before and after they generate their own artwork using a popular GenAI tool. As expected, when AI use was disclosed, attitudes towards the artist and the artwork revealed an anti-AI bias. Also, their general attitudes about AI and profile-viewing behavior served as significant moderators of the relationship between the presence of AI labels and attitudes toward the artist. Results showed strong support that the anti-AI bias could be muted by subjects’ positive AI attitudes, but more importantly, our hypothesis that producing their own GenAI was partially supported.

papers.title: Prepared or Pressured? Coping Configurations and Technostress in AI-Enabled Work Systems
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in organizational work systems, employees face AI-related demands that can generate diverse technostress experiences. While prior research conceptualizes coping primarily as an individual and reactive response to technostress creators, limited understanding exists of how coping is configured within AI-enabled work systems and how such configurations are associated with technostress experiences. Drawing on 62 semi-structured interviews with employees regularly using AI in their work, we develop a configurational theory of coping in AI-enabled work systems. Our findings show that coping unfolds as a multilevel and temporally distributed process comprising proactive and reactive coping practices across individual and organizational levels. We introduce a coping matrix that captures the configurational architecture of coping in AI-enabled work systems and show how coping configurations are associated with recurring patterns of techno-distress and techno-eustress creators, thereby extending technostress theory beyond linear coping assumptions.

papers.title: Trap or Catalyst? Expertise in Human-GenAI Creative Work
papers.abstract: Generative AI makes creative alternatives inexpensive to produce, allowing users to either explore qualitatively different directions or repeatedly develop an existing one. We examine how domain expertise shapes this choice in human–GenAI creative work. A pilot study shows that higher expertise is associated with stronger creative performance but also with greater relative emphasis on developing existing directions. Performance exhibits a suggestive inverted-U relationship with this exploitation: refinement initially supports performance, but excessive exploitation may reduce it by displacing the search for different alternatives. Pre-interaction mental imagery offers a cognitive explanation for this shift. Higher expertise is associated with clearer task-specific imagery before the first prompt, which in turn corresponds to greater exploitation. Together, these findings suggest an Expertise Paradox: expertise helps users develop promising directions, yet may also encourage commitment before sufficiently different alternatives have been considered.

papers.title: Toward Culturally Aligned Empathic AI: A Bibliometric Review and Design Framework for Organizational Readiness
papers.abstract: Empathic AI systems are increasingly integrated into organizational workflows, yet no comprehensive framework aligns their design with organizational culture. This paper presents a systematic bibliometric review of three key areas: empathic human-AI collaboration, trust calibration in automation, and the integration of organizational culture and technology. Analyzing 555 documents from an initial collection of 13,265 records across five databases, the study identifies four structural gaps: cultural fit, trust calibration, empathic interaction style, and ethical boundary conditions. These gaps inform the design requirements for a future diagnostic readiness instrument. The proposed conceptual model enables organizations to create differentiated readiness profiles by culture type rather than a single aggregate score. This paper offers a framework and a multi-phase validation roadmap as its main contribution to information systems research and practice.

papers.title: How Anthropomorphic Design Dimensions Influence User Responses: Evidence from a Field Experiment
papers.abstract: Although organizations rely on chatbots to collect user feedback, yet little is known about  how chatbot design influences the amount and quality of user-provided information. To  stimulate  user  responses  in  human-chatbot  interactions,  organizations  increasingly  implement anthropomorphic design dimensions. Drawing on anthropomorphism theory,  we hypothesize how verbal and nonverbal anthropomorphic design dimensions  shape  user responses. We tested these effects, used as experimental manipulations, on reciprocal courtesy, interaction continuity, emotional regulation, and information depth in a field experiment with 479 users of an online grocery retailer. Our  findings confirm that, as  hypothesized,  anthropomorphic  design  dimensions  increase  reciprocal  courtesy,  and  foster  more  emotionally  neutral  responses.  Contrary  to  our  hypothesizing,  anthropomorphic design dimensions also lead to more specific and actionable feedback,  while having no  significant  effect on  interaction  continuity. Overall, our  study  refines  theorizing  on  the  effect  of  chatbots  with  anthropomorphic  design  dimensions  and  provides useful design guidance for organizations.

papers.title: Who’s Got the Power? How Generative AI Shapes Power Dynamics in Team–GenAI Interaction
papers.abstract: Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming increasingly embedded in collaborative projects, research focusing specifically on team–GenAI interaction remains scarce. Drawing on an emergent-pluralist perspective on power, this paper explores how GenAI interaction shapes power dynamics within teams. We conducted a field study involving 60 management student teams (200 individuals). Our dataset includes team diaries, ethnographic observations, semi-structured interviews, and individual reflections. We observed that GenAI’s opaque and probabilistic nature induces uncertainty, which teams address through either collective coordination or individual coordination efforts. While collective coordination enables a heterarchical redistribution of power, individual coordination is associated with the emergence of informal hierarchies. Our paper offers insights into how the same GenAI tool can lead to divergent power structures across teams, links micro-level interaction patterns to team-level power structures, and derives implications for designing GenAI-supported teamwork.

papers.title: Opposite Minds: Product Description Divergence Between LLMs and Humans
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate consumer product search, understanding how they evaluate product information relative to human consumers becomes crucial. This study investigates whether GPT and human participants diverge in how they weight product description features, specifically length and technicality. Using a 2 × 2 within-subject experiment with sunscreen product, we compared rankings from GPT-o3 agents and human participants. Results reveal a systematic preference reversal: humans favoured short, lay-language descriptions, while GPT consistently ranked long, technical descriptions highest. Mixed-effects regression confirmed significant interaction effects for both length and technicality. We introduce information-format-sensitivity bias to capture this divergence, attributing it to differences between human cognitive constraints and LLM statistical processing. These findings have important implications for generative engine optimisation, content governance, and the alignment of AI-mediated recommendations with human consumer preferences.

papers.title: Synthesizing Factors of Human-AI Trust: Preliminary Meta-Analytic Evidence
papers.abstract: Trust is central to human-AI relationships, shaping how users engage with AI-based  systems and rely on their outputs, recommendations, or actions. However, the diversity  of trust antecedents in the literature creates a critical problem: practitioners lack  guidance on which factors foster trust in AI, while scholars lack clarity on their effects  across contexts. To address this problem, we conduct a meta-analysis of 131 empirical  studies comprising 521 bivariate relationships. We synthesize antecedents of trust in AI  and categorize them into system and user characteristics, human-like and system-like  trusting beliefs, technology acceptance factors, and contextual factors.
