Preliminary  findings show that all examined antecedents are positively associated with trust in AI,  indicating that trust-building requires not only technically reliable systems but also social  and human-centered design considerations. Our findings contribute to human- technology interaction research by synthesizing evidence on AI trust formation,  structuring trust antecedents across human-AI contexts, and informing AI system design.

papers.title: Critical Engagement with Generative AI: Development and Validation of a Scale
papers.abstract: The use of large language model-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in knowledge work differs fundamentally from traditional technologies, as these systems are probabilistic models trained on vast, diverse data. Their adoption by knowledge workers necessitates “skillful navigation”. Despite prior work on “effective” and “mindful” use, existing scales provide only a partial understanding of the nuances of GenAI interaction. To address this gap, we follow MacKenzie et al. (2011) and best practices in scale development to propose a multidimensional construct- Critical Engagement with GenAI. Drawing on the literature on critical thinking, problem-solving, and skepticism, and informed by focus group insights, we conceptualize this construct as reflective and refine the items into two sub-dimensions: Thoughtful Structuring of Input and Skeptical Review of Output, using content validity. Exploratory factor analysis supports this theoretical conceptualization, which we propose to further validate by using confirmatory factor analysis, providing a foundation for measuring skillful GenAI use.

papers.title: Can AI Understand Loneliness? Socio-Emotional Affordances of AEI Chatbots, Perceived Emotional Authenticity, and Loneliness Reduction
papers.abstract: Loneliness is among the most pressing public health challenges of the 21st century, and emotionally intelligent chatbots are increasingly promoted as a scalable, non-clinical source of socio-emotional support. Information Systems research has yet to explain how the relational capabilities of such artifacts translate into well-being outcomes. Drawing on affordance theory and the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm, we theorize two socio-emotional affordances of artificial emotional intelligence (AEI) chatbots, adaptive empathy and scripted empathy, and propose perceived emotional authenticity (PEA) as the mechanism through which these affordances reduce emotional and social loneliness, with trust in the chatbot as a boundary condition. We propose a six-week between-subjects experiment with pre- and post-interaction survey measurements. The study extends affordance theory to the emotional domain and contributes a validated PEA instrument for IS research.

papers.title: Generative AI and the Reorganization of Human Cognition: The Augmented Cognitive Extension Model
papers.abstract: Generative AI is becoming integrated into human cognition, yet the mechanisms shaping this cognitive coupling remain poorly understood. Using informed grounded theory, this paper introduces the Augmented Cognitive Extension (ACE) model, which explains how sustained generative AI use reorganizes cognition through five regulatory mechanisms. These are attentional synchronization, epistemic calibration, affective attunement, risk construal, and narrative preservation. The findings reveal a three-stage developmental trajectory from Engagement through Calibration to Integration, with Calibration serving as the critical regulatory window shaping long-term cognitive coupling. Each mechanism can produce productive cognitive extension or problematic dependency. This is the stabilization–destabilization spectrum, and the same user may show stabilizing patterns in some domains and destabilizing patterns in others. ACE provides an empirically grounded, mechanism-level account of human-AI interaction and challenges binary views of AI augmentation by showing that cognitive extension and cognitive erosion emerge from the same regulatory mechanisms.

papers.title: Understanding Users’ Trust Calibration Journeys in Human-Generative AI Interaction
papers.abstract: As organizations increasingly adopt generative AI (GenAI) assistants, understanding when and to what extent users should trust them becomes critical. Although prior research has established that trust is dynamic and shaped by various factors, little is known about how the process of trust calibration unfolds over time at the individual level. To address this gap, we conducted a qualitative study based on interviews with 23 industry professionals and developed the Trust Calibration Journey (TCJ) framework. The framework conceptualizes trust calibration as an individual, dynamic, and episode-based journey, in which different types of trust calibrators trigger changes in users’ trust. These changes can improve or worsen calibration depending on whether they move users’ trust closer to or further away from the GenAI assistant’s actual capabilities. We contribute to IS research by providing novel insights into how users’ trust changes over time and how these changes affect trust calibration in human-GenAI interaction.

papers.title: Agentic Automation and the Reorganization of Human Work in Small Open-Source Software Teams
papers.abstract: AI coding agents mark a shift from workflow automation to agentic automation, in which AI systems participate as semi-autonomous collaborators in software development. While prior research has focused on productivity and efficiency, less is known about how agentic automation reshapes human work within teams. This study examines changes in team structure and work allocation following AI-agent adoption in open-source software (OSS) projects. Using a panel of GitHub repositories and a propensity-score-matched difference-in-differences design, we analyze the short-run consequences of Claude Code usage. We find no statistically detectable reduction in active human contributors. Adoption is associated with a broader functional scope of human work, with a more pronounced increase in development-heavy projects. These findings indicate that the early organizational consequences of agentic automation are reflected in the reallocation and broadening of human work, highlighting augmentation and work reorganization as important dimensions of AI-enabled software development.

papers.title: When Human Assurance Matters: Task Complexity and Pre-Interaction Expected Satisfaction in Human-AI Hybrid Service Systems
papers.abstract: Consumers frequently disengage from AI service encounters because they doubt whether chatbots can resolve their requests. Although human–AI hybrid systems provide human backup, this capability is often concealed. Drawing on Uncertainty Reduction Theory and Cognitive Appraisal Theory, we examine when human assurance—an upfront statement that users may transfer to a human if the AI cannot resolve the request—improves pre-interaction expectations. A between-subjects online experiment (N = 217) and a within-subject EEG experiment (N = 35) show that assurance increases expected system capability and expected satisfaction, with larger effects under high task complexity. Expected system capability mediates this relationship. EEG results reveal early frontal theta synchronization followed by later frontal alpha desynchronization under high complexity, a temporal pattern consistent with affective engagement and cognitive elaboration. These findings identify human assurance as a task-contingent cue that makes hybrid systems’ recourse capability visible.

papers.title: Preserving Trust in Generative AI Scientific Communication
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) introduces new uncertainties to scientific communication without necessarily causing trust breaches. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 50 multi-stakeholder participants and Gioia qualitative analysis, this study investigates trust preservation—maintaining established trust amid technological disruption. We identify a two-phase process: an assessment phase diagnosing information vulnerabilities, and an active maintenance phase featuring two strategies: creating a shared mental model and balancing autonomy and control. Human-XAI (Explainable Artificial Intelligence) symbiosis, defined through an audit-oriented explainability lens, serves as the enabling mechanism. The study extends AI trust theory and offers practical implications for trustworthy GAI-mediated scholarly communication.

papers.title: Authorization in Agentic AI: How Interaction Modality Affects Privacy Disclosure
papers.abstract: While users readily delegate tasks to agentic AI systems, these systems’ proactive requests for authorization may prompt users to grant privacy permissions impulsively, leading to subsequent regret. This study investigates how the interaction modality of agentic AI influences users’ privacy authorization decisions. Specifically, we propose that the voice-based interaction, compared with text-based interaction, increases users’ excessive privacy disclosure and intensifies their subsequent regret. We further argue that users’ perspective on AI—either as an instrument or as a collaborator—moderates the effect of interaction modality on excessive privacy disclosure. We plan to test our hypotheses through two experiments. By adopting an interaction modality perspective, our work expects to deepen the understanding of how agentic AI interfaces shape user privacy decision-making and to contribute to human-technology interaction (HTI) literature. It also expects to offer practical implications for the design of agentic AI system interactions.

papers.title: What Algorithms Leave Behind: How Automatic Matching Reshapes Worker Capability in Ride-Hailing Platforms
papers.abstract: Algorithmic management increasingly delegates work decisions to platform systems. Prior research has largely focused on immediate efficiency gains, paying less attention to the longer-term implications of sustained algorithmic delegation for workers’ capabilities. We examine this question on a South Korean ride-hailing platform, where drivers transition into and out of a franchise-based automatic matching system that substantially reduces discretion over ride acceptance. Exploiting these transitions, we examine changes in drivers’ behavior during automatic matching and after discretion is restored. Automatic matching reduces cruising time and drivers’ alignment with both recurring and unusual demand conditions. After exit, alignment with recurring demand substantially recovers, whereas alignment with unusual demand recovers only partially. Automatic matching also broadens drivers’ spatial exposure and increases earnings. These findings suggest that the longer-term implications of algorithmic delegation may differ across dimensions of worker capability depending on the opportunities for practice, exposure, feedback, and relearning that the system preserves.

papers.title: Turning the Threat Around: Restoring Online Community Engagement with Generative AI
papers.abstract: Online knowledge communities face a threat from Generative AI (GenAI): Users can obtain answers without engaging with the communities that produced the underlying knowledge. We therefore ask: Can GenAI be designed to restore community engagement, and if so, under what conditions and with what constraints? Through a Design Science Research study of IKEAhackers, an online creative knowledge community for DIY furniture modification, we develop a domain-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot and evaluate it with 20 users. We identify generative concretization as a mechanism by which GenAI helps users articulate underspecified problems and connect them to potential solutions, exposing questions about enactment. Users may then return to community sources for verification, particularly when they need experiential evidence of a solution's feasibility. We derive three design tensions and principles for restoring engagement with community knowledge. We also discuss boundary conditions related to the creative problem-solving process and the type of knowledge required.

papers.title: Algorithmic Antidotes: Heuristic-Aligned Explanations for Debiasing Judgment
papers.abstract: Cognitive biases routinely impair human judgment, yet existing debiasing interventions are often narrow in scope, resource-intensive, and difficult to scale. We advance a heuristic-centered framework for algorithmic debiasing in which algorithms augment human judgment through real-time advice and explanations aligned with the psychological mechanisms of representativeness, anchoring, and availability. Across three experiments using a bankruptcy estimation task, we test how distinct forms of algorithmic explanations mitigate errors associated with each heuristic. Example-based explanations most effectively reduce representativeness errors, whereas feature-based explanations attenuate availability-driven distortions. For anchoring, accurate algorithmic advice reduces errors independent of explanation type. These findings demonstrate that effective algorithmic debiasing depends on aligning intervention design with the cognitive mechanism producing the bias. By embedding mechanism-aligned interventions within the decision process, algorithmic decision-support offers a scalable approach to real-time debiasing and provides actionable guidance for designing systems that counter predictable failures in human judgment.

papers.title: AI Does Not Work Until It Is Made to Work: A Sociomaterial Process Model of Generative AI Value Emergence (GAIVE)
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly diffusing across organizations, yet its anticipated value often remains uneven and difficult to transfer. We treat five identified mechanisms of this GenAI value gap as interrelated tensions whose management depends on the progressive temporal stabilization of sociomaterial practices. Based on a process-oriented study of a GenAI implementation in a large European bank, we develop the Generative AI Value Emergence (GAIVE) model to conceptualize how co-produced human–AI practice configurations stabilize over time. The model distinguishes three interrelated and overlapping modes: exploration, adaptation, and consolidation. The model shows that value does not arise from GenAI use per se, but from the extent to which practices become reproducible, shared, and organizationally embedded across users and contexts. By linking situated human-AI interaction to temporally structured processes, our findings explain how task-level benefits become more consistently realizable and transferable, contributing to research on AI, sociomateriality, and value creation.

papers.title: Blame the Prompt: How Experts Attribute AI Errors in Hybrid Teams
papers.abstract: As Agentic AI integrates into knowledge-intensive workflows, organizations anticipate  unprecedented productivity, yet hybrid teams frequently underperform. To explore this  collaborative paradox, we conducted an inductive qualitative study with management  professionals to investigate how experts dynamically negotiate trust following critical AI  failures. Our preliminary findings suggest a psychological defense mechanism termed the  Internalization of Machine Error. Instead of abandoning an erring AI, experts tend to  blame their own prompts, cognitively framing the system as a mere reactive tool. When  subsequent relational trust repair fails, users appear to establish rigid cognitive  boundaries that manifest as a Knowledge Paradox, in which experts micromanage highly  verifiable tasks while risking overreliance in unfamiliar domains. Ultimately, our  emerging model suggests that such behavioral adaptations deliberately silo the AI,  potentially hindering the successful integration of Transactive Intelligent Memory  Systems in professional practice.

papers.title: Who Am I When Using AI: How AI Influences Fashion Designer Identity
papers.abstract: AI is attracting interest in IS research for its role in reshaping professional identities, work process, and skill requirements; limited research has examined these dynamics within creative industries, particularly in the context of fashion design, where designers’ identity is intertwined with work practices. This study addresses this gap through ongoing qualitative research on fashion designers in mid-luxury and luxury sectors. Findings identify three identity orientations in response to generative AI: Fixed identities are associated with resistance to technological change and risk of deskilling, where designers do not comply with emerging norms. Evolving identities reflect reskilling, as designers adopt generative AI tools to maintain professional relevance. New identities are characterised by upskilling, in which designers embrace generative AI while maintaining confidence in creativity, craftsmanship, and uniqueness. Building on this, the study outlines a research agenda to examine the role of craftsmanship in mediating the relationships among AI, skills, and professional identity in creative domains.

papers.title: Too Clear to Question: AI Summarization and Overestimation in Managerial Decision Making
papers.abstract: Generative AI summaries are increasingly used to compress complex organizational information for managerial decision making. While often framed as productivity tools, summaries are not neutral reductions of evidence; they selectively emphasize, omit, and reorganize information before judgment occurs. This paper examines whether AI summarization weakens managerial decision quality while increasing decision makers’ overestimation of their own performance. Drawing on decision support research, dual-process theory, and overconfidence theory, we argue that fluent AI summaries may encourage heuristic processing and create an illusion of understanding. We further theorize that relevant industry experience attenuates this effect by improving domain schemas and metacognitive calibration. We propose a randomized experiment in which working adults complete an information-rich managerial decision task with or without an AI-generated summary. The study aims to contribute to information systems (IS) research by reframing AI-assisted decision making as a joint problem of performance and calibration.

papers.title: Cognitive Partner or Execution Tool? How Employees’ Perceptions of Generative AI Capabilities Shape Task Performance
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) produces strikingly uneven performance returns across employees. Drawing on technology affordance theory, this study develops and tests a moderated dual-mediation model that distinguishes perceived GenAI cognitive capabilities from perceived operational capabilities, tracing how each converts into task performance through matched actualization pathways. Using two-wave matched data from 346 Chinese employees, structural equation modeling reveals that perceived cognitive capabilities translate into performance primarily through GenAI learning motivation, whereas perceived operational capabilities translate into performance primarily through GenAI proactivity. Perceived organizational GenAI readiness positively moderates both first-stage links and strengthens the corresponding indirect effects, but does not exert a uniform influence. Supplementary analyses confirm that significant mediation appears only along these one-to-one capability–mechanism pairs, with no empirical support for cross-over paths. These findings suggest GenAI's performance value is produced through capability-specific actualization processes that organizational readiness selectively reinforces, rather than prewritten in technical functions or released uniformly upon adoption.

papers.title: Following the Machine, Doubting Yourself: Behavioral Reliance and Confidence Erosion in AI-Assisted Diagnosis
papers.abstract: AI-based diagnostic systems promise to improve medical decision-making, yet little is known about how the quality of their recommendations shapes behavioral reliance and users' confidence in their own expertise. We report a between-subjects online experiment in which 74 medical professionals interpreted 15 X-ray images with support from a simulated AI whose accuracy was manipulated (14 vs. 8 of 15 correct recommendations). Accurate AI advice increased reliance and diagnostic performance but lowered participants' confidence in their unaided judgment, consistent with social comparison theory. When the previously reliable AI produced a false negative, two thirds of participants who had initially identified the abnormality abandoned their correct diagnosis. A PLS-SEM analysis shows that domain self-efficacy raises diagnostic confidence, which in turn reduces calibrated diagnostic performance under accurate AI. The findings establish reliance and confidence as separable outcomes that can move in opposite directions and identify a boundary condition of self-efficacy in human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: From Tools to Partners: A Validated Three-Factor Uses-and-Gratifications Model of Generative AI Use
papers.abstract: This study investigates the underlying gratifications driving the acceptance and use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools among adults. Drawing on a national, census-balanced survey (n=1500), we applied an iterative, bootstrapped, exploratory analysis followed by confirmatory factor analysis across 100 random splits to identify a stable latent structure of GenAI motivations. After excluding non-users and invariant respondents, the analytic sample comprised 915 GenAI users. Results consistently supported a three-factor model encompassing Utilitarian, Creative Expression, and Hedonic/Parasocial dimensions. These factors capture distinct yet interconnected motives with strong internal consistency and good model fit. The prominence of creative gratification suggests that users increasingly view GenAI not merely as a functional or entertaining tool but as a collaborative partner in ideation and problem-solving. We conclude by proposing this validated three-factor structure as a measurement baseline for future structural modelling.

papers.title: “This is not a Human”: The Effect of Transparency Interventions on the Humanization of Relational Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: The rapid growth in the use of conversational agents (CAs) for relational purposes, such as companionship, has raised concerns about psychological risks associated with their humanization. Policymakers increasingly mandate transparency to mitigate these effects, yet the efficacy of current approaches, such as informational disclaimers, remains unclear. This study examines how different transparency interventions influence users’ humanization of an emotional support CA. In an experiment with 1,144 participants, respondents interacted with the CA under four conditions: no intervention, a neutral disclaimer, a strong warning, or AI identity signaling. Results show that AI identity and the warning significantly reduce perceived anthropomorphism and social presence, whereas the disclaimer produced no notable effect. Linguistic analyses further revealed shifts in users’ communication patterns across conditions. These results challenge prevailing practices that rely solely on disclaimers and offer guidance on mitigating risk and ethical liabilities in the use of relational CAs.

papers.title: Not All Engagement Is Equal: Active-Passive Interaction Asymmetry and Reversible Disengagement in Behavior Change Support Systems
papers.abstract: Engagement with Behavior Change Support Systems (BCSS) conditions their effect, since benefit accrues through repeated interaction over months rather than any single session. Yet engagement rarely follows a simple path of continued use or abandonment, unfolding through cycles of activity, inactivity, and return that binary post-adoption models do not capture. Using 52 weeks of behavioral log data from 605 users of a persuasive mobile health BCSS, engagement is classified into four longitudinal states distinguishing sustained and episodic use from prolonged disengagement with and without return. Disengagement is often reversible: 63.1% cross the prolonged-disengagement threshold, of whom 21.5% later re-engage. The study specifies active-passive interaction asymmetry: interactions requiring self-referential enactment predict sustained engagement more strongly than passively consumed content, revealing divergence within rather than only between persuasive feature categories. This predictive value weakens as structured support is reduced, identifying a scope condition for binary post-adoption models in long-duration BCSS.

papers.title: Losing Face but Winning Fame: Social Comparison and Streamer Performance in Livestreaming Platforms
papers.abstract: Digital platforms deploy competitive features to drive engagement. We study player knockout (PK) events, a livestreaming feature in which two streamers compete on a split screen for audience gifts, conceptualized as coopetitive social comparison. Study 1 applies Double Machine Learning over 500,000 sessions and shows that PK increases gifting, engagement, and follower acquisition through cooperative audience expansion and competitive support intensification. Study 2 analyzes over 130,000 Random PK pairings. Facing a bigger opponent lowers win probability but increases gifting and follower activity, while same-category pairing increases gifting and follower attraction without affecting win probability. Viewer-source patterns reveal intensified competition of existing supporters in upward comparison and cooperative discovery in same-category comparison. Our study extends social comparison theory by showing that third-party audiences can move from passive observers to active participants and advance coopetition research by identifying comparison structure governing the competition-cooperation balance.

papers.title: When Data Becomes Reality: Effective Use Under Opacity in Sleep Tracking
papers.abstract: Effective use—defined as engaging with an information system (IS) in ways that advance users’ goals—rests on the assumption that system representations faithfully reflect an underlying phenomenon. This assumption is challenged when IS represent a domain that is opaque. Under opacity, referents may be inaccessible, and representational faithfulness can therefore not be assessed easily. We examine how effective use unfolds when referential grounding is unavailable, specifically, how users obtain and act upon representations under these conditions in the context of consumer sleep tracking, where sleep is inherently unobservable and primarily known through system outputs. Drawing on narrative interviews with 37 users, we identify three generative mechanisms—reflexive performance, objectifying subjectivity, and rationalizing experience—that produce distinct patterns of effective use. Our findings shift representational faithfulness from an objective correspondence view to a perceptive notion and extend effective use by theorizing learning distributed across humans and systems.

papers.title: Designing Engagement in Gamified Open Data Platforms: A Comparative Study of Interaction Temporality
papers.abstract: Open data platforms enable value creation from public data, yet many struggle to foster meaningful engagement. While gamification research identifies social interaction as a motivational element to encourage engagement, we still have limited understanding of how interaction temporality shapes engagement in gamified contexts. This study examines synchronous and asynchronous interactions as design choices for engagement in gamified open data settings. Using Comparative Structured Observation (CSO) approach, we compare two gamified environments that differ in interaction temporality: an asynchronous data-oriented competition and synchronous gamified colloquium sessions. The findings suggest that interaction temporality shapes how engagement unfolds: asynchronous interaction enables reflective sensemaking over time, whereas synchronous interaction enables immediate sensegiving and richer social presence cues within constrained timeframes. These trade-offs highlight how temporal interaction design shapes value-oriented engagement in open data settings. This study contributes a comparative design framework that positions interaction temporality as a design condition in gamified open data platforms.

papers.title: Should I Tell? Navigating AI Usage Disclosure in AI-Supported Interpersonal Communication
papers.abstract: AI increasingly supports interpersonal communication by helping individuals create or refine messages, raising the question of whether such usage should be disclosed to message receivers. While prior research on AI usage disclosure has focused on organizational and academic contexts shaped by regulations, disclosure in interpersonal communication remains voluntary and underexplored. This research-in-progress paper investigates which relational patterns shape AI usage disclosure in AI-supported interpersonal communication. Drawing on an exploratory qualitative study based on five semi-structured interviews, we aim to identify relational patterns structured by communication type and receiver type. Our preliminary results suggest that AI usage disclosure is perceived as irrelevant in functional communication with distant receivers, permissible in functional communication with close receivers, precarious in intimate communication with distant receivers, and improbable in intimate communication with close receivers. We will contribute to literature by conceptualizing AI usage disclosure as a relational judgment.

papers.title: Empowering and Ensnaring? Compassionate AI’s Impact on User Dependency and Empowerment When Delivering Bad News
papers.abstract: Compassionate AI combines emotional support with helping responses. It holds promise for delivering negative news while supporting user well-being. However, it may also foster unhealthy dependency. This study investigates how components of compassionate AI differentially influence affective dependency, instrumental dependency, and AI empowerment. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, we propose that perceived warmth and competence mediate these dual outcomes. A preliminary workplace experiment compared compassion to help-only conditions, showing that adding emotional support simultaneously increases affective dependency and AI empowerment. This provides early evidence for compassionate AI’s double-edged nature. Full experiments will include four conditions: compassion, emotional support only, help offering only, and control. These will test generalizability and the mediating roles of warmth and competence. Findings will inform design guidelines for compassionate AI that empower users while mitigating over-reliance risks.

papers.title: A Two-Signal Approach to Measuring Reliance on AI Assistants for Analytical Work
papers.abstract: Knowledge workers increasingly use generative AI in analytical tasks, but high textual overlap with AI outputs does not necessarily indicate uncritical dependence. We propose that behavioral text adoption and self-reported reliance on AI can be combined as a diagnostic lens for distinguishing different forms of AI-assisted work. In a study of 102 business students completing a competitor analysis with access to a conversational AI assistant, more proficient participants were less likely to use the assistant in a single-shot manner and more likely to engage iteratively. Higher text adoption was associated with higher-quality outputs, but this association weakened as self-reported reliance increased. This pattern was statistically significant under both human and LLM-based evaluation. These findings suggest that the same degree of AI text adoption may reflect different human-AI processes and suggest caution in treating text overlap alone as a marker of overreliance.

papers.title: The Dark Side of the Evaluator: How Dark Triad Traits Shape Judgments of Human-Generative AI Co-Created Ideas
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports creative work, yet human gatekeepers often undervalue AI augmented ideas. This study examines how Dark Triad traits shape evaluations of start up ideas co created by humans and GenAI. In a 2 × 2 online experiment (N = 176), we manipulated true source (human vs. human-GenAI collaboration) and disclosed label (“human generated” vs. “human-GenAI co created”) and analyzed perceived creativity, originality, and effort using OLS regressions. Ideas developed through human-GenAI collaboration received higher ratings across all three evaluation dimensions, whereas GenAI labels reduced perceived creativity and effort, even when the underlying source is experimentally controlled. The Dark Triad trait Machiavellianism predicted higher evaluations and greater AI acceptance, while Narcissism and Psychopathy showed no robust main effects but moderated labeling penalties in opposite directions. The findings highlight the “dark side” of the evaluator as a key driver of algorithm aversion in creative settings and underscore the need for personality sensitive governance.

papers.title: Professional Identity Threats: Third-Party Appraisals of GAI-Enabled Knowledge Work
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is changing the role of knowledge workers, with implications for professional identity. While identity threats can emerge internally, professional identity is also socially constructed. To examine how GAI shapes identity through social evaluations, we draw on identity threat theory and study journalism, a profession dependent on audience judgments. We conducted an experiment in which participants were assigned to one of four GAI-enabled work practices defined by agency (automation vs. augmentation) and task centrality (core vs. peripheral), or to a control condition (no GAI). Participants read a scenario describing a fictitious news organization’s use of GAI and a standardized news article, then evaluated the organization, the journalist, and the article. Results indicate that automating core journalistic tasks is associated with higher audience-driven identity threats, and that GAI use elicits greater identity threats than manual work, irrespective of agency or task centrality.

papers.title: Devil’s AI Advocate: Understanding Affective and Cognitive Outcomes of AI Dissent in Team Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Dissent can improve team decisions, but its social costs often prevent human team members from voicing it. AI agents could help introduce dissent into team discussions, yet its effects may depend on how it is initiated. This study examines how proactivity and politeness of AI dissent shape affective and cognitive reactions. In a 2 × 2 vignette-based online experiment (N = 391), we found that proactive dissent increased perceived self-threat, whereas polite dissent reduced it. Self-threat, in turn, mediated the effects of both design features on willingness to work with the AI agent. Reactive and less polite dissent were found to increase decision reconsideration intention. These results extend emerging research on AI-enabled dissent by showing that its effects depend on how dissent is initiated and framed within an interaction. The study highlights a central design challenge between reducing affective costs and preserving the epistemic benefit of AI dissent.

papers.title: Ambient Connected Presence: Why Do Individuals Continuously Share Location Data With Each Other and How Does It Change Their Relationships?
papers.abstract: Continuous location sharing (CLS) has become a constitutive element of how individuals sustain ties with close others, yet its relational consequences remain underexplored. Drawing on a 14-day experience sampling study with nine dyads of peers and romantic partners, complemented by semi-structured individual interviews, this study inductively develops the theoretical model of ambient connected presence. The model comprises three phases: a goal-directed initial adoption motivated by the dyadic logistical need for coordination and the emotional need for reassurance, a habitualization stage in which CLS persists through silent practices, and the emergence of intended and unintended relational outcomes, including communication substitution and control ambivalence. Introducing a nuanced understanding of moving location coordinates into a silent phatic act that sustains relational presence without deliberate communication, we theorize how passive, automated visibility reconstitutes relational dynamics. We conclude with implications for users, designers, and regulators of location-based services.

papers.title: Beyond Rational Mediation: The Selective Behavioural Adoption Framework for AI Financial Tool Adoption
papers.abstract: Robo-advisors could democratise institutional-grade wealth management, yet institutional adoption exceeding 90% coexists with individual adoption near 5%. Rational adoption frameworks yield mixed findings on this paradox, pointing to theoretical inadequacy: frameworks developed in organisational contexts with distributed risk and institutional support cannot accommodate individual high-stakes decisions where personal capital vulnerability activates affective rather than deliberative processing. We advance the Selective Behavioural Adoption Framework, positioning behavioural finance as theoretical replacement rather than supplement. Proof-of-concept PLS-SEM analysis (N = 151) indicates that trust exerts a substantial direct effect on adoption and reduces all three psychological barriers examined, yet only financial uncertainty mediates the trust-adoption relationship, with ambiguity aversion and social influence remaining psychologically active but behaviourally inert. Digital literacy demonstrates an expertise backfire effect, amplifying rather than mitigating financial uncertainty's negative influence on adoption. Full confirmatory validation with construct separation is planned.

papers.title: When Membership and Participation Diverge: An Empirical Investigation into Cross-Group Participation in Online Health Groups
papers.abstract: Although online platforms often organize interaction through formally defined groups, users frequently participate beyond the boundaries of the group to which they belong. Drawing on a social capital perspective, this study examines cross-group participation in an online health platform where users belong to exactly one group but may freely post messages in other groups. The results show that users who participate across groups are less likely to exit their focal group, and that groups receiving external member participation experience higher subsequent message activity. These findings suggest that engagement in digital groups should not be understood only through a bounded-group view centered on internal member dynamics. In platforms with permeable group boundaries, engagement may also be sustained through participation flows across groups. This study extends research on online community engagement and digital health interventions while offering actionable implications for platform design in health behavior support contexts.

papers.title: Trust but Verify: Understanding Consumer Responses to Generative AI Review Summaries
Examining the Role of User Knowledge Contribution Portfolios in Their Responses to Generative AI Shock
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes knowledge-sharing communities by lowering barriers to knowledge contribution and improving efficiency, while also raising concerns about reduced user engagement and deterioration in content quality. Yet, existing research has not reached a consensus on how users respond to this technological shock in terms of both the quantity and quality of their contributions, despite highlighting substantial user heterogeneity. To address this gap, we adopt a portfolio perspective to uncover the complexity underlying user responses by conceptualizing knowledge contributions as the allocation of limited resources, such as effort, across domains to build social capital with heterogeneous returns. We aim to examine how users’ ex-ante portfolios condition their responses by shaping adjustments in expected returns, leading to differential behavioral changes. A preliminary study using data from a large knowledge-sharing community provides initial insights. This study enriches the theoretical understanding of knowledge contribution behavior and offers practical implications for managing GenAI.

papers.title: When AI Evaluates:  Emotional Pathways to Willingness to Pay
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly evaluates and selects content, shaping what users ultimately encounter. We examine whether content selected through AI evaluators differs from human-selected content in downstream emotional responses and willingness to pay (WTP). Professional experts created five text-based advertising storyboards, of which 176 human evaluators and nine LLM-based AI evaluators independently rated for emotional impact. The highest-rated storyboard from each source was used in a 2 × 2 experiment crossing selection source (AI-selected vs. human-selected) and media format (text vs. visual) with 713 participants. Participants exposed to AI-selected content reported stronger emotional responses and higher WTP, and mediation analysis identified a significant indirect pathway through emotion. Media richness did not consistently enhance WTP. These findings conceptualize AI evaluation as a selection process and identify emotion as one downstream pathway linking AI-based selection to economic valuation.

papers.title: May AI Be With You: A Star Wars Study of Human and AI Biases
papers.abstract: Biases are central to human decision-making, and their role grows more relevant as Generative AI enters judgment-intensive domains. This pilot study examines the halo effect in human participants and large language models (LLMs), testing whether AI reproduces or diverges from human judgment. We used a fictional, abstract persona – a Star Wars commander – to isolate impression formation from the accountability pressures of judging real individuals, such as job candidates. Assigning the character to a fleet (Imperial vs Rebel) served as a proxy for perception (villain vs hero), complemented by open-ended responses. No clear halo effect emerged in the binary measure, yet human and LLM decisions differed significantly, and qualitative findings revealed subtle bias patterns not captured quantitatively. LLMs appeared less prone to halo effects but reasoned differently, suggesting AI’s susceptibility may hinge on the evaluation’s stakes and realism – a boundary condition future HR research should test.

papers.title: When Online Shops Start Chatting: Exploring Design Requirements for Conversational Online Shops
papers.abstract: Conversational agents are becoming integral to e-commerce, reshaping how consumers search, compare, and purchase products. As large language models (LLMs) advance, companies increasingly integrate conversational assistants into online shops, creating hybrid interfaces that combine chat with traditional search, filter, and navigation elements. Yet, it remains unclear how such designs influence user behavior and decision-making. In the problem awareness phase of a design science research (DSR) project, we reviewed existing conversational shops and developed a hybrid conversational shop prototype featuring an LLM-based assistant for white goods. Using attention allocation theory and the theory of effective use, we examined the prototype’s impact in a mixed-method study involving eye-tracking, behavioral metrics, subjective assessments, and interviews. Findings indicate that conversational shopping reduces efficiency but maintains effectiveness compared to traditional shops. The paper contributes design knowledge for this emerging problem space and proposes five design requirements for creating conversational online shops that support effective use.

papers.title: From Compassion to Contribution: How Empathy and Perceived Urgency Shape Online Fundraising Performance
papers.abstract: As digital fundraising platforms expand, nonprofit fundraising increasingly relies on multimodal project presentations to solicit contributions. Drawing on empathy theory and urgency theory, this study examines how two empathy-related appeal features—individuation and negative sentiment—shape fundraising performance, and how perceived urgency conditions their effects. Based on a large-scale dataset of 38,947 projects from GlobalGiving, we applied computational text analysis and computer vision techniques to capture the textual and visual manifestations of these appeal features and used LLM-based annotation to measure perceived urgency. Multi-way fixed-effects estimations showed that both appeal features were positively associated with fundraising performance. Urgency showed asymmetric moderating effects on text-based features, weakening the positive effect of individuation while strengthening that of negative sentiment. This study contributes to the digital charitable fundraising literature by theorizing and demonstrating the contingent effectiveness of appeal features in multimodal fundraising presentations. Practically, it provides guidance for fundraisers in designing online appeals.

papers.title: Appropriating the Worker through AI? The Impact of Worker AI Models and Their Governance on Workers and Platforms
papers.abstract: Digital work platforms train AI models on individual workers and deploy them as what we call Worker AI Models, which act in the worker’s place. Platform governance literature treats AI as a tool for managing workers, but Worker AI Models take over part of workers’ value creation. We ask how workers respond to this datafication and how their responses shape platform participation. We theorize Worker AI Model ownership and autonomy as governance dimensions and manipulate both in a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment. Platform-owned models raise perceived organizational exploitation, while high-autonomy models raise self-threat from AI. Both raise the intention to opt out; only perceived organizational exploitation raises the intention to leave the platform. Workers thus leave not because the model takes over their work, but because the platform owns it. Platforms must govern not only what the AI does, but workers’ control over the value created from their datafied work.

papers.title: Fluent but False: The Oversight-Correction Gap in Generative AI Verification
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in knowledge work, requiring users to verify  fluent but error-prone outputs. We report a preregistered between-subjects experiment  with 280 participants from a university-centered convenience sample who verified three  AI-generated summaries containing planted surface, logic, and hallucination errors.  Participants received standard usage or one of three cognitive-forcing implementations:  a 20-second delay, pre-AI source notes, or a post-exposure category checklist. No  intervention detectably improved error detection in this continuous-text task; the pooled  contrast was near zero (d = −0.033, 95% CI [−0.293, 0.226]). Checklist and Decision First  increased task time, while Checklist increased self-reported critical evaluation; yet 51.3%  of error-linked checklist flags were not accompanied by error correction. These findings  establish, within this task, that oversight and effective correction are empirically  separable outcomes. They document an oversight-correction gap and motivate task intervention fit as a candidate boundary condition for cognitive forcing functions.

papers.title: The Status Motive for AI Adoption on Review Platforms
papers.abstract: This study examines whether renewable platform status recognition shapes contributors' adoption of generative AI and how AI-detected reviews differ in production characteristics and audience reception. Using Yelp's annually reassessed Elite program, I construct a fuzzy regression discontinuity design around a machine-learning-based predicted eligibility cutoff. Receiving Elite recognition increases subsequent AI-detected reviewing among users near the cutoff, with the effect concentrated among users who had no prior Elite experience before ChatGPT. These newly entering Elite users also exhibit larger increases in review count and review length, and the adoption effect strengthens near annual reassessment. Complementary review-level analyses show that AI-detected reviews are longer and more difficult to read, while receiving fewer helpful votes. Together, the findings show that renewable status incentives can shape technology adoption and create a production-reception tension between scalable contribution and audience-perceived value.

papers.title: Why the Elderly Show Resistance to Continued Use of AI-Powered Exercise Technologies?
papers.abstract: AI-powered exercise technologies are viewed as promising tools for supporting healthy aging, and their value depends largely on continued use. This study examines why the elderly may resist the continued use of AI-powered exercise technologies. Drawing on person-environment fit theory, we investigate misfits between the elderly’s values and the demands and supplies of exercise technologies. Phase 1 involved interviewing 30 elderly people and conducting two focus groups with HCI experts. We identified affordance intelligibility misfit, socioemotional misfit, and content-relevance misfit to explain why exercise technologies may fail to lead to sustained use. In Phase 2, we will apply fsQCA to examine how configurations of the misfits affect the outcome. This study contributes to the literature on continued use and the PE fit theory by extending it to the application of exercise technologies among the elderly. Practically, the findings offer design implications for exercise technologies that better align with the elderly.

papers.title: When Perfect Language Backfires: The Impact of Linguistic Accuracy on Review Helpfulness
papers.abstract: Traditional wisdom suggests that greater linguistic accuracy enhances the helpfulness of online reviews. With the rise of genAI, reviewers can now easily polish or even generate highly accurate text, making near-perfect language increasingly prevalent and often presumed to increase a review’s impact. Departing from this view, this study draws on attribution theory to propose that linguistic accuracy exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with perceived helpfulness in the genAI era. Using a dataset of 50,949 Yelp restaurant reviews collected after the release of ChatGPT, the results show that the accuracy of grammar, punctuation, and capitalization follows this inverted U-shaped pattern, whereas spelling does not. A follow-up experiment replicates the effect and uncovers the underlying mechanism: improvements from low to moderate levels of linguistic accuracy enhance helpfulness because they are attributed to human effort, whereas further increases from moderate to high levels reduce helpfulness because they trigger attributions of AI involvement.

papers.title: Antecedents and Outcomes of Cognitive Offloading in Human-GenAI Collaboration
papers.abstract: The powerful capabilities of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) applications enable working professionals to collaborate with these applications and offload cognitive effort during task execution, to improve work efficiency and performance. However, excessive cognitive offloading to GenAI may reduce users’ task engagement, weaken independent problem-solving, and foster long-term reliance. To better understand this user behavior, our study explores antecedents and outcomes of cognitive offloading in human-GenAI collaboration, in the context of academically focused knowledge work. We conducted interviews with 45 professionals at a business school within a U.S. public university and proposed an inductive model linking antecedents and outcomes of cognitive offloading in human-GenAI collaboration from our data. Theoretically, our study provides a preliminary conceptualization of cognitive offloading in human-GenAI collaboration and explains the rationales and consequences underlying users’ cognitive offloading decisions. Practically, our findings offer GenAI users with valuable implications for collaborating with GenAI efficiently and effectively in work settings.

papers.title: When Less is Worse Than More: AI Assistance Intensity and the Disengagement Zone in Writing
papers.abstract: AI writing assistants increasingly perform revision work, yet research commonly treats AI-generated revisions as a single acceptance rate. We argue that the mode of engagement matters more than aggregate acceptance because writers may evaluate changes individually, adopt AI-generated text wholesale, or disengage from the revision process entirely. In an ongoing randomized field experiment, 66 participants were blindly assigned to light, balanced, or deep assistance conditions, under which an AI assistant proposed revisions and user engagement was captured through interaction logs. Per-change acceptance was highest under light assistance and lowest under balanced assistance, with deep assistance falling in between, while disengagement was particularly pronounced in the balanced condition. We interpret this pattern as a displacement-without-exchange zone, in which moderate assistance may reduce writers’ sense of ownership without providing sufficient perceived benefit to motivate engagement. The sample is preliminary, so these patterns should be interpreted as directional.

papers.title: When Competence Matters: Rethinking Warmth in LLM-Based Conversational Agents for Prosocial Decisions
papers.abstract: As conversational agents increasingly support morally consequential decisions, it remains unclear whether anthropomorphic design promotes prosocial behavior. Integrating self-humanization theory with the stereotype content model, we examine how anthropomorphic cues shape perceived warmth, perceived competence and, in turn, algorithm aversion and prosocial behavior. In a preregistered, incentivized between-subjects experiment, 521 participants interacted with either a human-like conversational agent, a computer-like conversational agent, or a static text-based control before allocating money to an animal-related charity. Anthropomorphic cues increased both perceived warmth and perceived competence. However, only perceived competence was significantly associated with lower algorithm aversion and higher donation amounts, though the two paths did not differ significantly. Exploratory mediation analyses indicated an indirect association of anthropomorphic design with donations through competence. These findings qualify the presumed primacy of warmth in prosocial contexts and identify perceived competence as a pathway through which anthropomorphic conversational agents may support prosocial behavior.

papers.title: Before Reliance: Perceived Verification Potential in GenAI-Generated Outputs
papers.abstract: Reliance-centered explanations of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) use explain why users trust, evaluate, or accept GenAI-generated outputs, but not why they treat scrutiny as meaningful rather than futile. We introduce perceived verification potential (PVP): an inferred capacity assessment of whether the system-output-task context provides a basis for verification and whether what users learn can inform reliance. Drawing on Signaling Theory, we theorize that epistemic transparency signals and epistemic opacity signals shape PVP under information asymmetry. PVP, in turn, explains vigilant use as self-reported scrutiny-oriented engagement with GenAI-generated outputs rather than passive acceptance. We propose a 2×2 between-subjects experiment with employed adults to test this signaling chain. The model shifts explanations of GenAI engagement from whether users rely on outputs to whether they see outputs as claims that can be checked before reliance. Without PVP, reliance remains a decision about accepting an output. With PVP, it becomes conditional on scrutiny.

papers.title: Bonded by the Coin: How Artist Token Issuance Reshapes Audience Engagement on a Decentralized Music Platform
papers.abstract: This study explores how a creator-initiated relational commitment, via Artist Coin issuance on a decentralized music platform, affects audience engagement. Using transaction-level and audience data from Audius, along with a stacked difference-in-differences approach and propensity score matching, the analysis finds that coin issuance significantly boosts artist play counts, with effects lasting beyond coin holders. Engagement is notably higher among low-visibility artists, indicating the mechanism doesn't worsen the industry's long-tail distribution. The results show that coin issuance expands the total number of listeners without changing per-listener consumption, affecting the extensive but not the intensive margin. These findings advance understanding of audience engagement in creator economies, shedding light on creator–audience bond dynamics and positioning tokenization as a relational infrastructure rather than merely a financial tool.

papers.title: To Skip or Not to Skip: The Double-Edged Sword of AI-Generated Video Summaries in Utilitarian and Hedonic Contexts
papers.abstract: As AI-generated summaries (AIGS) increasingly transform video consumption, their effects on users’ cognitive perceptions and subsequent behaviors remain underexplored. Drawing on affordance theory and task–technology fit theory, this paper examines how different AIGS interaction forms—no AIGS, plain-text AIGS, and timestamp-enabled AIGS—shape user experiences across utilitarian and hedonic contexts. Based on a pilot online experiment that combines subjective perception surveys with objective system logs, preliminary findings reveal the double-edged effects of AIGS. Timestamp-enabled AIGS enhances perceived utilitarian value under a utilitarian orientation but reduces perceived hedonic value under a hedonic orientation. Moreover, initial evidence suggests that timestamp-enabled AIGS may impair objective knowledge acquisition performance, consistent with a cognitive offloading explanation. This research is expected to contribute to the AI-enabled media consumption literature by showing how AI affordances generate both value-enhancing and value-undermining effects in rich media contexts and offer implications for intent-aware interface design on video platforms.

papers.title: From Solo to Social: Access-Based Promotions and Subscription Conversion on Music Streaming Platforms
papers.abstract: Digital music platforms increasingly combine access-based promotions with synchronous social consumption, yet little is known about whether promotional effectiveness changes across listening contexts. We examine a limited-time full-access trial that simultaneously provides complete access to VIP songs and restricts that access temporally. Using two large-scale randomized field experiments involving nearly 50,000 users of a leading music streaming platform, we compare subscription responses in individual- and social-listening settings. The intervention significantly increases VIP subscription in individual listening but produces no significant average effect in joint listening. We theorize that this difference reflects value–restriction alignment: premium-content access is central to individual listening value, whereas social listening also generates value through interaction with the listening partner. We further consider partner type—friend versus platform-matched stranger—as a boundary condition. The study contributes to digital-promotion and platform research by showing how access-control and synchronous co-consumption affordances jointly shape subscription conversion.

papers.title: Invisible Redistribution: How Virtual Queues Increase Nearby Transactions Without Detectable
papers.abstract: Virtual queue (VQ) systems free consumers from standing in line while they wait for a table, yet where those released consumers go remains largely unexamined. We introduce algorithmic tethering to characterize this consumer-algorithm relationship and derive its economic implications. Using VQ's staggered adoption across 273 Busan restaurants (2022–2023), we estimate its effect on neighboring commerce with a difference-in-differences design. Adoption increases the number of transactions at neighboring establishments within 150 meters by approximately 7 percent, with no detectable effect at 250 meters or beyond. Effects on neighboring sales amount and average ticket are statistically indistinguishable from zero, indicating additional purchase occasions rather than higher spending per transaction. Effects on visitor, resident, and workplace population measures are also indistinguishable from zero, a decoupling we term invisible redistribution. Our findings extend retail-spillover theory to algorithmically mediated consumer behavior and inform platform governance and externality measurement.

papers.title: Why Do Employees Hide Their AI Use? A Disclosure Threat Model of Shadow AI Use
papers.abstract: Shadow AI use has emerged as a defining feature of generative AI, where employees increasingly conceal AI use. As generative AI takes on cognitive work that signals employees’ competence and effort, disclosing AI use has become a distinct interpersonal risk. When employees hide their AI use, organizations lose visibility into where AI adds value and introduces risk. Understanding why employees conceal AI use is therefore important. Grounded in psychological safety theory, our model identifies three individual-level perceived disclosure threats arising from distinct sources: AI competence attribution threat, AI-induced role threat, and AI governance uncertainty threat. These threats reduce psychological safety to disclose AI use and, in turn, drive shadow AI use. We also distinguish routine and cognitive tasks. To test the model, we plan a scenario-based experiment and a two-wave field survey within an organization. Upon completion, we expect the findings to yield significant implications for research and practice.

papers.title: Aligning Stakeholder Purpose to Foster Engagement in Online Communities
papers.abstract: While organizations increasingly create and sponsor online communities to advance their goals, many nascent communities fail because they lack meaningful user engagement. We argue that misalignment between organizational and member purposes is a critical but overlooked determinant of early engagement. Drawing on sensegiving and sensemaking, we propose a framework of purpose alignment organized around stakeholder configuration, motivational goals, and functional enactment. We define purpose alignment as an ongoing process through which community stakeholders develop, negotiate, and enact sufficiently compatible understandings of what the community is for and how it should function. When sufficient alignment fails to emerge, members are less likely to experience the meaning, relevance, and belonging needed to sustain participation. We conclude by proposing a research agenda to empirically refine the framework, with implications for theory on user engagement and for the design of digital environments that foster sustained participation.

papers.title: Push or Pull: AI Advice Initiation in Service Work Under Customer Incivility
papers.abstract: AI service copilots deliver advice reactively, when employees ask, or proactively, without a request. Deployments treat initiation as an implicit default rather than a design variable. Yet advice initiation allocates agency within AI-augmented work, creating a trade-off between an authorship pathway shaping experienced responsibility and an instrumental pathway shaping reliance and performance under demanding interactions. In a 3 (no advice, reactive, proactive) × 2 (civil, uncivil customer) between-subjects experiment, 176 participants with customer-facing experience handled a simulated voice call. Reactive advice lowered negative agency relative to proactive advice, indirectly increasing experienced responsibility regardless of incivility. Reactive and proactive advice performed similarly under civil customers, whereas proactive advice outperformed reactive advice under uncivil customers, with AI reliance as a possible pathway. We position advice initiation as a design variable allocating agency within augmentation and show that partially automating advice access can improve performance under incivility while weakening employees’ sense of authorship.

papers.title: Managing Information Cascades through Review Tags in Online Shopping
papers.abstract: Online shopping creates a paradox: consumers may follow others’ choices even when those choices conflict with their preferences, leading to regret or returns. An information cascade (IC) occurs when social information overrides private information, and consumers discount their own judgment. This research examines whether review tags, a platform-controllable review-summary feature, can steer IC in online shopping. Across four online experiments using realistic simulated shopping websites, we test whether review-tag volume strengthens IC as an indirect social-information cue, review-tag diagnostic weakens IC by reducing private-information acquisition costs, and their interaction shapes IC occurrence. We further test whether an IC-facilitating environment increases post-purchase regret and returns. By assigning the same private information to all participants and identifying choices that conflict with it, we reduce spurious IC and directly capture true IC. This research is expected to advance ICT by clarifying how platform-controllable review-tag features can manage IC occurrence and its post-purchase consequences.

papers.title: How the Design of Explanations Affects Intentionality Attributions and Appropriate Reliance in AI-Augmented Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Explainable AI research increasingly advocates interactive natural-language explanations to support appropriate reliance, yet dialogical designs may also alter how users interpret an AI system's intent. Drawing on attribution theory, this short paper proposes that interactive explanations heighten perceived humanness, thereby strengthening intentionality attributions — more strongly for perceptions that the system seeks to persuade than to assist — ultimately impacting reliance behavior. Additionally, decision-makers’ Locus of Control conditions whether perceived humanness is read as assistance or persuasion. Using a between-subjects online experiment in a deception-detection task, we compare recommendation-only, static explanation, and interactive explanation conditions and measure behavioral reliance on correct and incorrect AI advice. The study contributes to explainable AI research by showing how explanation design affects assistive and persuasive attributions of intent, which shape reliance behavior.

papers.title: AI Workforce Architecture and Digital Innovation: Complementarity, Governance, and the Value of Balance
papers.abstract: Firms with comparable artificial intelligence headcounts can distribute that talent very differently across the functions AI work requires. We distinguish Invention, Application/Design, and Scaling/Governance roles and link Revelio Labs workforce data to Compustat and KPSS patent data for 3,236 publicly traded U.S. firms from 2012 to 2022. In firm and year fixed-effects Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) models, the Invention × Application/Design staffing interaction is associated with broader digital technology scope and entry into new digital subclasses, but not with greater patent volume. The relationship with forward citations is stronger where Scaling/Governance staffing is higher, and firms with more balanced role composition exhibit broader exploratory search. Alternative taxonomies and specifications yield the same pattern. For research on digital innovation and AI capability, this locates one source of innovation heterogeneity in the architecture of the AI workforce: which functions a firm covers, and how they combine.

papers.title: Closed No More: How DeepSeek-R1 Reshaped the Productivity, Direction, and Openness of AI Innovation
papers.abstract: Open foundation models make trained capabilities reusable even when the processes that produced them remain only partially reproducible. We theorize this configuration as asymmetric openness and examine its consequences around DeepSeek-R1. Using a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences design on 3,787 Hugging Face organizations, we find that organizations with greater pre-event text-generation relatedness increase release volume and redirect their portfolios toward DeepSeek-derived and distilled models after R1; they also increase the permissive-license share across their overall release portfolios. These patterns reveal capability-based generativity: accessible weights expand follow-on production without equivalently lowering the cost of developing an independent alternative. The result is an openness–dependence paradox—greater ecosystem output accompanied by stronger concentration around a shared technical lineage. Prior related knowledge conditions which organizations can exploit this opportunity.

papers.title: Leveraging Intrinsically Interpretable Machine Learning for Startup Success Prediction
papers.abstract: Venture capital (VC) decision-making increasingly relies on data-driven approaches to reduce uncertainty in startup investments. However, while advanced machine learning models offer high predictive performance, their opacity limits transparency and trust. This study examines whether intrinsically interpretable machine learning (IIML) models, particularly advanced generalized additive models (GAMs), can achieve competitive performance while preserving interpretability. Following the knowledge discovery in databases process, we use data from 20,172 early-stage startups and compare advanced IIML models with traditional IIML models and black-box models in terms of predictive performance and functional interpretability. We further investigate the domain adaptability of advanced IIML models regarding interaction effects and monotonic constraints. Among other findings, our results show that IIML models achieve predictive performance comparable to black-box models while providing insights into key drivers. The study highlights the practical value of GAM-based approaches for VC decision support and contributes to research at the intersection of IIML and finance.

papers.title: Innovations Under Fire: Strategic Responses to Patent Trolls in Digital Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Innovation is vital to societal progress and economic development, yet it often takes place within a complex network of relationships and market dynamics. This study highlights the adverse effects of patent trolls—entities that exploit intellectual property rights to pursue litigation without contributing to technological advancement. Through a comparative case study of GNOME and Valve, two contrasting digital innovators, we examine how they respond to predatory patent assertions by Rothschild, a prominent patent troll. Our findings indicate that these conflicts extend beyond legal disputes, significantly influencing resource allocation, community mobilisation, and organisational strategy within innovation ecosystems. The study therefore emphasises the need to re-evaluate the intellectual property landscape to ensure that it more effectively supports sustainable innovation.

papers.title: Layered Temporality in Digital Service Innovation
papers.abstract: This paper develops a temporal perspective on digital service innovation by introducing layered temporality, defined as temporal differentiation across interdependent digital, organizational, infrastructural, and institutional layers. We argue that temporal differences across these layers are not inherently problematic but become consequential when digitally enabled recombinations depend on developments in another layer that are temporally out of step with what the recombination requires. We conceptualize such consequential temporal differences as temporal misalignment and examine how actors respond through temporal work. We outline an ongoing empirical study in the Finnish construction sector that will refine this framework. The paper contributes to digital service innovation research by theorizing the development of digitally enabled recombinations as a temporal accomplishment and to IS research on temporality by explaining how cross-layer interdependencies shape when temporal differences matter and how actors respond to them.

papers.title: CIO as Bricoleur: Fostering Organizational Agility Through IT Bricolage
papers.abstract: Organizational agility is critical in volatile digital environments, yet prior research often assumes firms can readily know and access the resources needed to build such capabilities. In practice, CIOs operate under constraints that limit conventional approaches to capability development. Drawing on Bricolage perspective, this study examines how CIOs leverage existing resources to achieve agility under such constraints. We develop a model in which CIO strategic decision-making authority, business knowledge, and network resources enable IT bricolage, thereby enhancing organizational agility. We further examine the moderating role of TMT trust in shaping this relationship. Using matched survey data from 218 CIO–TMT pairs and SEM, we find that IT bricolage enhances agility and links CIO resources to outcomes, with its effect strengthened by TMT trust. This study introduces bricolage as an improvisational mechanism connecting CIO resources to agility and highlights the enabling role of trust.

papers.title: The Artificial Intelligence Innovation Wager: How Organizations Integrate Artificial Intelligence into Product Innovation Processes
papers.abstract: How do firms integrate AI into their product innovation processes? Drawing on insights from a multiple-case study of eight firms that build AI-enabled physical products, we identify four main findings: AI accelerates and broadens the innovation process. AI-enabled products create a data-product intelligence loop. Firms couple and decouple units to organize AI work. Leaders treat AI investment as a wager because of the difficulty of calculating its returns. Based on the findings, we develop a multi-level model encompassing four propositions and four feedback loops. A data paradox constrains the loop: product data grows rapidly, but few firms can translate it into design choices. Individual champions, not formal structures, carry the coupling work that AI demands. Our results guide leaders who fund AI innovation under deep uncertainty. The model shows where innovation theory breaks down when AI is both the tool and the outcome of innovation.

papers.title: Individuals’ Minds as an Empirical Site in Digital Innovation Research
papers.abstract: Digital innovation is celebrated for its productivity gains and business value creation, yet its pervasive influence increasingly raises concerns about its negative consequences for society, especially for individuals. Beyond organizational perspectives, less is understood about individuals as stakeholders affected by digital innovation. Addressing this concern, this study examines what cognitive associations individuals hold toward digital innovation–if any–combining explicit self-report measures with a single-category implicit association test across four dimensions: evaluative valence, value orientation, locus of agency, and gender. The results reveal that digital innovation is evaluated positively and associated with economic value creation, organizational actors, and male gender. The findings demonstrate that individuals’ cognition serves as a meaningful empirical site for capturing the multidimensional nature of digital innovation. These insights call for a more holistic perspective on digital innovation research and greater consideration of diverse stakeholders in shaping and governing digital innovation.

papers.title: Platforms that Build Entrepreneurs: Generative Market Infrastructure in Rural Africa
papers.abstract: Digital platforms in development contexts are usually theorized as intermediaries that optimize existing exchange. How platforms construct the sociotechnical conditions for exchange, and what this enables for previously excluded participants, remains underspecified. Drawing on a retrospective longitudinal case study of Hello Tractor, a Sub-Saharan African agritech platform, based on 40 interviews across two field visits and extensive secondary data, we develop a process account of sociotechnical market construction. We show that each of five phases generates a specific output the next requires as input, in a sequence the platform could not successfully invert. We introduce generative market infrastructure: a pattern in which the constructed infrastructure produces its own entrepreneurs, who ascend a self-replenish ladder and generate innovations that extend the market beyond the platform’s design. The paper specifies the causal micro-mechanisms of inter-phase enablement and shows that platform-led construction can distribute entrepreneurial capacity while retaining centralized control over infrastructural resources.

papers.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Opportunity Framing Under Layered Uncertainty in B2B Platform Marketplaces
papers.abstract: B2B application marketplaces have become important entrepreneurial arenas in which software developers must attract attention, establish credibility, and communicate value under adoption uncertainty. Yet we know less about how developers' communicative choices shape marketplace evaluation across adoption stages. Drawing on a stage-contingent evaluation framework, we examine how three opportunity-framing dimensions, intensity, concreteness, and outcome orientation, interact with visual demonstration and platform endorsement cues to influence market popularity, evaluative divergence, and realized business value. Using large-scale Shopify App Store data and LLM-based measurement of app listing descriptions, we find that outcome-oriented framing has the most consistent positive association across stages. Concreteness framing increases post-adoption evaluative divergence by creating more precise performance expectations, while demo availability weakens the association between intensity framing and market popularity. These findings show that textual framing and other listing cues perform different evaluative functions under layered uncertainty.

papers.title: AlphaFold Shock: Innovation Reallocation in Structural-Biology Firms
papers.abstract: AlphaFold is a domain-specific AI that addresses a key bottleneck in early-stage drug discovery: predicting protein structures. Such a breakthrough might intuitively be expected to accelerate upstream innovation and alter how firms allocate innovation across the R&D pipeline. Prior studies mainly examine general-purpose AI or innovation outputs within a single R&D stage. Less is known about how firms shift innovation focus when domain-specific AI breaks through an industry’s core technology.
