Using the AlphaFold shock as a natural experiment, we construct patent-based measures of upstream and downstream R&D activities for structural biology firms and estimate a difference-in-differences model. Our results reveal a non-intuitive finding: both patent applications and granted patents decrease after the shock. Meanwhile, firms shift innovation focus from upstream drug discovery toward downstream stages closer to clinical trials and commercialization. These findings extend AI innovation research and inform biotech strategy and innovation policy.

papers.title: Productive Noise: Theorizing GenAI Hallucinations and Serendipitous Innovation
papers.abstract: Generative AI hallucinations are often framed as organizational liabilities that require suppression. We argue this framing, while appropriate for factual fabrications, is theoretically incomplete for speculative recombinations, hallucinations that cross semantic boundaries in generatively useful ways. Drawing on Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR) theory and serendipity research, we theorize speculative recombinations as productive noise: a novel form of machine-generated blind variation uniquely positioned to trigger true serendipity, the redirection of organizational goals rather than merely their advancement. Four propositions specify how hallucinations expand the organizational idea set (P1), structurally undermine selective retention through evaluative ambiguity (P2), trigger true serendipity when a prepared mind operates within enabling organizational conditions (P3), and amplify innovation outcome variance (P4). We contribute an extension of BVSR to machine-generated variation, a sharpened pseudo vs. true serendipity distinction for IS innovation research, and governance principles for responsibly harnessing hallucinations as strategic innovation resources.

papers.title: AI Policy and the Reweighting of Sentiment: Evidence from Crowdfunding
papers.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate entrepreneurial communication, but adoption of GenAI disrupts how linguistic signal convey value and credibility, especially in crowdfunding. Existing IS and signalling research assumes linguistic fluency and emotional tone remain stable predictors of success, offering limited understanding of how AI-mediated standardization reshapes their informational value across evaluation regimes. We ask how GenAI reshapes the informational value of sentiment in digitally mediated entrepreneurial evaluation. Using a quasi-exogenous institutional intervention (Kickstarter’s AI Disclosure Policy), and 22,000 campaigns, we analyze pre- and post-shifts in sentiment-funding relationships across performance and meaning-oriented categories. Results show sentiment gains predictive power in performance contexts after GenAI diffusion but remains weak or negative in meaning contexts, reflecting regime-contingent interpretive recalibration. We extend crowdfunding literature by introducing evaluative regimes and advance IS research on AI-mediated communication by showing how algorithmic standardization selectively reconfigures signal interpretation with implications for platform governance, trust, and market dynamics.

papers.title: Cloud Around Me: How National Cloud Ecosystems Shape Software Developer Cloud Platform Use and AI Tool Use
papers.abstract: Despite importance of cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) in software development, how national cloud ecosystems influence software developers’ AI-tool behavior is unclear. Addressing this gap enriches understanding of AI-enabled innovation, where infrastructure shapes developers’ participation in innovation. Empirical analysis of global cloud providers and software developers yields four findings. First, national cloud provider breadth is positively associated with developers’ cloud platform use breadth, whereas national cloud service breadth is negatively associated with developers’ cloud platform use breadth. Second, cloud platform use breadth is positively associated with AI tool use breadth. Third, national cloud service breadth indirectly influences AI tool use breadth through cloud platform use breadth. Finally, these effects are generally stronger for developers in small organizations and in-person work arrangements. Our study shows that participation in AI-enabled innovation is unevenly distributed across nations, as national cloud conditions, organization size, and work arrangements shape software developers’ use of AI tools.

papers.title: CIO Career Variety and Generative AI Innovation: A U-Shaped Perspective in the Upper Echelons of the Firm
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping firms, yet scholarly attention to organizational antecedents of GenAI innovation remains limited. Drawing on upper echelons theory, this study examines how chief information officers’ (CIOs) career variety influences firms’ GenAI innovation. We argue that GenAI innovation is higher in firms led by CIOs with either highly specialized or highly generalist career backgrounds than in firms led by CIOs with moderate career variety, consistent with a U-shaped association between CIO career variety and firm-level GenAI innovation. We further propose that this relationship is linked to the broader top management team (TMT), particularly a CEO’s tenure within the TMT and the chief financial officer’s (CFO) IT experience. Using generalized estimating equations and data from S&P 500 companies from 2014 to 2023, we find support for a U-shaped relationship between CIO career variety and GenAI innovation and show that this relationship is contingent on CEO TMT tenure and CFO IT experience.

papers.title: Reconfiguring Information Ecosystems: Referential, Curational, and Generative Intermediation
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how information is accessed, produced, and distributed, with implications that extend beyond organizational contexts. This paper develops an information ecosystem perspective that foregrounds the processes of intermediation reshaping informational and economic flows. We theorize three modes of information intermediation, referential, curational, and generative, each characterized by distinct technological logics and processes for organizing access to information. These modes, which have emerged over time, are not mutually exclusive but layered, blending into hybrid forms in modern information services and ecosystems. We show how the emergence of generative intermediation can reconfigure information ecosystems by shifting information flows from traceable sources to synthesized patterns and associated economic flows from traffic redistribution to centralized value capture. In doing so, we highlight how evolving forms of intermediation drive structural transformation in information ecosystems.

papers.title: Exploring the Roles of Non-Commercial Organizations in Open and Coopetitive Ecosystems: The Case of TensorFlow
papers.abstract: Open-source software ecosystems are increasingly coopetitive, hosting networks in which competing organizations cooperate in producing shared platforms. Yet the roles of non-commercial organizations in such ecosystems remain underexplored. We conduct an in-depth case study of the TensorFlow platform ecosystem spanning eleven years of development history (2015–2026). By combining social network analysis of over 4200 developers with LLM-assisted computational qualitative coding of pull-request data from 51 contributors affiliated with universities, research institutes, and open-source foundations. Non-commercial organizations occupy peripheral network positions yet maintain ties with most commercial actors at the core. Each type performs a distinct role: universities as problem-finders and power users, research institutes as specialized technical innovators, and open-source foundations as documenters and gatekeepers. We advance two propositions---on structurally parallel ties and functionally complementary roles---and extend the Triple Helix model to recognize open-source foundations as a distinct institutional actor.

papers.title: Balancing Identity and Transformation: The Digital and IT-Enabled Organizational Transformation of Hidden Champions
papers.abstract: Hidden champions (HCs) are highly specialized niche leaders whose competitive advantage is rooted in enduring identity anchors such as product excellence, craftsmanship, technological leadership, and customer intimacy. This makes HCs a theoretically salient context for studying digital transformation, as they must integrate digital technologies without undermining the identity foundations of their success. Drawing on a multiple mini-case study of 14 HCs, this study examines how digital and IT-enabled organizational transformation affect organizational identity. Building on and refining the distinction between digital transformation and IT-enabled organizational transformation, we show that transformation in HCs often unfolds as anchored digital transformation: digital initiatives may be strategically significant and organizationally far-reaching, yet remain tied to established product, service, or know-how logics. We contribute by introducing an identity-outcome typology comprising identity reinforcement, extension, and redefinition, explaining how HCs preserve identity continuity while integrating digital technologies.

papers.title: Platform Authority vs. Managerial Authority: Who Really Controls Work in Digitized Organizations
papers.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly determine whether organisational actions can proceed, even when managers remain formally responsible for the outcomes. As validation rules, predefined categories, and system thresholds become embedded in organisational processes, formal authority is separated from the practical control required to implement decisions. This study examines how platform architectures and technical intermediaries reconfigure authority within digitally mediated processes. Drawing on a qualitative, practice-based design, it traces authority across reporting, validation, and coordination activities. Findings identify three interconnected mechanisms: displacement, whereby managerial authority becomes decoupled from the capacity to make a decision operationally effective; mediation, whereby technical intermediaries broker alignment between managerial intent and system requirements; and reconstitution, whereby a provisional authority settlement forms around organisational usable output. Through these mechanisms, formal responsibility remains stable while operative control is distributed across managers, platform configurations, and intermediaries. The study advances a processual account of platform-mediated authority and governance in digitally dependent organisations.

papers.title: Valuing the Uncertain: Identifying AI Investment Preferences in Organizations
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has increased competitive pressure and made technology investment decisions more complex and strategically relevant. While IT investments have traditionally been evaluated using established financial metrics, artificial intelligence (AI) changes the underlying logic of investment decisions. AI systems are characterized as a bundle of heterogeneous capabilities, making it difficult to predict their performance prior to implementation. Moreover, realizing AI value typically depends on complementary organizational changes, such as process redesign and new decision routines, meaning that benefits emerge dynamically over time rather than being immediately observable. These characteristics challenge traditional investment appraisal approaches and suggest that different decision criteria may become more influential in AI contexts. Against this background, it remains unclear which attributes drive managerial preferences when allocating resources to AI technologies. This study addresses this question using a discrete choice experiment with a split-sample design to compare AI and BI investment scenarios.

papers.title: Business Models of AI-driven Sustainability Startups: A Taxonomy
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and sustainability efforts are fostering innovative business models that integrate both domains. This paper develops a taxonomy to classify business models for AI-driven sustainability startups. Following the methodological approach of Nickerson et al. (2013), a taxonomy comprising of 43 characteristics across nine dimensions was developed through five iterations utilizing the Business Model Canvas as a foundational framework. This taxonomy was developed and validated by analyzing 90 European startups, resulting in the categorization and clustering of five types of business models. By establishing a common vocabulary, this research addresses fragmentation and creates a foundation for comparative research and theory building in the intersection of AI and sustainability. The final taxonomy provides a tool for evaluation, classification and communication of business model types for both researchers and stakeholders, while remaining adaptable of future extensions and specifications to reflect innovation and evolution of AI-driven sustainability startups

papers.title: Tailoring Intelligence to Context: Configurational Pathways to Context-Oriented AI Innovation
papers.abstract: Generative AI is often celebrated as a general-purpose technology, yet its business value emerges when models are tailored to the contexts in which users act, decide, and create. This study examines context-oriented AI innovation, defined as the development of AI-enabled products, services, or processes that address user needs and create value under specific usage contexts. Drawing on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and a configurational view of innovation, we investigate how technological resources, organizational capabilities, and environmental pressures combine to drive context-oriented AI innovation. Using Chinese listed firms that have registered generative AI models, we plan to employ qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) to identify multiple pathways leading to the depth and breadth of context-oriented AI innovation. This paper intends to advance AI innovation research by foregrounding context, theorizing configurational pathways of context-oriented AI innovation, and revealing how distinct configurations produce different patterns of context-specific innovation.

papers.title: Build, Apply, Operate: AI Role Complementarities and Firm Value
papers.abstract: Firms increasingly compete not on whether they employ artificial intelligence talent but on how they organize it. We distinguish three functionally distinct forms of AI work — Build (proprietary AI creation), Apply (domain-specific deployment), and Operate (governance and infrastructure) — and ask whether the value associated with one depends on the presence of another. Using Revelio Labs workforce data matched to Compustat for 1,927 publicly traded U.S. firms from 2019 to 2025, we estimate firm and year fixed-effects models of Tobin's Q. Build and Apply talent are associated with higher firm value jointly rather than separately, and this association is stronger where Operate intensity is high and outside the technology sector. Results hold under alternative role taxonomies, alternative valuation and productivity outcomes, and dynamic specifications. We contribute a functional-configuration perspective on AI value, showing that complementarities arise within AI human capital itself, so that configuration, not scale alone, shapes returns.

papers.title: Data protection and servitization performance of manufacturing firms
papers.abstract: While digital technologies have been widely adopted in servitization of manufacturing firms, the influence of data protection, the central ethical tenet of digital technology adoption, on servitization remains uncertain. To address this research gap, we investigate how data protection may impact the servitization performance of manufacturing firms as well as the firm- and market- level contingencies in this context. We find that personal data protection has a positive influence on servitization performance of manufacturing firms. More importantly, consistent with the contingent resource-based view, we also find that the relationship between personal data protection and servitization performance is strengthened by financial resources, TMT oversea experience, and market competition. Our study contributes to the literature by explicating the effects of data protection on servitization and makes important and practical contributions to our understanding of how data protection can be valuable for promoting servitization of manufacturing firms.

papers.title: How Deterministic and Probabilistic Information Systems Shape Complicatedness, Complexity, and Performance in Knowledge Work
papers.abstract: Organizations deploy information systems to help knowledge workers manage portfolios of interconnected products and customers. Drawing on complexity science, we distinguish portfolio complicatedness, the number of interconnected components a worker carries, from complexity, which emerges when those interactions become ad hoc and nonlinear. We theorize that deterministic CRM features impose predefined structure keeping complicated portfolios tractable, whereas probabilistic GenAI features generate context-dependent outputs that fuel complexity dynamics. Using agent- and deal-level data from U.S. independent insurance distribution and a shift-share identification strategy, we find the opposite. CRM use negatively moderates the performance effects of product and customer complicatedness, while GenAI use positively moderates both. Predetermined structure is valuable when complicatedness creates coordination and retrieval demands, but constrains performance when those demands remain tractable. The findings extend complexity science by showing that information systems improve performance both by taming complexity and by increasing worker capacity under demanding interaction conditions.

papers.title: From Pilot to Production: Microfoundations and Responsibility Structures for Enterprise AI Projects
papers.abstract: Enterprise AI projects in firms frequently fail to transition from pilot to production. This study characterizes this transition through 14 projects across multiple industries. Using an inductive multiple-case design and a microfoundations lens grounded in the dynamic capabilities framework, we identify 38 microfoundations and 12 meso-level capabilities spanning sensing, seizing, and transforming. While sensing and seizing activities largely resemble prior digital transformation research, the transforming dimension diverges, centering on operational AI governance, knowledge institutionalization, and AI asset evolution. We further develop a two-dimensional framework of responsibility allocation across piloting and productionizing, identifying three responsibility patterns: domain-driven, handover, and tech-driven. For theory, the transforming dimension requires a microfoundation profile distinctive to AI projects, and responsibility allocation is a phase-sensitive structural variable rather than a steady-state governance property. For practice, AI competence distribution is the key precondition shaping which responsibility patterns are sustainable – and something firms can deliberately develop.

papers.title: Governing AI Scaling Through Temporal Alignment: A Process Model of Governance-Innovation Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, enables experimentation to spread faster than formal governance mechanisms can develop. Existing research often frames governance and innovation as a trade-off between control and flexibility, but this view offers limited insight into how both evolve during AI scaling. Drawing on a comparative qualitative case study of two universities in the United States and Germany, based on six semi-structured interviews, this study proposes a provisional process model of governance-innovation co-evolution. The findings suggest that innovation velocity and governance intensity are independent dimensions whose interaction produces evolving governance postures. When these dimensions develop unevenly, organizations may accumulate governance debt, where experimentation outpaces oversight, or innovation debt, where governance constrains capability development. The study contributes to digital innovation and IT governance research by conceptualizing temporal misalignment as a generative mechanism in AI scaling and by outlining how organizations may transition between stages of governance and experimentation.

papers.title: Lessons Learned from a Governance Transition in  Deep Learning Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Open-source software is the invisible infrastructure of the digital economy, yet little is known about how its governance shapes participation when projects transfer from a single sponsoring firm to a neutral foundation. In a quasi-experimental design, we modelled the PyTorch’s September 2022 transfer from Meta to the Linux Foundation as a treatment with TensorFlow, JAX, and Chainer as controls to estimate difference-in-differences effects on participation across three analytical levels (organisational breadth, institutional depth, community participation) and comparing post-transition developer mobility across two forms (adoption and migration). We also separate collaborative from isolated developers, a population typically neglected in co-editing-network studies. The transition was associated with breadth-and-community expansion with institutional depth contraction: more contributing organisations and substantially more independent contributors, but fewer external institutional developers. Migration into PyTorch was supported while adoption was not, indicating that collective governance attracts migrants rather than multi-homers. The findings extend prior work on governance transitions beyond the firm layer.

papers.title: AI Investment under Pressure
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central driver of firm productivity and innovation, yet little is known about how earnings pressure influences firms' AI investment decisions. We develop a model that yields two competing predictions. Under a cash-financing motive, AI is an inefficient target for cost relief, and any reduction would not depend on exploration intensity. Under a tolerance motive, exploration-loaded AI would be disproportionately affected because its value is harder to verify and its interim signals more closely resemble failure. Using a regression discontinuity design comparing firms just missing the analyst earnings per share (EPS) forecast with those just meeting it, we find that narrowly missing the target reduces AI investment over three years. The reduction concentrates among firms with high AI exploration share and is negligible among those with low exploration share. These findings show that earnings pressure selectively erodes tolerance for failure, the organizational precondition on which exploratory AI activity depends.

papers.title: Differentiated Value Realization Paths of Hospital Data Sharing in China: Data Types and Transaction Modes
papers.abstract: This study examines how Chinese public hospitals realize value from data sharing under heterogeneous regulatory and operational conditions. Drawing on eight theoretically sampled cases, 28 interviews, observations, and archival materials, we use Resource Orchestration Theory to analyze how data resources are structured, bundled, and leveraged. We identify four context-driven mechanisms across data type and transaction mode: Privacy-Encapsulated, Targeted Synergistic, Standardized Assetization, and Business Symbiotic Orchestration. Our findings show that differences in data sensitivity, standardizability, customization, and time sensitivity shape distinct orchestration requirements and the relative viability of alternative mechanisms. We further show that data transformation is a common process underlying value realization, while its form ranges from discrete derived-data products to continuous real-time integration. The study extends resource orchestration theory by explaining how contextual conditions shape differentiated pathways of hospital data value realization.

papers.title: From Digital Restoration to Synthetic Personas: Navigating the Systematic Tensions of AI in the Music Industry
papers.abstract: This research explores the paradoxical role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the music industry, illustrating how it both empowers and disempowers various actors within the creative ecosystem. While AI technologies enhance creativity and reduce production barriers, they can simultaneously diffuse accountability and threaten the economic viability of traditional artists. By examining two case studies—The Beatles’ AI-assisted track and the AI-generated project Breaking Rust—this study reveals how socio-technical configurations reshape empowerment dynamics. The findings suggest that greater access to AI tools can lead to conflicting outcomes for authorship, attribution, and remuneration, necessitating a reevaluation of music industry policy frameworks. Ultimately, this work contributes to the understanding of AI’s complex impact on creative industries and underscores the need for improved governance around technology use.

papers.title: Implications of AI Boundaries: Evidence from Finance and HR Professionals
papers.abstract: In response to risks arising from employees’ access to internet-based artificial intelligence (AI), organizations increasingly define formal rules and guidelines regarding the use of AI (hereafter, AI boundaries). Despite their increasing diffusion, little empirical evidence exists on their consequences. Drawing on information processing theory, we examine how the scope of AI boundaries shapes employees’ AI-related behavior. Using a large survey among finance and HR professionals, we find that more extensive AI boundaries are associated with lower perceived ambiguity regarding AI use among employees. Further, this reduced ambiguity is associated with lower shadow AI use and higher satisfaction with AI use. We also find that these associations vary with the sensitivity of the information employees work with and the presence of an organizational beliefs system that defines values regarding AI use. Overall, this study highlights an informational role of AI boundaries and suggests that its benefits depend on the organizational context.

papers.title: Making Sense of Responsible AI: An Institutional Complexity Perspective
papers.abstract: Responsible AI has received increasing attention, yet its implementation in organizational contexts remains insufficiently understood. This study examines how organizations experience and respond to challenges in Responsible AI by conducting a structured synthesis of prior research. The findings reveal that Responsible AI is shaped by interdependent demands related to innovation, compliance, and ethics, which give rise to persistent challenges that cannot be fully resolved. Building on this, the study conceptualizes AI governance as a process of mediating competing demands rather than translating principles into practice, and shows that organizational responses are constrained to forms of ongoing balancing, such as alignment, compromise, and workarounds. By integrating these insights, the study advances Responsible AI research beyond principle-based discussions and provides a more grounded understanding of how organizations navigate complexity in the governance of emerging digital technologies.

papers.title: Keeping Policy Operative: A Cybernetic Runtime Architecture for Governing User–GenAI Interaction in Educational Tutoring
papers.abstract: Organizations deploy generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in policy-sensitive settings where institution-specific policy must remain operative during user–GenAI interaction. Information systems research offers limited design knowledge for configuring and enacting such policy. Using cybernetic and organizational control theories in design science research, we derive five requirements for a runtime architecture that maintains policy as a reference condition, senses and compares interaction conditions, governs large language model (LLM) response generation and delivery within the configured policy. We instantiate it in an educational GenAI tutor and evaluate 64 cases across five conditions under conventional and runtime governance. Runtime control kept 89.1% of delivered responses within the instructor-specified boundary versus 60.9% conventionally. We show that institutional responsibility for GenAI policy extends from specification to runtime application and review.

papers.title: AI and the Red Queen Race: Coevolution on Rugged Landscapes
papers.abstract: What happens when AI can be leveraged by all firms within an industry? While growing evidence suggests that AI can generate performance gains for individual firms, less is known about how these gains unfold across interdependent firms. We address this question from a coevolutionary perspective by extending an NKC model in which firms use AI to reduce uncertainty in strategic decision making. Our analysis reveals a Red Queen race in which firms are compelled to use AI to improve immediate performance and survival. Yet as all firms do so, intensified competition erodes temporary advantages, reduces total industry performance, and may even create a lose-lose situation in which all firm performs worse. These findings suggest that the value of AI depends not only on how it improves firm decision making, but also on how it reshapes coevolutionary dynamics across firms.

papers.title: Beyond Strategy: A Practice-Based View  on Digital Transformation at the  Business Unit Level
papers.abstract: Given its profound impact on business, digital transformation has become a critical topic for executives and researchers. While effective digital transformation strategies are essential for maintaining competitiveness, existing research predominantly focuses on strategy development and execution at the organizational level. Digital transformation at the business unit level remains underexplored. Adopting a practice-based view, this study examines digital transformation strategy development and execution within a finance unit. Drawing on an in-depth single case study in a large pharmaceutical manufacturing firm, we make two contributions. First, we provide an empirical analysis of how digital transformation unfolds at the business unit level. Second, we inductively develop a practice-based model showing how interrelated practices, shaped by explanatory variables, drive transformation and improve operational performance. Our study demonstrates that digital transformation strategizing occurs not only at the organizational level but also within business units, highlighting the need to extend research to business unit contexts.

papers.title: Attention Externalities in Collective Complaints: How Platform Aggregation Reallocates Response Effort and Creates Unequal Satisfaction Outcomes
papers.abstract: Digital complaint platforms reshape negative word-of-mouth by aggregating grievances into visible collective complaint events. We examine how collective negative word-of-mouth (C-NWOM) affects post-complaint satisfaction in a dual-channel complaint environment, distinguishing aggregate satisfaction from individual complainants’ satisfaction outside the collective event. Using large-scale data from China’s leading automotive complaint platform, we document contrasting satisfaction outcomes: C-NWOM is associated with higher overall satisfaction but lower satisfaction among individual complainants of the same model. Drawing on the attention-based view, we explain this pattern as an attention externality: C-NWOM redirects managerial attention toward collective complaints and away from concurrent individual complaints, reducing response speed and prototypicality and thereby contributing to lower individual complainant satisfaction. This negative spillover is strongest during a model’s first C-NWOM shock and attenuates after firms accumulate C-NWOM experience. Our findings inform platform design by revealing how mechanisms that amplify collective voice can create inequities in service recovery for individual complainants.

papers.title: Adaptation, Assurance, and Control: How Agentic AI Reshapes SaaS Markets
papers.abstract: AI coding agents lower the cost of organization-specific software adaptation for both organizations and vendors, yet equal access need not produce symmetric sourcing effects. We model how residual control shapes adaptation investment when organization-specific changes cannot be fully specified in advance. Vendor control induces underinvestment that lowers joint value, and repricing cannot recover the lost surplus. Internal development therefore expands selectively, especially when adaptation matters more and governance burdens are lower. When the vendor offers low-assurance and assurance-certified options, higher agent capability reduces low-assurance demand and raises the assurance-certified share of remaining customers. Imperfect internal delegation weakens this shift, while better vendor-side specification and contracting can attenuate or locally reverse it. The model shows when symmetric access to agentic AI yields asymmetric sourcing responses across software categories.

papers.title: From Divergence to Stabilization: Governance Adaptation Through Conflict in Decentralized Banking Consortia
papers.abstract: Decentralized banking consortia reduce reconciliation through shared ledgers but require legally independent banks to jointly govern IT infrastructure while retaining individual risk and regulatory responsibilities. Because collective decisions require agreement, conflict can delay change and threaten continued operation. We reconstructed twelve conflicts in the SWIAT consortium through an embedded case study using interviews and internal documents. We find that members stabilize the consortium by translating broad disputes into concrete technical, contractual, or compliance questions and resolving them through direct coordination, formal commitments, and bounded assignments of coordination or operational responsibility. Conflict resolution can establish rules, roles, permissions, or procedures that shape later collective decisions, forming a governance adaptation loop. The loop explains how members restore joint action while changing the governance conditions under which subsequent conflicts are processed. Sustaining joint action therefore involves governing not only current conflicts but also what their resolution changes for later collective decisions.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs as Boundary Objects: A Sociotechnical Framework for Data Governance in Resource-Constrained Organizations
papers.abstract: More than ninety percent of organizations operate with limited resources, yet mainstream data governance frameworks assume enterprise-scale capacity. Drawing on the boundary-object concept (Star & Griesemer, 1989; Carlile, 2002, 2004), this paper proposes a sociotechnical framework that positions the knowledge graph as a shared artefact mediating between three governance communities: regulators and experts, ontology engineers, and organizations. A systematic review of forty-three studies shows that existing approaches treat knowledge graphs as technical artefacts, leaving resource-constrained organizations underserved along eight recurring dimensions. Reframing these as boundary-crossing needs, the framework explains how a knowledge graph transfers, translates, and transforms governance knowledge, making governance explicit and traceable while decisions remain with the communities. Nine design principles operationalize the framework. The paper offers researchers a new theoretical perspective, vendors an underserved market, and practitioners a feasible, constraint-aware approach.

papers.title: Knowledge Diversity and User Innovation in Online Communities: A Machine Learning-Enabled Analysis
papers.abstract: Distributed user innovation increasingly unfolds in online communities, yet little is known about how community-level knowledge structures relate to its outcomes. Prior research emphasizes individual innovators or single communities, leaving cross-community differences underexplored. We draw on a corpus of 157 million Reddit posts and implement a three-stage pipeline: First, a keyword-based semantic filter identifies problem-solving content. Second, supervised classification detects user-generated solutions and their novelty. Finally, on a stratified sample of 150,000 posts across 15 communities, we measure embedding dispersion and use embedding-based topic modeling to derive knowledge diversity components. Results indicate that different dimensions of knowledge diversity are associated with distinct and potentially non-monotonic patterns of solution emergence and novelty, while community evaluation appears to favor solution presence over novelty. These findings suggest that knowledge diversity may relate to the generation of distributed innovation and demonstrate a scalable approach to detecting distributed user innovation from digital trace data.

papers.title: Who Rises Online? Social Stratification Logics Across Social Media Platforms
papers.abstract: People increasingly manage their identities and social standing across multiple social media platforms, yet research largely examines social stratification within individual platforms. We lack a platform-level understanding of how platforms differ in the mechanisms through which social standing is constructed and how these differences shape the transfer of standing across platforms. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theorization of capital and its context-dependent value, we develop a typology based on platforms’ dominant social stratification logics. Status-Reflecting platforms foreground social standing developed and validated outside the focal platform through credentials, affiliations, and formal roles, whereas Status-Developing platforms foreground standing developed through activity and recognition within the platform. We derive propositions theorizing how these distinct logics shape social standing and how compatibility between platform stratification logics facilitates its cross-platform transfer. Our framework advances research on social stratification by conceptualizing platforms as distinct social contexts that determine which sources of standing are recognized and valued.

papers.title: Homophily or Heterophily? The Janus Face of Collaboration Tie Formation: Evidence from Polyadic Interaction Network Analysis
papers.abstract: As content creators strive to compete for limited viewer attention, they have been increasingly adopted collaborative content provision on digital content platforms. However, there remains a dearth of understanding about what antecedents drive collaboration tie formation. Utilizing 8,463 collaboration events involving 5,998 unique users retrieved from Bilibili, a prestigious digital creator platform, we construct a directed relational hyperevent model (RHEM) to capture the dynamics embedded in polyadic creator interaction network. We yield three key findings: (1) driven by the dynamic balance between resource complementarity acquisition and coordination cost reduction, homophily and heterophily effects coexist in the collaboration network; (2) structural features such as inertia and reciprocation are essential in predicting collaboration decision; (3) the virtual flow is hierarchical in nature, such that collaborations may go from higher-status to lower-status users, or vice versa. This study sheds lights on how to properly model polyadic collaboration network and offers valuable practical implications.

papers.title: The Ripple Effect: Analyzing Ecosystem-wide Value Spillovers from Digital Giants’ M&A
papers.abstract: This study investigates how M&A announcements by six dominant digital platform companies – termed Digital Giants (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, and Nvidia) – affect market valuations of competitors across distinct dimensions of rivalry. Applying an event study and multivariate regression to 889 M&A announcements from 2010 to 2024, we identify an asymmetric pattern across two rivalry dimensions. At the submarket level (Direct Rivals), diffuse signaling prevails: they show no systematic reactions, consistent with platform envelopment decoupling exposure from the product-market boundaries classical rival effect theory presupposes. At ecosystem level, ecosystem-wide exposure emerges: Indirect Rivals – Digital Giants competing for orchestration control – co-move with the acquirer’s valuation through overlapping governance and infrastructure interdependencies. A comparison against announcement-free days shows this co-movement is only partly continuous, with an announcement-specific component under the SIC-based rival definition. The findings establish a multi-dimensional rivalry framework extending classical rival effect theory to digital platform contexts.

papers.title: Safety as Strategy: Consumer Protection and Platform Leakage
papers.abstract: Platforms increasingly introduce safety policies (e.g., buyer protection, fraud reversal, trade locks) framed as consumer-protection measures rather than competitive instruments. Yet because such protections are typically enforceable only through the focal platform's infrastructure, they may simultaneously raise the cost of transacting on competing venues. We address this using Valve's Steam Trade Protection policy (July 2025), which imposed a seven-day reversal window on CS2 skin trades and asymmetrically affected peer-to-peer marketplaces dependent on rapid settlement. Combining a temporal difference-in-differences with an exposure-based triple-difference design on item-week transaction data from Steam and CSFloat, we find that the policy triggered a sharp contraction in third-party trading and partially consolidated liquidity on Steam. Items most embedded in CSFloat prior to the policy experienced the largest substitution toward Steam, consistent with demand leakage. The policy thus functioned simultaneously as consumer protection and ecosystem enclosure, underscoring the need for cross-platform impact assessments in platform governance.

papers.title: Political Bias in Crowdchecking and an Algorithmic Remedy
papers.abstract: Social media platforms are increasingly replacing professional fact-checking with crowdchecking to combat misinformation. Focusing on X's Community Notes program, we empirically investigate whether political bias exists in crowdchecking and whether algorithmic aggregation can mitigate it. We find that notes on politically divisive tweets receive 2.7% fewer helpfulness ratings and have 6.6% lower odds of receiving raters' support. A randomized online experiment confirms that this disparity stems from individual-level political bias among raters, who discount notes correcting tweets aligned with their own ideology. These individual biases further aggregate into politically biased outcomes, where notes on divisive tweets are 35.2% less likely to become public. The bridge-based aggregation algorithm not only fails to mitigate individual political bias but also exhibits excessive conservatism. We propose a discernment-based algorithm with an entropy-guided rotation, which substantially increases the misinformation labeling rate while maintaining precision, greatly improving the overall effectiveness of crowdchecking.

papers.title: Supplier Scale, Competition, and Consumer Experience in Platforms
papers.abstract: The relationship between supply-side competition and platform market dynamics has long been debated, yet the role of supplier scale remains underexplored. We study how competition from large-scale suppliers shapes platform outcomes and a platform's ability to compete with outside options. Using Airbnb as our empirical setting, we show that restricting large-scale suppliers generates only transient gains in price, demand, and revenue for incumbent suppliers. These gains are accompanied by declines in average consumer experience and increased demand for outside options, and they attenuate substantially over time. The findings suggest that competition among small individual suppliers alone may be insufficient to sustain the quality provision needed for platforms to compete effectively with external alternatives. More broadly, our results highlight an important role of large-scale suppliers beyond direct market competition: by sustaining consumer experience, they can contribute to the long-run competitiveness and sustainability of platform markets.

papers.title: Attracting Complementors to Social Mission Digital Platforms – A Convention Theory Perspective
papers.abstract: Social-mission platforms pursue societal goals while depending on complementors to create value and sustain their ecosystems. Yet attracting complementors proves particularly challenging when operational viability remains uncertain and participation may be evaluated through divergent principles. Drawing on a qualitative multiple-case study of four emerging social-mission news platforms, and incorporating both operator and complementor perspectives, we examine how complementor attraction unfolds through the lens of convention theory. Our analysis reveals a continuum of attraction ranging from robust to conditional and fragile configurations. These configurations differ in co-occurring patterns of shared or divergent orders of worth, the demandingness of participation tests, and the strength of devices. Crucially, attraction can persist without a shared evaluative basis when participation tests remain sufficiently accommodating and platform arrangements address different evaluative concerns. We contribute to research on social-mission platforms by explaining attraction under evaluative divergence and extending convention theory to platform-based coordination.

papers.title: Equal Access, Unequal Outcomes: Gender-Specific Challenges on Online Labor Platforms
papers.abstract: Online labor platforms (OLPs) have transformed access to and the organization of work and are often portrayed as vehicles for women’s economic inclusion. Yet women on OLPs earn on average 8–10% less than men in comparable tasks, cluster in lower-paid categories, and face distinct challenges often overlooked in IS research. This research-in-progress paper investigates how gender impacts opportunities and risks in the ride-hailing context. We integrate Wilson’s (2004) framework for studying gender with the job characteristics model and the algorithmic management literature to explain how platform artifacts interact with existing gender relations to produce different job characteristics for workers. Using a mixed-methods approach, we begin with semi-structured interviews with female ride-hailing drivers. Initial vignettes illustrate both the appeal of platform flexibility and the persistence of gendered constraints, including safety concerns, algorithmic opacity, and social isolation. We outline implications for IS research and next steps toward a validated framework.

papers.title: The Effect of Content Coherence on Content Consumption in User-Generated Content Platforms
papers.abstract: Although content coherence is widely regarded as a key dimension of content quality, its effect on content consumption on user-generated content (UGC) platforms remains unclear. In this work, we collaborated with a short-video platform in Asia to conduct a large-scale randomized experiment on UGC content in terms of user comments of videos. Specifically, we assigned approximately 500,000 users to either a pointwise or a listwise ranking algorithm for comments, with the latter designed to improve coherence across comments. We find that higher content coherence was associated with a 1.9% increase in users’ browsing duration. This effect decreased with user experience, with each additional year of experience associated with a 0.09% smaller effect, and was 0.7% larger for users with entertainment-seeking motivations than for those with information-seeking motivations. This study highlights the role of content coherence in shaping UGC consumption and offers insights for designing more engaging digital platform environments.

papers.title: When Generative AI Reshapes Platform Content Ecosystems: Evidence from Online Investment Community
papers.abstract: This study examines the introduction of virtual analyst reports on Seeking Alpha, an AI-generated feature launched in December 2024. Using a 13-month panel and a regression discontinuity in time (RDiT) design, we identify three effects of generative AI: a substitution effect, an augmentation effect, and a convergence effect. We find that virtual analyst reports exhibit a substitution effect by significantly reducing investor commenting activity while having no direct significant effect on liking behavior. They also generate an augmentation effect by increasing non-professional analysts’ content production. However, this effect is double-edged, as AI-generated content (AIGC) is associated with reduced analytical depth. Finally, virtual analyst reports create a convergence effect by reducing opinion dispersion. We further find that the effects of AIGC vary depending on the stock-level information environment. Overall, our findings highlight the multidimensional and tension-filled effects of generative AI in digital content ecosystems and offer implications for platform governance.

papers.title: Turning Followers into Patrons: How Social Media Value Converts Followers into Subscribers
papers.abstract: Subscription-based crowdfunding (SBC, i.e., paid subscriptions to content creators) is providing creators with an increasingly important income stream. However, it remains unclear how creators can convert their social media followers into paying supporters. We propose that the emotional and functional values of social media content contribute to SBC success by fostering parasocial relationships. Using YouTube content from 520 creators and their Patreon subscription counts, we test whether the content’s emotional value drivers (six basic emotions, emotional variety, and arousal) and functional value drivers (number of shared videos, video duration, and title novelty) predict subscriptions. For emotional value, surprise, anger, emotional variety, and arousal have positive effects, while fear has a negative effect. For functional value, all three components explain the number of Patreon subscriptions. A complementary survey shows that emotional and functional values predict parasocial relationships, which in turn are linked with followers’ intentions to pay for subscriptions.

papers.title: Should E-commerce Platforms Neutralize Emotion in Dispute? A Dual-Pathway Model of Perceived Fairness in Crowd Judging
papers.abstract: Although e-commerce platforms increasingly deploy crowd judging to resolve transaction disputes, the way dispute materials are presented remains a critical factor shaping jurors' fairness perceptions. This study examines whether platform-led emotion neutralization influences jurors' perceived fairness by altering their cognitive processing, and investigates how emotional expression structure and product type jointly moderate this relationship. Through a randomized experiment, we compare emotion preservation with emotion neutralization across three emotional expression structures—buyer-unilateral, seller-unilateral, and bilateral expressions—and two product types, namely utilitarian and hedonic disputes. We theorize that emotion neutralization operates as a dual-impact intervention, which enhances perceived objectivity but simultaneously undermines perceived representational fidelity. These competing mechanisms jointly shape jurors’ evaluations of platform governance fairness, with their relative dominance contingent on both the specific emotional expression structure and whether the disputed product is utilitarian or hedonic.

papers.title: Navigating the Ethical Challenges of Online Labor Platforms: A Case Study
papers.abstract: Online labor platforms (OLP) represent an appealing yet controversial business model. OLPs have faced criticism for transferring business risks to workers, exploiting regulatory loopholes, and misclassifying actual employees as independent contractors, among other concerns. Such unresolved ethical dilemmas increasingly affect more people as the volume of work conducted via these platforms expands, posing a compelling governance challenge. Drawing on the lenses of sociotechnical joint optimization and platform governance, we investigate how OLPs can treat their workers responsibly while retaining the unique advantages of the gig economy. Our revelatory case study of an OLP demonstrates a potential approach to striking this balance through three governance mechanisms that integrate elements of traditional staffing agencies with OLP characteristics. With some caveats, our findings reveal how OLPs can jointly optimize their social and technical system elements to produce positive instrumental and humanistic outcomes, enabling them to achieve profitability while managing complex ethical challenges.

papers.title: An Empirical Investigation of Algorithmic Failure in the App Store
papers.abstract: Platform ecosystems host millions of complementors whose reputation and market access depend on algorithmic systems they do not control. While research has documented harms from algorithms functioning as designed, algorithmic malfunction represents a fundamentally different failure mode whose occurrence is immediately apparent, yet how its costs are absorbed unequally across structurally different complementors is not. We study this using a natural experiment in Apple’s App Store in which a review-moderation algorithm malfunctioned, removing millions of legitimate reviews. Using anomaly detection, propensity score matching, and staggered difference-in-differences estimation, we find that the failure caused a significant average rating decline (β = -0.460, p < 0.001). Newer apps dropped -1.094 stars versus -0.382 for older apps, while low-review apps dropped -1.392 stars versus -0.243 for high-review apps. The algorithmic malfunction examined intensified preexisting structural inequalities, revealing that structurally weaker complementors bear a disproportionately larger cost from an ostensibly uniform algorithmic failure.

papers.title: Same Space, Different Sparks: Speech-Act Activation and Intervention in Online Support
papers.abstract: Promoting user contribution is central to online support communities. We study mutual activation, a scalable, decentralized mechanism in which early replies prompt later replies. On a leading social media platform, threads divide into venting and support seeking, and replies are assertive, expressive, or directive speech acts. We estimate a nonlinear multivariate Hawkes model with a bounded logistic link and thread-level cold-start heterogeneity on 1,375 threads and 90,984 replies. Expressive replies reach the highest fitted intensity in venting threads and assertive replies in seeking support threads, yet neither receives the most likes in its category. Replies in more balanced conversations receive more likes. Using the fitted model as a simulator, we learn a two-stage intervention policy through reinforcement learning. The policy targets threads that can still be moved, intervenes early, and gives the least budget to the speech act each category already produces most, outperforming equal-capacity benchmarks.

papers.title: Badges of Influence: How Digital Platforms Induce Decoy-Like Effects to Steer Consumer Choice
papers.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly use endorsement badges and punitive badges to steer consumer demand, yet their structural impact on choice remains under-explored. This research conceptualizes badges as choice architecture tools designed to induce "decoy-like effects" without altering choice set composition, simply by altering perceived dominance relationships. Through two randomized online experiments (N=1,400), we compare traditional decoy effects induced through choice set expansion against decoy-like effects induced through badges. Our results demonstrate that endorsement badges mimic traditional decoys, increasing the respective target choice share. Furthermore, punitive badges effectively steer demand toward intended targets by retroactively transforming existing options into asymmetrically dominated decoys. These findings contribute to digital platforms literature by framing the use of badges as a strategic manipulation of dominance relationships and highlight the potency of badges for platform governance.

papers.title: Interoperability versus Data Portability for Fostering Competition
papers.abstract: Data portability (DP) and interoperability (IO) are two openness mandates in digital markets with switching costs and network effects. We model price competition between an incumbent and an entrant and treat the two mandates as separate regulatory instruments. DP reduces switching friction, intensifies competition, and increases consumer surplus. IO shares network benefits across platforms and reduces the incumbent's demand advantage, but it softens price competition, raises both equilibrium prices, and decreases consumer surplus. When the two policies are used together, they are strategic substitutes in enhancing contestability. Their interaction on consumer surplus is conditional: they are complements where both policy levels are low and substitutes where interoperability is high. They are strategic complements with respect to total welfare. The results show that greater contestability, consumer welfare, and total welfare need not move together under openness mandates.

papers.title: Who Stays When AI Answers? Core-Periphery Resilience in Online Knowledge Communities
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers a low-cost substitute for community-based knowledge exchange, but its disruptive effects may vary across users and task contexts. Drawing on social exchange theory, embeddedness, and task-technology fit, we examine how ChatGPT’s public release reshaped participation and contribution in online knowledge communities. Using 52-week user-level panels covering 558,980 users on Stack Overflow and Mathematics Stack Exchange, we estimate difference-in-differences and triple-differences models. Peripheral users experienced sharper participation declines than core users, with the relative decline 15.4% greater on Stack Overflow than on Mathematics Stack Exchange (p = .009), consistent with stronger GenAI substitutability for programming tasks. Among users who remained active, peripheral users elaborated their contributions further, with average post length rising by 40.7 more characters, an increase unchanged when the sample is restricted to users active in both periods. These findings show that GenAI reconfigures who participates and how remaining users contribute, revealing differential resilience shaped by embeddedness and task-technology fit.

papers.title: Ranking Authority and Knowledge Production: How Ranking Design Shapes Participation on Digital Platforms
papers.abstract: Online question-and-answer platforms depend on voluntary contributions whose visibility is governed by ranking systems. We study how shifting default ranking authority from asker endorsement to peer vote aggregation affects participation and evaluation, exploiting Stack Overflow's 2021 policy change in a difference-in-differences design covering 1.14 million questions. At the question level, treated questions show lower acceptance rates, fewer answers, and reduced commenting and voting, indicating contraction rather than redistribution of engagement. At the answer level, promoted answers attract longer, more elaborated comments but receive fewer net votes, while demoted answers gain votes yet lose constructive discourse. These results suggest that ranking design operates as algorithmic governance, reshaping incentives for askers, answer providers, and evaluators rather than merely reorganizing retrieval. Findings contribute to research on digital platforms and crowd-based knowledge production by showing that crowd-based ranking signals can undermine the collaborative curation processes they are intended to support.

papers.title: When Models Arrive Before Papers: Temporal Coupling in Open AI Knowledge Production
papers.abstract: Open AI knowledge production increasingly unfolds through narrative papers and executable models, two distinct carriers that may become public at different times. We examine how these carriers are structurally connected and, within release-associated pairs, how their temporal ordering relates to infrastructural uptake. Using Hugging Face-linked arXiv traces from 2017–2025, we identify 12,361 papers, 183,697 paper-model links, and 8,176 conservatively classified release associations. Structural coupling varies substantially across task environments. Within release associations, 43.9% are paper-first, 44.9% near-simultaneous, and 11.2% model-first. Model-first releases are also modestly more likely to occupy dependency-bearing positions. We theorize these patterns through prospective, co-deployed, and retrospective attachment, showing how temporal coupling can reorder the relationship between infrastructural uptake, narrative articulation, and subsequent legitimation. The study adds a temporal dimension to research on digital infrastructures and platformized knowledge production.

papers.title: When Anyone Can Build, Who Evaluates? Use-Side Governance in AI Skill Ecosystems
papers.abstract: AI skills are shareable, reusable, task-specific instructions that AI agents interpret and execute to perform recurring workflows. They circulate through public repositories where anyone can publish or adopt one. AI has lowered the cost of producing these artifacts far faster than platforms have developed standards for verifying them, so users must judge what a skill does and whether to trust it from a listing alone. What governance work makes this abundant supply evaluable and usable? We study 49,332 skills from ClawHub, a public AI skill repository. Catalog and interface audits show that relevant skills can be retrieved while reliance-relevant evidence remains outside dedicated comparison fields. We develop a theory of use-side governance: how evaluation work is allocated across platforms, organizations, and users, with platform curation and AI fluency as complementary capabilities. When anyone can build, platform governance should shift from expanding supply toward supporting evaluation and use.

papers.title: Same Superstar, Different Spillovers: Product-Level Market Success and Inter-Complementor Spillovers
papers.abstract: Superstar complementors are a major driver of demand spillovers on digital platforms. However, existing research has primarily examined complementor prominence and product success as separate sources of spillover heterogeneity, overlooking that prominent complementors often offer portfolios of products with varying levels of market success. We examine this dynamic in Spotify’s editorial playlists, which curate tracks from both superstars and non-superstar artists and create interdependence among co-listed artists. Because release catalogs of superstar artists contain both hits and less popular tracks, playlists provide a rich setting to study how product-level success within prominent complementors’ portfolios shapes spillovers to co-listed peers. We find that playlist inclusion generates much greater growth in artists’ listener bases than in follower bases. Specifically, a higher proportion of superstar hit tracks within playlists strengthens the inclusion effect on co-listed artists’ follower growth whereas a higher proportion of superstar non-hit tracks strengthens inclusion effect on listener growth.

papers.title: Siphoning and Supplementing? Donor Reallocation and Match Funding Policy Design on a Crowdfunding Platform
papers.abstract: Match funding accelerates funding for a cause, but what happens to unmatched projects in a multi-project marketplace? I study a Google.org match for Special Needs projects on DonorsChoose. Funding rose sharply for eligible projects. Yet as matching became more prevalent around them, unmatched projects in the same school and grade received less, despite maintaining their donor counts, and donors shifted their first gifts toward matched projects. These patterns motivate a model of donor behavior that I use to compare campaign designs. Concentrating matches where Special Needs projects account for most local need attracts more donor funding and lowers sponsor spending, but does not address the lower funding of the unmatched. Matching every project in a subset of markets preserves more funding for neighbors than concentrated targeting, but costs the sponsor more. Match design therefore requires platforms to balance sponsor savings against funding for the wider marketplace.

papers.title: Digital Public Infrastructure Through the Lens of Dimensional Publicness
papers.abstract: Digital public infrastructure (DPI) – public foundational and reusable digital systems for e.g. digital identity, payment, and data-exchange – has become a high-stakes concept in digital government and global development. Yet, it is underspecified: discourse bundles legal, normative, and functional meanings of ‘‘public‘‘ without analytically distinguishing them. We ask how dimensional publicness (DmP) theory can be adapted into an analytical framework for assessing the publicness of DPI. Employing a two-step knowledge synthesis – a concept-centered systematic review of publicness literature and a deductive grey-literature document analysis of 61 DPI sources – we identify twelve DPI-relevant publicness dimensions, specify units of analysis in infrastructural settings, and synthesize into three layers: structural, normative-relational, and experienced-realized publicness. Three propositions link the layers to the building, governing, and use of DPIs, and a contrasting illustration of India's Aadhaar / UPI and the European Digital Identity Wallet cases demonstrates the framework's discriminating power.

papers.title: When Civil Servants Resist AI for Citizens: Privacy Concerns and Prosocial Resistance
papers.abstract: Civil servants handle personal data that citizens have no choice but to disclose. When an administration mandates that an artificial intelligence (AI) system process it, the citizen’s protection rests with the servant entrusted with the data, for whom resistance may become advocacy rather than inertia. Drawing on Communication Privacy Management (CPM) theory, the study theorizes “Custodial Boundary Turbulence” (CBT) as a state of conflict arising when institutional AI mandates clash with a bureaucrat’s benevolent obligation to protect sensitive citizen information. By modeling the boundary rule formation process, this work investigates how CBT arises under mandated disclosure and predicts that intentions to resist AI will be stronger for more prosocially motivated bureaucrats. Testing the model via a cross-sectional survey of civil servants across five public administrations using PLS-SEM, this study will contribute to the IS community by extending CPM to custodial settings and explaining resistance through benevolent motives.

papers.title: The Impacts of Public Data on AI Innovation: Open Government Data Initiatives Encourage Local Healthcare AI Investment
papers.abstract: Public data infrastructure is built primarily for transparency, yet it is costly, its innovation spillovers remain uncertain, and governments have adopted divergent data-opening strategies as a result. We examine whether and how the launch of open government data portals (OGDPs) affects local healthcare AI investment. Healthcare is a useful setting: it is data-intensive, faces substantial regulatory uncertainty, and depends on both data availability and institutional support for AI deployment. Using a panel of 258 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2012 to 2023 and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we measure investment through hospitals' procurement of diagnostic and operational AI systems, and find that OGDP launches generate sustained increases. Data provision operates as a necessary baseline input, while cross-city variation in the effect tracks governmental signaling rather than measured data supply. These findings position OGDPs as both digital infrastructure and institutional signal, and show that public data can shape local AI investment through cognitive as well as material channels.

papers.title: SVEA-in-the-Making: A Sociomaterial Genealogy of Public-Sector LLM Development in Sweden
papers.abstract: Governments are developing sovereign large language models (LLMs) to align generative AI with public-sector values and legal frameworks. Yet research still treats LLMs as stable artifacts, overlooking their continuous reconfiguration. This paper examines Sweden's SVEA initiative as public-sector AI-in-the-making, drawing on documents, interviews, and focus groups across two development phases. We identify four coexisting versions of SVEA—a technical model, a governance object, a political project, and a workplace tool—and three frictions through which they develop: an annotation knot binding retrieval accuracy to exhausting labor; a sovereignty gap in which political ambition and technical capability alike lack a legal form; and a localization cascade in which political boundaries become hardware contracts and then workplace capabilities. We contribute a four-version framework for public-sector AI infrastructures and show that national-scale versioning lacks an institutional stabilizer: versions are produced by institutions that cannot direct one another and must be held together jurisdictionally.

papers.title: Urban Mobility: Unveiling Research Trends and Future Pathways
papers.abstract: Smart urban mobility has emerged as a multidisciplinary field that integrates digital technologies, governance, and sustainability to address increasingly complex urban transportation challenges. Despite growing scholarly attention, knowledge remains fragmented and lacks a comprehensive synthesis. This study conducts a systematic literature review, following the PRISMA 2020 protocol and combining bibliometric analysis with thematic analysis. The findings identify six major thematic categories: Technological Integration; Sustainability and Environmental Impacts; Economic Impacts and Governance; Regional Contexts and Local Challenges; Prevailing Definitions and Dominant Concepts; and Accessibility and Social Inclusion. Results show that research has evolved from a predominantly technology-oriented perspective toward broader concerns involving governance, sustainability, and public policy. However, significant gaps remain regarding conceptual consensus, regional adaptation, and social inclusion. Based on this, this study proposes an integrative definition of smart urban mobility and outlines a research agenda on the subject that is more inclusive, context-sensitive, and theoretically grounded.

papers.title: Between Innovation and Risk Aversion: A Contextual Perception of AI Sourcing Risks in Public Organisations
papers.abstract: Efforts to map and understand the risks associated with artificial intelligence (AI) are growing. While much of the existing discourse focuses on post-deployment risks, the system sourcing phase, where problems are defined and system requirements are specified, receives less attention. This paper explores AI sourcing risks, particularly those that arise early with cascading effects on system development. Drawing on interviews with 33 AI sourcing actors, we reveal procedural and conceptual risks associated with system sourcing and, in relation to these risks, conceptualise three interrelated risk constructs: pre-deployment operationalisation risks, risk-aware vendor risks, and adaptive future-proofing risks. The findings indicate how internal misalignments and vendor dynamics can compromise the success of AI projects. We propose a theory of contextual AI sourcing risk aversion to show the evaluative, context-dependent, and reflexive process in which actors construe and respond to risk under uncertainty, particularly in the context of AI sourcing in public organisations.

papers.title: Configured to Care: How AI Emotional Expression Shapes User Engagement in Mental Health Support
papers.abstract: Conversational agents are becoming an important source of support on mental health peer-support platforms, where engagement is critical to realizing support value and emotional support is a central support type. Unlike human supporters, AI agents’ emotional expressions are designable. We conceptualize this emotional affordance through a valence–complexity taxonomy that captures emotional tone and nuance. Using data from a leading online mental health community, we find that negative emotional expressions, which may convey validation and emotional resonance in support contexts, are more effective than positive expressions in eliciting user engagement. In particular, negative secondary emotions, which convey greater nuance and sophistication, outperform alternative emotional categories. These findings suggest that users value resonance and emotionally attuned responses from AI supporters. Our study highlights emotional expression as a key design feature of AI support agents and offers a framework for understanding how agent emotions shape user outcomes in mental health contexts.

papers.title: Informal Infrastructuring as Drift: The  Case of Energy Management Systems
papers.abstract: This paper questions how infrastructure can be built and evolve outside state sponsorship and centralized control. To this end, we consider this process as linked to informal infrastructuring. While this concept is usually discussed in relation to the informal practices of the urban population, this study contextualizes informal infrastructuring to business practices through the empirical case of an Energy Management System (EMS) implementation. The study adopts a mixed-methods approach and uses assemblage theory as a theoretical lens. The results show that informal infrastructuring is driven by coexisting configurations shaped by two identified toggling dynamics: rerolling and rescaling. Our findings contribute to the literature on digital infrastructure by linking drift to informal infrastructuring, thereby complementing various approaches in IS research on drift and infrastructure evolution.

papers.title: Motivating Individual Effort in Collective Action Tasks in Local Government: An Experimental Evaluation of Expectancy Theory-Based Design Interventions
papers.abstract: Public administration increasingly relies on collective data work, yet motivating individual contributions remains difficult. Existing research offers limited insight into how information systems can motivate effort in such collective action tasks with intangible individual benefits. Drawing on Expectancy Theory, this study examines how design interventions targeting expectancy, instrumentality, and valence influence motivation in collective settings. We conduct a large-scale online experiment with 405 participants using a 2×2×2 between-subjects design with real-effort tasks reflecting collective-benefit structures. Results show that perceived expectancy and valence are associated with task completion, while perceived instrumentality and valence are associated with time spent working. Among the tested interventions, the valence-targeting treatment has significant impact. Our findings suggest that Expectancy Theory remains relevant in collective contexts and highlight the importance of making collective outcomes more salient in the design of information systems targeting the motivation of collective effort.

papers.title: Polycentric Governance of Nascent Digital Public Infrastructures: Insights from the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Digital public infrastructures have become foundational to the delivery of today’s public and private services. Yet, there is limited understanding of how governments can effectively govern infrastructure innovation during the early stages – especially when the infrastructure spans national borders. To address this gap, we conduct an inductive case study of the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure. Our analysis shows how nascent cross-border infrastructures can be organized through multi-layered and dynamically evolving polycentric governance configurations, in which distinct yet aligned sub-configurations are applied to the infrastructure core and complement layers over time. By unpacking how these configurations can be established and adapted, we contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the challenges inherent in nascent DPI governance and offer actionable insights into how governments can purposefully design and combine governance configurations to navigate this critical early stage.

papers.title: From Ordinary Cameras to Rehabilitation Information: A Dual-View TUG Artifact
papers.abstract: Specialized movement-analysis systems provide rehabilitation evidence but impose equipment, setup, and expertise demands that constrain routine access. This design science study develops a working dual-view Timed Up and Go (TUG) artifact that transforms ordinary front- and side-view video into phase-aware candidate measures and a therapist-facing report. Three frontline rehabilitation practitioners informed requirements, demonstrations, and output review; a rehabilitation physician participated in the broader project. A documented review raised 13 questions about phase scope, calculation, units, video-value disagreement, and acquisition conditions. We also report two therapist-performed same-episode comparisons between prototype and hospital reference outputs. Agreement varied by parameter: sit-to-stand times differed by 0.1 seconds, whereas turn timing, step counts, walking speed, step width, and some step-length estimates diverged substantially. The paper contributes an implemented capture-to-report artifact and nascent design knowledge: lower-infrastructure sensing becomes useful only when task decomposition, measurement qualification, information representation, and professional review are designed end to end.

papers.title: A Within-Person Privacy Calculus Perspective for Patient-Generated Health Data in Mental Health Care among Emerging Adults
papers.abstract: Patient-generated health data (PGHD) enable more personalized mental health care, but also raise privacy concerns. Building on Privacy Calculus theory, this study examines whether privacy concern varies not only between individuals but also within individuals across PGHD types, and how perceived treatment relevance and performance expectancy relate to these concerns. Based on an online survey of 439 emerging adults aged 18 to 29, participants rated 21 PGHD types for their treatment relevance for mental health and privacy concern.
