Our analysis of linear multilevel models shows that privacy concern is associated with both general privacy dispositions and data-type-specific relevance ratings. PGHD types perceived as more relevant to treatment are associated with stronger privacy concern. The relationship between relevance and privacy concern is stronger among respondents with higher performance expectancy. Our results suggest that, among emerging adults, the PGHD privacy concerns involve repeated, PGHD-type-specific appraisals rather than a single general evaluation.

papers.title: Multihospital System Affiliation and Patient Experience: The Cost of EHR Misalignment
papers.abstract: Multihospital system affiliation is widely pursued to improve efficiency, yet its patient-facing consequences remain unclear. We examine how affiliation affects patient experience and whether electronic health record (EHR) alignment moderates its effects. Using a longitudinal panel of affiliation histories, EHR vendors, and Google reviews covering nearly all U.S. general acute-care hospitals, we exploit variation in affiliation timing in a quasi-experimental design. Affiliation is associated with a 9.2% decline in average ratings, driven by more one-star and fewer five-star reviews. Although affiliated hospitals increasingly adopt their parent system’s primary EHR vendor, misalignment often persists. Rating declines are concentrated among hospitals remaining misaligned after affiliation. Topic modeling shows that dissatisfaction centers on billing and payment rather than clinical care, consistent with coordination frictions from incomplete digital integration. These findings show that ownership consolidation without EHR standardization may limit the coordination benefits of system affiliation.

papers.title: Defending Professional Identity: How Generative AI Promotes Physicians' Voluntary Knowledge Contribution in Online Health Communities
papers.abstract: Generative AI is transforming knowledge-sharing dynamics. While evidence suggests AI may reduce human participation in general settings, this study examines how technological encroachment affects experts' voluntary knowledge contributions through the lens of professional identity threat. Using a natural experiment involving two leading Chinese online health communities and a difference-in-differences approach, we find that AI’s emergence is associated with a significant increase in physicians' knowledge sharing. This suggests that physicians utilize proactive contribution as a strategic response to reaffirm their professional authority and unique value. Furthermore, we find that peer influence and individual experience are critical boundary conditions that moderate this behavior. This research offers a nuanced perspective on human-AI dynamics and the social mechanisms that sustain expert engagement amidst technological disruption. Practically, these findings provide actionable insights for platform managers to integrate AI strategically and empower human experts.

papers.title: Design Considerations for Generative AI Tools in Mental Healthcare
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools hold promise for expanding access to mental health support, yet prescriptive knowledge on how such systems should be designed remains limited. This study adopts a design science research approach to develop and evaluate a generative AI chatbot in the context of university students’ stress self-management. The project involved three phases: user needs identification through semi-structured interviews with Gen AI users, artifact instantiation, and artifact evaluation through an expert panel and task-based usability testing with students. Evaluation results indicated strong performance in plain language, empathy, usability, and satisfaction, but revealed gaps in evidence grounding, contextual understanding, cognitive manageability, and crisis recognition and escalation. Based on these findings, we derive ex post design guidelines to guide the future design and evaluation of Gen AI tools in mental healthcare.

papers.title: Prescription Without Pressure: Voluntary Use, Interstate Spillovers, and Interoperability in PDMP Effectiveness
papers.abstract: Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs are state-operated systems whose mandates stop at the state line, raising the question of what happens to physicians in neighboring states who face no change in their own obligations. Using physician-level system logs and prescription records for 16,445 Oregon prescribers from 2018 to 2022, we exploit mandates adopted in California and Washington, which differ in whether they share data with Oregon. Mandates in both states increased patient inflows to Oregon border regions. Oregon physicians responded by voluntarily increasing their use of the system, with larger increases where interoperability made cross-state histories available. Greater use was associated with reduced controlled substance prescribing and less doctor shopping, and these effects were stronger under interoperability. The results show that uncoordinated state mandates displace rather than resolve monitoring problems, and that interoperability can raise the informational value of a system enough to draw voluntary use without a mandate.

papers.title: Conversational Value Pathways in Generative Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Self-Care
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used as a first-contact interface for self-care, but its value depends on how lay users interpret, verify, and act on conversational outputs. This paper develops a conversation-to-value model of GenAI-mediated self-care by integrating Technology Affordance and Constraint Theory with IS value theorising. We argue that system response properties, user capabilities, and task characteristics shape conversational interrogation, which in turn shapes interpretive calibration, i.e., the correspondence between users’ judgements of credibility, uncertainty, and actionability and what the available evidence and self-care situation warrant. Calibration shapes downstream actions, whose consequences distribute value, burden, and risk across users, healthcare providers, and platforms. The model positions GenAI-mediated digital-health value as both interpretively contingent and distributively consequential and outlines a linked multi-method empirical design for future research.

papers.title: “Do you have a Digital Therapeutic for that?” Design and Evaluation of Conversational Virtual Patients for DTx Prescription Training in Medical Education
papers.abstract: Digital therapeutics (DTx) represent a class of software-based clinical interventions that remain underused, in part because physicians lack the knowledge to prescribe them confidently. We address this issue through the design of conversational virtual patients (CVP), an innovative training format with growing empirical support. We developed and evaluated four CVP personas, exhibiting varying DTx inquiry demeanor (proactive vs. reactive) and contraindication presence. Drawing on Kirkpatrick’s four-level evaluation framework, we derive six hypotheses and test them in an online experiment with 29 medical students and physicians. Three hypotheses were supported: satisfaction, willingness to engage with DTx, and prescription willingness increased significantly post-interaction. Authenticity, perceived skill development, and DTx knowledge gain did not reach significance. These findings suggest that simulated consultations can serve as a low-threshold lever for shifting prescriber attitudes toward DTx. A multi-site follow-up study using advanced path modeling is underway.

papers.title: Not Every Help is Helpful: Longitudinal Study on the Effects of GenAI Support on Users’ Well-being
papers.abstract: Rising levels of mental health challenges have intensified interest in ways to improve well-being. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used as a source of social support, yet its implications for users’ well-being remain little understood. Drawing on Social Support Theory, this study employs a longitudinal diary design to examine how within-person fluctuations in GenAI-based informational and emotional support relate to daily well-being. Focusing on ChatGPT, we find that GenAI-based informational support is a positive within-person predictor of daily well-being, whereas emotional support shows no significant effect. Moreover, trust in GenAI acts as a critical boundary condition, strengthening the beneficial effect of informational support, while perceived anthropomorphism does not moderate these relationships. These findings highlight the differential impact of GenAI support types and underscore the role of trust as a prerequisite for the psychological benefits of human-AI interaction to unfold.

papers.title: Persuasive System Design: Tailoring Digital Self-compassion Artifacts to Entrepreneurs
papers.abstract: Information Systems Research on digital well-being and behavioral interventions shows substantial benefits for general populations. Context-specific studies addressing entrepreneurs remain scarce, despite their relevance as time-constrained, high-stakes user group. Drawing on Stress Appraisal Theory and Persuasive System Design (PSD), we test whether a brief PSD-grounded self-compassion artifact shifts entrepreneurs’ secondary appraisal of a venture-related threat toward challenge to enable approach-oriented coping. In a pre-registered online RCT (N = 316), entrepreneurs are randomized to a self-compassion or an active control artifact, testing the effects on self-reported autonomous help-seeking probability and the underlying appraisal pathways. The artifact indirectly increases autonomous help-seeking probability via two pathways: lower help-seeking cost and greater self-improvement motivation. We extend the scarce IS digital well-being research on entrepreneurs, and anchor PSD in the state-based Stress Appraisal Theory, outlining its effects on cognitive appraisal mechanisms.

papers.title: The Impact of AI on Physician Diagnosis: Evidence from AI-enabled Medical Devices
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support clinical decision-making, yet evidence of the impact of information-generating AI, where AI produces new clinical information, on physician decision quality and efficiency remains limited. We examine the role of information-generating AI in the context of AI-augmented diagnostic procedures of coronary artery disease, which physicians can use to guide diagnostic and treatment decisions. By examining the impact of information-generating AI on physician care quality and efficiency, this study offers critical insights for hospitals, payers, and policymakers seeking to understand how AI can be integrated into diagnostic pathways to improve physician diagnosis and decision making to advance value-based care.

papers.title: Toward Intelligent Medical Decision Support: A Spatio-Temporal Reinforcement Learning Artifact for Ambulance Redeployment
papers.abstract: Emergency Medical Service systems face persistent supply-demand mismatches because emergency calls and ambulance availability evolve dynamically across time and space. This study develops an intelligent medical decision-support artifact for ambulance redeployment, consisting of a spatio-temporal reinforcement learning policy and a high-fidelity event-driven simulation environment. We formulate ambulance redeployment as a sequential decision problem and propose STAmbPG, which explicitly represents temporal demand-resource evolution and spatial inter-station dependencies before station scoring, translating these dependencies into adaptive redeployment decisions. To enable safe training and reproducible evaluation, we develop AmbGym, an open-source Gymnasium-compatible EMS simulator. Experiments against representative baselines show gains in response efficiency and survival-related metrics across resource levels, while ablation, fairness, and interpretability analyses support its representation design and balanced performance. Together, STAmbPG and AmbGym provide a testable and extensible foundation for EMS resource allocation.

papers.title: Emotional Availability in Chatbot Interaction: Understanding Perceptions and Expectations of Youth
papers.abstract: The use of chatbots by youth extends beyond information seeking to conversations about  emotionally challenging and potentially distressing topics, raising the question of which  interactional qualities they perceive as supportive. This exploratory study uses Emotional  Availability (EA) as an analytical lens to examine these perceptions. Based on 17 semi structured interviews with youth aged 18 to 21 and two EA expert interviews, a hybrid  thematic analysis combined deductive and inductive coding. Participants associated  supportive interaction less with emotional expressiveness than with concise validation,  structured but non-directive guidance, neutral and non-judgmental communication,  user-initiated interaction, and control over personal data. These accounts are interpreted  in relation to sensitivity, structuring, non-intrusiveness, and non-hostility, while  acknowledging the limitations of transferring EA from human relationships to human AI interaction. This study contributes an initial exploration of whether EA can be  transferred from human relationships to human-AI interaction and how youth perceive  its dimensions in chatbot communication.

papers.title: From Confusion to Clarity: Designing Generative AI to Reduce Illness Uncertainty in Chronic Disease Self-Management
Predicting Online-to-Offline Care Conversion in Internet Hospitals: A Theory-Guided Deep Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Internet hospitals increasingly serve as an entry point into integrated online-to-offline care pathways, but hospitals often lack timely tools to anticipate subsequent offline demand. Drawing on Protection Motivation Theory, this study develops PACC-Net, a theory-guided deep learning framework that predicts whether patients will seek offline outpatient care within 14 days after an online consultation. The model separately represents threat appraisal and coping appraisal by integrating consultation dialogues, patients’ prior healthcare utilization, and physician credential signals. Using linked online consultation and offline outpatient records from a large public hospital in China, we show that PACC-Net outperforms traditional machine learning, neural dialogue, and LLM-based baselines across multiple metrics. The findings demonstrate the value of appraisal-aware dialogue modeling for predicting short-term offline care-seeking and supporting proactive outpatient resource coordination.

papers.title: When Digital Punctuality Backfires: Queue Demotion and Congestion Externalities in Outpatient Care
papers.abstract: Hospitals increasingly embed appointment punctuality policies to reduce late check-ins and improve outpatient flow, yet such policies may also synchronize arrivals and create congestion in shared-capacity queues. Prior research explains how appointment schedules and incentive rules improve compliance and manage uncertainty, but pays less attention to how punctuality rules reshape patient demand timing and generate system-level externalities. Drawing on congestion externality theory, we exploit a quasi-natural experiment at a large tertiary hospital in China, using over 4.2 million patient visits and a difference-in-differences design to evaluate the appointment punctuality policy. We find that the policy improved compliance by reducing late check-ins and increasing on-time registration, but also concentrated check-ins, increased overall waiting time, and imposed waiting costs on patients not directly targeted by the penalty. This study shifts attention from compliance to collective flow consequences and offers guidance for designing appointment governance that balances punctuality with queue performance.

papers.title: Designing Frailty Feedback for Action: How Assessment Modality Shapes Older Adults’ Trust and Engagement with Health-Promoting Care
papers.abstract: Population aging is driving demand for scalable frailty assessment, and digital technologies now generate frailty risk information from electronic health records and wearable sensors. Yet scalable detection is not the same as effective intervention: older adults must understand, accept, and act on the information they receive. We propose a randomized longitudinal field experiment in which approximately 300 older adults are assigned to clinician-mediated assessment, passive electronic frailty index scoring, or wearable remote patient monitoring, then receive standardized frailty feedback and an identical intervention offer. Holding communication constant while varying the apparatus that generated the evidence separates two elements that existing theory conflates: the entity that produces risk information and the entity that communicates it. We theorize the recipient's own role in generating evidence about themselves as a distinct source cue, extending information adoption research to technology-mediated personal risk assessment more broadly.

papers.title: Fragmented and Trauma-Unaware: Health Information Systems for Refugees in Finland
papers.abstract: Ukrainian refugees under temporary protection in Finland have a full legal entitlement to healthcare. Yet, many remain unaware of, or unable to sustain their use of, the health information systems (IS) intended to serve them. Drawing on 75 interviews with refugees and organisational representatives, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis, we examine why health IS continue to produce refugee exclusion. We find that trauma reduces the cognitive capacity required for sustained engagement, identity-based authentication can exclude new arrivals who lack bank credentials, and portals may leave valued mental-health services undiscovered for months or years, despite positive experiences once accessed. We extend digital divide theory by specifying a trauma-driven mechanism within its motivational-access stage. We also contribute to research on digital identity infrastructures by showing that governance-level exclusion can persist despite full legal entitlement. We recommend interim authentication pathways, proactive multilingual dissemination, and trauma-informed design standards, while identifying implementation constraints.

papers.title: Thought-Bubbles in Therapy: The Effect of Conversational AI’s Transparency in Mental Health Contexts
papers.abstract: Users seek AI-based counseling to escape being judged by humans, yet perceived judgmentalness persists as a barrier even in AI counseling. Direct empathic expressions intended to alleviate such concerns, however, may be discounted as insincere. We address this limitation by introducing thought bubbles, a novel format that renders a chatbot’s pre-response processing as a given-off signal rather than a directed message. Two online lab studies show that empathetic thought bubbles increase perceived authenticity, which reduces perceived judgmentalness and, in turn, increases trust, satisfaction, disclosure, and compliance. A Clinical Study extends the generalizability of these findings to a real-world clinical setting and further shows stronger effects among patients with greater mentalizing difficulties and concerns about being judged. Together, these findings suggest that effective AI counseling depends not only on what message a chatbot delivers, but also on how that message is presented to users.

papers.title: Co-Designing AI Governance for Care Coordination in Community Mental Health: An Action Design Research Study
papers.abstract: AI governance in healthcare operates top-down, through enterprise frameworks and organizational policy. These approaches do not address how governance should be designed into a clinical artifact through iterative engagement with the providers and patients who use it. We report an in-progress Action Design Research study with a community mental health center, co-designing an AI care coordination agent that addresses the delivery and communication gaps in service quality. The study introduces governed emergence: the principle that governance must hold at the design process level and at the artifact's runtime behavior level. Practitioner evaluation in the first building-intervention-evaluation cycle reshaped the artifact's governance architecture and yielded three design principles, with a fourth following from problem formulation. The contribution is a co-design approach to AI governance that treats provider accountability and patient empowerment as interdependent requirements.

papers.title: Institutional Signals, Social Amplification, and Prescription Disruption: Evidence from the GLP-1 Drug Shortage
papers.abstract: During FDA-declared drug shortages, institutional risk signals and social media discussion form overlapping information environments that shape patient behavior. Applying the Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF), this study examines how adverse-event reports and Reddit discussion interact with prescription disruption for two semaglutide-based drugs. We estimate a partly recursive Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) on weekly data from April 2022 to December 2024 for Wegovy (weight management) and Ozempic (diabetes). Results reveal a mechanism-divided dual- channel system: adverse-event shocks significantly affect only Ozempic through clinical channels, whereas social-amplification shocks act on both populations with a delay and greater impact on Wegovy. The study contributes by (1) reconceptualizing medication information systems as closed-loop hierarchical structures, (2) proposing a theory- grounded SVAR identification strategy for healthcare IS, and (3) showing how patient- population characteristics drive differential responses to identical signals.

papers.title: Beyond Generic Empathy: Empirical Grounding for the Design of Transition-Sensitive AI Support in Later Life
papers.abstract: AI-enabled support systems increasingly address health, caregiving, and aging-related challenges, yet later-life support often requires more than generic empathy or factual advice. We develop transition-sensitive support matching to explain how transition contexts shape support needs, peer communities configure response functions, and support episodes continue through clarification and sensemaking. Using Mayo Clinic Connect, we screened 35,506 discussion threads and analyzed 651 high-relevance later-life transition threads, including 651 original posts, 20,866 peer replies, and 3,562 follow-up messages. LLM-assisted coding captured transition contexts, support needs, response functions, and follow-up signals. Findings show that needs vary across transition contexts, peer responses are experience-centered yet need-responsive, and specific early responses are associated with clarification-oriented continuation rather than return in general. The study shifts attention from support categories to support trajectories and derives empirically grounded design directions for transition-sensitive AI support systems.

papers.title: Unraveling the dimensions and transfer mechanisms of trust in AI health services: Does business origin matter?
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare, attracting both medical institutions and technical enterprises to develop AI health services. During this process, trust serves as a key psychological factor that shapes users’ evaluations and adoption willingness when facing different services. Existing studies conceptualize trust as a unidimensional construct and overlook the hybrid nature of AI health services. Hence, this study reconceptualizes trust as a two-dimensional construct (trust in technical capability and medical capability) and introduce business origin as a key antecedent that creates asymmetric initial trust and influences how trust transfers between these dimensions. By testing transfer paths across enterprise types, this study provides comparative evidence on the direction of trust transfer between two dimensions, with stronger support for the technical-to-medical path in the technical-origin condition. This study contributes by offering a capability-based trust framework and extending trust transfer theory beyond cross-object contexts, providing new insights into AI health services adoption.

papers.title: Noise-Robust Depression Screening using Smartphone-Generated Physiological Data: A Three-Module Framework
papers.abstract: Smartphone-generated physiological data (SGPD), such as remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) captured through a smartphone camera, offers a low-burden channel for population-scale depression screening, but real-world SGPD is noisy in ways prior work has not systematically addressed. We propose a three-layer noise taxonomy, human, technical, and contextual, and a three-module framework that operationalizes it: Confident Learning for label noise correction, a Biodynamics-Guided CNN embedding a first-order autonomic regulation constraint, and deep ensemble uncertainty quantification. Using SGPD from 67,801 participants in a nationwide occupational health examination, our model achieves balanced accuracy of 0.758, recall of 0.835, and AUROC of 0.822, rising to 0.909 balanced accuracy in a subgroup independently confirmed through suicidal-ideation disclosure. Ablations show that the biodynamics-guided constraint’s contribution to recall is conditional on prior label correction, consistent with the framework’s sequential design. Uncertainty analysis explains up to 35% of prediction-reliability variance, providing actionable guidance for equitable, noise-robust SGPD-based mental health screening.

papers.title: When Technology Ideas Retain Legitimacy Despite Failure: Insights from Danish General Practice
papers.abstract: AI-supported documentation is increasingly promoted to reduce clinicians’ documentation burden, promising efficiency and more time for patient care. Yet in a voluntary initiative in Danish general practice, an AI clinical scribe increased rather than reduced documentation work, while GPs continued to view AI-supported documentation as promising. Drawing on rationalized myth and institutional translation theory, we examine how a technology idea retains legitimacy despite poor performance. Through a qualitative case study, we identify two interpretive moves: GPs localize shortcomings to the artifact and workflow and temporalize expected benefits to later, more mature translations. These moves restrict what poor local performance is taken to disconfirm. We contribute to IS research on technology ideas by showing how professional users maintain a technology promise despite contradictory experience, and to institutional translation research by showing how localization and temporalization can preserve the legitimacy of a rationalized myth despite poor performance of a local translation.

papers.title: Toward Intelligent Caregiver Support: A Taxonomy-Guided LLM System for Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRDs) place substantial burdens on informal caregivers, who often rely on online health communities (OHCs) for support despite variability in information quality and structure. Using a computational design science approach, we develop a three-level taxonomy of ADRD caregiver support scenarios from 48,581 OHC threads and instantiate it in a taxonomy-guided LLM system. The taxonomy specifies scenario-specific requirements for empathy, actionability, uncertainty, and risk-sensitive escalation. In a preliminary within-subject experiment, the system received higher ratings than comparison conditions across usefulness, trust, empathy, contextual relevance, actionability, and perceived safety, and was preferred by 76.9–83.3% of participants in forced-choice evaluations. The study demonstrates how domain-specific taxonomic knowledge can guide responsible LLM adaptation for caregiver support in digital health contexts.

papers.title: Communication LLMs Increase Hospital Dwell Time: Evidence from the Early Nationwide Deployment in U.S. Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Hospitals have begun wiring large language models (LLMs) into the electronic health record (EHR) to draft replies to patient portal messages. Whether this changes in-person care is unknown. We study the April 2023 release of Epic’s MyChart In-Basket Augmented Response Technology (ART), an early large-scale U.S. deployment of a communication LLM inside EHRs, using a monthly panel of 1,014 hospitals linked to SafeGraph mobility traces. Difference-in-differences estimates with hospital and State×Month fixed effects show median per-visit dwell time rising 11.4% after deployment, a result that holds under falsification tests among planning hospitals, temporal and vendor placebos, randomization inference, and matching. The pattern is consistent with selective filtering, under which routine inquiries are disproportionately resolved digitally and the remaining in-person stream skews complex, though aggregate data cannot adjudicate this mechanism against alternatives. Communication LLMs may reshape in-person care rather than simply reduce it, with consequences for staffing, scheduling, and capacity planning.

papers.title: From Alert to Rescue: How National Culture Shapes Community First Responder Engagement
papers.abstract: Smartphone-dispatched community first responder (CFR) systems shorten the interval between out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and the first compressions delivered by a layperson. Engagement across these systems is uneven, but cross-national variation has been treated as an artefact of operational conditions, leaving the cultural dimension of volunteer behaviour untheorised. Building on a prior scoping review of 23 empirical CFR studies, we develop a stage-specific theory of how national culture shapes engagement. The theory contains eleven propositions linking Hofstede's dimensions to twelve behavioural decision points across five response stages, treated as additive over baseline technical attrition. We then show that when these stage-specific cultural effects operate sequentially, they progressively reshape the composition of the volunteer pool. We call this mechanism cultural filtering and offer it as the paper's central theoretical contribution. The paper closes with implications for IS research on prosocial technology and for the design of culturally adaptive CFR systems.

papers.title: Doctors Meet Patient AI
papers.abstract: Patients increasingly bring generative AI (GenAI) diagnoses into clinical encounters, yet little is known about how physicians use such patient-provided information. We conduct a randomized field experiment on an online medical consultation platform using 436 physicians and standardized dermatology cases with confirmed diagnoses. Physicians receive no external diagnosis, a correct diagnosis attributed to GenAI, or the identical diagnosis attributed to a physician. Correct GenAI-attributed diagnoses improve both benign/malignant and exact-diagnosis accuracy, but physicians still distinguish benign from malignant conditions in only about two-thirds of accepted consultations and identify the exact diagnosis in less than one-third. The GenAI gains are nearly eliminated for uncommon cases and are accompanied by more hedging and recommendations for further testing. Across the main outcomes, source attribution itself matters little. These findings highlight that highly useful patient-provided AI diagnoses can improve physician accuracy and shape clinical decisions, yet physicians make only partial use of the information provided.

papers.title: Push vs. Pull in Mobile Advertising: The Role of Cognitive Load in Consumer Response
papers.abstract: Mobile advertising relies on two delivery mechanisms: push notifications that proactively present content and pull-based interactions that require active user search. While prior research shows that push is often more effective, the behavioral mechanisms contributing to this advantage remain unclear. Drawing on cognitive load theory, we propose cognitive load as one mechanism: push can reduce cognitive effort by presenting a salient, pre-selected option, whereas pull requires active search and choice among alternatives. We test this mechanism in a 2×2×2 online experiment (N = 1,600) manipulating delivery mode, prior usage experience, and store density. Results show that push increases response likelihood and reduces cognitive load, which partially mediates the effect on response. This cognitive-load reduction is stronger under high store density. Prior usage experience reduces cognitive load but does not moderate the effect of push. Our findings identify cognitive load as one pathway contributing to the effectiveness advantage of mobile push.

papers.title: Livestreaming vs. Short-Video Selling in Social Commerce: Effects on Product Returns
papers.abstract: Product returns present a major challenge in content-driven social commerce, where sellers face strategic choices for both selling format and selling channel. Using data from a social commerce platform and a brand vendor, we examine the effect of livestreaming vs. short-video selling format on product returns, and its joint effect with selling channel. Results show that livestreaming (vs. short-video) has an insignificant overall effect on product returns. However, livestreaming (vs. short-video) in seller-operated channels has a 5.9 percentage points higher return likelihood compared to influencer-collaboration channels. Mechanism analyses show that the insignificant overall effect of livestreaming (vs. short-video) on product returns is driven by the coexistence of two countervailing effects — an informative effect that reduces returns and an impulsive effect that increases returns — that offset each other. The cross-channel difference in product return likelihood appears to arise from variations in the magnitude of livestreaming’s impulse-purchase inducement effect across channels.

papers.title: How User Approval and Cognitive Load Shape the Effectiveness of a Digital Swap Nudge
papers.abstract: Digital nudging has gained prominence as a tool to motivate behavior change in e-commerce. Just-in-time product swap recommendations have emerged as an effective intervention for promoting healthier food choices, yet retailers’ concerns over user reactance and overwhelm remain barriers to implementation. This study examines how user approval and cognitive load affect nudge effectiveness. We analyze data from a large-scale, multi-session online experiment (N = 1,201; three visits each) in which participants completed simulated shopping tasks in a realistic online grocery platform. Product labels indicated healthiness ratings, CO₂ impact, or both; a control group saw no labels. When participants selected poorly rated products, pop-up recommendations suggested category alternatives. Swap nudges significantly improved basket healthiness and reduced carbon footprint. Both user approval and increases in cognitive load over time correlated positively with behavioral change, suggesting a possible interpretation of approval and cognitive load as drivers, rather than barriers to nudge-induced behavior change.

papers.title: Seeing the Future, Selling the Present: AI-Generated Renovation Visualizations in Housing Transactions
papers.abstract: Housing platforms now use generative AI to show buyers how a home could look after renovation. Unlike listing photos or VR tours that reproduce a property’s current state, AI-generated renovation visualization (AIRV) depicts an unrealized future state. Using proprietary data from a leading Chinese housing platform and an instrumental-variable design based on listing-entry agents’ AIRV adoption propensity, we find that AIRV raises the probability of sale and lengthens time on market, with effects concentrated among hard-to-imagine listings (shell, never-occupied, and unfurnished units). Two opposing stage-specific patterns emerge. AIRV raises online-to-offline conversion and shortens the time to the first showing; yet it lengthens the post-showing stage, as buyers who visit are less likely to return and sellers make larger downward list-price adjustments, lowering transaction prices for these listings, consistent with expectation disconfirmation and seller price discovery. Expanded showings and price corrections jointly reconcile the sale-probability gain. This dual-stage tension is intrinsic to AI-generated future-state content and informs platform design and governance.

papers.title: Pricing the Outcomes under Endogenous Stochastic Quality
papers.abstract: Outcome-based pricing charges clients for realized task completion rather than for software access or usage. Although rare in traditional software markets, this model becomes viable for AI agents, which can perform tasks and embed verification rules within digital workflows. We develop a model in which an AI firm chooses quality, verification stringency, and contract terms for heterogeneous clients. The key mechanism is endogenous stochastic quality: one scalable AI investment generates different resolution rates across client types. This simple shift changes both payment differentiation and investment incentives. Low-complexity clients pay more because their tasks are resolved more often even under a uniform contract. Strict verification arises endogenously because more permissive rules increase billable outcomes but weaken the link between payments and genuine performance. Outcome-based pricing outperforms usage pricing when the revenue gain from heterogeneous performance exceeds verification cost. These findings show how AI’s stochastic task performance shapes pricing and quality-investment incentives.

papers.title: Attention Volatility in the Digital Economy: The Dual Role of Digital Assets
papers.abstract: Digital acquisitions do not necessarily translate into immediate use or uniform reallocation of attention. This study conceptualizes post-purchase behavioral attention volatility as two distinct facets: entry dynamics, or time to first observed use, and allocative displacement, or relative playtime allocated to newly acquired versus incumbent assets. Using a five-month panel of 3,695 Steam users, Cox proportional-hazards and two-way fixed effects models examine how inventory overhang and consumption capital are associated with these facets across discount-intensity and rare-deal environments. The results indicate that these portfolio-state associations differ across promotion conditions, with more consistent robustness for entry dynamics than for allocative displacement. The study extends post-adoption and cross-application research by anchoring activation timing and relative allocation to a discrete acquisition within a persistently owned portfolio. It also identifies entry latency and new-versus-incumbent allocation as complementary post-purchase indicators beyond transaction counts.

papers.title: When the Buyer Is a Machine: The Diagnosticity–Exploration Tradeoff in Agentic Commerce
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are beginning to browse, evaluate, and purchase products on behalf of consumers, raising a question for agentic commerce: do marketing strategies designed for humans influence machine shoppers, and do they affect search as well as choice? We build a sandboxed e-commerce environment with nine marketing cues drawn from 24 retail sites and run 23,015 trials across three models from two providers. Marketing cues affect product selection, but their effectiveness varies across cues and models; in the primary model, a Best Seller Badge raises target selection to 70.0% from 11.5% in control. Relative cue effectiveness shows both convergence and divergence from patterns documented in prior consumer research. More importantly, stronger selection effects are systematically associated with less exploration before commitment. We characterize this inverse relationship as the diagnosticity–exploration tradeoff, showing that marketing can shape not only what an AI agent chooses but how far it searches before choosing.

papers.title: When Machines Persuade Better Than Humans: Generative AI, Cognitive Constraints, and Promotional Effectiveness
papers.abstract: This study examines the effects of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-based product promotion on customer purchase decisions in the context of online food ordering. In partnership with a chain restaurant, we conducted a randomized field experiment comparing four message types: AI-generated personalized messages, AI-generated generic messages, human-generated generic messages, and coupons only. Both AI-generated formats outperformed human-generated messages in driving purchases. Personalized AI messages increased daily order amounts by 14.3%, while generic AI messages increased them by 10.4%. Moderation analyses show that generic AI messages are especially effective under high cognitive load (e.g., workplace), whereas personalized AI messages remain effective across contexts. We further utilize the Elaboration Likelihood Model to explain the results. The findings provide causal evidence for GenAI’s value in marketing and customer engagement strategies.

papers.title: Algorithmic Infrastructure and Market Coordination in Credit Markets
papers.abstract: Automated underwriting systems increasingly shape how mortgage credit is evaluated and allocated. While prior research focuses on individual loan decisions, less is known about market-level consequences as adoption expands across local credit markets. Using tract-year Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data, we examine automated underwriting as market-coordinating infrastructure. To address endogenous adoption, we use an instrumental-variables design based on lagged conforming-loan-limit changes that shift exposure to GSE-compatible underwriting pipelines. Naïve fixed-effects estimates show a positive association between AUS adoption and approval rates, whereas the local IV estimate is negative and statistically significant. The baseline relative-timing connected-market IV estimate is also negative and statistically significant, indicating that lagged neighboring AUS exposure is associated with lower local approval rates. Conditional on the maintained exclusion restriction, the findings indicate that policy-induced shifts in standardized-underwriting exposure are associated with credit allocation within and across connected local markets.

papers.title: The Negotiator's Dilemma at Scale: Creating Value in Agentic Negotiations
papers.abstract: Recent work uses negotiation to evaluate language-model capabilities. Evaluating the effects of widespread adoption requires understanding how negotiation agents interact and which agents principals have incentives to choose. We cross nine theory-grounded prompts and an unprompted baseline in 100 ordered pairings, with 30 runs per pairing in each of two multi-issue scenarios, and analyze payoff matrices as games of agent choice. In the main scenario, two decompositions attribute 69% and 81% of systematic variation to pair-specific interactions. Best responses for principals maximizing their payoff generally favor value claiming; with Ultimatum held out, all do. The most productive pairing combines preference elicitation with trade proposals, yet principals' incentives lead to equilibria with lower joint value. Pairing effects and welfare gaps recur in another scenario and model family. Platforms seeking to improve value creation through negotiation agents need to evaluate agents in pairs and account for principals' incentives when choosing designs.

papers.title: AI as Shopping Gatekeepers: Marketplace Cooperation with External LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are emerging as new shopping gatekeepers by mediating consumer search, product discovery, and recommendations. We study when marketplace platforms should cooperate with external LLMs and how such cooperation reshapes seller competition. We develop a stylized game-theoretic model in which cooperation introduces an LLM-mediated recommendation channel and sellers can engage in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). Our analysis shows that LLM-induced traffic may intensify price and GEO competition and reduce marketplace advertising. In contrast, higher LLM inference accuracy softens GEO-based competition and can complement platform advertising. Cooperation is profitable when the LLM provides sufficient traffic scale and inference accuracy. Moreover, sellers may be worse off under cooperation when the LLM places high weight on GEO, leading to a rent-dissipating GEO arms race. Overall, our study innovatively incorporates sellers’ GEO behaviors and provides several theoretical insights into LLM-mediated shopping.

papers.title: Learning from Counterfactual Feedback: Algorithmic Bidding in Display Ad Auctions
papers.abstract: Competition authorities increasingly mandate that programmatic ad platforms share post-auction information such as the minimum bid required to win. We study how such counterfactual feedback affects competition between learning bidders in repeated first-price auctions. In a $2\times2$ Q-learning design, we vary whether bidders use threshold feedback to update unchosen bids (all-bid updating) and whether they condition current bids on past bids (memory). First, all-bid updating is pro-competitive across exploration, learning rates, discount factors, and initialization rules, but the effect is systematically smaller with memory. Seller revenue rises by approximately 200\% without memory and 85\% with memory. Second, under memory, forced winning bids produce smaller post-deviation losses and deviation paths return to their paired no-deviation paths sooner under all-bid updating. For the tested bids under greedy continuation, this indicates weaker deviation discipline. The effect of threshold feedback therefore depends on bidder memory.

papers.title: Preview Before Blind Box Purchase? Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment
papers.abstract: Blind-box products have become increasingly popular worldwide. Recently, some blind- box companies have introduced a “preview” function, which allows users to try a blind box for free and view the option without paying. Some platforms also allow users to purchase the previewed item. However, there is little empirical evidence on how previews may influence consumers. Therefore, this research aims to fill the research gap by examining how the preview feature affects user engagement and purchase behavior. We conducted a randomized field experiment in collaboration with a major blind box digital platform in China. Using action-level data with product and date fixed effects, we find that previews can substantially increase immediate purchase likelihood, but the effect attenuates over time.

papers.title: Beyond Content: How Short-Form Video Feeds Reshape User Views and Engagement
papers.abstract: Short-form vertical video feeds are ubiquitous, yet their behavioral effects are difficult to isolate because cross-platform comparisons confound interface with content and within-platform adoption is endogenous. On a leading Chinese video platform, we use the average January vertical-upload share of creators watched by each user as an instrumental variable for February exposure to its TikTok-style Story mode. Because the platform preferentially surfaces vertical videos in Story, the instrument predicts exposure; its one-month lag makes it predetermined and limits confounding from contemporaneous choices. In a panel of 36,612 users and 259,624 user-weeks, 2SLS estimates show that Story exposure recomposes rather than expands activity: low-friction actions and content-category breadth increase, while viewing volume does not change significantly. Estimates for high-deliberation engagement and platform time are exploratory. The pattern is consistent with lower search and transition costs, with effects concentrated among already-active users.

papers.title: Beyond Retrieval: Generative Algorithms in Recommendation and Search
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is transforming how digital platforms connect users with information, products, and services, a task long performed by retrieval-based recommentaion and search algorithms. This shift raises a central question: how does deploying generative algorithms affect user engagement? Combining China’s mandatory algorithm filing records with app-level monthly active user data, we trace the diffusion of generative algorithms and estimate their engagement effects using staggered and stacked difference-in-differences designs. Generative recommendation and search algorithms diffuse rapidly across app categories and produce larger increases in monthly active users than their conventional counterparts. Their adoption also reduces competitors’ user engagement, indicating that generative capabilities reshape the allocation of attention within platform markets. These effects arise across both demand-formation and demand-fulfillment contexts. Our findings show that generative algorithms move digital intermediation beyond information retrieval, from ranking existing items to constructing answers.

papers.title: Delegated Incentive Allocation in Collective Finance: Evidence from a Digital Microfinance Platform
papers.abstract: Many collective finance platforms operate under All-or-Nothing models, in which project success hinges on meeting participation thresholds. To help reach these thresholds, conventional incentive allocation rewards participation asymmetrically, favoring those who commit under higher uncertainty. However, theoretically optimal allocations are often impractical, leading platforms to rely on simplified rules that can create incentive misalignments. This study examines whether introducing discretion into otherwise rule-based incentive allocation improves coordination outcomes. We exploit a policy change on a South Korean digital microfinance platform that delegated authority over a portion of the incentive budget to group leaders. Using a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we find that delegated incentive allocation increases the probability of successful group formation by 12.4 percentage points. Mechanism analyses show that delegation accelerates the filling of the slots that rule-based allocation under-incentivizes, consistent with leaders directing incentives toward participation bottlenecks. We contribute to research on coordination in collective finance and hybrid governance.

papers.title: Anchored at Fifty-Fifty: How LLM Agents Bargain Across Providers
papers.abstract: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed as bargaining agents in consumer and enterprise commerce, yet systematic evidence on their strategic behavior under formal incentive structures remains scarce. Bilateral bargaining is studied across 1,296 negotiations among 9 LLMs from 3 providers and 3 capability tiers, in three settings: a closed-form Rubinstein alternating-offers benchmark, a naturalistic procurement setting, and a scaffolded payoff maximization. Three patterns emerge. Agents reach agreement reliably but anchor on equal splits even when the equilibrium is markedly asymmetric. They routinely violate their own budget bounds and fail to walk away from infeasible deals, although a one-shot supervisory check removes three-quarters of out-of-bounds outcomes. A prompt-level treatment largely dislodges the equal-split anchor across all models, yet improves equilibrium alignment only for those with explicit reasoning capacity. Together, the findings show that the principal-agent gap in LLM bargaining is structural – closing it requires external scaffolding which effectiveness scales with, but cannot be replaced by, gains in model capability.

papers.title: When AI Enters Art Market: Substitution, Disclosure, and Strategic Responses
papers.abstract: Generative AI has transformed the digital art markets into a hybrid environment where UGC and AIGC coexist and compete. While AI-generated content (AIGC) is increasingly prevalent, empirical evidence regarding its direct economic consequences for user-generated content (UGC) demand and the effectiveness of platform governance remains limited. Utilizing data from a leading digital art platform and a Difference-in-Differences approach across two quasi-experimental designs, we find that AIGC entry significantly reduces UGC sales through visibility, value, and quality effects, with the value effect as the dominant driver. Additionally, the introduction of voluntary AIGC tags further decreases UGC demand due to strategic disclosure, as artists conceal AI works to bypass user filters and intensify substitution. These findings offer important theoretical and practical insights for platform governance.

papers.title: REIT Frameworks as FinTech Infrastructure: Banking Complementarity and Corporate Innovation in the EU
papers.abstract: Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) regimes bundle exchange listing, standardized electronic disclosure, automated settlement, and tax transparency into a single institutional arrangement. This paper treats that bundle as FinTech infrastructure and asks whether it raises business R&D intensity. Two-way fixed effects regressions on 2016–2023 data place the REIT premium between +0.18 and +0.26 percentage points of business enterprise R&D over GDP, stable across eight specifications, though design-based inference places it at the margin of conventional significance. A sample split at the median bank cost-to-income ratio appears to make the premium conditional, but a full-sample interaction test does not reject coefficient equality (p = 0.36). A sector-level decomposition across 22 manufacturing divisions, exploiting the staggered activation of the settlement layer in 21 member states, finds the premium uniform regardless of external financial dependence. For the Capital Markets Union agenda, REIT promotion does not require a prior banking-efficiency benchmark.

papers.title: Regulations as a Percolative and Turbulent Force in Cybersecurity
papers.abstract: The European Union's regulatory tsunami has confronted cybersecurity managers with an unprecedented wave of overlapping, ambiguous, and anticipatory demands. This paper examines how regulation shapes the ontological work of cybersecurity through temporal dynamics, illustrated by a qualitative case study of cybersecurity managers in European advanced machinery companies. Following Michel Serres, we theorize time as non-linear and contemporary, proposing percolation and turbulence as two distinct temporal forces through which past and future collapse into the present moment. This conceptualization reveals how cybersecurity actors continuously work out what is being secured, what it is becoming, and what responsibilities attach to it under conditions that structurally resist stabilization. We make three contributions: we move beyond sequential temporality in IS research; we develop ontological work as a distinct analytical concept for cybersecurity; and we show how regulation functions as a percolative and turbulent force that generates rather than resolves ontological work.

papers.title: Adaptive AI Regulation Beyond Aspiration: Regulatory Learning and the AI Act
papers.abstract: Information Systems (IS) research has predominantly treated regulation as stable and top-down: rules are set, and actors comply. This framing is inadequate for governing AI. Rapid technological change outpaces regulatory updates, rendering frameworks obsolete. Adaptive regulation addresses this by designing frameworks that learn from the actors they govern. The central mechanism is regulatory learning: generating and integrating evidence from practice to trigger updates. Drawing on the AI Act, where adaptive ambitions are explicitly codified in law, we show that the Act's adaptive infrastructure remains largely incomplete. The metrics, knowledge infrastructures, and coordination required to make regulatory learning operational do not yet exist. This gap opens three paths for IS research: (1) designing knowledge infrastructures that support regulatory learning; (2) empirically studying regulatory learning under ambiguity and resource constraints; and (3) engaging in IS policy research.

papers.title: The Influence of Regulatory Intermediaries on AI Deployment in Organizations
papers.abstract: Organizations are expected to develop and deploy AI quickly while ensuring that they are used safely and responsibly. These pressures are significant in regulated sectors such as healthcare, where organizations are subjected to external regulations via regulatory bodies and regulatory intermediaries. Our study examines how regulatory intermediaries (RIs) shape AI deployment. We studied a troubled AI chatbot project in a public hospital that had to comply with two regulatory chains comprising a regulator and a regulatory intermediary. The RI chains shaped the project through the way they translated external regulations. We developed a theoretical framework of organizational AI deployment under multiple RIs that shows how the regulatory chains’ translation created AI deployment tensions, and how the hospital enacted several responses to manage these tensions and move the project forward. However, it could not resolve conflicting requirements between the two regulatory chains, which contributed to the project’s eventual failure.

papers.title: From Human-in-the-Loop to Stakeholdersin-the-loop: A Multi-Stakeholder Governance Mechanism for AI Decision Making
papers.abstract: Efforts to institutionalize trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) rely on governance mechanisms, such as human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, human-in-command, which establish formal human oversight of automated decision-making (ADM). While these mechanisms provide foundational role-based oversight, oversight may be assigned to a designated human actor, with stakeholder perspectives entering, where considered, through consultation, representation, or surrounding organizational and regulatory arrangements. What remains less theorized is how plural stakeholder participation can function as an integral governance logic through which diverse perspectives and collective oversight are systematically incorporated into ADM governance. This study conceptualizes such logic within a generalizable AI governance mechanism. Drawing on stakeholder theory, it develops Stakeholders-in-the-loop (SITL), structuring plural oversight through asynchronous collection of evaluative, instructive, and authoritative stakeholder input, and its integration into ADM monitoring, supervision, and control. SITL complements existing role-based mechanisms by making stakeholder participation and collective governance an explicit oversight logic.

papers.title: Anticipatory Regulation of Digital Phenomena: The Case of Digital Nomadism
papers.abstract: This research-in-progress examines how multi-level governance (MLG) arrangements shape anticipatory regulation of emerging digital phenomena, using digital nomadism as an empirical case. Governments increasingly struggle to respond coherently to digital phenomena that scale across jurisdictions faster than regulatory categories can adapt, resulting in fragmented policy responses. Conceptually, the study frames anticipatory regulation as depending on recognition and coordination across actors, domains, and levels. Empirically, we draw on document analysis of official government sources across nine jurisdictions, with Australia as a focal case without a dedicated arrangement. Findings suggest that responses are largely migration-first and entry-focused, addressing mobility while leaving cross-domain coordination unresolved. Only two jurisdictions specify how tax treatment applies, despite arrangements authorizing stays that may engage domestic tax residence rules. The study contributes to an initial conceptualization of how the anticipatory regulation of digital phenomena occurs, positioning digital nomadism as a case of regulatory ambiguity.

papers.title: Governing Open Finance: A Comparative Analysis of Regulation, Standards, and Stakeholder Strategy
papers.abstract: Open Finance extends Open Banking by enabling customer-authorised data sharing across financial products through APIs. This paper examines Open Finance as an IS governance problem in which shared digital infrastructure is governed through the interaction of regulatory pressure, stakeholder strategy and standards development. Drawing on institutional isomorphism and stakeholder theory, we develop a framework linking coercive, mimetic and normative pressures to stakeholder positions on participation, liability, data protection and standards governance. Based on preliminary analysis of institutional documents from the UK, EU and US, supplemented by exploratory interviews, we identify three tensions: mandatory versus voluntary participation, liability and data protection, and standards governance. We show how these tensions vary across regulatory spaces, comparing the UK’s regulator-led approach with the EU’s legislative model and the US’s industry-led standard-setting regime.

papers.title: Rights by Architecture: A Human-Compatible Sociotechnical Layer for Digital Protection Across Regulatory Regimes
papers.abstract: Digital rights increasingly exist in law but remain difficult to exercise through the information systems that mediate them. Using disciplined conceptual synthesis and problematization, this critical-conceptual IS paper explains the gap through the interaction of legal heterogeneity, conflicting organizational and commercial incentives, fragmented architectures, and asymmetrical control over rights-relevant acts. It then theorizes a human-compatible rights layer: a governed sociotechnical capability for standardized, machine-readable, bidirectional, and jurisdictionally plural communication of requests, consent, refusal, withdrawal, objection, records, and support. Comparing California-style opt-out signals, the EU's mixed lawful-basis regime, and P3P, DNT, GPC, and ADPC, the paper derives seven normative requirements, develops rights by architecture as a bounded emancipatory policy argument, and treats a proposed GDPR provision on automated and machine-readable privacy management as a policy case for moving from banner-based compliance toward rights-supporting digital infrastructure.

papers.title: AI Regulation and Venture Capital Investment
papers.abstract: This study examines how comprehensive AI regulation affects venture investment. Using venture capital investment data from January 2022 through December 2025 and a difference-in-differences design that compares EU countries with U.S. states across the phased EU AI Act, we find no significant decline at the Parliament vote or entry into force, but a substantial reduction when concrete obligations begin to apply. Effects are uneven across regulatory exposure, venture size and age, syndication, and investment stage. The key mechanism is that financial risk serves as a moderating factor: ventures and deal structures with less capacity to absorb or share downside risk experience larger reductions.

papers.title: Governance Remediation in Supranational Digital Infrastructure Initiatives - Harmonizing EU Maritime Reporting Data
papers.abstract: Creating supranational digital infrastructures that harmonize cross-border data exchange presents a complex governance challenge. While the literature has investigated initial or localized infrastructure initiative challenges, we know little about how regulatory bodies remediate failed infrastructure initiatives via governance redesign. To address this gap, we draw upon a longitudinal case study of the EU Maritime Single Window to investigate why an initial 2010 Directive resulted in fragmentation and how a subsequent 2019 Regulation was designed to remediate this failure. Our findings show that the initial ‘hands-off’ governance failed to incentivize architectural changes of installed bases to achieve supranational interoperability. We further show that effective remediation involves redistributing regulatory and technical control across architectural layers to balance supranational and local needs, centralizing where interoperability is non-negotiable while preserving local control elsewhere. Our study contributes to digital infrastructure literature and offers practical implications for policymakers.

papers.title: Data Is Key: AUDI 'S Journey to Data‐Driven Business Models
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Car manufacturers excel in leveraging new digital technologies through vehicle design but face challenges in using the data these technologies provide for innovation. In this practitioner paper, we analyse and report on the process AUDI, a German original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of premium automobiles, went through in developing and managing data‐driven business models. A detailed description of the three phases of the carmaker's journey from creating to scaling to capturing identifies the automotive industry's urgent need to standardise data, prioritise customer integration and overcome difficulties in determining the price of data. For other (European) car manufacturers developing and managing data‐driven business models, we also derive five lessons learned from our case regarding AUDI's efforts to address issues when leveraging car‐related data and present an industry outlook with remaining challenges.

papers.title: Emerging Resistance in the Digital Transformation of Public Transport: Older Passengers With Dementia and Experiences of Ecobiographical Disruption
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The digital transformation of public transport is prone to resistance. Among the discontents of such transformation, older people and those living with cognitive impairments are repeatedly identified. Stereotypes assuming their innate resistance to technological change are widespread, but research shows that older people with dementia can have rich digital lives. This paper reports findings from an ethnography of public transport digital transformation with older passengers living with dementia in Greater Manchester, UK. Combining interviews, photography, poetry, route maps and contextual statistics, four cases illustrate the emergence of resistance to digital displays, cashless exchange, e‐ticketing and live routing. They reveal subtle, nuanced and contextually contingent resistances that emerge from digital transformation disrupting passenger ecobiographies—the rootedness of their lives in longstanding ecosystems. Findings show that everyday resistance can be small, transient and relational, and should be taken seriously as an indicator of potential injustices. Future initiatives should meaningfully include older and disabled users throughout to increase alertness to ecobiographical disruption and emerging resistance.

papers.title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
papers.abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02761 .

papers.title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
papers.abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors acknowledge funding from the University of Konstanz for Study 2, Harvard University Pershing Square Foundation for Human Research, and Harvard Business School. The funders had no role in data collection and analysis, the decision to publish, or preparation of this manuscript. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files …

papers.title: Dialysis Clinic Patient Flow and Work Design
papers.abstract: Problem Definition: For 433,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatments cost over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment “put-on” task and a post-treatment “take-off” task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safety and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations through better patient flow. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-ons as soon as a technician and station are free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons and the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. We derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s makespan under constant treatment durations and show that interlaced schedules achieve the shortest completion time, whereas tandem configurations can reduce labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations and stochastic task times and arrivals to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, …

papers.title: Enhancing Safety Signaling: Integrating Clinical Trials and Post-Marketing Adverse Event Reports
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) cause numerous emergency room visits and thousands of deaths annually in the U.S. Although regulators like the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) aim to detect safety issues during clinical trials, these trials are often too small, short, or restrictive to capture rare or delayed ADRs. Consequently, regulators rely on spontaneous adverse event reporting systems (eg, FAERS) to identify potential safety issues—termed safety signals—by detecting side effects that occur disproportionately among patients taking a particular drug. However, these observational data are subject to selection and reporting biases, which can lead to false signals or missed risks. Methodology/results: We propose a Bayesian framework to enhance the hypothesis generation step in safety signaling, offering two methodological advances over standard approaches that rely solely on observational data. First, it integrates pre-approval clinical trial and post-approval observational data. Second, it uses information from common ADRs to estimate and correct bias in rare ADRs. We assess the approach using an analytical model and a large-scale numerical study with real clinical trial and FAERS data. Incorporating clinical trial data substantially reduces signaling costs, and using a common ADR for debiasing yields further gains. This refinement improves decisions for about 1% of ADRs, translating to expected cost savings of 1.5–2.3% (approx. $32–159 million), with …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Multi-Self Presentation and Knowledge Contribution in Platform Operations: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
papers.abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users' formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others' questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature's multi-self presentation function: First, the new feature increases high adopters' engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; Second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Mind the Cost of Disturbance: Firm-Level Supply Chain Risk and the Bank Loan Cost
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive — the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Pricing and Information Provision in Service Platforms with Heterogeneous Customers
papers.abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers' decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
papers.abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm.
