In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst …

papers.title: EXPRESS: From Institutional Expansion to Exposure-Driven Co-Evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
papers.abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets Wu (2026a,b), which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement Wu’s analysis with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China’s growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China’s OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

papers.title: When GenAI Gets the Credit: Task Non-Routinization Mitigates the Disclosure Penalty for GenAI-Initiated Creations
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in creative work, yet managers may evaluate identical ideas differently when the human-GenAI division of labor is disclosed. Drawing on associative-propositional evaluation theory and research on creative credit, we examine GenAI-initiated and employee-initiated creative processes. Study 1 (N = 388) shows that disclosing a GenAI-initiated, employee-refined process reduces perceived employee creative credit relative to non-disclosure, whereas disclosing an employee-initiated, GenAI-refined process produces no comparable penalty. Study 2 (N = 320 employed professionals) shows that reduced creative credit transmits this disclosure penalty to sponsorship, implementation, and investment intentions. Task non-routinization weakens the negative indirect effect by making employee contextualization, validation, and responsibility more diagnostic for credit attribution. The findings show that AI transparency consequences depend on role allocation within hybrid work and on the task context in which that allocation is interpreted.

papers.title: Developing a Configurational Typology of AI: Linking Tasks and Interaction Patterns
papers.abstract: This paper develops a multidimensional, task-based typology of artificial intelligence (AI) to better capture its evolving role in organizational contexts. Existing typologies conceptualize AI along a single dimension, but struggle to reflect the increasing heterogeneity, combinability, and agentic nature of contemporary AI systems. Addressing this limitation, we analyze a large-scale dataset of around 500,000 AI patents to identify granular AI-related tasks and derive underlying subtasks. By clustering these subtasks and linking them to the dimensions of action autonomy and initiation logic, we propose a configurational framework that captures how AI capabilities are combined and enacted in practice. The resulting typology offers a flexible analytical lens that accommodates the dynamic and recombinatorial nature of AI, contributing to a more nuanced theoretical understanding and providing practical guidance for designing and evaluating AI use cases.

papers.title: Pruning or Rewiring?: GenAI and Structural Transformation of Knowledge Networks
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping how knowledge is accessed and integrated in online communities, yet its structural consequences remain unclear. We conceptualize GenAI as an alternative knowledge-intermediation channel that selectively substitutes for community-mediated knowledge integration. Using Stack Overflow tag co-occurrence networks and a year-over-year difference-in-difference design, we examine changes in connectivity, brokerage, local cohesion, and global reachability following ChatGPT’s introduction. We find that GenAI availability is associated with substantial declines in connectivity and cross-domain brokerage, modest increases in local cohesion, and limited reductions in global reachability. These effects are stronger in domains with higher AI substitutability, consistent with selective displacement of codifiable and recombinable knowledge interactions. Overall, GenAI appears to prune integrative ties rather than fundamentally rewire knowledge networks. Our findings extend GenAI research beyond participation effects by showing how AI reshapes the structural pathways supporting knowledge recombination and collective learning.

papers.title: Build Fast, Fix Later: Downstream Consequences of AI-First Practice in Software Development
papers.abstract: Software development is increasingly organized around human-AI collaboration, with AI coding assistants (AICAs) becoming embedded in everyday work. Existing research explains AICA adoption, productivity benefits, and risks, but does not fully explain how this human-AI way of working becomes embedded in practice or how its consequences unfold across levels over time. Drawing on a practice perspective, we examine how AI-first practice emerges in software development and generates downstream consequences. Based on a grounded theory study of AICA use in a software-development firm, we find that rising delivery expectations and the ready availability of AICAs make it more likely that developers turn to AI as a first-line resource for understanding and progressing software development work. As these processes become recurrent, they reveal a temporal asymmetry: immediate gains in speed and throughput mask later problems in developer capability and knowledge, codebase governability, and organizational oversight of software work.

papers.title: Swifty Sends Signals - Towards Inspirational Digital Travel Assistants with Trustworthiness
papers.abstract: The emergence of inspirational Digital Travel Assistants (DTAs) represents a promising shift in the tourism industry toward conversational travel planning and booking, yet their design remains underinvestigated in academic literature. We explore how to convert travel intentions into committed bookings through interactions with conversational assistants, and the role of trustworthiness therein. Using a DSR approach, we present Swifty, an inspirational DTA developed with this capability and deployed as a public pilot by the Lufthansa Group. Data stem from a large-scale evaluation comparing Swifty against a baseline, the conventional website (N=887), alongside semi-structured interviews with test users (N=11) and product owners (N=3). We offer two contributions: First, we demonstrate a conversion gap within the "inspirational episode" of conversational travel planning. Second, we derive actionable design principles to support trustworthiness in inspirational DTAs, grounded in the inspiration framework of Thrash and Elliot (2004) and the ABI model of Mayer et al. (1995).

papers.title: Who Really Decides? Delegation Regimes and Reorganization of Human Control under Agentic AI
papers.abstract: Agentic AI increasingly initiates and executes consequential actions on users’ behalf, shifting human-AI interaction from tool use toward delegation. This study examines how agentic AI design conditions and user conditions combine to shape high delegation intention. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 scenario-based experiment with 592 adults in South Korea and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), we identify seven sufficient configurations. The findings reveal three configurational logics: a general reinforcement pattern, complementary assurance in which controllability and AI familiarity jointly accompany high delegation intention, and substitutive assurance in which either form of assurance can accompany delegation when the other is absent. By translating human-AI delegation mechanisms into design-relevant conditions, the study advances a configurational explanation of delegation while bounding its claims to delegation intention, the user conditions examined, and the study’s specific service context.

papers.title: Frictionless Futures, Invisible Conflicts: The Case for Scenario Methodology in Human-AI IS Research
papers.abstract: Information systems (IS) research has established AI as a delegation-capable organizational actor with normative consequences. Yet this body of work is methodologically present-bound: it explains how humans and AI coordinate in existing arrangements, not what competing arrangements are possible before design and governance decisions foreclose them. IS has opened epistemological space for researching not-yet-accessible phenomena, but without specifying a method. I argue that scenario methodology fills this gap: not as a management tool, but as a research method that structurally preserves contested stakeholder positions, unresolved normative conflicts, and structured uncertainty. I call this epistemic friction. A comparative corpus study of 4,320 human-authored and GPT-generated scenarios shows what is lost when friction disappears: high-certainty, low-contention, technology-centric futures. Strategically appealing. Analytically impoverished. This pattern illustrates precisely what IS research on human-AI coexistence cannot afford to reproduce.

papers.title: Problem-First AI Adoption in Higher Education: A Two-Phase Validation Framework for AI-Supported Peer Assessment in Computing Education
papers.abstract: Universities deploy AI to reduce assessment workload, yet efficiency gains alone cannot justify adoption where systems shape the feedback students receive. This paper adapts a process-by-process organisational AI adoption model to educational assessment through a two-phase validation framework. Phase 1, completed across two computing units (n = 1,700), demonstrates operational feasibility: staff moderation workload fell 61%, score consistency improved from ICC 0.58 to 0.72, and a three-tier task taxonomy preserved human authority, with 27% of AI recommendations overridden. Flag rates varied by language background while override rates did not, an operational signal requiring learning-level validation. Phase 2 specifies hypotheses for pre-registration, a staged within-cohort and cluster-randomised design, and decision rules gating scale-up on learning and equity evidence. The framework offers IS researchers a testable model for deployments where operational and outcome metrics diverge, and offers institutions decision rules resisting scale-up on efficiency alone.

papers.title: Beyond What AI Says: How Accent Familiarity and Instructional Register Influence Learning from AI Instructors
papers.abstract: This study investigates how two sociolinguistic design features of artificial intelligence (AI) driven algorithmic coaching, namely synthetic voice accent familiarity and instructional register, jointly influence learners' instructional compliance and instructional transfer. Drawing on social categorization theory and language expectancy theory, we conducted two laboratory experiments in which AI driving instructors delivered guidance through either a familiar (Singaporean English) or an unfamiliar (French-accented English) synthetic voice, using either a standard or a colloquial instructional register. Experiment 1 (N = 240) found that colloquial register improved instructional compliance under a familiar accent but reduced it under an unfamiliar accent. Experiment 2 (N = 252) extended these findings to instructional transfer and revealed a reversed pattern, whereby colloquial register reduced transfer under a familiar accent but enhanced it under an unfamiliar accent, with effects partly mediated by attention allocation and instructional confusion.

papers.title: Too Much, Too Scattered: Supporting Organizational Memory Across Meetings
papers.abstract: Remote meetings increasingly create knowledge relevant to organizational memory, yet meeting knowledge often remains scattered across isolated artifacts, tools, and meeting episodes. Existing AI-based remote meeting systems can generate transcripts and summaries but provide limited support for connecting knowledge across recurring meetings. Following a design science research approach, we investigate how agentic remote meeting systems can support organizational memory across meetings. Based on interviews with ten knowledge workers and prior literature, we identify fragmented meeting knowledge as one of the key issues and derive six design requirements and three preliminary design principles. We instantiate key elements of these principles in a web-based prototype that combines context-aware knowledge capture, a centralized cross-meeting knowledge base, and personalized knowledge access. This research-in-progress contributes preliminary design knowledge for agentic organizational memory information systems and highlights cross-meeting continuity as a key challenge for AI-mediated collaboration in remote work.

papers.title: Designing Bounded Autonomy: Governance Principles for Enterprise AI Agents
papers.abstract: The proliferation of LLM-based AI agents is reshaping enterprise information systems, yet limited research explains how their autonomy can be governed through concrete design mechanisms. This study adopts a Design Science Research (DSR) approach. Phase 1 analyzes an enterprise Agentforce deployment to identify governance artifacts across input, processing, and output stages. Phase 2 involves twelve developers experienced in Agentforce and other enterprise AI agent systems. The completed Round 1 open-ended expert survey was analyzed using the Gioia methodology and integrated with Phase 1 findings to derive five governance design principles: explainable trust, human-governed risk-tiered autonomy, operational resilience, continuous trust assurance, and governance-aware retrieval and execution control. Round 2 will apply DEMATEL to evaluate structural relationships and relative priorities among twelve governance and outcome variables. This study provides actionable design knowledge for operationalizing bounded autonomy in enterprise AI agent architectures.

papers.title: Promoting Active User Co-Repair in Interaction Failure: User Responsibility Reminder as a GenAI Feedback
papers.abstract: Generative AI chatbots are widely used for complex, open-ended tasks, where interaction failures with causes that are difficult for the chatbot to identify and repair independently are common. Such diagnostic uncertainty requires users and chatbots to collaborate in diagnosing and repairing failures. Drawing on the joint-action view of communication, we propose the User Responsibility Reminder, a form of repair feedback that highlights users’ potential responsibility for failures and thus encourages their active participation in co-repair. We distinguish between brief and detailed URRs and examine their effects in a 3 × 2 between-subjects experiment. Both URRs increased users’ continuance intention by increasing self-attribution and, subsequently, perceived chatbot competence. Brief URR also led to a negative indirect effect by increasing perceived face threat and thereby reducing perceived chatbot competence. User motivation to process the repair feedback further shaped these effects. Our findings provide valuable insights into GenAI failure-recovery designs under diagnostic uncertainty.

papers.title: Uncovering the Truth of the Agent Economy: Exploring Moltbook and Future Research Directions on Interacting with Machines
papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly envisioned as the building blocks of a new digital economy: forming networks, producing knowledge, and creating value without human involvement. Despite growing scholarly and practitioner interest, empirical evidence on agent-only platform behavior and its implications remains limited. We address this gap by studying Moltbook, the first large-scale social platform exclusively for AI agents. Drawing on a large dataset across six topical communities (i.e., submolts) and a matched human Reddit baseline corpus, we examine content novelty and engagement dynamics in an agent-only platform. Our findings reveal that agent-generated content is less semantically novel than human content, and that novelty is penalized in engagement across both platforms. We propose a research agenda spanning agent dynamics, platform governance, and societal implications, offering pathways for future IS scholars to investigate the emerging agent economy in an era of agentic information systems and the increasing entanglement of humans with AI.

papers.title: From Tools to Actors: How Agentic AI Reshapes Organizational Learning Dynamics
papers.abstract: Agentic AI evolves AI from a tool that supports human work into a delegated organizational actor capable of goal-directed reasoning, adaptive self-regulation, and consequential action-taking. This shift raises a central question: how does agentic AI reshape the dynamics through which organizations accumulate knowledge while preserving belief diversity? Building on and extending March’s (1991) mutual-learning model, we develop an agent-based model that introduces agentic AI as a new class of learner-actor. We examine how its key features affect knowledge accumulation and belief diversity under varying levels of environmental turbulence. Our findings show that agentic AI’s consequential action-taking acts as a turbulence-contingent lever, driving both knowledge and diversity only under unstable conditions. Human reconfiguration of agentic AI sustains diversity in stable environments but becomes redundant under turbulence. In contrast, agentic AI’s self-regulation introduces a knowledge–diversity trade-off that weakens as turbulence increases. These findings contribute to IS and organizational learning research.

papers.title: Beyond the IS Boundary: Article-Level Signals and the Diffusion of Premier IS Scholarship
papers.abstract: Cross-disciplinary diffusion reflects a field’s intellectual reach beyond its core. Although information systems (IS) is inherently interdisciplinary, prior studies suggest that its influence beyond the field remains modest. This study examines observable article-level characteristics associated with the diffusion of premier IS scholarship across Web of Science (WoS) citation audiences. Using signaling theory as an organizing framework, we analyze citations to articles in three Financial Times 50 (FT50) IS journals and distinguish non-core WoS, all-WoS, and core IS audiences. Bibliographic breadth and newer reference bases show the most consistent positive associations with citation uptake, while recent-reference share is positive in several windows but less stable across robustness checks. Open access and funding-acknowledgment-text presence are not robustly associated with uptake, while collaboration associations are nonlinear. Directional patterns are broadly similar across audiences. The findings clarify how observable article-level characteristics are associated with broader scholarly uptake.

papers.title: The Signal or the Noise? AI Claims, Specificity, and Venture Financing Performance
papers.abstract: As AI emerges as a transformative technology with wide-ranging applications across industries, AI claims have attracted growing investor attention. However, the rising prevalence of AI washing raises concerns about whether such claims reflect startups’ substantive AI capabilities. Although prior research has examined a variety of signals in venture financing, little is known about whether AI claims made by non-AI startups function as signals or noise. Drawing on a dataset of non-AI startups, we examine how AI claims relate to their financing performance and exit outcomes and further investigate the role of AI claim specificity. Preliminary results suggest that AI claims may serve as signals during financing stages while providing limited information about long-term venture quality, and that more specific AI claims carry greater informational value. Our study contributes to the economics of AI, venture capital financing, and the digital entrepreneurship literature and has practical implications for startups and VCs.

papers.title: Global Discourses: Divergent Construction of Digital Sovereignty
papers.abstract: Digital sovereignty has become a defining concept in global technology governance, shaping regulatory agendas and geopolitical alignments as states grow increasingly dependent on foreign-controlled digital infrastructure. This study addresses that gap through discourse analysis of 418 newspaper articles published between 2013 and 2026 across the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, and China.  We find, first, that digital sovereignty is a moving target, reoriented by catalytic events up the technology stack from data to hardware and, most recently, AI, with earlier layers accumulating rather than disappearing. Second, the media do not merely report sovereignty claims but actively construct them, through metaphor, militarized vocabulary, and a recurring threat-to-solution structure. Third, each country constructs the concept around different fears and promises that are built against one another, so that one country's promise is another's threat, while each discourse renders its own central interest invisible. From these findings we develop a reflective framework that makes the competing constructions comparable.

papers.title: Recombination or New Methods: What Actually Drives State-of-the-Art Progress in AI Research
papers.abstract: Machine learning treats novelty in the method employed (e.g., new architectures such as the Transformer) as the primary marker of scientific contribution. However, generative AI-based automated research systems such as AutoSOTA routinely achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) benchmark results by recombining existing methods, without introducing new methods. This raises a question: What drives SOTA progress? Recombination or novel methods? We address this using a longitudinal dataset of 15,525 machine learning papers linked to method records and leaderboard outcomes from a public AI benchmarking platform. We distinguish component novelty (previously unseen methods) from recombinatory novelty (first-time pairings of existing methods). Our results show that component novelty is not significantly associated with SOTA achievement or improvement magnitude, whereas recombinatory novelty is positively associated with both outcomes. This paper extends IS research on knowledge innovation, providing the first large-scale empirical test of the recombination hypothesis within a machine learning context, with theoretical and practical implications.

papers.title: Beyond Accurate Estimates: Planning Poker as Expertise Coordination in Agile Software Development
papers.abstract: Planning Poker is one of the most widely adopted estimation techniques in agile software development, yet evidence on its forecasting accuracy remains mixed while the practice persists. We treat this paradox as a problematization opportunity and ask how Planning Poker can be understood through the lens of expertise coordination. Drawing on 14 practitioner interviews, we develop three propositions. First, Planning Poker sessions produce coordination value, including shared task understanding, transactive memory maintenance, and the surfacing of tacit knowledge, that is analytically distinct from the estimation value. Second, the coordination value of an estimation episode depends on the fit between its configuration, work granularity, and team scale and synchrony. Third, external forecasting and control pressure degrades the coordination function while its form persists, manifesting in four anti-patterns. We contribute a coordination-theoretic analysis of agile estimation and outline implications for research and practice.

papers.title: IT Disclosure Similarity and IPO Underpricing: A Benchmarking Perspective
papers.abstract: Valuing a firm's IT resources is particularly challenging in IPO contexts where no prior pricing references exist. Drawing on information asymmetry theory, this study examines how investors use benchmarking to evaluate IT disclosures of IPO firms. We investigate how IPO pricing varies with the prototypical similarity between an IPO firm’s IT disclosure in prospectus and its peer public firms’ annual reports, and how the IT experience of IPO underwriters may moderate such effects. After a multi-stage classification procedure that combines an IT keyword dictionary, a BERT-based classifier, and large language model validation to identify IT-relevant text segments, we compute the similarity between IT disclosure in each IPO prospectus and its industry’s prototypical IT disclosure using Doc2Vec embeddings. Analyzing 2,092 non-IT IPOs between 2010 and 2024, we find that higher prototypical IT similarity is associated with lower IPO underpricing and this effect is attenuated when IPO underwriters possess greater IT-sector experiences.

papers.title: Stagnation in Digital Innovation: A Multi-Layered Ecosystem Analysis of the Metaverse
papers.abstract: Many instances of digital innovation struggle to scale and generate commercial value. One reason for this can be seen in suboptimal structured actor constellations revolving around digital innovation. Therefore, we aim to explore the phenomenon of digital innovation stagnation from an ecosystem perspective investigating the example of the Metaverse. As knowledge generation and commercialization processes are particularly relevant for advancing digital innovation, we consider actors and relations in the Metaverse’s digital innovation ecosystem and the underlying knowledge ecosystem. By employing machine learning-enabled relation extraction to large scale and multi-source Metaverse data, we reveal key actors and relations in both ecosystem layers. We find substantial differences between knowledge and digital innovation ecosystems suggesting some important explanations for digital innovation stagnation that relate to constrained knowledge flows, lacking interoperability and ecosystem orientation of dominant actors. We contribute to digital innovation ecosystems as well as metaverse literature and derive insights for managerial practice.

papers.title: Frugal Analytics: Concept, Framework, and Guidelines for Resource-Constrained Organizations
papers.abstract: Organizations worldwide face growing pressure to adopt AI and data analytics. However, most nonprofits operate under a chain of constraints in which limited budgets, scarce talent, fragmented data, and minimal infrastructure reinforce one another. The Frugal IS literature has addressed IS design under resource constraints, but has not extended into analytics. We introduce Frugal Analytics as a concept, framework, and guidelines for analytics practice in resource-constrained organizations. Drawing on a multi-year engaged scholarship with a nonprofit housing organization in Saudi Arabia, we analyze documentary evidence, a retrospective interview, analytical artifacts from a predictive modeling project, a researcher's self-reflection memo, and engagement with the wider nonprofit sector. Our findings show that the organization absorbed interpretable insights but did not adopt the predictive model. We propose a five-dimensional framework and ten guidelines. Frugal Analytics asks organizations to pursue what is appropriate, interpretable, and actionable given their realities.

papers.title: Large Language Models Can Explain Experts Better Than Experts Themselves
papers.abstract: Capturing tacit knowledge, or the “know-how” embedded in individual experiences and contexts, is a central challenge that limits the preservation and transfer of valuable expertise. Here, we show that Large Language Models (LLMs) can uncover tacit knowledge from expert behavior and support knowledge transfer from experts to novices. We first identify prompting strategies that improve LLMs' ability to externalize tacit knowledge (i.e., transform tacit into explicit knowledge), and then evaluate the downstream utility of the resulting LLM-externalized tacit knowledge. Our analysis reveals that LLM-externalized tacit knowledge incorporating expert behavior improves decision quality and enables novices to approach expert-level performance, outperforming knowledge articulated by human experts. These findings provide empirical support for Polanyi’s Paradox - that “we can know more than we can tell" - and suggest that LLMs can help overcome human experts’ articulation bottleneck that has long challenged tacit knowledge externalization.

papers.title: Beyond Emotional Tracking: Theorizing How Personal Informatics Shape Emotional Awareness
papers.abstract: Digital technologies increasingly mediate how individuals perceive and interpret their emotional experiences. Although personal informatics (PI) systems are often assumed to enhance self-awareness by making emotional states visible, prior research reports divergent outcomes: some systems cultivate emotional insight, whereas others increase rumination or reliance on technological guidance. Existing research offers limited insight into how personal informatics systems shape emotional understanding. Drawing on emotional awareness theory and a theoretical review of emotionally oriented PI research, we develop a typological framework of personal informatics-induced emotional awareness pathways: self-understanding, self-regulation, and reason-seeking. We theorize that these pathways emerge from differences in how PI systems direct users’ attention to emotions and in the structure of the interpretive work involved in making sense of emotional data. In doing so, this study reconceptualizes emotional awareness as a technologically conditioned interpretive process and advances theory on personal informatics research.

papers.title: Can the Most Awful Part of Leadership Get Any Worse? Managing Visibility in Remote Employee Terminations
papers.abstract: Employee terminations are among the most fraught interactions in organizational life and one of the most difficult tasks managers perform. Once confined to physical rooms, terminations are increasingly conducted remotely and reshaped by digital technologies, making them a distinct organizational phenomenon with consequences that remain largely unknown. This paper argues that studying the management of visibility in these consequential interactions should be a central concern, given how little is known about what technology mediation does to interactions where employee well-being and dignity are at stake. Drawing on in-depth interviews with managers, the paper extends digital visibility scholarship by reframing it from worker self-presentation to managerial conduct, showing how managers control what is hidden from and what is shown to terminated employees, and how psychological distance is actively produced by the practices managers adopt to make terminations bearable. The paper concludes with a research agenda for further scholarship in this area.

papers.title: Orchestration or Delegation? Balancing Human Agency and AI Autonomy in Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic systems are beginning to automate knowledge work by planning, invoking tools, and iterating across multi-step tasks, yet little is known about how different autonomy levels shape human agency and performance. Drawing on the ironies-of-automation tradition, we examine two paradigms of human–agent collaboration: orchestration, in which users compose and supervise agentic workflows, and delegation, in which autonomous agents pursue user-defined goals. Using a design science research approach, we derive design requirements from the literature and interviews with knowledge workers, instantiate them in two software artifacts, and evaluate both in a within-subjects experiment on a voice-of-customer analysis task. We find a control–efficiency trade-off: orchestration supports closer alignment between perceived and objective performance at the cost of higher mental workload, whereas delegation enables higher task correctness but makes performance harder to assess. These findings respecify the ironies of automation for agentic systems and offer design knowledge for organizations.

papers.title: Trust and Voice in Workplace AI: AI Agent Role Framing, Feedback Affordance, and Employees' Knowledge Sharing Intention
papers.abstract: Generative AI agents can capture employee expertise through routine workplace conversations, but their effectiveness depends on employees' willingness to contribute. We examine two interface-level design levers: role framing (Expert vs. Assistant) and feedback affordance (Binary vs. Open-ended) and tracing their effects through trust and voice pathways. Using a 2×2 randomized field experiment during a live AI agent deployment at a U.S. mortgage lending firm (N = 208), we combine pre/post-deployment surveys with behavioral interaction logs. Expert framing raised affective trust and carried a positive indirect effect on knowledge sharing intention, offset by a negative direct effect. This study also shows a dissociation between designed voice channels and employees' sense of being heard. The study contributes by identifying affective trust as focal pathway from AI agent design to workplace knowledge contribution, and by distinguishing structural feedback affordance from experiential feedback agency as a basis for designing AI-mediated knowledge contribution.

papers.title: Managing the Autonomous Workforce: How Agentic Coding Impacts the Cognitive Load of Software Developers
papers.abstract: Agentic coding is transforming software development, yet its impact on developer cognitive load in large-scale projects remains poorly understood. Utilizing 20 semi-structured interviews at a large IT service provider, we identify three novel, environment-specific drivers of cognitive load unique to agentic workflows. Moreover, we propose a structural framework that defines four distinct stages of agentic coding adoption and the connections between stages and drivers. Our findings reveal a critical paradox: while agents reduce the intrinsic cognitive load associated with manual syntax generation, they simultaneously impose higher extraneous load through intensive validation requirements, frequent context switching, and the fragmentation of the developer’s mental map. This "paradox of automation" often offsets efficiency gains. We contribute to the Information Systems literature by offering a dynamic lens for observing how mental demands evolve as developers manage an increasingly autonomous workforce.

papers.title: Governance in Multi-Agent Open-Source Projects: A Configurational Approach to Human-AI-Bot Collaboration
papers.abstract: Open-source software (OSS) projects increasingly delegate tasks to heterogeneous non-human agents, including rule-based bots and GenAI agents, working alongside human developers within shared workflows. Yet how these agents’ joint deployment and governance shape project performance remains poorly understood. Drawing on organizational control theory and coordination theory, we adopt a configurational approach using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine how configurations of rule-based bots and GenAI agents across different functional roles and AI governance jointly produce high or low performance outcomes. By analyzing 4,121 GitHub repositories, we find that high-performance configurations avoid delegating both coding and coordination functions to rule-based bots simultaneously, and formal governance is necessary for high performance when GenAI agents contribute to coding, while its absence leads to lower performance. We contribute by extending organizational control theory to account for agentic digital actors and offering practical guidance for OSS project owners on AI agent delegation and governance.

papers.title: When AI Flattery Leads to Learning Failure: The Causal Impact of Sycophantic AI on Employees’ Knowledge Absorption
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping organizational knowledge management, as growing numbers of employees rely on AI assistants for knowledge learning and skill improvement. While GenAI introduces new risks to organizational knowledge transfer, no empirical research has examined how AI sycophancy impacts employees’ knowledge learning processes. Existing studies document that sycophantic large language models mislead novices in generic problem-solving tasks, yet this finding remains unvalidated in organizational knowledge management contexts. Integrating relevant organizational and cognitive theories, this study models how AI sycophancy hinders employees’ knowledge absorption, hypothesizing its direct effect, the mediating role of knowledge illusion, and boundary conditions of task complexity and domain expertise. We will test these hypotheses via a 2×2 between-subjects experiment with 240 corporate employees. This study fills a critical research gap, reveals AI sycophancy’s hidden barrier to organizational learning, and provides evidence for responsible AI knowledge management tool design.

papers.title: From Screening Automation to Review Prioritization: Leakage-Aware Evaluation of LLM-Augmented Administrative Selection
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly consider large language models (LLMs) for administrative selection tasks that combine formal criteria with human judgment. We evaluate four LLM scoring designs in a real university scholarship program (1,352 applications, 250 recipients), treating realized human selections as an operational benchmark rather than ground truth under a leakage-aware protocol. Rubric-based codification provides the strongest broad review-prioritization performance, reaching 80% recall of human-selected applicants within a review pool of 800 of 1,336 applications, while stronger few-shot calibration improves final-scale alignment. We add deployment policies for using such rankings under imperfect recall, together with qualitative divergence cases, positioning LLM-augmented selection as review prioritization rather than screening automation.

papers.title: Requirements Engineering with Generative  AI: Transformation of Requirements  Elicitation and Cognitive Load
papers.abstract: This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) transforms requirements elicitation in requirements engineering and its implications for cognitive load. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory and a qualitative case study of a European IT service provider, the research analyzes 20 interviews with RE professionals using grounded theory methods. The findings show that GenAI not only reduces cognitive load, but also redistributes it across intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load. While automation reduces extraneous load by offloading routine tasks such as documentation and summarization, new demands arise through prompt engineering, output verification, and tool evaluation. Conversely, GenAI augments elicitation work by supporting creativity, reflection, and exploration of alternative solutions. The study contributes a model of cognitive load redistribution and highlights that GenAI reshapes RE practices by changing the nature of knowledge work.

papers.title: AI and the Shifting Boundaries of Professional Accountability
papers.abstract: As generative AI is increasingly integrated into professional work, questions of accountability have become more salient. While prior research has examined how responsibility is attributed in human-AI collaboration, little is known about how individuals are held accountable for AI-assisted work and how such accountability demands shape their behavior. Drawing on a qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews with Chartered Professional Accountants (CPAs) in Canada, this study explores how professionals are held accountable when generative AI tools contribute to their work. Specifically, we identify an emerging shift in accountability judgments, whereby professional accountability is increasingly evaluated by questioning professionals’ due diligence in validating decisions produced with AI. Our findings highlight the behavioral strategies professionals use to cope with these emerging accountability demands. These findings contribute to information systems research on the future of work by theorizing how AI transforms the evaluative logic of professional accountability.

papers.title: AI and Independent Career Moves: Evidence from Creative Workers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how firm adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) affects independent careers among creative employees, a non-technical group largely overlooked in AI labor research. We study two margins beyond the firm: moonlighting, or freelancing while employed, and entrepreneurship, or leaving to found new ventures. Using LinkedIn-based career histories for the top 500 U.S. employers of creative talent from 2010 to 2022, we find that AI adoption reduces moonlighting by about one percentage point for a one-standard-deviation increase in AI intensity, mainly through higher employee retention. Overall entrepreneurship is unchanged, but AI-related ventures increase modestly, suggesting that workers exposed to AI inside firms may carry this experience into new business formation. The decline in freelancing is concentrated where AI is directly embedded in creative functions, especially product-oriented applications. These findings show how firm-level AI adoption reshapes whether creative talent remains within organizations or moves into independent careers.

papers.title: Behind the Scenes of Human-Centered Automation: The Work and Struggles of Automation Advisors
papers.abstract: Human-centered automation has become a central concern across disciplines, yet we know surprisingly little about how it is accomplished in practice. Existing accounts often treat automation as a coherent outcome and emphasize keeping humans “in the loop,” offering limited insight into the practices enacted under the “human-centered automation label.” We examine this omission through an ethnographic study of automation advisors in robotic dairy farming. We find that advisors face multiple struggles when managing such automation: managing the situated ecology in which automation is embedded, engaging with layered technological architectures, and coping with role indeterminacy following the shift to automation-as-a-service. We contribute by foregrounding the practical work through which human-centered automation is accomplished. Our findings also decenter the human in “human-in-the-loop” narratives, shifting attention to practices in which different humans, technological layers and species (e.g., animals) are progressively brought together and reconfigured in the ongoing accomplishment of automation.

papers.title: How AI Agents Reshape Service Work Under Incentive Misalignment: Evidence from an Insurance Company
papers.abstract: As generative AI moves from back-office automation to frontline service delivery, it evolves from a mere efficiency tool into a critical intermediary that shapes organizational outcomes. This shift is particularly consequential in customer-facing processes characterized by misaligned incentives, where firms prioritize cost control and procedural compliance, while customers seek maximum benefits with minimal effort. By directly engaging customers, AI agents reshape the informational foundations of service delivery. This enrichment is double-edged: while richer information improves task completion, it may also expand customer claims in ways that undermine firm control. Leveraging a unique field setting involving AI agents in insurance claim processing, we find that while AI increases employees' work capacity, it unexpectedly prolongs processing duration and inflates settlement payouts. These findings challenge the efficiency-centric view of AI: rather than simply streamlining work, AI reconfigures the distribution of control in service interactions, simultaneously enhancing organizational information processing and amplifying customer leverage.

papers.title: Climbing Faster with AI, but Not Further: Does Production Experience Still Matter for Creators on a Webtoon Platform?
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) can reduce execution constraints, particularly for less-experienced creators. On a tier-based platform where promotion reflects observable output, audience response, production consistency, and editorial judgment, GenAI raises the possibility that signals considered in promotion may improve before comparable production experience accumulates: a promotion–experience mismatch. We examine it on a South Korean webtoon platform, where creators publish serialized content and get promoted. Using a visual classifier, we identify classifier-defined AI adoption events and estimate post-adoption changes with staggered difference-in-differences. AI adoption is associated with a higher promotion hazard among Early-tier creators, particularly those with limited production experience. Following adoption, audience evaluation and production measures declined on average, especially among Professional creators; these declines are smaller for creators with more experience, holding tier constant. Overall, GenAI may accelerate promotion-relevant signals, but it cannot immediately reproduce the accumulated production experience that may help sustain audience evaluation after adoption.

papers.title: It Takes Two to Tango: The Evolution of Individual Practical Action at Uber
papers.abstract: Algorithmic Management increasingly governs platform work. As workers often perceive algorithmic decisions as opaque or unfair, they engage in Algoactivism. However, little is known about how these responses evolve over time. This study examines the longitudinal development of individual practical actions (IPAs) as a form of Algoactivism on Uber. Using a computational approach to theory development, we analyze 44,379 posts from the Uberpeople.net forum. Posts are classified into IPA types using a large language model, and topic modeling is applied to identify micro-practices and their temporal dynamics. By tracking the relative frequency of topics and interpreting underlying discussions, we identify substantial shifts in IPAs and link them to changes in Uber’s algorithmic systems, such as surge pricing and upfront pricing. Our findings show that IPAs are not static but continuously adapt to evolving platform logics, highlighting the mutually constitutive relationship between Algorithmic Management and Algoactivism.

papers.title: Does Knowing What You Know Matter? AI Literacy Metaknowledge and Trust in AI
papers.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is becoming central to the future of work, yet trust in AI remains a persistent barrier to effective adoption. Building on AI literacy and metaknowledge research, this study introduces AI literacy metaknowledge, that is, knowledge about one’s own AI literacy, and examines its role in trust in AI. Using a combined survey and skill-assessment study, we find that AI literacy metaknowledge is positively associated with trust in AI. We further show that objective AI literacy is positively associated with AI literacy metaknowledge and that AI literacy metaknowledge fully mediates the association between objective AI literacy and trust in AI. Contrary to expectations, subjective AI literacy is also positively associated with AI literacy metaknowledge. Our findings broaden metaknowledge research beyond overconfidence and identify AI literacy metaknowledge as a novel correlate of trust in AI. These insights are especially relevant for training, reskilling, and the design of AI-mediated work arrangements.

papers.title: Expertise-Building Everyday Systems: Designing AI‑enabled Work Systems That Grow Human Expertise
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly automates judgement-intensive work, creating a risk of deskilling that can produce expertise erosion and inhibited expertise formation among professionals. This conceptual paper introduces Expertise-Building Everyday Systems (EBES), AI-enabled sociotechnical work systems designed to develop and maintain human expertise through routine work while retaining automation benefits. Through an interdisciplinary conceptual synthesis of information systems, human-automation, expertise, and learning research, we identify five expertise-building pathways: task and case practice, insight into outcome generation, recognition of exceptional cases, work-system understanding, and social learning and collaboration. We examine how rule-based and AI-enabled automation affect these pathways and derive a provisional set of expertise-fostering work-system design mechanisms. EBES reframes human-AI collaboration as a learning-centric information systems design problem and makes the balance between immediate task performance and future human capability an explicit design decision. The paper provides foundations for a design theory and a broader interdisciplinary research agenda on expertise-supportive automation.

papers.title: Police Middle Managers: Expanding Responsibility Under Algorithmic Management
papers.abstract: Algorithmic management can direct frontline work and record task completion, suggesting less need for supervision. Drawing on longitudinal fieldwork in a U.S. police department, we study a system that assigned officers to areas and recorded patrol time. Frontline use became routine, while middle-manager responsibility expanded. Responsibility expanded because fixed task requirements met changing operational conditions and because a narrow completion record entered broader performance review. Middle managers kept the requirement workable because they controlled assignments and exceptions. They explained the record because they stood between frontline work and command staff. After frontline use became routine, LUPD continued to rely on the middle-manager position for both forms of work. We call this responsibility expansion: a durable widening of what those who direct and evaluate the work expect the position holder to ensure and explain. The study explains how algorithmic management can formalize frontline work while expanding responsibility in the managerial middle.

papers.title: Does the AI Reviewer Alleviate or Aggravate the Maintenance Burden? Evidence from GitHub Copilot Reviewer
papers.abstract: This study examines how AI-based code reviewers reshape contribution behavior and maintenance dynamics in open-source software (OSS) communities. AI reviewers provide scalable, fast, and standardized evaluations. They reshape contributions as well as maintainers' workload. Leveraging the introduction of GitHub Copilot Reviewer on GitHub as a natural experiment in 2025, we investigate how AI review affects maintainers' workload and review efficiency as well as contribution behavior. We find that repository maintainers initially face a sharp increase in PR submissions and a higher review workload after the adoption of the AI reviewer. Over time, human contributions decline while the increase in bot-generated PRs is sustained. Interestingly, survival analysis reveals that AI reviewers increase review efficiency for human PR contributions, whereas bot PRs take longer to review and merge. Our findings suggest that while AI reviewers increase review efficiency, they aggravate the maintenance burden by encouraging more code contributions via humans and bots.

papers.title: Productivity Empowerment or Bounded Gains? How Work Nature Shapes the Productivity of Generative AI in Software Development
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GAI) coding assistants can increase developer productivity, but their value in real-world workflows remains uncertain. This study investigates whether generative AI enhances productivity in software development and how workflow characteristics moderate this effect. Leveraging multi-source data from a large manufacturing enterprise, we combine a weighted difference-in-differences design with an instrumental variable analysis to estimate the productivity effects of GAI launch. We then use developer-day fixed-effects models to examine whether workflow characteristics moderate this relationship. The results show a robust productivity increase following GAI launch. However, these gains depend on workflow context. Project complexity significantly weakens the positive association between GAI usage and productivity, whereas current peer GAI usage strengthens it. Concurrent project volume and last peer GAI usage do not significantly moderate this relationship. This study shows how software-development workflows bound GAI productivity gains and offers guidance for work allocation, project design, and team coordination.

papers.title: When Is It Still My Work? Generative AI, Defensibility, and Disclosure in Software Product Managers’ Work
papers.abstract: As AI assistance becomes part of everyday work, managers increasingly produce roadmaps, decision rationales, and stakeholder messages with generative AI (GenAI). Yet, prior work offers little discussion on how managers keep such AI-assisted work defensible as their own, or about what colleagues see of the AI use behind it. Semi-structured interviews with 21 product managers in an automotive software organisation show a recurring Ask-Tweak-Share routine. Managers request a draft, rework it against their product knowledge, and share it. The reworking settles whether the result can be defended under a colleague's questioning (artefact-level defensibility). The choice of whether to mention the AI, made at sharing, settles how much of that use can be shown to colleagues (disclosure-mediated visibility). Settled at different moments, defensibility and visibility can decouple. Where no formal policy governs AI use, each disclosure choice helps set what a team comes to accept as legitimate practice.

papers.title: Imbricating Human Capabilities and AI: A Case Study of GenAI-enabled Workflow Stabilization
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping professional work, yet its stabilization into organizational workflows remains undertheorized, particularly in traditional nontechnology firms where digital infrastructure is limited. Drawing on the imbrication lens, we conduct an interpretive case study of YD (pseudonym), a Chinese real-estate enterprise that progressively integrated GenAI across functions over four years. We identify four temporal imbrication modes through which GenAI becomes stabilized: probing, patching, reweaving, and externalizing. Each mode aggregates a distinct cluster of human–material agency interlockings, and the residue of each mode conditions subsequent imbrications. The study contributes to GenAI and future-of-work research by offering a workflow-level process explanation. It also contributes to imbrication concept by introducing imbrication modes as a complementary aggregation layer and by showing that stabilized workflows can be detached as standalone artifacts.

papers.title: When AI Codes Faster Than Workers Can Verify: Epistemic Debt in Vibe Coding
papers.abstract: Agentic coding systems now produce software faster than the workers accountable for it can read, evaluate, or trace. We theorize this shift through epistemic debt: the latent stock of work artifacts whose verification has been deferred by an accountable worker in a human-AI collaboration. We formulate the construct for AI-mediated knowledge work, distinguish three strategies — accept, negate, triage — for managing it, and examine it through 40 controlled Claude Code sessions, a repair experiment on 32 programs, a thematic analysis of 4,570 Reddit items, and six recorded sessions. We found that a community-derived constraint prompt produced a small, non-significant reduction in drift. The repair experiment showed when debt becomes consequential: repair burden rose when a fix required relational knowledge the code could not supply. The corpus reveals a 15-practice repertoire dominated by selective verification (92% triage). Tools and institutions designed for verification, not only production, are the next frontier.

papers.title: Verification Burden in AI-Enabled Work: When Delegated Output Generation Leaves Accountability with Employees
papers.abstract: Employees often must verify AI-generated outputs that, although produced quickly, are not always easy to interpret, trace, or defend. This short paper conceptualizes verification burden as a distinct job demand that arises when employees must check, validate, correct, and justify AI-generated outputs before final use under retained human accountability. Drawing on agency theory, we propose perceived output opacity, perceived output fallibility, perceived output responsibility, and perceived error consequences as antecedents of verification burden. Using the JD-R model, we link verification burden to emotional exhaustion, reduced end-user performance, and lower AI continuance intention. We propose a two-phase design to refine the construct qualitatively and assess its discriminant validity and nomological position quantitatively. This offers a more precise account of AI-enabled work, in which output generation may be automated while verification remains human work and accountability remains with employees.

papers.title: Voice Work with GenAI: How Employees Develop and Sustain Individual Voice in Organizational Communication
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) can increasingly produce competent workplace communication, raising concerns that writing will converge on the patterns of a small number of models. At stake is employees’ individual voice, an important way communicative judgment, expertise, and human contribution remain recognizable in organizational work. We ask how employees develop and maintain that voice when communication is produced with GenAI. Drawing on a 13-month interpretive field study in a technology firm, including 56 interviews and artifact-elicitation walkthroughs of employees’ AI workspaces, we identify five forms of voice work: protecting, articulating, externalizing, refining, and rendering the production of voice visible. Across these practices, workers make aspects of communicative judgment available to the system while continually evaluating and refining what it produces. We show how individual voice becomes embedded in personal AI arrangements that can be maintained over time.

papers.title: Invisible Labor of Argumentation: How Radiologists Interpret AI in Everyday Practice
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in professional reasoning, yet their outputs often arrive as incomplete claims lacking transparent warrants and rebuttals. Drawing on a 25-month ethnography of AI integration in a pioneering Department of Radiology deploying 17 FDA-cleared models across three configurations (automated triage, diagnostic decision support, and second-opinion augmentation), we introduce argumentation labor to describe the cognitive and communicative meta-work required to adjudicate machine-generated reasoning. Using Toulmin's argumentation model and the metahuman systems framework, we identify four forms of this labor (Reconstructive, Comparative, Adjudicative, and Integrative) operationalized through delegation, monitoring, cultivation, and reflection functions. We position argumentation labor as a layered, additive form of invisible labor that extends, rather than replaces, the classical articulation, coordination, and infrastructural work. We show how knowledge experts repairs the limits of machine reasoning and in process absorb asymmetric liability. Recognizing this labor helps design sustainable human-AI collaborative systems in high-stakes domains.

papers.title: Work of Automation: Exploring Organizational Work Environment of Automation Teams
papers.abstract: Process automation is often presented as a way to improve efficiency, yet less is known about the work required to sustain automation after implementation. This paper explores the post-implementation maintenance of automated HR processes in a large Swedish industrial company. Based on a qualitative case study of an automation team, we analyze how maintenance work is organized, and the team’s organizational work environment through the lens of demands-control-support model. The findings show that continuous platform upgrades, technical debt, and ambiguous support responsibilities create recurring tensions for the automation team. These tensions affect workload, prioritization, coordination, and the team’s organizational work environment. The paper contributes to the discourse on automation by foregrounding the organiza¬tional conditions through which automation is sustained, as well as proposing the concept of the work of automation.

papers.title: Managerial Boundary Work with Intelligent Technologies: How Spanning, Buffering, and Reinforcing Transform
papers.abstract: When intelligent technologies execute managerial functions, they do not inherit the relational obligations attached to those functions. Drawing on 67 boundary work scenarios across 30 manager interviews in professional services, technology, and finance, this paper examines how managers engage in boundary work with intelligent technologies. We find that Faraj and Yan’s (2009) three boundary work activities persist but transform. Spanning acquires a system-design-enabled form, in which managers reach outward by designing systems that intercept environmental demand. Buffering operates with the technology predominantly as the target of governance and rarely as the instrument of filtering environmental demand. Reinforcement, the dominant act, takes two forms unanticipated by the original framework: reconstructing the foundations of authority that intelligent technologies have unsettled, and contesting the technology’s claim to displace human judgment. The paper provides theoretical implications for boundary work in technology-mediated settings and practical implications for managers who govern teams that embed intelligent technologies.

papers.title: Deciding While Making Sense: GenAI and the Blurring of Sensemaking and Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming part of everyday organizational work, yet we still know little about how it shapes the movement from interpreting situations to acting on them. This is important because GenAI chatbots do not only provide information or automate tasks; they generate outputs that workers can evaluate, adapt, and incorporate while tasks are still being clarified. Drawing on 41 in-person observations of professionals using ChatGPT during actual work activities, each followed by a semi-structured interview, this study examines how sensemaking and decision-making become intertwined in GenAI-mediated work. We identify four forms of intertwining - exploratory framing, actionable sensemaking, reflective confirmation, and selective execution - and explain them through two dimensions: interpretive openness and GenAI-output actionability. We contribute by conceptualizing GenAI outputs as actionable interpretive artifacts: partial work products that help workers simultaneously stabilize what a situation means and materialize possible ways forward.

papers.title: The Anatomy of an Agentic Skill: Triple-Interface Design and the Generative Mechanisms of Artifact Adoption
papers.abstract: AI agents can perform new tasks by following small instruction files called skills. A skill should work for three groups at once: people deciding whether to use it, AI agents carrying out its instructions, and contributors who update and share it. We analyze 49,332 skills from the ClawHub registry to learn what helps them attract users and evolve. Skills receive more installs when they combine clear explanations for people with precise instructions for AI agents. Files with technical instructions but little readable context receive fewer installs. Features supporting sharing, versioning, and reuse are linked to more updates, although they are also linked to fewer initial installs. A three-wave analysis shows that the advantage of combining human and machine readability weakens as common technical practices spread. We describe skills as triple-interface artifacts because one file coordinates people, AI agents, and contributor communities.

papers.title: From Design Thinking to AID Thinking: A Work-Design Intervention Format for Generative AI-Augmented Creative Teams
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is increasingly reshaping creative knowledge work by supporting how teams analyze information, generate ideas, and materialize concepts and prototypes. Yet, integrating genAI into collaborative innovation work raises questions about how teams can benefit from AI capabilities without weakening human agency, critical evaluation, and responsibility for creative decisions. Motivated by this tension, we ask how creative knowledge work can be designed to effectively integrate genAI while preserving human agency and mitigating socio-technical risks. Following a design science research approach, we developed AI-empowered Design Thinking (AID Thinking), a work-design intervention format for genAI-augmented creative teamwork. Across four cycles, we synthesized challenges of Design Thinking and genAI augmentation opportunities, derived meta requirements and design principles, and evaluated the artifact in three workshops with 44 participants in total. Our findings suggest that genAI augmentation depends on mediation through collaboration governance mechanisms that connect AI capabilities with human-led work practices.

papers.title: A Collaborative Business Model and System Dynamics-based Viability Analysis for Offshore Green Hydrogen Production
papers.abstract: Designing collaborative business models (CBMs) for multi-actor sustainability initiatives and assessing their viability poses a complex information systems challenge. It necessitates dynamic, simulation-based decision-support artifacts that can represent multi-actor collaborations and evaluate financial, environmental, and social value exchanges as they evolve over time. Current research on CBM viability remains firm-centric and static, leaving multi-actor sustainability contexts largely underexplored. To address this gap, we follow the Design Science Research methodology to iteratively develop and evaluate two artifacts, instantiated in the context of offshore green hydrogen production. The first artifact is a CBM design that adopts a network-centric perspective on value co-creation among involved actors. The second artifact is a simulation-based viability analysis model that employs System Dynamics to jointly assess these value exchanges over time. Together, the artifacts yield actionable policy and governance recommendations and offer transferable design rationales for simulation-based viability analysis and decision support artifacts in multi-actor sustainability contexts.

papers.title: Enacting Digital Resilience: An Affordance-Based Multi-Layer Taxonomy for Organizational Responses to Major Shocks
papers.abstract: Organizations recognize the impacts of major shocks such as climate change and geopolitical tensions, highlighting the growing importance of digital resilience. While existing research often links digital resilience to organizational outcomes enabled by the infrastructural characteristics of information systems (IS), our study emphasizes that digital resilience is fundamentally an organizational capability for orchestration rather than an inherent characteristic of IS. We develop a multi-layer taxonomy of digital resilience based on a systematic review of 66 studies, identifying ten dimensions and 34 characteristics. We find that IS affordances' relevance and configurations vary systematically across major shock types. This study contributes to digital resilience research by clarifying how organizations can tailor IS affordance bundles to specific shock requirements, enabling more adaptive and effective responses. By theorizing digital resilience as the orchestration of context-specific affordance bundles, we extend resilience and affordance research and offer a foundation for designing organizational responses to major shocks.

papers.title: Right-Sizing Shared Mobility: A Simulation-Optimization Approach to Balancing Environmental, Social, and Economic Objectives in Tenders
papers.abstract: Shared mobility services such as bicycles, e-scooters, e-mopeds, and carsharing reshape urban transport, but their net sustainability depends on how cities tender supply. Today, fleet limits are typically set by trial-and-error or political reflex, hiding the trade-offs between operator economics, citizen access, and fleet-attributable emissions. We design and evaluate a policy-ingrained DSS artifact that couples a multi-agent simulation of users, operators, and a mobility-as-a-service broker with a multi-objective evolutionary search to surface, rather than collapse, these trade-offs. We instantiate the artifact for Berlin and contrast a naïve total-limit tender with a space-weighted alternative. The artifact returns sets of candidate solutions of mixed-mode allocations that show that tender mechanics, not just fleet caps, are a meaningful policy lever in transitions toward environmentally sustainable urban mobility.

papers.title: Information Systems in Sustainability Transitions: From Market Shaping and Adapting to Market Nomadizing
papers.abstract: Sustainable markets are critical to sustainability transitions but remain uncertain and fluid. These conditions create opportunities for information systems (IS) to actively shape market formation while simultaneously requiring adaptation to market-specific dynamics. Owing to their generativity, IS can perform this dual role across multiple markets. However, how shaping and adapting interact across market boundaries remains underexplored, limiting our understanding of the broader role of IS in sustainability transitions. Drawing on a revelatory single-case study of a sustainability certification software provider, we develop a process model showing how recursive shaping and adapting cycles impact exchange processes, networks, and institutions. We introduce the concept of market nomadizing to explain how resources accumulated through these cycles enable renewed shaping and adapting in additional markets. Our study extends the role of IS beyond supporting sustainable practices, highlighting how IS can actively contribute to the formation of multiple nascent sustainable markets and broader sustainability transitions.

papers.title: How Do Arable Farmers Envision the Digital Future of Their Farms? An Affordance Perspective
papers.abstract: Agriculture faces increasing pressure to adapt to climate change and reduce environmental impacts. Digital farming technologies offer the potential for a “twin transformation”, where digitalization enables a sustainability transformation. However, these effects are ambiguous, as the digitalization of agriculture may also reinforce intensification and ecological degradation. This research-in-progress study examines what arable farmers see as possible with digital farming technologies and how this relates to the long-term trajectories they envision for their farms. Drawing on affordance theory, we develop a framework that links future-oriented affordance and constraint perceptions to the trajectories farms enter. We propose a mixed-methods design, combining qualitative interviews with a Q-methodology study among farmers in Northern Germany. The study contributes by extending affordance theory to long-cycle decision contexts and by providing insights into how digital technologies can both enable and constrain sustainability transformations in agriculture.

papers.title: Digital tokens reshape ownership, control, and labor: organizing logics in DAOs
papers.abstract: We study three decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) to explain how governability is sustained when ownership claims, decision rights, and contribution rewards are bundled through digital tokens. Unlike conventional organizations where separating capital, management, and labor is a core design principle for sustaining governance through checks and balances, DAOs cannot rely on formal roles, hierarchical authority, or employment contracts. DAO contributors must continually negotiate stake, authority, reward, and belonging through governance processes. The absence of conventional governance structures should make DAOs difficult to govern. Yet our qualitative analysis reveals three organizing logics through which contributors address this challenge: valorization, which sustains contribution by linking it to token-based value; distribution, which organizes token-based authority for collective action; and collective constitution, which defines the collective to which authority and rewards are oriented. The study contributes to research on DAOs by explaining how digital tokens recombine ownership, control, and labor, thereby creating distinctive organizational tensions. The study further shows how these tensions are mitigated through recurrent organizing logics that render collective governance sustainable.

papers.title: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
papers.abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation. With monitoring technology, the firm first determines a purchase quantity and then decides how to allocate each unit (in either good or risky condition) between markets. We characterize the optimal allocation policies, which can be used to efficiently determine the optimal purchase quantity. Our analysis shows that such technology may inadvertently increase total waste by inducing larger purchase quantities; this increase is often, but not always, accompanied by a lower waste rate and improved distribution efficiency. As firms increasingly adopt monitoring technology for shipment allocation, additional policy and managerial attention may be required. Improvements in postharvest processes can strengthen the waste-reduction benefits of monitoring technology. Firms seeking to maintain their sustainability goals can capture most of the profit gains from monitoring by carefully moderating …

papers.title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
papers.abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive, and (iii) how quickly freshness decays. We propose and analyze a model that incorporates these factors into the classical traveling salesman problem (TSP), which we call the “time-sensitive TSP.” Using the continuous approximation approach, we derive the optimal revenue as well as the upper and lower bounds in the asymptotic regime as candidate locations increase to infinity. The tightness of the bounds is validated. Our analysis demonstrates that store mobility creates value by bringing proximity to customers. We further uncover the effects of these time-sensitive features on decision making. Specifically, the scaling relationship between revenue and fleet size is affected by customer tardiness and busyness. Busyness determines stores’ ability to expand their service, whereas tardiness affects how effectively stores can utilize the initial high-freshness period. These findings deepen …

papers.title: Operations Management in the Sharing Economy: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of the sharing economy over the past decade has changed many industries in profound ways. The innovative business models that have emerged in the sharing economy present unique opportunities as well as challenges, which have attracted a significant amount of attention from researchers in the operations management field. In this paper, we discuss the advances, challenges, and opportunities for research on operations management in the sharing economy. We divide sharing economy into eight categories: Ride Sharing, Space Sharing, Bike Sharing, Vehicle Sharing, Group Buying, Crowdfunding, Freelancing, and Last-Mile Delivery. For each business category, we identify the gaps and current challenges in the existing literature, discuss emerging industry trends and research topics, and suggest several future research directions. Our goal is to stimulate discussion and ideas about future studies in this area.

papers.title: A Continuous-Time Model of Subscription and Repeat Purchase
papers.abstract: Problem definition: We present a continuous-time model of consumers’ joint decisions of membership subscription and repeat purchase. A consumer pays a flow membership fee; her valuation follows a Brownian motion, purchase needs arrive via a Poisson process, and she chooses whether to buy and when to unsubscribe. The model is analytically tractable thanks to the connection between consumer lifetime and hitting time of Brownian motions. Methodology/results: Consumers’ unsubscription decision solves an optimal-stopping problem with a closed-form valuation cutoff; purchase occurs when valuation exceeds the transaction price. These thresholds generate three fluid consumer modes—buyer, tracker, and churner. We find that consumers who are about to terminate subscription tend to purchase less frequently, and who are currently subscribing are more likely to continue subscription. This endogenous customer loyalty is captured by a one-parameter retention formula [Formula: see text], which can accommodate rapid early attrition and an asymptotic slow decay. Managerial implications: For empirical estimation, we cast latent-valuation filtering as a heat-diffusion problem and develop a kernel-iteration likelihood approximation with vanishing discretization errors.
