Three empirical studies that feature two distinct firm-customer relationships demonstrate that our model performs on par with or better than existing models. Based on the model estimates, firms can infer consumers’ latent …

papers.title: Response efficiency versus response customization: An examination of firms’ responses to platform-empowered group complaints
papers.abstract: The rise of group complaints on digital platforms, where consumers can publicly voice collective concerns, presents significant challenges for firms’ service recovery operations. Prior research assessing service operations on digital platforms has focused primarily on individual complaints, and less is known about how firms respond to platform-empowered (PE) group complaints. We examine this question through the lens of a trade-off between response efficiency and response customization and argue that this trade-off evolves as group complaints develop over time. Based on a large-scale dataset from Tousu, a leading complaint platform in China, we find that group complaints paradoxically increase response time and decrease empathy and explanation in firms’ responses. Further analyses indicate that these effects depend on dynamic group size and dynamic need diversity. When dynamic need diversity is low, larger groups are associated with more standardized, efficiency-oriented responses, whereas when dynamic need diversity is high, larger groups are associated with slower but more customized responses. These findings extend research on service operations by showing how PE group complaints reshape firms’ complaint handling. Our study also provides operational guidance for managing group complaints more effectively.

papers.title: Inter-organisational Capabilities and the Transformation of Trust in Blockchain-based Smart Contracts: A Framework for SME Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Blockchain-based smart contracts embed agreement enforcement within executable code, constraining the partner discretion that inter-organisational relationships (IORs) have traditionally coordinated through trust, communication, and relational governance. This raises a question that popular accounts tend to foreclose: whether automated enforcement makes inter-organisational trust unnecessary, or whether trust instead changes in function and object. Drawing on expert consultation with 28 blockchain specialists and 25 in-depth interviews with executives, we conduct an inductive study of how IORs transform as organisations adopt smart contracts. We develop a framework in which intensive relational exchange enables organisations to build two inter-organisational capabilities, Distributed Transparency Capability and Algorithmic Coordination Capability, through which they actualise the affordances that smart contracts offer. Through this capability development a distinctive inter-organisational trust form emerges, System-based Trust, defined as warranted reliance on coordinating infrastructure that partner organisations jointly construct. System-based Trust complements rather than replaces relational trust: it carries operational coordination and frees relational trust for strategic collaboration and exception handling, producing Hybrid Inter-organisational Relationships as the outcome of successful transformation. The framework applies to small and medium-sized enterprise …

papers.title: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
papers.abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: R. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant 31-R833984]. Supplemental Material: The internet appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07607 .

papers.title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
papers.abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

papers.title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
papers.abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03238 .

papers.title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
papers.abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: Financial support from the Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe Experiment Center Frankfurt [Grant 232406], the Interdisciplinary Public Policy Mainz [Grant A2021011], and the Mainzer Wissenschaftsstiftung is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01818 .

papers.title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
papers.abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

papers.title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
papers.abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

papers.title: The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
papers.abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and two coupons for a plasma donation. Informing donors about the existing rewards increases plasma donations by 4.6% during the nine-month information period, although this effect fades with repeated reminders. Rewarding plasma donors with an extra coupon raises plasma donations by an additional 7.1% during the six-month reward period; this effect grows during the reward period but disappears immediately afterward. We also document a substitution effect; the plasma reward reduces blood donations by 3.3%. Survey evidence suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts eliciting reciprocity and that our findings may extend to volunteering decisions more broadly. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, Behavioral Economics and Decision Analysis. Funding: This paper is based on research funded by the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders; the content reflects solely the …

papers.title: From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market
papers.abstract: Using a field experiment with 550 Rwandan firms, we show marketing analytics causally enhances entrepreneurs’ cognition and raises firm sales and profits.

papers.title: Can Facebook Ads Prevent Malaria? Two Field Experiments in India
papers.abstract: Two field experiments evaluate a nationwide Facebook malaria prevention campaign in India, finding effects concentrated in urban, more advantaged populations.

papers.title: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
papers.abstract: While many business situations relevant to production and operations management (POM), such as supply chain coordination or sustainable operations, involve some form of collective action; managerial frameworks for collective action rarely appear in POM contexts. Valuable insights may thus be missed, reducing the effectiveness and implementability of the proposed POM solutions. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a framework for collective action that has its roots in the organizational behavior literature. We formalize it mathematically not only to offer definitional clarity, but also to relate it to common POM modeling approaches. We then illustrate its relevance to POM by mapping it to case studies in supply chain coordination and sustainable operations. The proposed framework, named the Strategy–Operations–People (SOP) framework, is structured in three levels, comprising three elements, two elements, and one element, respectively. First, the Strategy level induces and enforces solidarity among all team members by specifying common goals, shared values, and well-defined rules. Second, the Operations level organizes the decentralized execution of collective action in autonomous subgroups through a detailed specification of roles and processes. Third, the People level requires the individual commitment of all team members to the proposed collective action program, since a team’s performance rests on the individual contributions of its members. The framework thus …

papers.title: Collective Activism
papers.abstract: Can investor stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism be satisfied by an Investor Collective Action Organization (ICAO)? In an ICAO, investors work collectively, like a large shareholder, to monitor management and increase value. We analyze the endogenous formation of an ICAO and its equilibrium size, considering free-rider problems and coordination costs. While the ICAO overcomes free-rider problems among its members, it exacerbates them between the ICAO and solo activists. The benefit of joining an ICAO is hump-shaped in size. With moderate coordination costs, ICAO formation features multiple equilibria. Small changes in coordination costs significantly influence ICAO formation and activism. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: L. Yang thanks the support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grants 435-2021-0040, 435-2026-0060] and the Bank of Canada [Fellowship]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02975 .

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
papers.abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, and cascading partner failures, and can rapidly reconfigure whole‑network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness–resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass pre‑shock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness–resilience perspective opens for the study of network change.

papers.title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
papers.abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting …

papers.title: Colleagues that work together move together: How co-moving among newcomers affects individual and team performance.
papers.abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. …
